questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For the reaction, $\mathbf{X}(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{Y}(s)+\mathbf{Z}(g)$, the plot of $\ln \frac{p_{\mathbf{Z}}}{p^{\theta}}$ versus $\frac{10^{4}}{T}$ is given below (in solid line), where $p_{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the pressure (in bar) of the gas $\mathbf{Z}$ at temperature $T$ and $p^{\theta}=1$ bar.

(Given, $\frac{\mathrm{d}(\ln K)}{\mathrm{d}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)}=-\frac{\Delta H^{\theta}}{R}$, where the equilibrium constant, $K=\frac{p_{z}}{p^{\theta}}$ and the gas constant, $\mathrm{R}=8.314 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ )

The value of standard enthalpy, $∆ {H}^{o}$ (in $kJ{mol}^{- 1}$) for the given reaction is ___.
questions.solution:
Slop $g$ the Given graph

$\dfrac{dln\dfrac{{p}_{z}}{{p}^{ϕ}}}{d\left(\dfrac{{10}^{4}}{T}\right)} = \dfrac{- 7 + 3}{12 - 10} = - 2$

$\dfrac{dln\dfrac{{p}_{z}}{{p}^{ϕ}}}{d\dfrac{1}{T}} - 2 \times {10}^{4} = - \dfrac{{\Delta H}^{o}}{R}$

${\Delta H}^{o} = 2 \times {10}^{4} \times R$

$= 2 \times 8 .314 \times 10kJ / mol$

$= 166 . 28$

The value of $∆ {S}^{o}$ (in $kJ{mol}^{- 1}$) for the given reaction, at $1000K$ is ___.
questions.solution:
According to graph when $T = 1000K$ and $\dfrac{{10}^{4}}{T} = 10$ then $ln\dfrac{{p}_{z}}{{p}^{ϕ}} = - 3$

Now, ${\Delta G}^{o} = {\Delta H}^{o} - T{\Delta S}^{o}$

$- RT{lnK}_{p} = {\Delta H}^{o} - T{\Delta S}^{o}$

$Rln{K}_{p} = {\Delta S}^{o} - \dfrac{{\Delta H}^{o}}{T}$

${\Delta S}^{o} = {RlnK}_{p} + \dfrac{{\Delta H}^{o}}{T}$

${lnK}_{p} = ln\dfrac{{p}_{z}}{{p}^{ϕ}} = - 3$

${\Delta S}^{o} = - 3R + \dfrac{166 .28 \times {10}^{3}J}{1000}$

$166 .28 - 3 \times 8 .314$

${\Delta S}^{o} = 141 .34$

In thermodynamics, the $P - V$ work done is given by $w = - ∫ {dVP}_{ext}$. For a system undergoing a particular process, the work done is,

$w = - ∫ dV\left(\dfrac{RT}{V - b} - \dfrac{a}{{V}^{2}}\right)$. This equation is applicable to a
options: system that satisfies the van der Waals equation of state.
process that is reversible and isothermal.
process that is reversible and adiabatic.
process that is irreversible and at constant pressure.
questions.solution:
\(W=-\int P_{\text{ext }} d v\)

From van der waal equation of state for one mole gas \(p+\frac{a}{v^{2}}(v-b)=\mathrm{RT}\)

\(p=\frac{\mathrm{RT}}{(v-b)}-\frac{a}{v^{2}}\)

For reversible process

\(p_{\text{ext }}=p_{\text{gas }}\)

\(W=-\int \frac{\text{RT }}{(v-b)}-\frac{a}{v^{2}}\)

process is only not applicable for irreversible process.

questions.q:
The surface of copper gets tarnished by the formation of copper oxide. ${N}_{2}$ gas was passed to prevent the oxide formation during heating of copper at 1250 K. However, the ${N}_{2}$ gas contains 1 mole % of water vapour as impurity. The water vapour oxidises copper as per the reaction given below:



$2Cu\left(s\right) + {H}_{2}O\left(g\right) \to C{u}_{2}O ( s ) + {H}_{2} ( g )$



${P}_{{H}_{2}}$ Is the minimum partial pressure of ${H}_{2}$ (in bar) needed to prevent the oxidation at 1250 K. The value of $ln ⁡ \left(p{H}_{2}\right)$ is ____.



(Given: total pressure = 1 bar, R (universal gas constant) $= 8J{K}^{- 1}mo{l}^{- 1}, ln ⁡ \left(10\right) = 2.3 . Cu ( s ) andC{u}_{2}O ( s )$ are mutually immiscible.



At $1250K: 2Cu\left(s\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2}\left(g\right) \to C{u}_{2}O ( s ) ; ∆ {G}^{⊝} = - 78,000Jmo{l}^{- 1}$



${H}_{2}\left(g\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2}\left(g\right) \to {H}_{2}O ( g ) ; {∆}^{⊝} = - 1,78,000Jmo{l}^{- 1}; G$ is the Gibbs energy)
questions.solution:
$2Cu\left(s\right) + \dfrac{1}{4}{O}_{2}\left(g\right) \to 1C{u}_{2}O\left(s\right) ∆ {G}^{0} = - 78kJ$
$\left[{H}_{2}\left(g\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2} \to {H}_{2}O\left(g\right) ∆ {G}^{o} = - 178kJ\right] \times \left(- 1\right)$
Hence, $2Cu\left(s\right) + {H}_{2}O\left(g\right) \to C{u}_{2}O + {H}_{2}\left(g\right) ∆ {G}^{o} = + 100kJ$
$∆ G = ∆ {G}^{o} + RTln ⁡ Q$
$0 = + 100 + \dfrac{8}{1000} \times 1250ln ⁡ \dfrac{{P}_{{H}_{2}}}{P{H}_{2}O}$
$- \dfrac{100 \times 1000}{8} = 1250ln ⁡ \dfrac{{{P}_{H}}_{2}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{100} \times 1\right)}$
$ln ⁡ {P}_{{H}_{2}} = - 14.6$

questions.q: For a reaction taking place in a container in equilibrium with its surroundings, the effect of temperature on its equilibrium constant $K$ in terms of change in entropy is described by:
options: with increase in temperature, the value of $K$ for exothermic reaction decreases because the entropy change of the system is positive.
with increase in temperature, the value of $K$ for endothermic reaction increases because unfavourable change in entropy of the surroundings decreases.

with increase in temperature, the value of $K$ for endothermic reaction increases because the entropy change of the system is negative.
questions.solution:
${\Delta S}_{surrounding} = \dfrac{- {q}_{process}}{{T}_{surrounding}}$

questions.q:
One mole of an ideal gas at $300K$ in thermal contact with its surroundings expands isothermally from $1 . 0L to 2 . 0L$ against a constant pressure of $3 . 0atm$. In this process, the change in entropy of the surroundings $\left(∆ {S}_{surr}\right) in J{K}^{- 1}$ is:
$\left(1Latm = 101 . 3J\right)$
questions.solution:
From ${1}^{st}$ law of thermodynamics,
${q}_{sys} = ∆ U - w = 0 - \left[- {P}_{ext} . ∆ V\right]$
$= 3.0atm \times \left(2.0L - 1.0L\right) = 3.0Latm$
$∴ ∆ {S}_{surr} = \dfrac{{\left({q}_{rev}\right)}_{surr}}{T} = - \dfrac{{q}_{sys}}{T}$
$= - \dfrac{3.0 \times 101.3J}{300K}$
$= - 1 .013 J / K$
Alternate solution:
$∆ {S}_{surr} = \dfrac{{q}_{surr}}{T} = - \dfrac{{q}_{sys}}{T} = \dfrac{{W}_{sys}}{T}$
$∵$ For the isothermal process:
$∆ U = 0$ ${q}_{sys} = - {W}_{sys}$
$∆ {S}_{surr.} = \dfrac{- {P}_{ext}\left({V}_{f} - {V}_{i}\right)}{T}$
$= \dfrac{- 3 ( 2 - 1 )}{300} \times 101.3$
$= - 1.013J / K$

questions.q: The standard enthalpies of formation of $C{O}_{2} ( g )$ ${\text{, H}}_{2} \text{O} \left(\text{l}\right)$ and glucose (s) at $2 {5}^{\text{o}} C$ are $- \text{400 kJ} / \text{mol}$, $- \text{300 kJ} / \text{mol}$ and $- \text{1300 kJ} / \text{mol}$, respectively. The standard enthalpy combustion per gram of glucose at $2 {5}^{\text{o}} C$ is $( \Delta{H}_{f}^{0} = - 1300kJmo{l}^{-} for\text{glucose} )$
questions.solution:
Heat of combustion : It is the amount of heat evolved or absorbed (i.e. change in enthalpy) when one mole of the substance is completely burnt in air or oxygen.

Standard enthalpy of combustion of glucose reaction is given as
​${\text{C}}_{6} {\text{H}}_{1 2} {\text{O}}_{6 \left(\text{s}\right)} + 6 {\text{O}}_{2 \left(\text{g}\right)} \to 6 {\text{CO}}_{2 \left(\text{g}\right)} + 6 {\text{H}}_{2} \text{O} \left(\text{l}\right)$
$\Delta {\text{H}}_{\text{C}}^{\text{o}} = {Σ}_{\text{Product}} \Delta {\text{H}}_{\text{f}}^{\text{o}} - {Σ}_{\text{Reactant}} \Delta {\text{H}}_{\text{f}}^{\text{o}}$
$= {\left\{6 \left(- 4 0 0\right) + 6 \left(- 3 0 0\right)\right\}}_{\text{Product}} - {\left\{- 1 3 0 0 \times 1 + 6 \times 0\right\}}_{\text{Reactant}}$
$= - 2400 - 1800 + 1300 = - {\text{2900 kJ mole}}^{-1}$
Molecular mass of glucose $= 7 2 + 1 2 + 9 6 = \text{180 g} / \text{mole}$
$\Delta {\text{H}}_{\text{C}}^{\text{o}} / \text{gram of glucose} = \dfrac{- 2 9 0 0}{1 8 0} = - \text{16.11 kJ} / \text{g}$.

questions.q: Using the data provided, calculate the multiple bond energy $\left(\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}\right)$ of a $\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}$ bond in $\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}$. That energy is (take the bond energy of a $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}$ bond as $350 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ ) $2 \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{~g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{HC}=\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{g}) ; \Delta \mathrm{H}=225 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} 2 \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g}) ; \Delta \mathrm{H}=1410 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{~g}) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{g}) ; \Delta \mathrm{H}=330 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$
questions.solution:
(i) $2 \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{~g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{g})$

$\Delta \mathrm{H}=225 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

(ii) $2 \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g}) \Delta \mathrm{H}=1410 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

(iii) $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ (g) $\longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}$ (g) $\Delta \mathrm{H}=330 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

From equation (i) :

$\begin{array}{l}

225=\left[2 \times \Delta \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})}+1 \times \mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}}\right] \\

-\left[2 \times \mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}}+1 \times \mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}}\right] \\

225=[1410+1 \times 330]-\left[2 \times 350+1 \times \mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}}\right] \\

225=[1410+330]-\left[700+\mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}}\right] \\

225=1740-700-\mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}} \\

\mathrm{BE}_{\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}}=815 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}

\end{array}$

questions.q: For an ideal gas, consider only P-V work in going from an initial state $\mathrm{X}$ to the final state $\mathrm{Z}$. The final state $\mathrm{Z}$ can be reached by either of the two paths shown in the figure. Which of the following choice(s) is (are) correct? questions.q: Match the transformation in Column I with appropriate options in Column II.
options:
(A) p,q,r,s, (B) r,s, (C) t, (D) p,q

(A) p,s, (B) p,s, (C) s, (D) p,q,s

(A) p,s, (B) q,r, (C) s, (D) p,q

(A) p,r,s, (B) r,s, (C) t, (D) p,q,t
questions.solution:
(A) $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~s}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
It is just a phase transition (sublimation) as no chemical change has occurred. Sublimation is always endothermic. Product is gas, more disordered, hence $\Delta s$ is positive.
(B) $\mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{~s}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
It is a chemical decomposition, not a phase change. Thermal decomposition occur at the expense of energy, hence endothermic. Product contain a gaseous species, hence, $\Delta S>0$.
(C) $2 \mathrm{H} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
A new $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}$ covalent bond is being formed, hence, $\Delta H < 0$.
Also, product is less disordered than reactant, $\Delta S < 0$.
(D) Allotropes are considered as different phase, hence $\mathrm{P}_{\text{(white, solid) }} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}_{\text{(red, solid) }}$ is a phase transition as well as allotropic change.
Also, red phosphorus is more ordered than white phosphorus, $\Delta S < 0$.

questions.explanation:
(A) $\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~s}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
It is just a phase transition (sublimation) as no chemical change has occurred. Sublimation is always endothermic. Product is gas, more disordered, hence $\Delta s$ is positive.
(B) $\mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{~s}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s})+\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
It is a chemical decomposition, not a phase change. Thermal decomposition occur at the expense of energy, hence endothermic. Product contain a gaseous species, hence, $\Delta S>0$.
(C) $2 \mathrm{H} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g})$
A new $\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{H}$ covalent bond is being formed, hence, $\Delta H < 0$.
Also, product is less disordered than reactant, $\Delta S < 0$.
(D) Allotropes are considered as different phase, hence $\mathrm{P}_{\text{(white, solid) }} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}_{\text{(red, solid) }}$ is a phase transition as well as allotropic change.
Also, red phosphorus is more ordered than white phosphorus, $\Delta S < 0$.

questions.q: In a constant volume calorimeter, $3.5 \mathrm{~g}$ of a gas with molecular weight $=28$ was burnt in excess oxygen at $298.0 \mathrm{~K}$. The temperature of the calorimeter was found to increases from $298.0 \mathrm{~K}$ to $298.45 \mathrm{~K}$ due to the combustion process. Given, that the heat capacity of the calorimeter is $2.5$ $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{K}^{-1}$, the numerical value for the enthalpy of combustion of the gas in $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ is
questions.solution:
The temperature rise is : $\Delta T=T_2-T_1=298.45-298=0.45 \mathrm{~K}$
This indicates that heat produced from combustion of $3.5 \mathrm{~g}$ of compound rises temperature of calorimeter by $0.45 \mathrm{~K}$.
Heat produced $=0.45 \mathrm{~K} \times 2.5 \mathrm{k} \mathrm{JK}^{-1}=1.125 \mathrm{~kJ}$
$\Rightarrow$ Heat produced from $28 \mathrm{~g}$ of compound $(1.0 \mathrm{~mol})=\frac{1.125}{3.5} \times 28=9 \mathrm{~kJ}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Consider the function $f: (0, \infty) \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty)$ given by

$f(x) = \sqrt{x}\, \log_e(x) - x + 1$.

Then which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The derivative of the function $f$ is decreasing in the interval $(0, 1)$
The function $f$ has a local maximum at some point $a \in (0, \infty)$
The function $f$ has a local minimum at some point $b \in (0, \infty)$
The function $f$ has NEITHER a point of local maximum NOR a point of local minimum in the interval $(0, \infty)$
questions.solution:
Given $f(x) = \sqrt{x} \log_e(x) - x + 1$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$f'(x) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \log_e(x) + \sqrt{x} \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) - 1$

$f'(x) = \dfrac{\log_e(x)}{2\sqrt{x}} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - 1$

Differentiating again with respect to $x$:

$f''(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} x^{-1/2} \log_e(x) + x^{-1/2} - 1 \right)$

$f''(x) = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} x^{-3/2} \log_e(x) + x^{-1/2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} \right) - \dfrac{1}{2} x^{-3/2}$

$f''(x) = -\dfrac{\log_e(x)}{4x^{3/2}} + \dfrac{1}{2x^{3/2}} - \dfrac{1}{2x^{3/2}}$

$f''(x) = -\dfrac{\log_e(x)}{4x^{3/2}}$

For $x \in (0, 1)$, $\log_e(x) < 0$, which implies $f''(x) > 0$. Thus, $f'(x)$ is strictly increasing in $(0, 1)$.

For $x \in (1, \infty)$, $\log_e(x) > 0$, which implies $f''(x) < 0$. Thus, $f'(x)$ is strictly decreasing in $(1, \infty)$.

Therefore, $f'(x)$ attains its maximum value at $x = 1$.

Maximum value of $f'(x) = f'(1) = \dfrac{\log_e(1)}{2} + 1 - 1 = 0$.

Since the maximum value of $f'(x)$ is $0$, we have $f'(x) \le 0$ for all $x \in (0, \infty)$, with equality holding only at $x = 1$.

This means $f(x)$ is a strictly decreasing function on $(0, \infty)$.

Hence, $f(x)$ has neither a point of local maximum nor a point of local minimum in the interval $(0, \infty)$.

Answer: The function $f$ has NEITHER a point of local maximum NOR a point of local minimum in the interval $(0, \infty)$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $P$ be the point on the parabola $y = x^2$ such that the slope of the tangent to the parabola at the point $P$ is $4$. Let $Q$ be the point in the first quadrant lying on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ such that the slope of the tangent to the circle at the point $Q$ is $-1$. Let $R$ be the point in the first quadrant lying on the ellipse $x^2 + 4y^2 = 8$ such that the slope of the tangent to the ellipse at the point $R$ is $-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Then the radius of the circle passing through the points $P, Q$ and $R$ is
questions.solution:
For the point $P$ on the parabola $y = x^2$, the slope of the tangent is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2x$.
Given $2x = 4 \Rightarrow x = 2$.
Substituting $x = 2$ in $y = x^2$, we get $y = 4$.
Thus, the coordinates of $P$ are $(2, 4)$.

For the point $Q$ on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 2$, differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $2x + 2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y}$.
Given $-\dfrac{x}{y} = -1 \Rightarrow x = y$.
Since $Q$ lies in the first quadrant, substituting $x = y$ in $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ gives $2x^2 = 2 \Rightarrow x = 1, y = 1$.
Thus, the coordinates of $Q$ are $(1, 1)$.

For the point $R$ on the ellipse $x^2 + 4y^2 = 8$, differentiating with respect to $x$ gives $2x + 8y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{4y}$.
Given $-\dfrac{x}{4y} = -\dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow x = 2y$.
Since $R$ lies in the first quadrant, substituting $x = 2y$ in $x^2 + 4y^2 = 8$ gives $4y^2 + 4y^2 = 8 \Rightarrow 8y^2 = 8 \Rightarrow y = 1, x = 2$.
Thus, the coordinates of $R$ are $(2, 1)$.

The points are $P(2, 4)$, $Q(1, 1)$, and $R(2, 1)$.
The line segment $PR$ lies on the vertical line $x = 2$, and the line segment $QR$ lies on the horizontal line $y = 1$.
Since $PR$ is perpendicular to $QR$, the angle $\angle PRQ = 90^{\circ}$.
Therefore, the triangle $PQR$ is a right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse $PQ$.
The circumcircle of $\triangle PQR$ has $PQ$ as its diameter.
The length of the diameter is $PQ = \sqrt{(2 - 1)^2 + (4 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{1^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{10}$.
The radius of the circle is $\dfrac{PQ}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}}$

Thus, the coordinates of $R$ are $(2, 1)$.

The points are $P(2, 4)$, $Q(1, 1)$, and $R(2, 1)$.
The line segment $PR$ lies on the vertical line $x = 2$, and the line segment $QR$ lies on the horizontal line $y = 1$.
Since $PR$ is perpendicular to $QR$, the angle $\angle PRQ = 90^{\circ}$.
Therefore, the triangle $PQR$ is a right-angled triangle with the hypotenuse $PQ$.
The circumcircle of $\triangle PQR$ has $PQ$ as its diameter.
The length of the diameter is $PQ = \sqrt{(2 - 1)^2 + (4 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{1^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{10}$.
The radius of the circle is $\dfrac{PQ}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{10}}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}}$

Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Define the function $f: \mathbb{R \rightarrow \mathbb { R }}$ by
$f(\mathrm{x})=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}2-2 x^2-x^2 \sin\frac{1}{x} & \text{ if } x \neq 0 \\ 2 & \text{ if } x=0\end{array}\right.$
Then which one of the following statements is TRUE ?
options: $\text{ The function } f \text{ is NOT differentiable at } x=0$
There is a positive real number $\delta$, such that $f$ is a decreasing function on the interval $(0, \delta)$
For any positive real number $\delta$, the function $f$ is NOT an increasing function on the interval $(-\delta, 0)$
$x=0$ is a point of local minima of $f$
questions.solution:
(A)
RHD at $x=0: \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\left(2-2 h^2-h^2 \sin \frac{1}{h}\right)-2}{h}=0$
Similarly LHD at $\mathrm{x}=0$ is also equal to 0 .
$\therefore$ Differentiable at $\mathrm{x}=0$
(B) $f^{\prime}(x)=-4 x-2 x \sin \frac{1}{x}-x^2\left(\cos \frac{1}{x}\right)\left(\frac{-1}{x^2}\right) \begin{aligned}
& f^{\prime}(x)=-\left(4 x+2 x \sin \frac{1}{x}\right)+\cos \frac{1}{x} \\
& f^{\prime}(x)=-\left(2 x\left(4-\sin \frac{1}{x}\right)\right)+\cos \frac{1}{x}
\end{aligned}$
for $\mathrm{x} \in(0, \delta) \Rightarrow$ We can't say $f(x)$ is decreasing on $(0, \delta)$ as $\cos \frac{1}{x}$ oscillates.
(C) for $x \in(-\delta, 0)$, for any $\delta>0 \Rightarrow f(x)$ is not increasing on $(-\delta, 0)$ as $\cos \frac{1}{x}$ oscillates from -1 to 1.
(D) $f(0)=2 \begin{aligned}
& f(0+h) <2 \\
& f(0-h) <2
\end{aligned} \therefore \mathrm{x}=0$ is local maxima

LIST - I LIST - II
(P) The minimum value of $n$ for which the function $f(x)=\left[\frac{10 x^3-45 x^2+60 x+35}{n}\right]$ is continuous on the interval $[1,2]$,is (1) 8
(Q) The minimum value of $n$ for which $g(x)=\left(2 n^2-13 n-15\right)\left(x^3+3 x\right),x \in \mathbb{R}$,is an increasing function on $\mathbb{R}$,is (2) 9
(R) The smallest natural number $n$ which is greater than 5,such that $x=3$ is a point of local minima of $h(x)=\left(x^2-9\right)^{\mathrm{n}}\left(x^2+2 x+3\right)$,is (3) 5
(S) Number of $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $l(x)=\sum_{k=0}^4\left(\sin |x-k|+\cos \left|x-k+\frac{1}{2}\right|\right),x \in \mathbb{R}$,is NOT differentiable at $x_0$,is (4) 6
(5) 10
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& P(x)=10 x^3-45 x^2+60 x+35 \\
& P^{\prime}(x)=30(x-1)(x-2)
\end{aligned} \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{x})$ decreases in $[1,2] \Rightarrow$ Range of $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{x})=[55,60] f(\mathrm{x})=\left[\frac{\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{x})}{\mathrm{n}}\right] \min$ value of $\mathrm{n}=9$

Derivative must change sign at $x=3 \begin{aligned}
& \because \mathrm{n}-1=\text{ odd } \\
& \mathrm{n}=\text{ even } \\
& \mathrm{n}=6
\end{aligned}$

$\Rightarrow \sin |\mathrm{x}-\mathrm{k}|$ is NOT diff. at $\mathrm{k}=0,1,2,3,4$

questions.q:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be defined by
$f(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{6 x+\sin x}{2 x+\sin x} & \text{ if } x \neq 0 \\ \frac{7}{3} & \text{ if } x=0\end{cases}$
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The point $x=0$ is a point of local maxima of $f$
The point $x=0$ is a point of local minima of $f$
Number of points of local maxima of $f$ in the interval $[\pi, 6 \pi]$ is 3
Number of points of local minima of $f$ in the interval $[2 \pi, 4 \pi]$ is 1
questions.solution:
since $3>\frac{7}{3} \Rightarrow 3>f(0)$ $\Rightarrow x=0$ is local minima ....option (B) is correct Now, $\begin{aligned} & f(x)=\frac{6 x+\sin x}{2 x+\sin x}=1+\frac{4 x}{2 x+\sin x} \\ & f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{4[(2 x+\sin x) \cdot 1-x(2+\cos x)]}{(2 x+\sin x)^2}=\frac{4(\sin x-x \cos x)}{(2 x+\sin x)^2} \\ & =\frac{4 \cos x(\tan x-x)}{(2 x+\sin x)^2} \end{aligned}$
Options (C) \& (D) are also correct.

For $f \in S$, let ${X}_{f}$ be the number of points $x \in \left(- 1, 1\right)$ for which $f\left(x\right) = x$. Then which of the following statements is(are) true?
options: There exists a function $f \in S$ such that ${X}_{f} = 0$
For every function $f \in S$, we have ${X}_{f} \le 2$

There does NOT exist any function f in S such that ${X}_{f} = 1$
questions.solution:
Given,

${f}^{"} ( x ) > 0 \text{$ and } f ( x ) - x = 0

$g\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right) - x$

Now differentiating above equation we get,

$⇒ {g}^{'}\left(x\right) = {f}^{'}\left(x\right) - 1$

Again differentiating we get,

${g}^{"} ( x ) = {f}^{"} ( x ) > 0 ⇒ \text{concave up}$

So, possible graphs will be,

Here in above graph ${X}_{f} = 0$ as there is no point for which $f\left(x\right) = x$

Now here ${X}_{f} \le 2$ as there will be minimum two points when $y = x$ will cut the given graph,

Now in above graph ${X}_{f} = 1$ so there will minimum one intersection between line $y = x$ and the given graph so option $\left(D\right)$ is wrong.

Let $f_{1}:(0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $f_{2}:(0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be defined by



f_{1}(x)=\int_{0}^{x} \prod_{j=1}^{21}(t-j)^{j} d t, \quad x>0



and

$

f_{2}(x)=98(x-1)^{50}-600(x-1)^{49}+2450, \quad x \gt 0

$

where, for any positive integer $n$ and real numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{i}$ denotes the product of $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} .$ Let $m_{i}$ and $n_{i}$, respectively, denote the number of points of local minima and the number of points of local maxima of function $f_{i}, i=1,2$, in the interval $(0, \infty)$.

The value of~$2{m}_{1} + 3{n}_{1} + {m}_{1}{n}_{1}$& is _____.
questions.solution:
Given

${f}_{1}\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{x}\left(t - 1\right){\left(t - 2\right)}^{2}......{\left(t - 2t\right)}^{21}dt$

$⇒ {f}^{'}1\left(x\right) = \left(x - 1\right){\left(x - 2\right)}^{2}.....{\left(x - 21\right)}^{21}$

Checking critical points

At all odd integers from $1$ to $21$ $f\left(x\right)$ will have an extrema with $1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21$ being points of minima & $3, 7, 11, 15, 19$ being points of maxima.

So ${m}_{1} = 6$ & ${n}_{1} = 5$

Hence $2{m}_{1} + 3{n}_{1} + {m}_{1}{n}_{1} = 57$

Question: Which of the following statements is TRUE ?
options: For every $x > 1$, there exists an $\alpha \in \left(1, x\right)$ such that ${ψ}_{1}\left(x\right) = 1 + \alphax$

questions.solution:

$f\left(x\right) = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}\left(t - {t}^{2}\right){e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt; x > 0$

$g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{t}{e}^{- 1}dt; x > 0$
put $t = {u}^{2}$
$∴ g\left(x\right) = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}{u}^{2}{e}^{- {u}^{2}}du = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}{t}^{2}{e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$

now, $f\left(x\right) + g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{x}2t{e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt = 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}}$

$⇒ f ( \sqrt{ln3} ) + g ( \sqrt{ln3} ) = 1 - {e}^{- ln3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

(B) for $\alpha \in ( 1, x ) ,$ ${ψ}_{1} ( x ) = 1 + \alphax$

$⇒ {e}^{- x} + x - 1 - \alphax = 0$

Paragraph: Let $\psi_{1}:[0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \psi_{2}:[0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, f:[0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $g:[0, \infty) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be functions such that $f(0)=g(0)=0$, $\psi_{1}(x)=e^{-x}+x, \quad x \geq 0$, $\psi_{2}(x)=x^{2}-2 x-2 e^{-x}+2, \quad x \geq 0$, $f(x)=\int_{-x}^{x}\left(|t|-t^{2}\right) e^{-t^{2}} d t, \quad x>0$ and $g(x)=\int_{0}^{x^{2}} \sqrt{t} e^{-t} d t, \quad x>0$
Question: Which of the following statements is TRUE ?
questions.solution:
(A) Given

${ψ}_{1}\left(x\right) = {e}^{- x} + x, x \ge 0$

${ψ}^{'}1\left(x\right) = - {e}^{- x} + 1, x \ge 0$

${ψ}^{'}1\left(x\right)$ is increasing function.

${ψ}_{1}\left(x\right) > {ψ}_{1}\left(0\right) ∀ x \ge 0$

${ψ}_{1}\left(x\right) \ge 1$

So,

${e}^{- x} + x < 1$ for $x \in ( 0, \infty )$ is incorrect.

LHS is increasing and unbounded function.

(B) Given${ψ}_{2}\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} - 2x - 2{e}^{- x} + 2, x \ge 0$

${ψ}^{'}2\left(x\right) = 2x - 2 + 2{e}^{- x}, x \ge 0$

${ψ}^{'}2\left(x\right) = 2{ψ}_{1}\left(x\right) - 2 \ge 0, x \ge 0$

So, ${ψ}_{2}\left(x\right)$ is increasing function.

${x}^{2} - 2x - 2{e}^{- x} + 2 < 1$
for $x \in ( 0, \infty )$ is incorrect because LHS $\to \infty$ when $x \to \infty$

(C) $f\left(x\right) = 2{∫}_{0}^{x}\left(t - {t}^{2}\right){e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$

$f\left(x\right) = {\left(- {e}^{- {t}^{2}}\right)}_{0}^{x} - 2{∫}_{0}^{x}{t}^{2}{e}^{- {t}^{2}}dt$

$= 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}} - 2{∫}_{0}^{x}{t}^{2}\left(1 - {t}^{2} + \dfrac{{t}^{4}}{2 !} ⋯ . .\right)$

$= f\left(x\right) - 1 + {e}^{- {x}^{2}} + \dfrac{2{x}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{2{x}^{5}}{5} < 0$ in $\left(0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

$g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{t}{e}^{- 1}dt$

Put $t = {z}^{2}$

$g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{x}2{z}^{2}{e}^{- {z}^{2}}dz$

$= {∫}_{0}^{x}2{z}^{2}\left(1 - {z}^{2} + \dfrac{{z}^{4}}{2 !} \ldots . .\right)dz$

$g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{2{x}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{2{x}^{5}}{5} + \dfrac{2{x}^{7}}{2 . 7} - \dfrac{2 \cdot {x}^{9}}{9 . 6} - \ldots \ldots$

$g\left(x\right) - \dfrac{2{x}^{3}}{3} + \dfrac{2{x}^{5}}{5} - \dfrac{2{x}^{7}}{2 . 7} \le 0$

$= 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}} - \dfrac{2{x}^{3}}{3} + \dfrac{2{x}^{5}}{5} - \dfrac{2{x}^{7}}{2} + \dfrac{2{x}^{9}}{6} \ldots \ldots \ldots$

Now $f\left(x\right) + g\left(x\right) = 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}} - g\left(x\right)$

$⇒ f\left(x\right)$ \le 1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}} - $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3} - \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{5}\right)$

(D) $g\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{t}{e}^{- t}dt$

$⇒ g \left(x\right) \le {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{t}\left(1 - t + \dfrac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)dt ⇒ g \left(x\right) \le \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3} - \dfrac{2}{5}{x}^{5} + \dfrac{1}{7}{x}^{7}$

$g\left(x\right) \ge {∫}_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{t}\left(1 - t\right)dt ⇒ g \left(x\right) \ge \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3} - \dfrac{2}{5}{x}^{5}$

questions.q:
Let $f: R \to R$ be defined by $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{x}^{2} - 3x - 6}{{x}^{2} + 2x + 4}$

Then which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{x}^{2} - 3x - 6}{{x}^{2} + 2x + 4}$

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\left({x}^{2} + 2x + 4\right)\left(2x - 3\right) - \left({x}^{2} - 3x - 6\right)\left(2x + 2\right)}{{\left({x}^{2} + 2x + 4\right)}^{2}}$

$= \dfrac{5{x}^{2} + 20x}{{\left({x}^{2} + 2x + 4\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{5x ( x + 4 )}{{\left({x}^{2} + 2x + 4\right)}^{2}}$

Hence, it is increasing in $( - \infty , - 4 ] ∪ [ 0, \infty )$

Now as $x \to - \infty$ then $f\left(x\right) = 1,$also, $x \to \infty$ then $f\left(x\right) = 1$

$f\left(- 4\right) = \dfrac{16 + 12 - 6}{16 - 8 + 4} = \dfrac{22}{12} = \dfrac{11}{6}$

$f\left(0\right) = \dfrac{- 3}{2}$

Hence, range is $\left[\dfrac{- 3}{2}, \dfrac{11}{6}\right]$, and the function is into.

questions.q: Let the function $f: \left(0, \pi\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f\left(\theta\right) = {\left(sin\theta + cos\theta\right)}^{2} + {\left(sin\theta - cos\theta\right)}^{4}$. Suppose the function $f$ has a local minimum at $\theta$ precisely when $\theta \in \left\{{\lambda}_{1}\pi, \ldots , {\lambda}_{r}\pi\right\},$ where $0 <$${\lambda}_{1} < ⋯ < {\lambda}_{r} < 1 .$ Then the value of ${\lambda}_{1} + ⋯ + {\lambda}_{r}$ is_______
questions.solution:
$f\left(\theta\right) = 1 + sin2\theta + {\left(1 - sin2\theta\right)}^{2}$

$= \sin^{2}2\theta - sin2\theta + 2$

$= {\left(sin2\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} + \dfrac{7}{4}$

It has minima when $sin2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} = sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}$

$\theta \in \left(0, \pi\right)$

$2\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$

$\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$

${\lambda}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{12}, {\lambda}_{2} = \dfrac{5}{12}$

$sum = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: Let $a, b$ and $\lambda$ be positive real numbers. Suppose $P$ is an end point of the latus rectum of the parabola ${y}^{2} = 4\lambdax$, and suppose the ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1$ passes through the point $P$. If the tangents to the parabola and the ellipse at the point $P$ are perpendicular to each other, then the eccentricity of the ellipse is
questions.solution:
${y}^{2} = 4\lambdax ⇒ {\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{P} = 1 = {m}_{1}$

Also, $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}} = 1 ⇒ {\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{P} = \dfrac{- {b}^{2}}{2{a}^{2}} = {m}_{2}$

Given both tangents are perpendicular.

$⇒ {m}_{1} ⋅ {m}_{2} = - 1 ⇒ {b}^{2} = 2{a}^{2}$

And ${a}^{2} = {b}^{2}\left(1 - {e}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ 1 = 2\left(1 - {e}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ e = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.solution:
$2sin2{\theta}_{1} = 2sin2{\theta}_{2}$ $⇒ 2{\theta}_{1} = \pi - 2{\theta}_{2}$ $⇒ {\theta}_{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - {\theta}_{1} \ldots . ( 1 )$
Now perimeter $p\left({\theta}_{1}, {\theta}_{2}\right) = 2\left\{\left({\theta}_{2} - {\theta}_{1}\right) + 2sin2{\theta}_{1}\right\}$ $⇒ p\left({\theta}_{1}\right) = 2\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2{\theta}_{1} + 2sin2{\theta}_{1}\right]$ $⇒ {p}^{'}\left({\theta}_{1}\right) = 2\left(- 2 + 4cos2{\theta}_{1}\right)$ Also, ${p}^{"}\left({\theta}_{1}\right) = 2\left(- 8sin2{\theta}_{1}\right) < 0$ For maximum perimeter, ${p}^{'}\left({\theta}_{1}\right) = 0 & {p}^{"}\left({\theta}_{1}\right) < 0$ $⇒ cos2{\theta}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ 2{\theta}_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} ⇒ {\theta}_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ Now area at ${\theta}_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ will be

questions.q: For a polynomial $g\left(x\right)$ with real coefficients, let ${m}_{g}$ denote the number of distinct real roots of $g\left(x\right)$. Suppose $S$ is the set of polynomials with real coefficients defined by $S = \left\{{\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2}\left({a}_{0} + {a}_{1}x + {a}_{2}{x}^{2} + {a}_{3}{x}^{3}\right): {a}_{0}, {a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3} \in R\right\}$. For a polynomial $f$, let $f '$ and ${f}^{″}$ denote its first and second order derivatives respectively. Then the minimum possible value of $\left(m{f}^{′} + m{f}^{″}\right)$, where $f \in S$, is ____
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right)$ is a polynomial in $x$ such that $f\left(x\right) = \left\{{\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2}\left({a}_{0} + {a}_{1}x + {a}_{2}{x}^{2} + {a}_{3}{x}^{3}\right): {a}_{0}, {a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3} \in R\right\}$

So, ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left({x}^{2} - 1\right)\left[q\left(x\right)\right]$ where $q\left(x\right)$ is polynomial roots of ${f}^{′}\left(x\right) = - 1, 1$

So, by Rolle’s theorem, $f\left(1\right) = 0 = f\left(- 1\right) ⇒ f ' \left(\alpha\right) = 0$, where $\alpha \in \left(- 1, 1\right)$

$⇒$ minimum $m{f}^{′} = 3$

Again by Rolle’s theorem, at least one real root lies in $\left(- 1, \alpha\right)$ and at least one real root lies in $\left(\alpha, 1\right)$ of ${f}^{″}\left(x\right)$

So, minimum $m{f}^{″} = 2$

questions.question: For a polynomial $g\left(x\right)$ with real coefficients, let ${m}_{g}$ denote the number of distinct real roots of $g\left(x\right)$. Suppose $S$ is the set of polynomials with real coefficients defined by $S = \left\{{\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2}\left({a}_{0} + {a}_{1}x + {a}_{2}{x}^{2} + {a}_{3}{x}^{3}\right): {a}_{0}, {a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3} \in R\right\}$. For a polynomial $f$, let $f '$ and ${f}^{″}$ denote its first and second order derivatives respectively. Then the minimum possible value of $\left(m{f}^{′} + m{f}^{″}\right)$, where $f \in S$, is ____
questions.explanation:
$f\left(x\right)$ is a polynomial in $x$ such that $f\left(x\right) = \left\{{\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2}\left({a}_{0} + {a}_{1}x + {a}_{2}{x}^{2} + {a}_{3}{x}^{3}\right): {a}_{0}, {a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3} \in R\right\}$

So, ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left({x}^{2} - 1\right)\left[q\left(x\right)\right]$ where $q\left(x\right)$ is polynomial roots of ${f}^{′}\left(x\right) = - 1, 1$

So, by Rolle’s theorem, $f\left(1\right) = 0 = f\left(- 1\right) ⇒ f ' \left(\alpha\right) = 0$, where $\alpha \in \left(- 1, 1\right)$

$⇒$ minimum $m{f}^{′} = 3$

Again by Rolle’s theorem, at least one real root lies in $\left(- 1, \alpha\right)$ and at least one real root lies in $\left(\alpha, 1\right)$ of ${f}^{″}\left(x\right)$

So, minimum $m{f}^{″} = 2$
$⇒$ Minimum possible value of $\left(m{f}^{′} + m{f}^{″}\right) = 5$

questions.q:
Let $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{sin ⁡ \pix}{{x}^{2}}, x > 0 .$
Let ${x}_{1} < {x}_{2} < {x}_{3} < \ldots < {x}_{n} < \ldots$ be all the points of local maximum of $f$ and ${y}_{1} < {y}_{2} < {y}_{3} < \ldots < {y}_{n} < \ldots$ be all the points of local minimum of $f .$
Then which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
$f'\left(x\right) = \dfrac{2xcos ⁡ \pix\left(\dfrac{\pix}{2} - tan ⁡ \pix\right)}{{x}^{4}}$ …(i)
$⇒$ for maxima/minima ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$
$\begin{cases}⇒ cos ⁡ \pix = 0 & or\dfrac{\pix}{2} = tan ⁡ \pix\end{cases}$
$\begin{cases}∵ cos ⁡ \pix \ne 0 & & \left\{∵ tan ⁡ \pixwillnotbedefined\right\}\end{cases}$
$∴$ maxima/minima will occur
Where $tan ⁡ \left(\pix\right) = \dfrac{\pix}{2}$

Case $I:$
$\left(i\right)$ For example
In $x \in \left(2n, 2n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ at point ${P}_{2}, x \in \left(2, \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$
$cos ⁡ \left(\pix\right) > 0$
and at ${P}_{2}^{+}, tan ⁡ \left(\pix\right) > \dfrac{\pix}{2}$
at ${P}_{2}^{-}, tan ⁡ \left(\pix\right) < \dfrac{\pix}{2}$
hence from equation (i)
in $x \in \left(2n, 2n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right), {f}^{'}\left(x\right)$ goes from positive to negative
hence ${P}_{2}$ is maxima
Similarly ${P}_{2}, {P}_{4}, {P}_{6}$ … are point of maxima and all lies in $x \in \left(2n, 2n + \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$
Case $II$
In $x \in \left(2n + 1, 2n + \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$
$\left(ii\right)$ for example at ${P}_{1}, x \in \left(1, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$
$cos ⁡ \left(\pix\right) < 0$
at ${P}_{1}^{+}, tan ⁡ \left(\pix\right) > \dfrac{\pix}{2}$
and at ${P}_{1}^{-}, tan ⁡ \left(\pix\right) < \dfrac{\pix}{2}$
hence from equation (i)
in $x \in \left(2n + 1, 2n + \dfrac{3}{2}\right), {f}^{'}\left(x\right)$ goes from negative to positive
$⇒$ so, for the minima ${y}_{1}: 1 < {y}_{1} < \dfrac{3}{2}$
${y}_{2}: 3 < {y}_{2} < \dfrac{7}{2}$
${y}_{3}: 5 < {y}_{3} < \dfrac{11}{2}$
and for the maxima ${x}_{1}: 2 < {x}_{1} < \dfrac{5}{2}$
${x}_{2}: 4 < {x}_{2} < \dfrac{9}{2}$
${x}_{3}: 6 < {x}_{3} < \dfrac{13}{2}$
Hence ${x}_{n} > {y}_{n}$ … $\left(a\right)$
$⇒$ now,
${x}_{1} > {y}_{1}$
$tan ⁡ \left(\pi{x}_{1}\right) > tan ⁡ \left(\pi{y}_{1}\right)$
$tan ⁡ \left(\pi{x}_{1}\right) > tan ⁡ \left(\pi + \pi{y}_{1}\right)$
$tan ⁡ \left(\pi{x}_{1}\right) > tan ⁡ \left(\pi\left(1 + {y}_{1}\right)\right)$
$\pi{x}_{1} > \pi\left(1 + {y}_{1}\right)$
${x}_{1} > 1 + {y}_{1}$
Similarly, ${x}_{n} > 1 + {y}_{n}$
${x}_{n} - {y}_{n} > 1$ …(b)
$\left|{x}_{n} - {y}_{n}\right| > 1$
$⇒ {y}_{2} > {x}_{1}$
$tan ⁡ \left(\pi{y}_{2}\right) > tan ⁡ \left(\pi{x}_{1}\right)$
$tan ⁡ \left(\pi{y}_{2}\right) > tan ⁡ \left(\pi + \pi{x}_{1}\right) ⇒ {y}_{2} > {x}_{1} + 1$
$⇒ {y}_{n + 1} > {x}_{n} + 1$
Therefore ${x}_{n} 1$ …(c)
Now consider ${x}_{n + 1} - {x}_{n} = \left({x}_{n + 1} - {y}_{n + 1}\right) + \left({y}_{n + 1} - {x}_{n}\right)$
From (b) and (c)
${x}_{n + 1} - {x}_{n} > 2$

questions.q: Let $f: R \to R$ be given by $f\left(x\right) = \left(x - 1\right)\left(x - 2\right)\left(x - 5\right) .$ Define $F\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{x}f\left(t\right)dt, x > 0 .$ Then which of the following options is/are correct?
options: $F$ has two local maxima and one local minimum in $\left(0, \infty\right)$
questions.solution:
$F\left(x\right) = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{x}f\left(t\right) . dt$
${F}^{'}\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right) = \left(x - 1\right)\left(x - 2\right)\left(x - 5\right)$

$⇒ F\left(x\right)$ has maxima at $x = 2$
and minima at $x = 1$ and $x = 5$
now $F\left(2\right) = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{2}\left({x}^{3} - 8{x}^{2} + 17x - 10\right) . dx$
$= {\left[\dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{8{x}^{3}}{3} + \dfrac{17{x}^{2}}{2} - 10x\right]}_{0}^{2}$
$F\left(2\right) = \dfrac{- 10}{3}$ which is a maxima in $x \in \left(0, 5\right)$
$F\left(0\right) = 0$

Hence $F\left(x\right) < 0 ∀ x \in \left(0, 5\right)$

Let $f: R \to R$ be given by $f\left(x\right)$ $= \left\{\begin{cases}{x}^{5} + 5{x}^{4} + 10{x}^{3} + 10{x}^{2} + 3x + 1, & x < 0; \\ {x}^{2} - x + 1, & 0 \le x < 1; \\ \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3} - 4{x}^{2} + 7x - \dfrac{8}{3}, & 1 \le x < 3; \\ \left(x - 2\right){\log}_{e}\left(x - 2\right) - x + \dfrac{10}{3}, & x \ge 3\end{cases}\right$
Then which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
As given $f: R \to R$
$f\left(x\right)= \left\{\begin{cases}{x}^{5} + 5{x}^{4} + 10{x}^{3} + 10{x}^{2} + 3x + 1 & x < 0 \\ {x}^{2} - x + 1 & 0 \le x < 1 \\ \dfrac{2}{3}{x}^{3} - 4{x}^{2} + 7x - \dfrac{8}{3} & 1 \le x < 3 \\ ( x - 2 ) ln ( x - 2 ) - x + \dfrac{10}{3} & x \ge 3\end{cases}\right$
$f ( {0}^{} ) = f ( {0}^{+} ) = f ( 0 ) = 1$
$f\left({1}^{}\right) = f\left({1}^{+}\right) = f\left(1\right) = 1$
$f\left({3}^{}\right) = f\left({3}^{+}\right) = f\left(3\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$
Hence $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous everywhere.
Now, $\lim_{x \to \infty}f\left(x\right) = - \infty$ and $\lim_{x \to \infty}f\left(x\right) = + \infty$
Hence, range of $f ( x )$ is $\left(- \infty, \infty\right)$
Consider $f ' \left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}5{x}^{4} + 20{x}^{3} + 30{x}^{2} + 20x + 3 = 5{( x + 1 )}^{4} - 2 & x 3\end{cases}\right$
Option $( B ) :$
For $x < 0{f}^{′}\left(x\right) = 5{\left(x + 1\right)}^{4} - 2,$ which takes both positive and negative values.
Hence, $f ( x )$ is non-monotonic for $x < 0$
Option $( A ) :$
${f}^{″} \left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}20{( x + 1 )}^{3} & x 3\end{cases}\right$
Now, $f”\left({1}^{′}\right) = 4 < 0$ and $f”\left({1}^{-}\right) = 2 > 0$
Given of f′ ( x ) in $x \in \left(0,3\right)$

$x = 1$ is maxima for ${f}^{′}\left(x\right) -----Option \left(D\right)
and ${f}^{′}$\left(x\right)$ is not differential at $x = 1$
Option $( C ) :$
$\lim_{x \to \infty}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to \infty}\left(x - 2\right)ln ⁡ \left(x - 2\right) - x + \dfrac{10}{3}$
$\lim_{x \to \infty}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to \infty}\left(x - 2\right)\left(ln ⁡ \left(x - 2\right) - 1\right) + \dfrac{4}{3} = \infty$
$\lim_{x \to - \infty}f\left(x\right) = - \infty$
Hence, range of f  $\in \left(- \infty, \infty\right)$

questions.q: For every twice differentiable function $f: \mathbb{R} \to \left[- 2, 2\right]with{\left(f\left(0\right)\right)}^{2} + {\left({f}^{′}\left(0\right)\right)}^{2} = 85$ , which of the following statement(s) is (are) TRUE?
options: There exist  $r, s \in \mathbb{R}, wherer < s,$ such that  $f$  is one-one on the open interval  $( r, s )$
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right)$ can't be constant throughout the domain. Hence we can find $x \in \left(r, s\right)$ such that $ƒ ( x )$ is one-one option $( A )$ is true.
$( B )$ $\left|{f}^{′}\left(x\right)\right| = \left|\dfrac{f\left(0\right) - f\left(- 4\right)}{4}\right| \le 1\left(LMVT\right)$
$( C )$ $f\left(x\right) = sin ⁡ \left(\sqrt{85x}\right)$ satisfies given condition
But $\lim_{x \to \infty} ⁡ sin ⁡ \left(\sqrt{85}\right)D . N . E$
$⇒$ Incorrect
$\left(D\right)$ $g\left(x\right) = {f}^{2}\left(x\right) + {\left({f}^{′}\left(x\right)\right)}^{2}$
$\left|{f}^{′}\left({x}_{1}\right)\right| \le 1$ (by LMVT)
$\left|f\left({x}_{1}\right)\right| \le 2$ (given)
$⇒ g\left({x}_{1}\right) \le 5 ∃ {x}_{1} \in \left(- 4,0\right)$
Similarly $g\left({x}_{2}\right) \le 5 ∃ {x}_{2} \in \left(0,4\right)$
$g\left(0\right) = 85 ⇒ g\left(x\right)$ has maxima in $\left({x}_{1}, {x}_{2}\right)sayat\alpha$
${g}^{′}\left(\alpha\right) = 0andg\left(\alpha\right) \ge 85$
$2{f}^{′}\left(\alpha\right)\left(f\left(\alpha\right) + {f}^{′′}\left(\alpha\right)\right) = 0$
If ${f}^{′}\left(\alpha\right) = 0 ⇒ g\left(\alpha\right) = {f}^{2}\left(\alpha\right) \ge 85$ not possible
$⇒ f\left(\alpha\right) + {f}^{′′}\left(\alpha\right) = 0 ∃ \alpha \in \left({x}_{1}, {x}_{2}\right) \in \left(- 4,4\right)$
$( D )$ correct

questions.q:
The number of real solutions of the equation $\sin^{- 1} ⁡ \left(\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{x}^{i + 1} - x\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}^{i}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \cos^{- 1} ⁡ \left(\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{\left(- \dfrac{x}{2}\right)}^{i} - \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{\left(- x\right)}^{i}\right)$ lying in the interval $\left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is____.
(Here, the inverse trigonometric functions $\sin^{- 1} ⁡ xand\cos^{- 1} ⁡ x$ assume values in $\left[- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]and\left[0, \pi\right]$
respectively.)
questions.solution:
$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{x}^{i + 1} = \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{1 - x}$
$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)}^{i} = \dfrac{x}{2 - x}$
$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{\infty}{\left(- \dfrac{x}{2}\right)}^{i} = \dfrac{- x}{2 + x}$

questions.q: Let $f: R \to \left(0, 1\right)$ , be a continuous function then, which of the following function(s), has(have) the values zero at some point in the interval, (0,1)?
questions.solution:
For option (i),

Let $M\left(x\right) = x - {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x}f\left(t\right) \cdot costdt$

$∴ M\left(0\right) = 0 - {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}f\left(t\right) . costdt < 0$

Also, $M\left(1\right) = 1 - {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1}f\left(t\right) . costdt > 0$

$⇒ M\left(0\right) . M\left(1\right) < 0$ (so $M ( x )$ can be zero)

For option (ii),

Let, $k\left(x\right) = {x}^{9} - f\left(x\right)$

Now, $k\left(0\right) = - f\left(0\right) < 0$, as $f \in \left(0, 1\right)$

Also, $k\left(1\right) = 1 - f\left(1\right) > 0\left(Asf \in \left(0,1\right)\right)$

$⇒ k\left(0\right) . k\left(1\right) < 0$ (so $k ( x )$ can be zero)

Let $g\left(x\right) = {e}^{x} - {∫}_{0}^{x}f\left(t\right)sintdt$

$∴ g ' \left(x\right) = {e}^{x} - \left(f\left(x\right) \cdot sinx\right) > 0 ∀ x \in \left(0, 1\right)$ (as $f ( x ) \cdot \text{sin x}$ , is less than 1)

$⇒ g\left(x\right)$ is strictly increasing function.

Also, $g\left(0\right) = 1$, (so $g ( x )$ is, never zero)

$⇒ T\left(x\right) > 0 ∀ x \in \left(0, 1\right)\left(Asf \in \left(0, 1\right)\right)$ (so $T ( x )$ can not be zero)

A cylindrical container is to be made from certain solid material with the following constraints: It has a fixed inner volume of $Vm{m}^{3}$, has a 2 mm thick solid wall and is open at the top. The bottom of the container is a solid circular disc of thickness 2mm and is of radius equal to the outer radius of the container.
If the volume of the material used to make the container is minimum when the inner radius of the container is 10mm, then the value of $\dfrac{V}{250\pi}$ is
questions.solution:
Volume of material used
${V}_{1} = \pi{\left(r + 2\right)}^{2}h - \pi{r}^{2}h + \pi{\left(r + 2\right)}^{2} . 2$
$= 4\pih\left(r + 1\right) + 2\pi{\left(r + 2\right)}^{2}$
$= \dfrac{4V}{{r}^{2}}\left(r + 1\right) + 2\pi{\left(r + 2\right)}^{2}$
$\left(∵ h = \dfrac{V}{\pi{r}^{2}}\right)$
$\dfrac{d{V}_{1}}{dr} = 4V\left(- \dfrac{1}{{r}^{2}} - \dfrac{2}{{r}^{3}}\right) + 4\pi\left(r + 2\right)$
Where $r = 10, \dfrac{d{V}_{1}}{dr} = 0$
$⇒ 4V\left(- \dfrac{1}{100} - \dfrac{- 2}{1000}\right) + 48\pi = 0$
$⇒ 4V\left(\dfrac{12}{1000}\right) = 48\pi$
$∴ \dfrac{V}{250\pi} = 4$

questions.solution:
$2\left(y - {x}^{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx} - 5{x}^{4}\right)$
$= 1{\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)}^{2} + \left(x\right)\left(2\left(1 + {x}^{2}\right)\left(2x\right)\right)$
Now put $x = 1, y = 3$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = m .$
$2\left(3 - 1\right)\left(m - 5\right) = 1\left(4\right) + \left(1\right)\left(4\right)\left(2\right)$
$m - 5 = \dfrac{12}{4}$
$m = 5 + 3 = 8$
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = m = 8 .$

questions.q: The function $\text{f}\left(x\right) = 2\left|x\right| + \left|x + 2\right| - \left|\left|x + 2\right| - 2\left|x\right|\right|$ has a local minimum or a local maximum at $x =$
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = 2\left|x\right| + \left|x + 2\right| - \left|\left|x + 2\right| - 2\left|x\right|\right|$

CASE 1:

For $x \le - 2,$

$\left|x\right| = - x$ and $\left|x + 2\right| = - \left(x + 2\right)$ $( ∵ x, x + 2 < 0 )$

$⇒ f ( x ) = - 3x - 2 - \left|x - 2\right|$

$= - 3x - 2 + ( x - 2 ) ( ∵ x - 2 < 0 )$

$= - 2x - 4 . . . ( 1 )$

CASE 2:

For $- 2 < x \le 0,$

$\left|x\right| = - x\left(∵ x 0 )$

$⇒ f ( x ) = - 2x + ( x + 2 ) - \left|( x + 2 ) + 2x\right| = - x + 2 - \left|3x + 2\right|$

$= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}- x + 2 + ( 3x + 2 ) , - 2 < x \le \dfrac{- 2}{3} \\ - x + 2 - ( 3x + 2 ) , \dfrac{- 2}{3} < x \le 0\end{array}\right\}$

$= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}2x + 4, - 2 < x \le \dfrac{- 2}{3} \\ - 4x, \dfrac{- 2}{3} < x \le 0\end{array}\right\} . . . ( 2 )$

CASE 3:

For $x > 0,$

$\left|x\right| = x \text{ and } \left|x + 2\right| = ( x + 2 )$

$⇒ f ( x ) = 2x + ( x + 2 ) - \left|( x + 2 ) - 2x\right| = 3x + 2 - \left|- x + 2\right|$

$= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}3x + 2 - ( - x + 2 ) , 0 < x \le 2 \\ 3x + 2 + ( - x + 2 ) , 2 < x\end{array}\right\}$

$= \left\{\begin{array}{ll}4x, 0 < x \le 2 \\ 2x + 4, 2 < x\end{array}\right\} . . . ( 3 )$

From $( 1 ) , ( 2 ) \text{ and } ( 3 ) ,$ we get
$\text{f}\text{(}\text{x}\text{)=}\left\{\begin{cases}- 2x - 4, & x \le - 2 \\ 2x + 4, & - 2 2\end{cases}\right\}$


From graph, $y = f ( x )$ has local minima at $x = - 2, 0$ and local maxima at $x = \dfrac{- 2}{3} .$

Paragraph: Let $f:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ (the set of all real numbers) be a function. Suppose the function $f$ is twice differentiable, $f(0)=f(1)=0$ and satisfies $f^{\prime \prime}(x)-2 f^{\prime}(x)+f(x) \geq e^{x}, x \in[0,1] .$
Question: Which of the following is true for $f(x)$ ?
questions.solution:
${\text{f}}^{″} \left(\text{x}\right) - 2 {\text{f}}^{′} \left(\text{x}\right) + \text{f} \left(\text{x}\right) \ge {\text{e}}^{\text{x}}$
${\text{f}}^{″} \left(\text{x}\right) \cdot {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} - {\text{f}}^{′} \left(\text{x}\right) {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} - {\text{f}}^{′} \left(\text{x}\right) {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} + \text{f} \left(\text{x}\right) {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} \ge 1$
$\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{dx}} \left({\text{f}}^{′} \left(\text{x}\right) {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}}\right) - \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{dx}} \left(\text{f} \left(\text{x}\right) \cdot {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}}\right) \ge 1$
$\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{dx}} \left({\text{f}}^{′} \left(\text{x}\right) {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} - \text{f} \left(\text{x}\right) {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}}\right) \ge 1$
$⇒ \dfrac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{{\text{dx}}^{2}} \left({\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} \text{f} \left(\text{x}\right)\right) \ge 1$ $∀ \text{x} \in \left[0 \text{,} 1\right]$
Let $ϕ \left(\text{x}\right) = {\text{e}}^{- \text{x}} \text{f} \left(\text{x}\right)$
$⇒ ϕ \left(\text{x}\right)$ is concave upward
$f ( 0 ) = f ( 1 ) = 0$
$⇒ ϕ \left(0\right) = 0 = ϕ \left(1\right)$
$⇒ \text{f} \left(\text{x}\right) < 0$
$⇒ ϕ \left(\text{x}\right) < 0$

$f\left(\infty\right) = \infty$

$f\left(- \infty\right) = \infty$

$\dfrac{dV}{da} = 6{a}^{2} - 46ax + 60{x}^{2}$
${\left(\dfrac{dV}{da}\right)}_{at a = 5} = 0$
$∴ x = 3$ and $\dfrac{5}{6}$
$\dfrac{{d}^{2}V}{d{a}^{2}} = 6a - 23x$

questions.q: Let $f(x)=(1-x)^{2} \sin ^{2} x+x^{2}$ for all $x \in I R$ and let $g(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\left(\frac{2(t-1)}{t+1}-\ln t\right) f(t) d t$ for all $x \in(1, \infty)$. Question: Which of the following is true?
options: $g$ is increasing on $(1,2)$ and decreasing on $(2, \infty)$
$g$ is decreasing on $(1,2)$ and increasing on $(2, \infty)$
questions.solution:
$g(x)=\int_{1}^{x}\left(\frac{2(t-1)}{t+1}-\ln t\right) f(t) d t$, $\therefore \quad g^{\prime}(x)=\left[\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}-\ln x\right] f(x)$

Here $f(x)>0, \forall x \in(1, \infty)$

Let $h(x)=\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}-\ln x$

$\therefore \quad h^{\prime}(x)=\frac{4}{(x+1)^{2}}-\frac{1}{x}=\frac{-(x-1)^{2}}{(x+1)^{2} x} < 0, x \in(1, \infty)$

$\Rightarrow h(x)$ is decreasing function.

Hence, for $x>1, h(x) < h(1) \Rightarrow h(x) < 0 \forall x>1$

$\Rightarrow g^{\prime}(x) < 0 \forall x \in(1, \infty)$

Therefore, $g(x)$ is decreasing on $(1, \infty)$.

questions.q: If $f(x)=\int_{0}^{x} e^{t^{2}}(t-2)(t-3) d t$ for all $x \in(0, \infty)$, then
questions.solution:
$f(x)=\int_{0}^{x} e^{t^{2}}(t-2)(t-3) d t$

$\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)=e^{x^{2}} \cdot(x-2)(x-3)$

Put $f^{\prime}(x)=0 \Rightarrow x=2,3$

$f^{\prime \prime}(x)=e^{x^{2}} \cdot 2 x\left(x^{2}-5 x+6\right)+e^{x^{2}}(2 x-5)$

$f^{\prime \prime}(2)=-$ ve and $f^{\prime \prime}(3)=+$ ve

$\therefore \quad x=2$ is a point of local maxima.

and $x=3$ is a point of local minima.

Also for $x \in(2,3), f^{\prime}(x) < 0$

$\Rightarrow \quad f$ is decreasing on $(2,3)$.

Also we observe $f^{\prime \prime}(0) < 0$ and $f^{\prime \prime}(1)>0$

$\therefore \quad$ There exists some $C \in(0,1)$ such that $f^{\prime \prime}(C)=0$

Hence all the options are correct.

questions.q: Let $f: I R \rightarrow I R$ be defined as $f(x)=|x|+\left|x^{2}-1\right|$. The total number of points at which $f$ attains either a local maximum or a local minimum is
questions.solution:
$f(x)=|x|+\left|x^{2}-1\right|=\left\{\begin{array}{c}-x+x^{2}-1, x < -1 \\ -x-x^{2}+1,-1 \leq x \leq 0 \\ x-x^{2}+1,0 < x < 1 \\ x^{2}+x-1, \quad x \geq 1\end{array}\right.$

$\therefore \quad f^{\prime}(x)=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}

2 x-1 & , & x < -1 \\

-2 x-1 & , & -1 \leq x \leq 0 \\

-2 x+1 & , & 0 < x < 1 \\

2 x+1 & , & x>1

questions.q: Let $f(x)$ be a non-constant twice differentiable function defined on $(-\infty, \infty)$, such that $f(x)=f(1-x)$ and $f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=0$. Then,
options:
$f^{\prime}(x)$ vanishes atleast twice on $[0,1]$

$f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0$

$\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{\frac{1}{2}} f\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right) \sin x d x=0$

$\int_0^{\frac{1}{2}} f(t) e^{\sin \pi t} d t=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^1 f(1-t) e^{\sin \pi t} d t$
questions.solution:
Given that, $f(x)=f(1-x)$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get

f^{\prime}(x)=-f^{\prime}(1-x)

Let us put $\quad x=\frac{1}{2}$
\Rightarrow \quad 2 f^{\prime}$\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=$0 \Rightarrow f^{\prime}$\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=$0

Since, $f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=0$ and $f^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=0\Rightarrow f^{\prime \prime}(x)=0$ at two points in $[0,1]$.
Now, $\int_{-1 / 2}^{1 / 2} f\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right) \sin x d x=0$
As, $f\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right) \sin x$ is an odd function which is clear from the following explanation.
Let $g(x)=f\left(x+\frac{1}{2}\right) \sin x$,

g(-x)=f$\left(\frac{1}{2}-$x\right) \sin (-x)=-\sin x f$\left(1-\left(\frac{1}{2}-$x\right)\right)=-\sin x f$\left(\frac{1}{2}+$x\right)=-g(x)

Moreover, $\int_{1 / 2}^1 f(1-t) e^{\sin (\pi t)} d t=\int_0^{1 / 2} f(u) \cdot e^{\sin \pi u} d u$ where, $1-t=u$.

questions.q:
Passage: Consider the curve $C_1$ given by $y = e^{-x}$ for $x \in [0, 10\pi]$, and the curve $C_2$ given by $y = e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x)$ for $x \in [0, 10\pi]$. Let $n$ be the total number of points of intersection of the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$. Suppose that $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n \in [0, 10\pi]$ are the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that $\alpha_1 < \alpha_2 < \cdots < \alpha_n$.

Question: Let $\beta$ be the area of the region enclosed between the curves $C_1$, $C_2$, and the lines $x = \alpha_1$ and $x = \alpha_4$. Then the value of $-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\log_e\left(\beta - 2 e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}}\right)$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
To find the points of intersection of the curves $C_1$ and $C_2$, we equate their equations:

$e^{-x} = e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x)$

Since $e^{-x} \neq 0$, we have:

$\sin x + \cos x = 1$

$\Rightarrow \sqrt{2}\sin\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \sin\left(x + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

The general solution is $x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2k\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ or $x + \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 2k\pi + \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ for any integer $k$.

Thus, $x = 2k\pi$ or $x = 2k\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

For $x \in [0, 10\pi]$, the first four points of intersection are:

$\alpha_1 = 0$

$\alpha_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$\alpha_3 = 2\pi$

$\alpha_4 = 2\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{5\pi}{2}$

The area $\beta$ enclosed between the curves from $x = \alpha_1$ to $x = \alpha_4$ is given by:

$\beta = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{5\pi}{2}} |e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x - 1)| dx$

We analyze the sign of $\sin x + \cos x - 1$ in the intervals $(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$, $(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 2\pi)$, and $(2\pi, \dfrac{5\pi}{2})$:

For $x \in (0, \dfrac{\pi}{2})$, $\sin x + \cos x > 1$

For $x \in (\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 2\pi)$, $\sin x + \cos x < 1$

For $x \in (2\pi, \dfrac{5\pi}{2})$, $\sin x + \cos x > 1$

Let $I = \int e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x - 1) dx$. Using integration by parts or standard formulas, we get:

$\int e^{-x}\sin x dx = -\dfrac{e^{-x}}{2}(\sin x + \cos x)$

$\int e^{-x}\cos x dx = \dfrac{e^{-x}}{2}(\sin x - \cos x)$

$\Rightarrow \int e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x) dx = -e^{-x}\cos x$

Thus, $I = -e^{-x}\cos x + e^{-x} = e^{-x}(1 - \cos x)$.

Now, we evaluate the area $\beta$ by splitting the integral:

$\beta = \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x - 1) dx - \int_{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{2\pi} e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x - 1) dx + \int_{2\pi}^{\dfrac{5\pi}{2}} e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x - 1) dx$

$\beta = \left[ e^{-x}(1 - \cos x) \right]_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} - \left[ e^{-x}(1 - \cos x) \right]_{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}^{2\pi} + \left[ e^{-x}(1 - \cos x) \right]_{2\pi}^{\dfrac{5\pi}{2}}$

$\beta = (e^{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}} - 0) - (0 - e^{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}}) + (e^{-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}} - 0)$

$\beta = 2e^{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}} + e^{-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}}$

We are required to find the value of $-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\log_e\left(\beta - 2 e^{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\right)$:

$\beta - 2 e^{-\dfrac{\pi}{2}} = e^{-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}}$

$\Rightarrow -\dfrac{1}{\pi}\log_e\left(e^{-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{\pi} \times \left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5$

Answer: $2.5$

Passage: Consider the ellipses given by $x^2 + 4y^2 = 1$ and $4x^2 + y^2 = 1$.

Question: If $\alpha$ is the area of the common region that lies inside both the given ellipses, then the value of $\cot\alpha$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
The given ellipses are $E_1: x^2 + 4y^2 = 1$ and $E_2: 4x^2 + y^2 = 1$.

By symmetry, the common region is symmetric about both the coordinate axes and the lines $y = x$ and $y = -x$. The total area $\alpha$ is $8$ times the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

In polar coordinates, substituting $x = r\cos\theta$ and $y = r\sin\theta$ into the equation of $E_2$ (which is the inner boundary for $0 \le \theta \le \dfrac{\pi}{4}$), we get:
$4r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta = 1 \Rightarrow r^2 = \dfrac{1}{4\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta}$

The area of this sector is given by:
$A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} r^2 d\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{1}{4\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta} d\theta$

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $\cos^2\theta$:
$A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{4 + \tan^2\theta} d\theta$

Substituting $t = \tan\theta$, we have $dt = \sec^2\theta d\theta$. The limits change from $0$ to $1$:
$A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dt}{4 + t^2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} \arctan\left(\dfrac{t}{2}\right) \right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{4} \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

The total area $\alpha$ of the common region is:
$\alpha = 8A = 8 \times \dfrac{1}{4} \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

We need to find the value of $\cot\alpha$:
$\cot\alpha = \cot\left(2 \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)$

Let $\phi = \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, which implies $\tan\phi = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Using the double angle formula for tangent:
$\tan(2\phi) = \dfrac{2\tan\phi}{1 - \tan^2\phi} = \dfrac{2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}{1 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{4}{3}$

Therefore, $\cot\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\tan(2\phi)} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Answer: $3/4$

The area of this sector is given by:

Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $\cos^2\theta$:
$A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}} \dfrac{\sec^2\theta}{4 + \tan^2\theta} d\theta$

The total area $\alpha$ of the common region is:

We need to find the value of $\cot\alpha$:
$\cot\alpha = \cot\left(2 \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)$

Let $\phi = \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, which implies $\tan\phi = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

Using the double angle formula for tangent:

Therefore, $\cot\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\tan(2\phi)} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

questions.q: Let $f: \left[0, 1\right] \to \left[0, 1\right]$ be the function defined by $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} - {x}^{2} + \dfrac{5}{9}x + \dfrac{17}{36}$. Consider the square region $S = \left[0, 1\right] \times \left[0, 1\right]$. Let $G = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in S: y > f\left(x\right)\right\}$ be called the green region and $R = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in S: y < f\left(x\right)\right\}$ be called the red region. Let ${L}_{h} = \left\{\left(x, h\right) \in S: x \in \left[0, 1\right]\right\}$ be the horizontal line drawn at a height $h \in \left[0, 1\right]$. Then which of the following statements is(are) true?
options: There exists an$h \in \left[\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]$ such that the area of the green region above the line ${L}_{h}$ equals the area of the green region below the line ${L}_{h}$
There exists an $h \in \left[\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]$ such that the area of the red region above the line ${L}_{h}$ equals the area of the red region below the line ${L}_{h}$
There exists an $h \in \left[\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]$ such that the area of the green region above the line ${L}_{h}$ equals the area of the red region below the line ${L}_{h}$
There exists an $h \in \left[\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]$ such that the area of the red region above the line ${L}_{h}$ equals the area of the green region below the line ${L}_{h}$
questions.solution:
Given,

Function $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} - {x}^{2} + \dfrac{5}{9}x + \dfrac{17}{36}$

Square region $S = \left[0, 1\right] \times \left[0, 1\right]$

Green region given by $G = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in S: y > f\left(x\right)\right\}$

Red region is given by $R = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in S: y < f\left(x\right)\right\}$

And ${L}_{h} = \left\{\left(x, h\right) \in S: x \in \left[0, 1\right]\right\}$ be the horizontal line drawn at a height $h \in \left[0, 1\right]$

Now plotting the diagram of the above function we get,

Now differentiating the function,

$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} - {x}^{2} + \dfrac{5}{9}x + \dfrac{17}{36}$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} - 2x + \dfrac{5}{9}$

For maxima/minima, ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0 ⇒ x = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Now finding the area of red region we get,

${A}_{R} = {∫}_{0}^{1}f\left(x\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So, area of the green region will be,

${A}_{G} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, as total area is $1$ sq.unit

Now solving option $\left(A\right)$ we get,

$1 - h = h - \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ h = \dfrac{3}{4}, \dfrac{3}{4} > \dfrac{2}{3}$

So, option $\left(A\right)$ is incorrect

For option $\left(B\right)$ $h = \dfrac{1}{2} - h ⇒ h = \dfrac{1}{4}$

So, option $\left(B\right)$ is correct as $h \in \left[\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]$

Now solving option $\left(C\right)$ we get,

${∫}_{0}^{1}f\left(x\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{2}, {∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{2}dx = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ {∫}_{0}^{1}\left(f\left(x\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)dx = 0$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So, option $\left(C\right)$ is correct.

$\left(D\right)$ $∵$ Option $\left(C\right)$ is correct $⇒$ option $\left(D\right)$ is also correct.

Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number and $f: \left[0, 1\right] \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined by

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}n\left(1 - 2nx\right) & if & 0 \le x \le \dfrac{1}{2n} \\ 2n\left(2nx - 1\right) & if & \dfrac{1}{2n} \le x \le \dfrac{3}{4n} \\ 4n\left(1 - nx\right) & if & \dfrac{3}{4n} \le x \le \dfrac{1}{n} \\ \dfrac{n}{n - 1}\left(nx - 1\right) & if & \dfrac{1}{n} \le x \le 1\end{cases}\right$

If $n$ is such that the area of the region bounded by the curves $x = 0, x = 1, y = 0$ and $y = f\left(x\right)$ is $4$, then the maximum value of the function $f$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}n\left(1 - 2nx\right), 0 \le x\right$

Here, $x \in \left[0, 1\right]$

Now $f\left(x\right) = n - 2{n}^{2}x$ is decreasing in $\left[0, \dfrac{1}{2n}\right]$

And $f\left(x\right) = 4{n}^{2}x - 4n$ increasing in $\left[\dfrac{1}{2n}, \dfrac{3}{4n}\right]$

And $f\left(x\right) = 4n - 4{n}^{2}x$ decreasing in $\left[\dfrac{3}{4n}, \dfrac{1}{n}\right]$

And $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{n}^{2}x - n}{n - 1}$ increasing in $\left[\dfrac{1}{n}, 1\right]$

Now plotting the graph of above function we get,

Also, $f\left(x\right) \in \left[0, n\right]$

Now from above diagram area will be,

$A = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{n - 1}{2} = 4$ $\left\{\text{as}n \ge 2\right\}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{n - 1}{2} = 4$

$⇒ \dfrac{n}{2} = 4$

$⇒ n = 8$

So, $f{\left(x\right)}_{max} = n = 8$

Consider the functions $f, g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} + \dfrac{5}{12}$ and $g\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}2\left(1 - \dfrac{4\left|x\right|}{3}\right), & \left|x\right| \le \dfrac{3}{4}, \\ 0, & \left|x\right| > \dfrac{3}{4}\end{cases}\right$
If $\alpha$ is the area of the region $\left\{\left(x, y\right) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}: \left|x\right| \le \dfrac{3}{4}, 0 \le y \le min\left\{f\left(x\right), g\left(x\right)\right\}\right\}$, then the value of $9\alpha$ is _____ .
questions.solution:
Plotting the diagram of the given function we have,

Now by diagram we can see twice of ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$ will be the required area,

So, required area $= 2 \cdot \left({A}_{1} + {A}_{2}\right)$

$⇒ \alpha = \left({∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}\left({x}^{2} + \dfrac{5}{12}\right)dx + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}\right) \times 2$

$⇒ \alpha = \left({\left\left(\dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} + \dfrac{5x}{12}\right)\right|}_{0}^{\dfrac{1}{2}} + \dfrac{1}{2} ⋅ \dfrac{1}{4} ⋅ \dfrac{2}{3}\right) \times 2$

$⇒ \alpha = \left(\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{12}\right) \times 2$

$⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{2}{3} ⇒ 9\alpha = 6$

$\left\{( x, y ) : 0 \le x \le \dfrac{9}{4}, 0 \le y \le 1, x \ge 3y, x + y \ge 2\right\}$ is
questions.solution:
The region is a quadrilateral $ABCD$

Now, area of the quadrilateral $ABCD =$area of triangle $ABD +$area of the triangle $BCD$

So, area $= \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{cases}\dfrac{3}{2} & \dfrac{1}{2} & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ \dfrac{9}{4} & \dfrac{3}{4} & 1\end{cases}\right| + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \left(\dfrac{9}{4} - 2\right) \times \dfrac{3}{4}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left\{- 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{3}{4}\right) - \left(\dfrac{9}{8} - \dfrac{9}{8}\right)\right\} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{3}{4}$

$= \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{32} = \dfrac{11}{32}$

questions.q:
Let the functions $f: R \to R$ and $g: R \to R$ be defined by
$f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{- \left|x - 1\right|}$ and $g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)$.
Then the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves $y = f\left(x\right), y = g\left(x\right)$ and $x = 0$ is
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{- \left|x - 1\right|} = \left\{\begin{cases}0, & x \le 1 \\ {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x}, & x > 1\end{cases}\right$ and

$g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)$

At $x = 0, f\left(0\right) = 0 & g\left(0\right) = \dfrac{e + {e}^{- 1}}{2}$

At $x = 1, f\left(1\right) = 0 & g\left(1\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{1 - 1} + {e}^{1 - 1}\right) = 1$

For point of intersection of the two curves for $x > 1$, $f\left(x\right) = g\left(x\right)$

$⇒ {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)$

$⇒ 2{e}^{x - 1} - 2{e}^{1 - x} = {e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}$

$⇒ {e}^{x - 1} = 3{e}^{1 - x}$

$⇒ {\left({e}^{x - 1}\right)}^{2} = 3$

$⇒ x = 1 + ln\sqrt{3}$

$∴$Required area $=$ Area of the shaded region

$= {∫}_{0}^{1}g\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}\left\{g\left(x\right) - f\left(x\right)\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)dx + {∫}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}\left\{\dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right) - \left({e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x}\right)\right\}dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{0}^{1}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)dx + \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}\left(3{e}^{1 - x} - {e}^{x - 1}\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{\left[{e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x}\right]}_{0}^{1} - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left[3{e}^{1 - x} + {e}^{x - 1}\right]}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(e - {e}^{- 1}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\left[2\sqrt{3} - 4\right]$

$= \dfrac{e - {e}^{- 1}}{2} + \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)$
questions.question:
Let the functions $f: R \to R$ and $g: R \to R$ be defined by
$f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{- \left|x - 1\right|}$ and $g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)$.
Then the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curves $y = f\left(x\right), y = g\left(x\right)$ and $x = 0$ is
questions.explanation:
$f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{- \left|x - 1\right|} = \left\{\begin{cases}0, & x \le 1 \\ {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x}, & x > 1\end{cases}\right$ and

$g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)$

At $x = 0, f\left(0\right) = 0 & g\left(0\right) = \dfrac{e + {e}^{- 1}}{2}$

At $x = 1, f\left(1\right) = 0 & g\left(1\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{1 - 1} + {e}^{1 - 1}\right) = 1$

For point of intersection of the two curves for $x > 1$, $f\left(x\right) = g\left(x\right)$

$⇒ {e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)$

$⇒ 2{e}^{x - 1} - 2{e}^{1 - x} = {e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}$

$⇒ {e}^{x - 1} = 3{e}^{1 - x}$

$⇒ {\left({e}^{x - 1}\right)}^{2} = 3$

$⇒ x = 1 + ln\sqrt{3}$

$∴$Required area $=$ Area of the shaded region

$= {∫}_{0}^{1}g\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}\left\{g\left(x\right) - f\left(x\right)\right\}dx$

$= {∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)dx + {∫}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}\left\{\dfrac{1}{2}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right) - \left({e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x}\right)\right\}dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{0}^{1}\left({e}^{x - 1} + {e}^{1 - x}\right)dx + \dfrac{1}{2}{∫}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}\left(3{e}^{1 - x} - {e}^{x - 1}\right)dx$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}{\left[{e}^{x - 1} - {e}^{1 - x}\right]}_{0}^{1} - \dfrac{1}{2}{\left[3{e}^{1 - x} + {e}^{x - 1}\right]}_{1}^{1 + ln\sqrt{3}}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(e - {e}^{- 1}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\left[2\sqrt{3} - 4\right]$

$= \dfrac{e - {e}^{- 1}}{2} + \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)$

questions.q: The area of the region $\left\{\left(x, y\right)$: xy \le 8, 1 \le y \le {x}^{2}\right\}$ is$
questions.solution:
To draw the inequality, let us draw the equation
$xy = 8$ and $y = 1$ and $y = {x}^{2}$
For point of intersection
(i) $xy = 8$ and $y = 1 ⇒ A ( 8,1 )$
(ii) $xy = 8$ and $y = {x}^{2} ⇒ {x}^{3} = 8 ⇒ x = 2 ⇒ B ( 2, 4 )$
(iii) $y = {x}^{2}$ and $y = 1 ⇒ C\left(1, 1\right)$ and $D\left(1, 1\right)$
Now $xy \le 8 ⇒$ region which contains origin
$y \ge 1 ⇒$ region above line $y = 1$
$y \le {x}^{2} ⇒$ region outside the parabola
Now required area
Method I:
Using x-axis:
$A = \mathop{∫}_{1}^{2}\left({x}^{2} - 1\right) ⋅ dx + \mathop{∫}_{2}^{8}\left(\dfrac{8}{x} - 1\right) ⋅ dx$
$A = {\left[\dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} - x\right]}_{1}^{2} + {\left[8lnx - x\right]}_{2}^{8}$
$A = - \dfrac{14}{3} + 16ln2$
Method II:
Using y-axis:
$A = \mathop{∫}_{1}^{4}\left(\dfrac{8}{y} - \sqrt{y}\right) ⋅ dy$
$A = {\left[8lny - \dfrac{2}{3}{y}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right]}_{1}^{4} ⇒ A = - \dfrac{14}{3} + 16ln2$
Note: The question should include bounded area term as in ${2}^{nd}$ quadrant there exist a area which satisfy the inequality and is unbounded.

questions.q: A farmer ${F}_{1}$ has a land in the shape of a triangle with vertices at $P ( 0, 0 ) , Q ( 1, 1 )$ and $R ( 2, 0 ) .$ From this land, a neighbouring farmer ${F}_{2}$ takes away the region which lies between the side $PQ$ and a curve of the form $y = {x}^{n}, n > 1$. If the area of the region taken away by the farmer ${F}_{2}$ is exactly $30%$ of the area of $∆ PQR,$ then the value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
Area $= \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(x - {x}^{n}\right)dx = \dfrac{3}{10}$
${\left[\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{{x}^{n + 1}}{n + 1}\right]}_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{3}{10}$
$\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{n + 1} = \dfrac{3}{10}$ $∴ n + 1 = 5$
$⇒ n = 4$

questions.q: If the line $x = \alpha$ divides the area of the region $R = { \left(x, y\right) \in {R}^{2}: {x}^{3} \le y \le x, 0 \le x \le 1 }$ into two equal parts, then
questions.solution:
$A = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Area of curvilinear triangle $OPQ = \dfrac{A}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

$⇒ \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\left(x - {x}^{3}\right)dx = \dfrac{1}{8} ⇒ 2{\alpha}^{4} - 4{\alpha}^{2} + 1 = 0$

$⇒ {\left({\alpha}^{2} - 1\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} ⇒ {\alpha}^{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2} - 1}{\sqrt{2}}$

so α lies between 0.5 and 1

questions.q: Area of the region ${ \left(x, y\right) \in {R}^{2}: y \ge \sqrt{\left|x + 3\right|},$ $5y \le x + 9 \le 15 }$ is equal to
questions.solution:
If $x + 3 < 0 ⇒ y \ge \sqrt{- ( x + 3 )} & y \ge 0$
If $x + 3 \ge 0 ⇒ y \ge \sqrt{( x + 3 )} & y \ge 0$
Also
$5y \le x + 9 \le 15$
$⇒ x - 5y + 9 \ge 0 & x \le 6$
Intersection point of line & parabolas
$5y = x + 9 & {y}^{2} = | x + 3 | ( y \ge 0 )$
${( \dfrac{x + 9}{5} )}^{2} = | x + 3 |$
${x}^{2} + 18x + 81 = 25x + 75or - 25x - 75$
${x}^{2} - 7x + 6 = 0or{x}^{2} + 43x + 156 = 0$
$x = 1, 6orx = - 39, - 4$
So Clearly,  $x = 1, y = 2$
and when  $x = - 4, y = 1$ are required points
Drawing all these, we get this graph.

Shaded portion is required area.
Clearly required area = area (trapezium ABCD) - $\left({A}_{1} + {A}_{2}\right)$ .......(i)
area (trapezium ABCD) $= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + 2\right)\left(5\right) = \dfrac{15}{2}$
${A}_{1} = \mathop{∫}_{- 4}^{- 3}\sqrt{- \left(x + 3\right)}dx$

$∴$ From equation (i), we get required area $= \dfrac{15}{2} - \left(\dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{16}{3}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.q: The area enclosed by the curves $y = sinx + cosx$ and $\text{y} = \left|\text{cos x} - \text{sin x}\right|$ over the interval $\left[0 \text{,} \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ is
questions.solution:
The given curves are $y = sinx + cosx \text{ and } y = \left|cosx - sinx\right|$

${\text{y}}_{1} = \text{sin x} + \text{cos x} = \sqrt{2} \text\sin \left(\text{x} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$
${\text{y}}_{2} = \sqrt{2} | \text\sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \text{x}\right) |$
So, Required Area$= \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\left(\left(\text{sin x} + \text{cos x}\right) - \left(\text{cos x} - \text{sin x}\right)\right)\text{dx} + \mathop{∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\left(\left(\text{sin x} + \text{cos x}\right) - \left(\text{sin x} - \text{cos x}\right)\right)\text{dx}$
$2{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}sinxdx + 2{∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}cosxdx$
$= 4 - 2\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)$.

questions.solution:
The given curve $y=e^{-x^{2}}$ Draw a rough sketch of curve at $x=0, y=1$ and at $x=1, y=1 / e \because y=e^{-x^{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=-2 x e^{-x^{2}} < 0 \quad \forall x \in(0,1) \therefore y=e^{-x^{2}}$ is decreasing on $(0,1)$

Hence its graph is as shown in figure given below

Now, $\mathrm{S}=$ area exclosed by curve $=\mathrm{XYCO} 

and area of rectangle  \mathrm{OCYL}= \frac{1}{e}$

Clearly $S>\frac{1}{e}$ \quad \therefore$ a is true.

For $x \in[0,1] \Rightarrow x^{2} < x $\begin{array}{l}

\Rightarrow-x^{2}>-x \quad \Rightarrow e^{-x^{2}} \geq e^{-x} \forall x \in[0,1] \\

\Rightarrow \int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^{2}} d x>\int_{0}^{1} e^{-x} d x=1-\frac{1}{e} \\

\Rightarrow S>1-\frac{1}{e} \quad \therefore \text{ (b) is true. }

\end{array}$

Also as $\frac{1}{4}\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\right) < 1-\frac{1}{e} \quad \therefore$ (c) is incorrect.

questions.q: The area of the region between the curves $y=\sqrt{\frac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}}$ and $y=\sqrt{\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos x}}$ bounded by the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ is
options:
$\int_0^{\sqrt{2}-1} \frac{t}{\left(1+t^2\right) \sqrt{1-t^2}} d t$

$\int_0^{\sqrt{2}-1} \frac{4 t}{\left(1+t^2\right) \sqrt{1-t^2}} d t$

$\int_0^{\sqrt{2}+1} \frac{4 t}{\left(1+t^2\right) \sqrt{1-t^2}} d t$

$\int_0^{\sqrt{2}+1} \frac{t}{\left(1+t^2\right) \sqrt{1-t^2}} d t$
questions.solution:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Required area }=\int_0^{\pi / 4}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}}-\sqrt{\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos x}}\right) d x \quad\left[\because \frac{1+\sin x}{\cos x}>\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos x}>0\right] \\
& \left.=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \sqrt{\frac{1+\frac{2 \tan \frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}}{\frac{1-\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}}} \sqrt{\frac{1-\frac{2 \tan \frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}}{\frac{1-\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}}}\right) d x \\
& \left.=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \sqrt{\frac{1+\tan \frac{x}{2}}{1-\tan \frac{x}{2}}}-\sqrt{\frac{1-\tan \frac{x}{2}}{1+\tan \frac{x}{2}}}\right) d x \\
&
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{1+\tan \frac{x}{2}-1+\tan \frac{x}{2}}{\sqrt{1-\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}} d x=\int_0^{\pi / 4} \frac{2 \tan \frac{x}{2}}{\sqrt{1-\tan ^2 \frac{x}{2}}} d x
$$
Put $\tan \frac{x}{2}=t$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2} \sec ^2 \frac{x}{2} d x & =d t \\
\therefore \text { Required area } & =\int_0^{\tan \frac{\pi}{8}} \frac{4 t d t}{\left(1+t^2\right) \sqrt{1-t^2}} \\
& =\int_0^{\sqrt{2}-1} \frac{4 t}{\left(1+t^2\right) \sqrt{1-t^2}} d t \quad\left[\text { astan } \frac{\pi}{8}=\sqrt{2}-1\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.q: Paragraph: Consider the functions defined implicitly by the equation $y^3-3 y+x=0$ on various intervals in the real line. If $x \in(-\infty,-2) \cup(2, \infty)$, the equation implicitly defines a unique real valued differentiable function $y=f(x)$. If $x \in(-2,2)$, the equation implicitly defines a unique real valued differentiable function $y=g(x)$, satisfying $g(0)=0$.Question: The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$, the $X$-axis and the lines $x=a$ and $x=b$, where $-\infty < a < b < -2$, is
options:
$\int_a^b \frac{x}{3\left[f(x)^2-1\right]} d x+b f(b)-a f(a)$

$-\int_a^b \frac{x}{3\left[(f(x))^2-1\right]} d x+b f(b)-a f(a)$

$\int_a^b \frac{x}{3\left[(f(x))^2-1\right]} d x-b f(b)+a f(a)$

$-\int_a^b \frac{x}{3\left[f(x)^2-1\right]} d x-b f(b)-a f(a)$
questions.solution:
Required area $=\int_a^b y d x=\int_a^b f(x) d x$
=[f(x) $\cdot$x]_a^b-\int_a^b f^{\prime}(x) $\cdot$x d x=b f(b)-a f(a)-\int_a^b f^{\prime}(x) $\cdot$x d x

=b f(b)-a f(a)+\int_a^b $\frac{x}{3\left[(f(x))^2-1\right]}$d x

As, $\quad f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{d y}{d x}=-\frac{1}{3\left(y^2-1\right)}=-\frac{1}{3\left[(f(x))^2-1\right]}$

questions.q: The product of all positive real values of $x$ satisfying the equation ${x}^{\left(16{\left({\log}_{5}x\right)}^{3} - 68{\log}_{5}x\right)} = {5}^{- 16}$ is
questions.solution:
Taking log to the base $5$ on both sides

$\left(16{\left({\log}_{5}x\right)}^{3} - 68\left({\log}_{5}x\right)\right)\left({\log}_{5}x\right) = - 16$

Let $\left({\log}_{5}x\right) = t$

$16{t}^{4} - 68{t}^{2} + 16 = 0$

$⇒ 4{t}^{4} - 16{t}^{2} - {t}^{2} + 4 = 0$

$⇒ \left(4{t}^{2} - 1\right)\left({t}^{2} - 4\right) = 0$

$⇒ t = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}, \pm 2$

So ${\log}_{5}x = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\pm 2$

$⇒ x = 5\dfrac{1}{2}, 5\dfrac{- 1}{2}, {5}^{2}, {5}^{- 2}$

Hence, the product is $\sqrt{5} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \times 25 \times \dfrac{1}{25} = 1$

questions.q: Let $\left(x_0, y_0\right)$ be the solution of the following equations $(2 x)^{\log 2}=(3 y)^{\log 3}$, $3^{\log x}=2^{\log y}$, then $x_0$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Taking log on both sides,
$$
\log 2 \cdot \log (2 x)=\log 3(\log 3 y)
$$


$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & \log 2\{\log 2+\log x\} \\
& =\log 3\{\log 3+\log y\} \\
\text{ and } & \log x \cdot \log 3=\log y \log 2 \\
& \log y=\frac{\log x \cdot \log 3}{\log 2}
\end{array}
$$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \log 2\{\log 2+\log x\} \\
&=\log 3 \cdot\left\{\log 3+\frac{\log x \cdot \log 3}{\log 2}\right\} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(\log 2)^2+\log 2 \cdot \log x \\
&=(\log 3)^2+\frac{(\log 3)^2}{(\log 2)} \cdot \log x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \log x\left\{\frac{(\log 3)^2}{\log 2}-\log 2\right\} \\
&=(\log 2)^2-(\log 3)^2
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \log x=-\log 2=\log 2^{-1} \\
& \therefore \quad x=\frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{23}$ be real numbers such that
$\left(1+\frac{2}{5} x\right)^{23}=\sum_{i=0}^{23} a_i x^i$
for every real number $x$. let $a_r$ be the largest among the numbers $a_j$ for $0 \leq j \leq 23$.
The the value of $r$ is ______
questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{x}=1 \left(1+\frac{2}{5}\right)^{23}=a_0+a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_{23}$
for numerically greatest term
$\frac{n+1}{1+\left|\frac{a}{b}\right|}=\frac{23+1}{1+\frac{5}{2}}=\frac{48}{7} \Rightarrow\left[\frac{48}{7}\right]=6=\mathrm{m}$ (where [.] greatest integer function)
so, $\mathrm{T}_7$ is numerical greatest term
Hence $r=6$

questions.q: Let $a$ and $b$ be two nonzero real numbers. If the coefficient of ${x}^{5}$ in the expansion of ${\left(a{x}^{2} + \dfrac{70}{27bx}\right)}^{4}$ is equal to the coefficient of ${x}^{- 5}$ in the expansion of ${\left(ax - \dfrac{1}{b{x}^{2}}\right)}^{7}$, then the value of $2b$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

The coefficient of ${x}^{5}$ in ${\left(a{x}^{2} + \dfrac{70}{27bx}\right)}^{4}$ is equal to coefficient of ${x}^{- 5}$ in ${\left(ax - \dfrac{1}{b{x}^{2}}\right)}^{7}$,

Now finding the coefficient of ${x}^{5}$ in ${\left(a{x}^{2} + \dfrac{70}{27bx}\right)}^{4}$ we get,

${T}_{r + 1} = Cr 4 {\left(a{x}^{2}\right)}^{4 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{70}{27bx}\right)}^{r}$

$⇒ {T}_{r + 1} = Cr 4 {\left(a\right)}^{4 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{70}{27b}\right)}^{r} \cdot {x}^{8 - 2r - r}$

So, $8 - 2r - r = 5 ⇒ r = 1$

So, ${T}_{2} = C1 4 {a}^{3} \cdot \dfrac{70}{27b} \cdot {x}^{5}$

Now finding the coefficient of ${x}^{- 5}$ in ${\left(ax - \dfrac{1}{b{x}^{2}}\right)}^{7}$ we get,

${T}_{r + 1} = Cr 7 {\left(ax\right)}^{7 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b{x}^{2}}\right)}^{r}$

$⇒ {T}_{r + 1} = Cr 7 {\left(a\right)}^{7 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{r} \cdot {x}^{7 - r - 2r}$

So, $7 - r - 2r = - 5 ⇒ r = 4$

So, ${T}_{5} = C4 7 {\left(a\right)}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{4} \cdot {x}^{- 5}$

Now equating the coefficient of ${x}^{5} \text{ and } {x}^{- 5}$ we get,

$C4 7 {\left(a\right)}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{4} = C1 4 {a}^{3} \cdot \dfrac{70}{27b}$

$⇒ 35{a}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{4} = 4{a}^{3} \cdot \dfrac{70}{27b}$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{3} = 4 \times \dfrac{2}{27}$

$⇒ b = \dfrac{3}{2} ⇒ 2b = 3$
