$⇒ {T}_{r + 1} = Cr 4 {\left(a\right)}^{4 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{70}{27b}\right)}^{r} \cdot {x}^{8 - 2r - r}$

So, $8 - 2r - r = 5 ⇒ r = 1$

So, ${T}_{2} = C1 4 {a}^{3} \cdot \dfrac{70}{27b} \cdot {x}^{5}$

Now finding the coefficient of ${x}^{- 5}$ in ${\left(ax - \dfrac{1}{b{x}^{2}}\right)}^{7}$ we get,

${T}_{r + 1} = Cr 7 {\left(ax\right)}^{7 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b{x}^{2}}\right)}^{r}$

$⇒ {T}_{r + 1} = Cr 7 {\left(a\right)}^{7 - r} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{r} \cdot {x}^{7 - r - 2r}$

So, $7 - r - 2r = - 5 ⇒ r = 4$

So, ${T}_{5} = C4 7 {\left(a\right)}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{4} \cdot {x}^{- 5}$

Now equating the coefficient of ${x}^{5} \text{ and } {x}^{- 5}$ we get,

$C4 7 {\left(a\right)}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{4} = C1 4 {a}^{3} \cdot \dfrac{70}{27b}$

$⇒ 35{a}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{4} = 4{a}^{3} \cdot \dfrac{70}{27b}$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{b}\right)}^{3} = 4 \times \dfrac{2}{27}$

$⇒ b = \dfrac{3}{2} ⇒ 2b = 3$

For nonnegative integers $s$ and $r$, let $\left(\begin{array}{ll}s \\ r\end{array}\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{s !}{r ! \left(s - r\right) !} & \text{if}r \le s \\ 0 & \text{if}r > s\end{cases}\right$. For positive integers $m$ and $n,$ let $g\left(m, n\right) = \mathop{∑}_{p = 0}^{m + n}\dfrac{f\left(m, n, p\right)}{\left(\begin{array}{ll}n + p \\ p\end{array}\right)}$, where for any nonnegative integer $p$,
$f\left(m, n, p\right) = \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p}\left(\begin{array}{ll}m \\ i\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}n + i \\ p\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}p + n \\ p - i\end{array}\right)$. Then which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: $g\left(m, n\right) = g\left(n, m\right)$ for all positive integers $m, n$
$g\left(m, n + 1\right) = g\left(m + 1, n\right)$ for all positive integers $m, n$
$g\left(2m, 2n\right) = 2g\left(m, n\right)$ for all positive integers $m, n$
$g\left(2m, 2n\right) = {\left(g\left(m, n\right)\right)}^{2}$ for all positive intergers $m, n$
questions.solution:
$f\left(m, n, p\right) = \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p}\left(\begin{array}{ll}m \\ i\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}n + i \\ p\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}p + n \\ p - i\end{array}\right)$

$= \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p} Ci m \cdot \dfrac{\left(n + i\right) !}{p ! \left(n + i - p\right) !} \cdot \dfrac{( p + n ) !}{\left(p - i\right) ! \left(n + i\right) !}$

$= \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p} Ci m \cdot \dfrac{( p + n ) !}{p ! n !} \cdot \dfrac{n !}{\left(n + i - p\right) ! \left(p - i\right) !}$

$= \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p} Ci m . Cp p + n \cdot Cp - i n$

$Cp p + n \cdot \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p} Ci m \cdot Cp - i n$

$\left(∵ \mathop{∑}_{i = 0}^{p} Ci m \cdot Cp - i n = Cp m + n\right)$

$∴ f\left(m, n, p\right) = Cp p + n . Cp m + n$

$⇒ \dfrac{f\left(m, n, p\right)}{Cp p + n} = Cp m + n$.

$g\left(m, n\right) = \mathop{∑}_{p = 0}^{m + n} Cp m + n = {2}^{m + n}$

(A) $g ( 2m, 2n ) = {2}^{2m + 2n}$

$2g\left(m, n\right) = 2 . {2}^{m + n}$

(B) $g\left(m, n + 1\right) = {2}^{m + n + 1} = g\left(m + 1, n\right)$

(C) $g\left(2m, 2n\right) = {2}^{2m + 2n} = {\left({2}^{m + n}\right)}^{2} = {\left(g\left(m, n\right)\right)}^{2}$

(D) $g\left(m, n\right) = g\left(n, m\right)$.

questions.solution:
$\text{n} + 5{\text{C}}_{\text{r} - 1}\text{:}\text{n} + 5{\text{C}}_{\text{r}}\text{:}\text{n} + 5{\text{C}}_{\text{r} + 1} = \text{5 : 10 :14}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(n + 5\right) !}{\left(r - 1\right) ! \left(n - r + 6\right) !}: \dfrac{\left(n + 5\right) !}{\left(r\right) ! \left(n - r + 5\right) !}: \dfrac{\left(n + 5\right) !}{\left(r + 1\right) ! \left(n - r + 4\right) !} = \text{5 : 10 :14}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\left(r - 1\right) ! \left(n - r + 6\right) !}: \dfrac{1}{\left(r\right) ! \left(n - r + 5\right) !}: \dfrac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) ! \left(n - r + 4\right) !} = \text{5 : 10 :14}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(r + 1\right)r}{\left(n - r + 6\right) !}: \dfrac{r + 1}{\left(n - r + 5\right) !}: \dfrac{1}{\left(n - r + 4\right) !} = \text{5 : 10 :14}$

$⇒ \left(r + 1\right)r: \left(r + 1\right)\left(n - r + 6\right): \left(n - r + 6\right)\left(n - r + 5\right) = \text{5 : 10 :14}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(r + 1\right)\left(n - r + 6\right)}{\left(r + 1\right)r} = \dfrac{10}{5}\text{and}\dfrac{\left(n - r + 6\right)\left(n - r + 5\right)}{\left(r + 1\right)\left(n - r + 6\right)} = \dfrac{14}{10}$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(n - r + 6\right)}{r} = 2\text{and}\dfrac{\left(n - r + 5\right)}{\left(r + 1\right)} = \dfrac{7}{5}$

$⇒ n = 3r - 6\text{and}\text{n} = \dfrac{12r - 18}{5}$

$⇒ 3r - 6 = \dfrac{12r - 18}{5} = n$

$⇒ 15r - 30 = 12r - 18$

$⇒ r = 4$

$⇒ n = 6$

(P) The circle with centre $(1, 2)$ and touching the straight line $3x + 4y = 1$, passes through(1) the point $(1, 1)$
(Q) The common tangent to the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 2$ and the parabola $y^2 = 8x$ with positive slope, passes through(2) the point $(7, 9)$
(R) Let $M$ be the end point of the latus rectum of the ellipse $3x^2 + 4y^2 = 48$ such that $M$ lies in the first quadrant. Then the normal to the ellipse drawn at $M$ passes through(3) the point $(3, 2)$
(S) Let $H$ be the hyperbola whose centre is at the origin, one of the foci is at $(5, 0)$, and one directrix is $5x + 16 = 0$. Then $H$ passes through(4) the point $(2, 5)$
(5) the point $(8, 3\sqrt{3})$
questions.solution:
For (P):
The radius of the circle is the perpendicular distance from $(1, 2)$ to $3x + 4y - 1 = 0$.
$r = \dfrac{|3(1) + 4(2) - 1|}{\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$
The equation of the circle is $(x - 1)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 4$.
Checking the given points, $(3, 2)$ satisfies the equation.
Thus, (P) $\rightarrow$ (3).

For (Q):
The equation of a tangent to $y^2 = 8x$ with slope $m$ is $y = mx + \dfrac{2}{m}$.
Since it is also a tangent to $x^2 + y^2 = 2$, the perpendicular distance from $(0, 0)$ to the line $mx - y + \dfrac{2}{m} = 0$ is equal to the radius $\sqrt{2}$.
$\dfrac{\left|\dfrac{2}{m}\right|}{\sqrt{m^2 + 1}} = \sqrt{2}$
$\dfrac{4}{m^2} = 2(m^2 + 1)$
$m^4 + m^2 - 2 = 0$
$(m^2 + 2)(m^2 - 1) = 0$
Since $m$ is real and positive, $m = 1$.
The equation of the common tangent is $y = x + 2$.
Checking the given points, $(7, 9)$ satisfies the equation.
Thus, (Q) $\rightarrow$ (2).

For (R):
The equation of the ellipse is $\dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{y^2}{12} = 1$.
Here $a^2 = 16$ and $b^2 = 12$.
Eccentricity $e = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{12}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
The end point of the latus rectum in the first quadrant is $\left(ae, \dfrac{b^2}{a}\right) = \left(4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{12}{4}\right) = (2, 3)$.
The equation of the normal at $(2, 3)$ is $\dfrac{16x}{2} - \dfrac{12y}{3} = 16 - 12$.
$8x - 4y = 4 \Rightarrow 2x - y = 1$.
Checking the given points, $(1, 1)$ satisfies the equation.
Thus, (R) $\rightarrow$ (1).

For (S):
The centre is $(0, 0)$. The focus is $(ae, 0) = (5, 0) \Rightarrow ae = 5$.
The directrix is $x = -\dfrac{16}{5} \Rightarrow \dfrac{a}{e} = \dfrac{16}{5}$.
Multiplying the two equations gives $a^2 = 16$.
Dividing the two equations gives $e^2 = \dfrac{25}{16}$.
$b^2 = a^2(e^2 - 1) = 16\left(\dfrac{25}{16} - 1\right) = 9$.
The equation of the hyperbola is $\dfrac{x^2}{16} - \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$.
Checking the given points, $(8, 3\sqrt{3})$ satisfies the equation.
Thus, (S) $\rightarrow$ (5).

Answer: (P) $\rightarrow$ (3), (Q) $\rightarrow$ (2), (R) $\rightarrow$ (1), (S) $\rightarrow$ (5)

questions.q: Let ${C}_{1}$ be the circle of radius $1$ with center at the origin. Let ${C}_{2}$ be the circle of radius $r$ with center at the point $A = ( 4, 1 )$, where $1 < r < 3$. Two distinct common tangents $PQ$ and $ST$ of ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ are drawn. The tangent $PQ$ touches ${C}_{1}$ at $P$ and ${C}_{2}$ at $Q$. The tangent $ST$ touches ${C}_{1}$ at $S$ and ${C}_{2}$ at $T$. Midpoints of the line segments $PQ$ and $ST$ are joined to form a line which meets the $x$-axis at a point $B$. If $AB = \sqrt{5}$, then the value of ${r}^{2}$ is
questions.solution:
Plotting the diagram of the given value we get,

Now let $M$ and $N$ be midpoints of $PQ$ and $ST$ respectively.
$⇒ MN$ is a radical axis of two circles

${C}_{1}: {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 1$

${C}_{2}: ( x - 4{)}^{2} + ( y - 1{)}^{2} = {r}^{2}$

$⇒ {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 8x - 2y + 17 - {r}^{2} = 0$

Now subtracting equation of both above circles we get,

Equation of $MN: 8x + 2y - 18 + {r}^{2} = 0$

Now the line $MN$ intersect the $x - \text{axis}$ at $B$

So, $B$ will be,

$⇒ B\left(\dfrac{18 - {r}^{2}}{8}, 0\right)$

Also given, $AB = \sqrt{5}$

Now using distance formula we get,

$\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{18 - {r}^{2}}{8} - 4\right)}^{2} + 1} = \sqrt{5}$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{18 - {r}^{2}}{8} - 4\right)}^{2} = 4$

$⇒ \dfrac{18 - {r}^{2}}{8} - 4 = \pm 2$

Taking positive sign we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{18 - {r}^{2}}{8} = 6 ⇒ {r}^{2} = - 30\left(\text{rejected}\right)$

Now taking negative sign we get,

$⇒ \dfrac{18 - {r}^{2}}{8} = 2 ⇒ {r}^{2} = 2$

Hence, ${r}^{2} = 2$

questions.q: Let $G$ be a circle of radius $R > 0$. Let ${G}_{1}, {G}_{2}, \ldots , {G}_{n}$ be $n$ circles of equal radius $r > 0$. Suppose each of the $n$ circles ${G}_{1}, {G}_{2}, \ldots , {G}_{n}$ touches the circle $G$ externally. Also, for $i = 1, 2, \ldots , n - 1$, the circle ${G}_{i}$ touches ${G}_{i + 1}$ externally, and ${G}_{n}$ touches ${G}_{1}$ externally. Then, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Plotting the diagram of given condition we have,

Now each radius of smaller circle will make $\dfrac{\pi}{n}$ angle at centre of bigger circle,

Now applying the sine rule, we get

$\dfrac{sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)}{sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}} = \dfrac{r}{R + r}$

$⇒ \dfrac{R}{r} + 1 = cosec \left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)$

$⇒ R = r\left[cosec \left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)\right]\left[- 1\right]$

Now checking all options we get,

(A) $n = 4, R = r\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)$

(B) $n = 5, R = r\left(cosec \dfrac{\pi}{5} - 1\right)$

$⇒ R < r\left(cosec \dfrac{\pi}{6} - 1\right) ⇒ R < r$

(C) $n = 8, R = r\left[cosec \left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) - 1\right]$

$⇒ R > r\left(cosec \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) - 1\right)$

$⇒ R > r\left(\sqrt{2} - 1\right)$

(D) $n = 12, R = r\left[cosec \left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right) - 1\right]$

$⇒ R = \left[\sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{3} + 1\right) - 1\right]r$

$⇒ R < \sqrt{2}\left(\sqrt{3} + 1\right)r$

questions.q: A line $y = mx + 1$ intersects the circle ${\left(x - 3\right)}^{2} + {\left(y + 2\right)}^{2} = 25$ at the points $P$ and $Q .$ If the midpoint of the line segment $PQ$ has $x -$coordinate $- \dfrac{3}{5},$ then which one of the following options is correct?
questions.solution:
Equation of line $PQ: y = mx + 1$ Let $R$ be the mid point of $PQ$, so its $x$-coordinate of midpoint $= - \dfrac{3}{5}$ Hence, coordinates of midpoint $R\left(- \dfrac{3}{5}, - \dfrac{3m}{5} + 1\right)$ Let centre of circle is $O\left(3, 2\right)$ Since, perpendicular dropped from centre upon any chord divides it in two equal parts. Hence, line $PQ$ will be perpendicular to $RO$ $⇒ {m}_{RQ} ⋅ {m}_{RO} = - 1$ $⇒ m\left(\dfrac{- \dfrac{3m}{5} + 1 + 2}{- \dfrac{3}{5} - 3}\right) = - 1$ $⇒ m\left(\dfrac{- 3m + 15}{- 18}\right) = - 1$ $⇒ {m}^{2} - 5m + 6 = 0$ $⇒ m = 2, 3$

$⇒ 2 \le m < 4$

questions.q: Let $T$ be the line passing through the points $P\left(- 2, 7\right) and Q \left(2, - 5\right). Let ${F}_{1}be the $set of all pairs of circles \left({S}_{1}, {S}_{2}\right) such that$T$ is tangents to ${S}_{1}$ at $P$ and tangent to ${S}_{2}$ at $Q$, and also such that ${S}_{1} and {S}_{2}$ touch each other at a point, say, $M$. Let ${E}_{1}$ be the set representing the locus of $Mas the $pair \left({S}_{1}, {S}_{2}\right) varies in${F}_{1}$. Let the set of all straight line segments joining a pair of distinct points of ${E}_{1}$ and passing through the point $R$\left(1,1\right)$ be ${F}_{2}$ . Let ${E}_{2}$ be the set of the mid-points of the line segments in the set ${F}_{2}$ . Then, which of the following statement(s) is (are) TRUE?
options: The point $\left(\dfrac{4}{5}, \dfrac{7}{5}\right)$ does NOT lie in ${E}_{2}$
The point $\left(0, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$ does NOT lie in ${E}_{1}$
questions.solution:
$AP = AQ = AM$ So $∠ PMQ = 90 °$
Locus of $M$ is a circle having $PQ$ as its diameter
Hence, ${E}_{1}: {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 2y - 39 = 0, x \ne \pm 2$
Clearly $\left(- 2, 7\right)$ is not included in the locus because we can not consider point circles, and $\left(0, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$ does not lie on ${E}_{1}$ as it does not satisfy the equation above.

The equation of chord with $B\left(h, k\right) as mid point will be given by $T = {S}_{1}$ or

$xh + yk - y - k - 39 = {h}^{2} + {k}^{2} - 2k - 39$

or $xh + yk - y + k = {h}^{2} + {k}^{2}$

It passes through $R$\left(1, 1\right)$. So,

$h + k - 1 + k = {h}^{2} + {k}^{2}$

or the locus of ${E}_{2}$ is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - x - 2y + 1 = 0$

But if $P$ is not the part of locus of $M$ then $PQ$ is not the chord of locus of $M$. So point $\left(\dfrac{4}{5}, \dfrac{7}{5}\right)$ does not lie in ${E}_{2}$. $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 1\right)$ does not satisfy the equation hence does not lie in ${E}_{2}$.

Question : Let ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}$ and ${F}_{1}{F}_{2}$ be the chords of $S$ passing through the point ${P}_{0} ( 1,1 )$ and parallel to the $x$ – axis and the $y$ – axis, respectively. Let ${G}_{1}{G}_{2}$ be the chord of $S$ passing through ${P}_{0}$ and having slope $- 1 .$ Let the tangents to $S$ at ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ meet at ${E}_{3}$, the tangents to $S$ at ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ meet at ${F}_{3},$ and the tangents to $S$ at ${G}_{1}$ and ${G}_{2}$ meet at ${G}_{3}$. Then, the points ${E}_{3}, {F}_{3},$ and ${G}_{3}$ lie on the curve
questions.solution: Co - ordinates of ${E}_{1}and{E}_{2}$ are obtained by solving $y = 1and{x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 4 ∴ {E}_{1}\left(- \sqrt{3}, 1\right)$and{E}_{2}$\left(\sqrt{3}, 1\right)$ Co - ordinates of ${F}_{1}and{F}_{2}$ are obtained by solving $x = 1and{x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 4 {F}_{1}\left(1, \sqrt{3}\right)and{F}_{2}\left(1, - \sqrt{3}\right) Tangent at ${E}_{1}: - \sqrt{3}x + y = 4$ Tangent at ${E}_{2}: - \sqrt{3}x + y = 4 ∴ {E}_{3}$\left(0, 4\right)$ Tangent at ${F}_{1}: x + \sqrt{3}y = 4$ Tangent at ${F}_{2}: x - \sqrt{3}y = 4 ∴ {F}_{3}\left(4, 0\right)$ And similarly{G}_{3}$\left(2, 2\right) \left(0, 4\right)$, $\left(4, 0\right)$and $\left(2, 2\right)$liesonx + y = 4$ Alternate solution 2: The required curve will be the polar of the pole ${P}_{0} ( 1, 1 )$w.rt. the circle S Hence its equation is $T = 0 ⇒ x.1 + y.1 = 4 ⇒ x + y = 4$ Alternate solution 3: Let $Q( h, k )$ is a general point on the curve containing points ${E}_{3} , {F}_{3} $\text{$ and } {G}_{3}$ and a pair of tangents are drawn to the circle S from Q then the equation of the chord of contact will be $T = xh + yk - 4 = 0$ since the chord of contact passes through ${P}_{0} ( 1, 1 )$ hence $1.h + 1.k - 4 = 0 ⇒$ The point $Q( h, k )$ lies on the line $1.x + 1.y - 4 = 0 ⇒ x + y - 4 = 0

questions.q: For how many values of $p$, the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2x + 4y - p = 0$ and the coordinate axes have exactly three common points?
questions.solution:
We shall consider 3 cases.

Case I: When p = 0

(i.e., circle passes through origin)

Now, equation of circle becomes

${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2x + 4y = 0$

Case II: When circle intersect x-axis at 2 distinct points and touches y-axis.

${g}^{2} - c > 0$ and ${f}^{2} = c$

$1 + p > 0$ and $p = - 4$ so, this case is not possible

Case III: When circle intersect y-axis at 2 distinct points and touches x-axis

Now, ${g}^{2} - c = 0$  and ${f}^{2} - c > 0$

$⇒ 1 - \left(- p\right) = 0$ and $4 - \left(- p\right) > 0$

$⇒ p = - 1$  and, $p > - 4$

$∴ p = - 1$ is possible.

$∴$   Finally, we conclude that $p = 0, - 1$.

$⇒$Two possible values of p.

questions.q: Let RS be the diameter of the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 1$ where, $S$ is the point$( 1, 0 )$. Let $P$be a variable point (other than $R \text{ and } S$) on the circle and tangents to the circle at $S \text{ and } P$meet at the point$Q$. The normal to the circle at P intersects a line drawn through$Q$ parallel to $RS$ at point $E$ . Then, the locus of $E$ passes through the point (s):
questions.solution:
$Let P be ( cos \theta, sin \theta )$, where
$\theta \ne 0, \pi$
Tangent at $P: xcos ⁡ \theta + ysin ⁡ \theta = 1$ ........(i)
Tangent at $S: x = 1$ .........(ii)
$∴$ By (i) and (ii) : $Q\left(1, \dfrac{1 - cos ⁡ \theta}{sin ⁡ \theta}\right)$
Line through Q parallel to RS :
$y = \dfrac{1 - cos ⁡ \theta}{sin ⁡ \theta} ⇒ y = tan ⁡ \dfrac{\theta}{2}$ ..........(iii)
Normal at $P: y = \dfrac{sin ⁡ \theta}{cos ⁡ \theta}x ⇒ y = tan ⁡ \theta . x$ $⇒ y = \left(\dfrac{2tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}}{1 - t{an}^{2}\dfrac{\theta}{2}}\right)x$ ........(iv)  
Point of intersection of equation (iii) and (iv), $E: h = \dfrac{1 - \tan^{2} ⁡ \dfrac{\theta}{2}}{2}; k = tan ⁡ \dfrac{\theta}{2}$
Eliminating $\theta: h = \dfrac{1 - {k}^{2}}{2} ⇒ {y}^{2} = 1 - 2x$
$( \dfrac{1}{3} , \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} ) & ( \dfrac{1}{3} , - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} )$  satisfy the locus.

questions.q: The circle ${C}_{1}: {x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 3,$ with centre at O, intersects the parabola ${x}^{2} = 2y$ at the point P in the first quadrant. Let the tangent to the circle ${C}_{1}$ at P touches other two circles ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ at ${R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{3}$ , respectively. Suppose ${C}_{2}$ and ${C}_{3}$ have equal radii $2\sqrt{3}$ and centres ${Q}_{2}$ and ${Q}_{3}$ , respectively. If ${Q}_{2}$ and ${Q}_{3}$ lie on the y - axis, then
questions.solution:
On solving ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 3 and {x}^{2} = 2y$ we get point $P\left(\sqrt{2}, 1\right)
Equation$ of tangent at P
\sqrt{2}x + y = 3$
Let ${Q}_{2}$ be (0, k) and radius is $2\sqrt{3}$
$∴ $\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{2}\left(0\right)$ + k - 3}{\sqrt{2 + 1}}\right| = 2\sqrt{3}$
$∴ k = 9, - 3 {Q}_{3}$
${Q}_{2}$\left(0, 9\right)$ and {Q}_{3} ( 0, - 3 ) { $\begin{array}{ll}{C}_{2} : {( x - 0 )}^{2} + {( y - 9 )}^{2} = 12 \\ {C}_{3} : {( x - 0 )}^{2} + {( y + 3 )}^{2} = 12\end{array}$
Hence ${Q}_{2}{Q}_{3} = 12$

${⇒ a}^{2} + 12 = 36$
$⇒ a = 2\sqrt{6}$
${R}_{2}{R}_{3} = 2a = 4\sqrt{6}$
Perpendicular distance of origin O from ${R}_{2}{R}_{3}$ is equal to distance of O from tangent $\sqrt{2}x + y = 3$ which is same as radius of circle ${C}_{1} = \sqrt{3}$
Hence area of $\DeltaO{R}_{2}{R}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \left({R}_{2}{R}_{3}\right)\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} . 4\sqrt{6} . \sqrt{3} = 6\sqrt{2}$
Perpendicular Distance of P from ${Q}_{2}{Q}_{3} = \sqrt{2}$
$∴$ Area of $\DeltaP{Q}_{2}{Q}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times$ 12 \times \sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{2}

questions.solution:
Given circles

${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 1 = 0$
Radical axis $x + 7 = 0$ ......(i)
Centre of circle lies on (i)

Orthogonallity gives
$- 14 = c - 15 ⇒ c = 1$ .......(ii)
$\left(0, 1\right) \to 1 - 2k + 1 = 0 ⇒ k = 1$

questions.solution:
Let the circle be

${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$

According to the question,

${g}^{2} - c = 0 ⇒ {g}^{2} = c . . . . \left(i\right)

and

$2\sqrt{{f}^{2} - c} = 2\sqrt{7} ⇒ {f}^{2} - c = 7 . . . . . $\left(ii\right)$

The circle passes through the point $\left(3, 0\right)$, then
$9 + 0 + 6g + 0 + c = 0$
$⇒ 9 + 6g + {g}^{2} = 0,$ by $\left(i\right)$
$⇒ ( g + 3{)}^{2} = 0 ⇒ g = - 3$
∴c = 9 and ${f}^{2} = 16 ⇒ f = \pm 4$

So the required circles are

${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 6x \pm 8y + 9 = 0$.

questions.q: A tangent $P T$ is drawn to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ at the point $P(\sqrt{3}, 1)$. A straight line $L$, perpendicular to $P T$ is a tangent to the circle $(x-3)^{2}+y^{2}-1$. Question: A possible equation of $L$ is
questions.solution:
Equation of tangent $P T$ to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=4$ at the point $P(\sqrt{3}, 1)$ is $x \sqrt{3}+y=4$ Let the line $L$, perpendicular to tangent $P T$ be $x-y \sqrt{3}+\lambda=0$

As it is tangent to the circle $(x-3)^{2}+y^{2}=1 \therefore \quad$ Length of perpendicular from centre of circle to the Tangent $=$ radius of circle.

$\Rightarrow\left|\frac{3+\lambda}{2}\right|=1 \Rightarrow \lambda=-1 \text{ or }-5 \therefore$ Equation of $L$ can be $x-\sqrt{3} y=1$ or $x-\sqrt{3} y=5$

questions.q: The locus of the mid-point of the chord of contact of tangents drawn from points lying on the straight line $4 x-$ $5 y=20$ to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$ is
questions.solution:
Any point $P$ on line $4 x-5 y=20$ can be considered as $\left(\alpha, \frac{4 \alpha-20}{5}\right)$. Equation of chord of contact $A B$ to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$ drawn from point $\mathrm{P}\left(\alpha, \frac{4 \alpha-20}{5}\right)$ is x. $\alpha+$ y. $\left(\frac{4 \alpha-20}{5}\right)=9...(i)$
Also the equation of chord $A B$ whose mid point is $(h, k)$ is $h x+k y=h^{2}+k^{2}....(ii)$ $\because \quad$ Equations (i) and (ii) represent the same line, $\therefore \quad \frac{h}{\alpha}=\frac{k}{\frac{4 \alpha-20}{5}}=\frac{h^{2}+k^{2}}{9}$ $\Rightarrow 5 k \alpha=4 h \alpha-20 h$ and $9 h=\alpha\left(h^{2}+k^{2}\right)$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{20 h}{4 h-5 k} \quad$ and $\alpha=\frac{9 h}{h^{2}+k^{2}}$ $\Rightarrow \quad \frac{20 h}{4 h-5 k}=\frac{9 h}{h^{2}+k^{2}} \Rightarrow 20\left(h^{2}+k^{2}\right)=9(4 h-5 k)$ $\therefore \quad$ Locus of $(h, k)$ is $20\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)-36 x+45 y=0$

\therefore & & x & =-1,-4
\end{array}$

Let centre of circle $C$ be $(h, k)$.

questions.solution: $\text{ Here, equation of }$C_2:(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=($\sqrt{2})^$2 $\text{ and }$C_1:(x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=(1)^2 $\begin{aligned}$& \therefore P(1+\cos $\theta,$1+\sin $\theta)$\\ & $\text{ and }$Q(1+$\sqrt{2} \sin \theta,$1+$\sqrt{2} \sin \theta)$\\ & \therefore P A²+P B²+P C²+P D² \\ & =$\left$\{(1+\cos $\theta)^$2+(1+\sin $\theta)^$2\right\} \\ & +$\left$\{(\cos $\theta-$1)^2+(1+\sin $\theta)^$2\right\} \\ & +$\left$\{(1+\cos $\theta)^$2+(1-\sin $\theta)^$2\right\} \\ & +$\left$\{(1-\cos $\theta)^$2+(1-\sin $\theta)^$2\right\} \\ & =16 \\ & \therefore \quad $\frac{\Sigma Q A^2}{\Sigma P A^2}=\frac{12}{16}=$0.75 \\ & \end{aligned} Hence (a) is the correct answer.

For a non-zero complex number $z$, let $\arg (z)$ denote the principal argument of $z$, with $-\pi <\arg (z) \leq \pi$. Let $\omega$ be the cube root of unity for which $0 <\arg (\omega) <\pi$. Let $\alpha=\arg \left(\sum_{n=1}^{2025}(-\omega)^n\right)$.
Then the value of $\frac{3 \alpha}{\pi}$ is ___________
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \alpha=\arg \left(-\omega+\omega^2-\omega^3+\ldots \ldots \ldots+(-\omega)^{2025}\right) \\ & \alpha=\arg \left(\frac{-\omega\left((-\omega)^{2025}-1\right)}{-\omega-1}\right) \\ & \alpha=\arg \left(\frac{-\omega}{-\omega-1}(-2)\right) \\ & \alpha=\arg \left(\frac{-2 \omega}{\omega+1}\right) \\ & \alpha=\arg \left(\frac{-2 \omega}{-\omega^2}\right) \\ & \alpha=\arg \left(\frac{2}{\omega}\right) \\ & \alpha=\arg \left(2 \omega^2\right) \\ & \alpha=\frac{-2 \pi}{3} \\ & \frac{3 \alpha}{\pi}=-2\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $A = \left\{\dfrac{1967 + 1686isin\theta}{7 - 3icos\theta}: \theta \in R\right\}$. If $A$ contains exactly one positive integer $n$, then the value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
Let $z = \dfrac{1967 + 1686isin\theta}{7 - 3icos\theta}$ is a positive integer.

$⇒ z = \dfrac{\left(1967 + 1686isin\theta\right)\left(7 + 3icos\theta\right)}{\left(7 - 3icos\theta\right)\left(7 + 3icos\theta\right)}$

$⇒ z = \dfrac{1967 \times 7 - 1686 \times 3sin\thetacos\theta + i\left(1686 \times 7sin\theta + 1967 \times 3cos\theta\right)}{49 + 9\cos^{2}\theta}$

Now taking imaginary part as zero we get,

$1686 \times 7sin\theta + 1967 \times 3cos\theta = 0$

$⇒ \left(281 \times 6\right) \times 7sin\theta + \left(281 \times 7\right) \times 3cos\theta = 0$

$⇒ 42sin\theta + 21cos\theta = 0$

$⇒ tan\theta = - \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \cos^{2}\theta = \dfrac{4}{5} \text{ and } sin\thetacos\theta = - \dfrac{2}{5}$

Now putting the value in $z$we get,

$z = \dfrac{\left(281 \times 7 \times 7\right) - \left(281 \times 6\right) \times 3 \times \left(- \dfrac{2}{5}\right)}{49 + 9 \times \dfrac{4}{5}}$

$⇒ z = \dfrac{281\left(49 + \dfrac{36}{5}\right)}{\left(49 + \dfrac{36}{5}\right)} = 281$

Hence, the value of $n$ is $281$

Let $z$ be a complex number satisfying ${\left|z\right|}^{3} + 2{z}^{2} + 4\overset{¯}{z} - 8 = 0$, where $\overset{¯}{z}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z$. Let the imaginary part of $z$ be nonzero.

Match each entry in List-I to the correct entries in List-II.

List-I List-II
$\left(P\right)$ ${\left|z\right|}^{2}$ is equal to $\left(1\right)$ $12$
$\left(Q\right)$ ${\left|z - \overset{¯}{z}\right|}^{2}$ is equal to $\left(2\right)$ $4$
$\left(R\right)$ ${\left|z\right|}^{2} + {\left|z + \overset{¯}{z}\right|}^{2}$ is equal to $\left(3\right)$ $8$
$\left(S\right)$ ${\left|z + 1\right|}^{2}$ is equal to $\left(4\right)$ $10$
$\left(5\right)$ $7$

The correct option is
questions.solution:
Given,

${\left|z\right|}^{3} + 2{z}^{2} + 4\overset{¯}{z} - 8 = 0 . . . . . . . \left(1\right)$

Now on taking conjugate both side we get,

${\left|z\right|}^{3} + 2\overset{¯}{z}2 + 4z - 8 = 0 . . . . . . . . \left(2\right)$

$\left\{\text{Note}\left|\overset{¯}{z}\right| = \left|z\right|\right\}$

Now subtracting both equations we get,

$2\left({z}^{2} - \overset{¯}{z}2\right) + 4\left(\overset{¯}{z} - z\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(z - \overset{¯}{z}\right)\left[2\left(z + \overset{¯}{z}\right) - 4\right] = 0$

$∵ z = \overset{¯}{z}$ (not possible) or $4x = 4 ⇒ x = 1$ $\left\{\text{as}z + \overset{¯}{z} = 2x\right\}$

So, $z = 1 + \lambdai$

$⇒ \left|z\right| = \sqrt{1 + {\lambda}^{2}} \text{ and } \overset{¯}{z} = 1 - \lambdai$

Now putting the value of $z, \left|z\right| \text{ and } \overset{¯}{z}$ in given equation we get,

${\left(1 + {\lambda}^{2}\right)}^{3 / 2} + 2\left(1 - {\lambda}^{2} + 2\lambdai\right) + 4\left(1 - \lambdai\right) - 8 = 0$

$⇒ {\left(1 + {\lambda}^{2}\right)}^{3 / 2} + 2\left(1 - {\lambda}^{2}\right) = 4$

$⇒ {\left(1 + {\lambda}^{2}\right)}^{3 / 2} = 2\left(1 + {\lambda}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ \left(1 + {\lambda}^{2}\right)\left[\sqrt{1 + {\lambda}^{2}} - 2\right] = 0$

$⇒ {\lambda}^{2} = 3$

Now solving,

$\left(P\right)$ ${\left|z\right|}^{2} = 1 + {\lambda}^{2} = 1 + 3 = 4$

$\left(Q\right)$ ${\left|z - \overset{¯}{z}\right|}^{2} = {\left|1 + \lambdai - \left(1 - \lambdai\right)\right|}^{2} = {\left|2\lambdai\right|}^{2} = 4{\lambda}^{2} = 12$

$\left(R\right)$ ${\left|z\right|}^{2} + {\left|z + \overset{¯}{z}\right|}^{2} = 4 + {\left|\left(1 + \lambdai\right) + \left(1 - \lambdai\right)\right|}^{2} = 4 + 4 = 8$

$\left(S\right)$ ${\left|z + 1\right|}^{2} = {\left|1 + \lambdai + 1\right|}^{2} = 4 + {\lambda}^{2} = 4 + 3 = 7$

$∴ P \to \left(2\right), Q \to \left(1\right), R \to \left(3\right), S \to \left(5\right)$

If $z$ is a non-zero complex number for which both real and imaginary parts of ${\left(\overset{¯}{z}\right)}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{z}^{2}}$ are integers, then which of the following is/are possible value(s) of $\left|z\right|$ ?
questions.solution:
Let $z = r . {e}^{i\theta}$

So, ${\left(\overset{¯}{z}\right)}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{z}^{2}} = \left({r}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{r}^{2}}\right){e}^{- 2i\theta} = a + ib$ (say), given $a, b \in Z$

Now taking mod both side and squaring we get,

${\left({r}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{r}^{2}}\right)}^{2} = {a}^{2} + {b}^{2}$

$⇒ {r}^{8} - \left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2} - 2\right){r}^{4} + 1 = 0$

$⇒ {r}^{4} = \dfrac{\left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2} - 2\right) \pm \sqrt{{\left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2} - 2\right)}^{2} - 4}}{2}$

Now comparing from option we get, for ${a}^{2} + {b}^{2} = 45$ (i.e $\left(a, b\right) = \left(\pm 6, \pm 3\right)$ or $\left(\pm 3, \pm 6\right)$

We get $r = \left(\dfrac{43 + 3\sqrt{205}}{2}\right)\dfrac{1}{4}$

questions.question:
Let ${\theta}_{1}, {\theta}_{2}, \ldots , {\theta}_{10}$ be positive valued angles (in radian) such that ${\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2} + ⋯ + {\theta}_{10} = 2\pi$. Define the complex numbers ${z}_{1} = {e}^{i{\theta}_{1}}, {z}_{k} = {z}_{k - 1}{e}^{i{\theta}_{k}}$ for $k = 2, 3, \ldots , 10$, where $i = \sqrt{- 1}$. Consider the statements $P$ and $Q$ given below:
$P: \left|{z}_{2} - {z}_{1}\right| + \left|{z}_{3} - {z}_{2}\right| + ⋯ + \left|{z}_{10} - {z}_{9}\right| + \left|{z}_{1} - {z}_{10}\right| \le 2\pi$
$Q: \left|{z}_{2}^{2} - {z}_{1}^{2}\right| + \left|{z}_{3}^{2} - {z}_{2}^{2}\right| + ⋯ + \left|{z}_{10}^{2} - {z}_{9}^{2}\right| + \left|{z}_{1}^{2} - {z}_{10}^{2}\right| \le 4\pi$
questions.explanation:
Given, ${\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2} + . . . . . + {\theta}_{10} = 2\pi$, ${z}_{1} = {e}^{i{\theta}_{1}}, {z}_{k} = {z}_{k - 1}{e}^{i{\theta}_{k}}$

Now, ${z}_{k} = {z}_{k - 1}{e}^{i{\theta}_{k}}$

$⇒ {z}_{2} = {z}_{1}{e}^{i{\theta}_{1}}, {z}_{3} = {z}_{2}{e}^{i{\theta}_{2}}, \ldots \ldots$

As, ${z}_{1} = {e}^{i{\theta}_{1}}⇒ \left|{z}_{1}\right| = 1$

${z}_{2} = {z}_{1}{e}^{{}_{i\theta}}⇒ \left|{z}_{2}\right| = \left|{z}_{1}\right| = 1$

Similarly $\left|{z}_{1}\right| = \left|{z}_{2}\right| \ldots = \left|{z}_{k}\right| = 1$

$⇒ {z}_{1}, {z}_{2}, \ldots , {z}_{k}$ lies on a circle of unit radius.

We know, $\left|{z}_{k} - {z}_{k - 1}\right|$ represents a line segment joining ${z}_{k} \text{$ and } {z}_{k - 1}.

Both ${z}_{k} \text{$ and } {z}_{k - 1} lies on a unit circle

Since ${\theta}_{1} + {\theta}_{2} + . . . . + {\theta}_{10} = 2\pi$

We get

So, $\left|{z}_{2} - {z}_{1}\right|, \left|{z}_{3} - {z}_{2}\right|$, \ldots , $\left|{z}_{1} - {z}_{10}\right|$ are the sides of a decagon circumscribed by a circle of unit radius

We know, the sum of the length of sides of a decagon is less than the circumference of its circumcircle.

$⇒ \left|{z}_{2} - {z}_{1}\right| + \left|{z}_{3} - {z}_{2}\right| + ⋯ + \left|{z}_{10} - {z}_{9}\right| + \left|{z}_{1} - {z}_{10}\right| \le 2\pi$

Hence, $P$ is true.

Similarly, ${\left({z}_{1}\right)}^{2} = {e}^{i2{\theta}_{1}}, {\left({z}_{k}\right)}^{2} = {\left({z}_{k - 1}\right)}^{2}{e}^{i2{\theta}_{k}}, \ldots \ldots$

So, $\left|{z}_{2}^{2} - {z}_{1}^{2}\right|$, $\left|{z}_{3}^{2} - {z}_{2}^{2}\right|$, $\left|{z}_{4}^{2} - {z}_{3}^{2}\right|$, $\left|{z}_{5}^{2} - {z}_{4}^{2}\right|$, $\left|{z}_{6}^{2} - {z}_{5}^{2}\right|$ are
the sides of a pentagon circumscribed by a circle of unit radius

So, $\left|{z}_{2}^{2} - {z}_{1}^{2}\right|$ + $\left|{z}_{3}^{2} - {z}_{2}^{2}\right|$ + \ldots $\left|{z}_{6}^{2} - {z}_{5}^{2}\right|$ \le 2\pi$

Similarly, \left|{z}_{7}^{2} - {z}_{8}^{2}\right| + \ldots + \left|{z}_{1}^{2} - {z}_{10}^{2}\right| \le 2\pi$

Adding these equations, we get

$\left|{z}_{2}^{2} - {z}_{1}^{2}\right|$ + $\left|{z}_{3}^{2} - {z}_{2}^{2}\right|$ + ⋯ + $\left|{z}_{10}^{2} - {z}_{9}^{2}\right|$ + $\left|{z}_{1}^{2} - {z}_{10}^{2}\right|$ \le 4\pi$

Hence, $Q$ is true.

Given, ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 5x - 3y + 4 = 0$

Centre $\left(\dfrac{- 5}{2}, \dfrac{3}{2}\right), r = \sqrt{\dfrac{25}{4} + \dfrac{9}{4} - 4} = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$

Angle made by $( - \alpha, 0 ) \text{$ and $} ( - \beta, 0 )$ at the centre $C$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Using rotation of complex numbers, we get

$\dfrac{- \alpha - \left(- \dfrac{5}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2}i\right)}{- \beta - \left(- \dfrac{5}{2} + \dfrac{3}{2}i\right)} = 1 \cdot {e}^{i\dfrac{\pi}{2}} = i$

$- \alpha + \dfrac{5}{2} - \dfrac{3}{2}i = - i\beta + \dfrac{5}{2}i + \dfrac{3}{2}$

$\alpha - i\beta = 1 - 4i$

$∵ \alpha, \beta \in R$

$⇒ \alpha = 1, \beta = 4$

$⇒ \left|z + \dfrac{1}{2}\right| \in \left[1, \sqrt{7}\right]$

questions.q: Let $S$ be the set of all complex numbers $z$ satisfying $\left|z - 2 + i\right| \ge \sqrt{5} .$ If the complex number ${z}_{0}$ is such that $\dfrac{1}{\left|{z}_{0} - 1\right|}$ is the maximum of the set $\left\{\dfrac{1}{\left|z - 1\right|}: z \in S\right\},$ then the principal argument of $\dfrac{4 - {z}_{0} - \overset{¯}{z}0}{{z}_{0} - \overset{¯}{z}0 + 2i}$ is
questions.solution:
The region represented by $\left|z - 2 + i\right| \ge \sqrt{5}$ will be region outside and on circle with centre $\left(2, - 1\right)$ and radius $\sqrt{5} .$ $\left|z - 2 + i\right| \ge \sqrt{5}$ Let $z = x + iy$ $⇒ \left|x + iy - 2 + i\right| \ge \sqrt{5}$ $⇒ \left|\left(x - 2\right) + i\left(y + 1\right)\right| \ge \sqrt{5}$ $⇒ \sqrt{{\left(x - 2\right)}^{2} + {\left(y + 1\right)}^{2}} \ge \sqrt{5}$ $⇒ {\left(x - 2\right)}^{2} + {\left(y + 1\right)}^{2} \ge 5$ Now, for $\dfrac{1}{\left|{z}_{0} - 1\right|}$ to be maximum, $\left|{z}_{0} - 1\right|$ must be minimum.

We need to find the $B\left({z}_{0}\right)$ which is in given region and nearest to point $A\left(1, 0\right),$ hence nearest point from $A\left(1, 0\right)$ will be on the line joining $A$ and $C .$ Method 1 Let ${z}_{0} = x + iy$, then $x < 2$ and $y > 0$ (from diagram) Consider $w = \dfrac{4 - {z}_{0} - \overset{¯}{z}0}{{z}_{0} - \overset{¯}{z}0 + 2i} = \dfrac{4 - \left(x + iy\right) - \left(x - iy\right)}{\left(x + iy\right) - \left(x - iy\right) + 2i} = \dfrac{4 - 2x}{i\left(y + 2\right)} = \dfrac{1}{i}\left(\dfrac{4 - x}{y + 2}\right)$ $w = - i\left(\dfrac{4 - x}{y + 2}\right)$ $w = i\left(K\right),$ where $K = \dfrac{4 - x}{y + 2}$ As $x < 2$ and $y > 0 ⇒ K > 0$ $w = - iK,$ will lie on negative imaginary axis $Arg\left(w\right) = - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ Alternate: As $B\left({z}_{0}\right)$ lies on line $AC,$ Equation of $AC$: $\left(y + 1\right) = \dfrac{0 - \left(- 1\right)}{1 - 2}\left(x - 2\right)$ $⇒ y + 1 = \dfrac{1}{- 1}\left(x - 2\right)$ $⇒ x + y = 2 . . . . \left(i\right)$ Let ${z}_{0} = x + iy$ Consider $w = \dfrac{4 - {z}_{0} - \overset{¯}{z}0}{{z}_{0} - \overset{¯}{z}0 + 2i}$ $w = \dfrac{4 - x}{i\left(y + 2\right)}$ From equation $\left(i\right)$ $w = \dfrac{4 - x}{i\left(2 - x + 2\right)}$ $w = \dfrac{1}{i}$ $w = - i$ $Arg\left(w\right) = - \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

questions.q: Let $a, b, x$ and $y$ be real numbers such that $a - b = 1$ and $y \ne 0$ . If the complex number $z = x + iy$ satisfies $Im\left(\dfrac{az + b}{z + 1}\right) = y,$ then which of the following is (are) possible value (s) of $x ?$
questions.solution:
$Im\left(\dfrac{az + b}{z + 1}\right) = y$ and $z = x + iy$

$∴ Im\left(\dfrac{a\left(x + iy\right) + b}{x + iy + 1}\right) = y$

multiply and divide by $x + 1 - iy$ and equate imaginary part

$⇒ - y\left(ax + b\right) + ay\left(x + 1\right) = y\left({\left(x + 1\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ \left(a - b\right)y = y\left({\left(x + 1\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2}\right)$

$∵ y \ne 0anda - b = 1$

$⇒ {\left(x + 1\right)}^{2} + {y}^{2} = 1$

$⇒ x = - 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - {y}^{2}}$

Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & \omega & \omega^2 \\ \omega & \omega^2 & 1 \\ \omega^2 & 1 & \omega\end{array}\right]$
Now, $\quad A^2=\left[\begin{array}{lll}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]$

questions.solution:
Let $z_1=\frac{w-\bar{w}_z}{1-z}$, be purely real.
$ \begin{array}{rlrl}
\Rightarrow & z_1 & =\bar{z}_1 \\
& \therefore & \frac{w-\bar{w} z}{1-z} & =\frac{\bar{w}-w \bar{z}}{1-\bar{z}} \\
\Rightarrow & & w-w \bar{z}-\bar{w} z+\bar{w} z \cdot \bar{z} & =\bar{w}-z \bar{w}-w \bar{z}+w z \cdot \bar{z} \\
\Rightarrow & & (w-\bar{w})+(\bar{w}-w)|z|^2 & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & & (w-\bar{w})\left(1-|z|^2\right) & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & & |z|^2 & =1 \\
\Rightarrow & & |z| & =1 \text{ and } z \neq 1 .
\end{array}   \text{ [as, }$ w-\bar{w} \neq 0 $\text{, since }$ \beta \neq 0 $\text{ ] } $

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $f : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be an arbitrary function and let $g : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined by

$g(x) = x f(x)$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The function $g$ is always continuous at $x = 0$
If $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$
If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$, then $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$
If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$, then $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$ exists
questions.solution:
Given $g(x) = x f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

For option A:
Let $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ for $x eq 0$ and $f(0) = 0$.
Then $g(x) = 1$ for $x eq 0$ and $g(0) = 0$.
$\lim_{x o 0} g(x) = 1 eq g(0)$.
Thus, $g$ is not necessarily continuous at $x = 0$. Option A is false.

For option B:
The derivative of $g$ at $x = 0$ is given by:
$g'(0) = \lim_{x o 0} \dfrac{g(x) - g(0)}{x - 0} = \lim_{x o 0} \dfrac{x f(x) - 0}{x} = \lim_{x o 0} f(x)$.
If $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$, then $\lim_{x o 0} f(x) = f(0)$.
Since $f(0)$ is a finite real number, $g'(0)$ exists and $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$. Option B is true.

For option C:
Let $f(x) = 0$ for $x eq 0$ and $f(0) = 1$.
Then $g(x) = 0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
Here, $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$ with $g'(0) = 0$.
However, $\lim_{x o 0} f(x) = 0 eq f(0)$, so $f$ is not continuous at $x = 0$. Option C is false.

For option D:
If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$, then $g'(0)$ exists.
Since $g'(0) = \lim_{x o 0} \dfrac{g(x) - g(0)}{x} = \lim_{x o 0} f(x)$, the limit $\lim_{x o 0} f(x)$ must exist. Option D is true.

Answer: If $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$; If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$, then $\lim_{x o 0} f(x)$ exists

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Consider the function $f : \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty)$ defined by

$f(x) = (|x| + |x - 1|) \sin x + [x \sin x]$,

where $[x \sin x]$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x \sin x$.

Let $\alpha$ be the total number of points in the interval $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ at which $f$ is NOT continuous, and let $\beta$ be the total number of points in the interval $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ at which $f$ is NOT differentiable.

Then the value of $\alpha + \beta$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
Let $f(x) = g(x) + h(x)$, where $g(x) = (|x| + |x - 1|) \sin x$ and $h(x) = [x \sin x]$.

First, we analyze $h(x) = [x \sin x]$ on the interval $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
The function $y = x \sin x$ is an even function. For $x \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $x \sin x$ is strictly increasing.
At $x = 0$, $x \sin x = 0$.
As $x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x \sin x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$.
Thus, $x \sin x \in [0, 1.57)$ for $x \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.
The value of $[x \sin x]$ will be $0$ when $0 \le x \sin x < 1$, and $1$ when $1 \le x \sin x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Let $x_1 \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ be the unique point where $x_1 \sin x_1 = 1$. By symmetry, $-x_1$ is the unique point in $\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$ where $(-x_1) \sin(-x_1) = 1$.
Therefore, $h(x)$ has jump discontinuities at exactly two points: $x = x_1$ and $x = -x_1$.
At $x = 0$, $x \sin x = 0$ and is non-negative in its neighborhood, so $[x \sin x] = 0$ around $x = 0$, making $h(x)$ continuous and differentiable at $x = 0$.

Next, we analyze $g(x) = (|x| + |x - 1|) \sin x$.
The absolute value functions have critical points at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.
For $x$ in a small neighborhood of $0$ (specifically $x \in (-1, 1)$):
If $x \in [0, 1)$, $g(x) = (x - (x - 1)) \sin x = \sin x \Rightarrow g'(0^+) = \cos 0 = 1$.
If $x \in (-1, 0)$, $g(x) = (-x - (x - 1)) \sin x = (1 - 2x) \sin x \Rightarrow g'(0^-) = -2 \sin 0 + 1 \cdot \cos 0 = 1$.
Since $g'(0^+) = g'(0^-)$, $g(x)$ is differentiable at $x = 0$.

For $x$ in a small neighborhood of $1$:
If $x \in (0, 1]$, $g(x) = \sin x \Rightarrow g'(1^-) = \cos 1$.
If $x \in \left(1, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $g(x) = (x + (x - 1)) \sin x = (2x - 1) \sin x \Rightarrow g'(1^+) = 2 \sin 1 + 1 \cdot \cos 1$.
Since $g'(1^-) \neq g'(1^+)$, $g(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = 1$.

Now, combining the results for $f(x) = g(x) + h(x)$:
1. Discontinuities: $g(x)$ is continuous everywhere. $h(x)$ is discontinuous at $x_1$ and $-x_1$. Thus, $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $2$ points. $\Rightarrow \alpha = 2$.
2. Non-differentiability: $f(x)$ is not differentiable where it is discontinuous ($x_1$ and $-x_1$). Additionally, at $x = 1$, $h(x)$ is constant ($0$) because $1 \cdot \sin 1 \approx 0.84 < 1$, meaning $h(x)$ is differentiable at $x = 1$. However, $g(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = 1$. Thus, $f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x = 1$.
This gives $3$ points of non-differentiability: $-x_1, 1, x_1$. $\Rightarrow \beta = 3$.

Finally, $\alpha + \beta = 2 + 3 = 5$.

Answer: $5$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
For a real number $\alpha$, let $[\alpha]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $\alpha$. For a finite set $S$, let $|S|$ denote the number of elements in the set $S$.
Consider the functions $f : (-3, 3) \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty)$ and $g : (-3, 3) \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty)$ defined by
$f(x) = [x^3]\log_e(1 + \sin^2(\pi(x - [x])))$
and
$g(x) = x^3 \sin^2(\pi \log_e(1 + x - [x]))$.
Let
$A = \{x \in (-3, 3) : f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\}$
and
$B = \{x \in (-3, 3) : g \text{ is discontinuous at } x\}$.
Then the value of $|A| + 2|B| - |A \cap B|$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
For the function $f(x) = [x^3]\log_e(1 + \sin^2(\pi(x - [x])))$, we can simplify the argument of the sine function. Since $[x]$ is an integer, $\sin(\pi(x - [x])) = \sin(\pi x - \pi[x]) = \pm \sin(\pi x)$. Thus, $\sin^2(\pi(x - [x])) = \sin^2(\pi x)$.

The function $f(x)$ can be rewritten as $f(x) = [x^3]\log_e(1 + \sin^2(\pi x))$.
The term $\log_e(1 + \sin^2(\pi x))$ is continuous everywhere. The term $[x^3]$ has jump discontinuities where $x^3$ is an integer. For $x \in (-3, 3)$, $x^3 \in (-27, 27)$. The integer values of $x^3$ in this interval are $k \in \{-26, -25, \dots, 26\}$, which gives $53$ points of the form $x = k^{1/3}$.

At these points, $[x^3]$ is discontinuous. For $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x = k^{1/3}$, the continuous factor must be zero:
$\log_e(1 + \sin^2(\pi x)) = 0 \implies \sin^2(\pi x) = 0 \implies x$ is an integer.
The integers in $(-3, 3)$ are $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$. Their cubes are $-8, -1, 0, 1, 8$, which are $5$ values among the $53$ points. At these $5$ points, $f(x)$ is continuous. At the remaining $53 - 5 = 48$ points, $f(x)$ is discontinuous.
Thus, $|A| = 48$.

For the function $g(x) = x^3 \sin^2(\pi \log_e(1 + x - [x]))$, we can write $x - [x] = \{x\}$, which is the fractional part of $x$.
The function $g(x) = x^3 \sin^2(\pi \log_e(1 + \{x\}))$ is continuous everywhere except possibly at the integers, where $\{x\}$ is discontinuous.
The integers in $(-3, 3)$ are $c \in \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$.
Let's check the continuity at $x = c$:
Right-hand limit ($x \to c^+$): $\{x\} \to 0$, so $g(x) \to c^3 \sin^2(\pi \log_e 1) = 0$.
Left-hand limit ($x \to c^-$): $\{x\} \to 1$, so $g(x) \to c^3 \sin^2(\pi \log_e 2)$.

For $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x = c$, we must have $c^3 \sin^2(\pi \log_e 2) = 0$. Since $\log_e 2 \approx 0.693$, $\pi \log_e 2$ is not an integer multiple of $\pi$, meaning $\sin^2(\pi \log_e 2) \neq 0$. Therefore, we must have $c^3 = 0 \implies c = 0$.
So, $g(x)$ is continuous at $x = 0$ and discontinuous at $x \in \{-2, -1, 1, 2\}$.
Thus, $B = \{-2, -1, 1, 2\}$ and $|B| = 4$.

Since $A$ contains no integers and $B$ contains only integers, $A \cap B = \emptyset$, which means $|A \cap B| = 0$.

Finally, we calculate the required value:
$|A| + 2|B| - |A \cap B| = 48 + 2(4) - 0 = 48 + 8 = 56$.

Answer: $56$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let $f: \left(0, 1\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined as $f\left(x\right) = \left[4x\right]{\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, where $[ x ]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Then which of the following is(are) true?
options: The function $f$ is discontinuous exactly at one point in $( 0, 1 )$
There is exactly one point in $( 0, 1 )$ at which the function $f$ is continuous but NOT differentiable
The function $f$ is NOT differentiable at more than three points in $( 0, 1 )$
The minimum value of the function $f$ is $- \dfrac{1}{512}$
questions.solution:
Given,

$f: ( 0, 1 ) \to \mathbb{R}$

$f\left(x\right) = \left[4x\right]{\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

We know that, $\left[4x\right]$ will be discontinuous function at integer points,

So, $\text{critical point} = \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{3}{4}$ as $x \in \left(0, 1\right)$

And function will be discontinuous at $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$ because for $\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ and } \dfrac{1}{4}$, $\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \text{ and } {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}$ will make the function continuos

Hence, the function is discontinuous exactly at one point in $\left(0, 1\right)$, so option $\left(A\right)$ is correct,

Now,

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}0, 0 < x < \dfrac{1}{4} \\ 1 \cdot {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right), \dfrac{1}{4} \le x < \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 2 \cdot {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right), \dfrac{1}{2} \le x < \dfrac{3}{4} \\ 3 \cdot {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right), \dfrac{3}{4} \le x < 1\end{array}\right$

Now differentiating the above function we get,

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}0, 0 < x < \dfrac{1}{4} \\ {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2} + 2\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right), \dfrac{1}{4} \le x < \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 4 \cdot \left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 2{\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2}, \dfrac{1}{2} \le x < \dfrac{3}{4} \\ 3 \cdot {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{2} + 6\left(x - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right), \dfrac{3}{4} \le x < 1\end{array}\right$

Now from above function we get,

${f}^{'}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} -\right) = {f}^{'}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} +\right) = 0$ so function is differentiable at $x = \dfrac{1}{4}$

And ${f}^{'}\left(\dfrac{1}{2} -\right) = \dfrac{1}{16} \text{ and } {f}^{'}\left(\dfrac{1}{2} +\right) = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{1}{8}$ so function is non-differentiable at $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, hence option $\left(B\right)$ is correct,

questions.q: Let the functions $f: \left(- 1, 1\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g: \left(- 1, 1\right) \to \left(- 1, 1\right)$ be defined by $f\left(x\right) = \left|2x - 1\right| + \left|2x + 1\right| \text{$ and $} g\left(x\right) = x - \left[x\right]$, where $\left[x\right]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to$x$. Let $f ∘ g: \left(- 1, 1\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ be the composite function defined by $\left(f ∘ g\right)\left(x\right) = f\left(g\left(x\right)\right)$. Suppose $c$ is the number of points in the interval $\left(- 1, 1\right)$ at which $f ∘ g$ is not continuous, and suppose $d$ is the number of points in the interval $\left(- 1, 1\right)$ at which $f ∘ g$ is not differentiable. Then the value of $c + d$ is _____________
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \left|2x - 1\right| + \left|2x + 1\right| = \left\{\begin{cases}- 4x & , & x \dfrac{1}{2}\end{cases}\right$

$g\left(x\right) = \left\{x\right\}$

$f\left(g\left(x\right)\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}- 4g\left(x\right), & g\left(x\right) \dfrac{1}{2}\end{cases}\right$

Graph of $g\left(x\right)$ is

$f\left(g\left(x\right)\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}2 & , x \in \left(- 1, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) ∪ \left(0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ 4\left(x + 1\right) & x \in \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, 0\right) \\ 4x & x \in \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 1\right)\end{cases}\right$

$c = 1$ at $x = 0$

$d = 3$ at $x = - \dfrac{1}{2}, 0, \dfrac{1}{2}$,

$∴ c + d = 4$.

questions.q: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions satisfying $f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + f\left(x\right)f\left(y\right)\text{and}f\left(x\right) = xg\left(x\right)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R} .$ If $\lim_{x \to 0}g\left(x\right) = 1,$ then which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: If $g\left(0\right) = 1,$ then $g$ is differentiable at every$x \in \mathbb{R}$
questions.solution:
Given $f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + f\left(x\right)f\left(y\right)$
Put $x = y = 0$ in given relation.

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = f\left(0\right) + f\left(0\right) + {f}^{2}\left(0\right)$

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = 0$ or $- 1$

$∵ f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + f\left(x\right) \cdot f\left(y\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{f\left(x + y\right) - f\left(x\right)}{y} = \dfrac{f\left(y\right)\left(1 + f\left(x\right)\right)}{y}$

$⇒ \lim_{y \to 0}\left(\dfrac{f ( x + y ) - f ( x )}{y}\right) = \lim_{y \to 0}\left(1 + f\left(x\right)\right) \cdot \dfrac{f\left(y\right)}{y}$

$∵ \lim_{x \to 0}g\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{x} = 1$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 1 + f\left(x\right)$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(0\right) = 1 + f\left(0\right)$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(0\right) = 1 + 0$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(0\right) = 1$

Again $\dfrac{{f}^{'}\left(x\right)}{1 + f\left(x\right)} = 1 ⇒ ∫ \dfrac{{f}^{'}\left(x\right)dx}{1 + f\left(x\right)}dx = ∫ dx$

$⇒ ln\left(1 + f\left(x\right)\right) = x + C$

$⇒ ln\left[1 + f\left(x\right)\right] = x\left(∵ C = 0\right)$

$⇒ 1 + f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x} - 1 ⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = {e}^{x}$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(1\right) = e$

Also, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable for every $x \in R$.

$g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{x} = \dfrac{{e}^{x} - 1}{x}{y}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{g\left(0 + h\right) - g\left(0\right)}{h}$

If $g\left(0\right) = 1$ then ${g}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\dfrac{{e}^{h} - 1}{h} - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{{e}^{h} - 1 - h}{{h}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

${g}^{'}\left({0}^{-}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{g\left(0 - h\right) - g\left(0\right)}{- h} = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{{e}^{- h} - 1}{\dfrac{- h}{- h}}$

$\lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{{e}^{- h} - 1 + h}{{h}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$g\left(x\right)$ is differentiable for every $x \in R$.

Also, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable for every $x \in R$.

$g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{x} = \dfrac{{e}^{x} - 1}{x}{y}^{'}\left({0}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{g\left(0 + h\right) - g\left(0\right)}{h}$

questions.q: Let the function $f: R \to R$ be defined by $f\left(x\right) = {x}^{3} - {x}^{2} + \left(x - 1\right)sinx$ and let $g: R \to R$ be an arbitrary function. Let $fg: R \to R$ be the product function defined by $\left(fg\right)\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right)g\left(x\right)$. Then which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: If $g$ is continuous at $x = 1$, then $fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$
If $fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, then $g$ is continuous at $x = 1$
If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, then $fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$
If $fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, then $g$ is differentiable at $x = 1$
questions.solution:
Differentiability of $fg$ at $x = 1$

Left-hand derivative :

${\left(fg\right)}^{'}\left({1}^{-}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{fg\left(1 - h\right) - fg\left(1\right)}{- h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left\{{\left(1 - h\right)}^{3} - {\left(1 - h\right)}^{2} - hsin\left(1 - h\right)\right\}g\left(1 - h\right) - 0}{- h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\left\{{\left(1 - h\right)}^{2} + sin\left(1 - h\right)\right\}g\left(1 - h\right) . . . . . . . \left(i\right)$

Right-hand derivative :

${\left(fg\right)}^{'}\left({1}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{fg\left(1 + h\right) - fg\left(1\right)}{h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left\{{\left(1 + h\right)}^{3} - {\left(1 + h\right)}^{2} + hsin\left(1 + h\right)\right\}g\left(1 + h\right) - 0}{h}$

$= \lim_{h \to 0}\left\{{\left(1 + h\right)}^{2} + sin\left(1 + h\right)\right\}g\left(1 + h\right) . . . . . . . \left(ii\right)$

If $g$ is continuous at $x = 1$, then

$\lim_{h \to 0}g\left(1 + h\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}g\left(1 - h\right) = g\left(1\right) . . . . . . . . . \left(iii\right)$

From equations $\left(i\right), \left(ii\right) \text{ and } \left(iii\right)$, we get

$\lim_{h \to 0}{\left(fg\right)}^{'}\left({1}^{+}\right) = \lim_{h \to 0}{\left(fg\right)}^{'}\left({1}^{-}\right) = \left(1 + sin1\right)g\left(1\right)$

$∴ fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$.

So, option $\left(A\right)$ is correct.

Now, from equations $\left(i\right) \text{ and } \left(ii\right)$, we can say that for $fg$ to be differentiable, we need only $g\left(1 + h\right) = g\left(1 - h\right)$.

But for $g$ to be continuous, we need $g\left(1 + h\right) = g\left(1 - h\right) = g\left(1\right)$.

So, option $\left(B\right)$ is incorrect.

Now, if $g$ is differentiable at $x = 1$ and $f$ is already differentiable at $x = 1$ as ${f}^{'}\left({1}^{-}\right) = {f}^{'}\left({1}^{+}\right) = 1 + sin1$, so product of two differentiable functions is also differentiable.

$∴ fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$.

So, option $\left(C\right)$ is correct.

Now, from option $\left(B\right)$, if $fg$ is differentiable at $x = 1$, we cannot guarantee $g$ to be continuous at $x = 1$.

So, we also cannot guarantee $g$ to be differentiable at $x = 1$.

So, option $\left(D\right)$ is incorrect.

(i) ${f}_{1}\left(x\right) = sin\sqrt{1 - {e}^{- {x}^{2}}}$. Clearly ${f}_{1} ( x )$ is continuous at $x = 0$ and $f\left(0\right) = 0$

$⇒$ ${f}_{2}\left(x\right)$ is not continuous at $x = 0$

(iii) In the close neighborhood of $x = 0$ given function ${f}_{3} ( x ) = 0$ hence ${f}^{′} 3 ( x ) = 0$ also ${f}^{′} 3 ( x )$ is continuous at $x = 0$

So $S \to 3$

questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = xcos ⁡ \left(\pix + \left[x\right]\pi\right)$

$[ x ]$ is discontinuous at all integers and $xcos\pix$ is continuous everywhere.

questions.q: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f\left(x\right) = acos ⁡ \left(\left|{x}^{3} - x\right|\right) + b\left|x\right|sin ⁡ \left(\left|{x}^{3} + x\right|\right)$ . Then $f$ is -
questions.solution:
If ${x}^{3} - x \ge 0 ⇒ cos ⁡ \left|{x}^{3} - x\right| = cos ⁡ \left({x}^{3} - x\right)$
${x}^{3} - x < 0 ⇒ cos ⁡ \left|{x}^{3} - x\right| = cos ⁡ \left({x}^{3} - x\right)$
Similarly $b\left|x\right|sin ⁡ \left|{x}^{3} + x\right| = bxsin ⁡ \left({x}^{3} + x\right)$ for all $x \in R$
$∴$ $f\left(x\right) = acos ⁡ \left({x}^{3} - x\right) + bxsin ⁡ \left({x}^{3} + x\right)$
Which is composition and sum of differentiable functions therefore always continuous and differentiable.

questions.q: Let $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function with $g\left(0\right) = 0, {g}^{′}\left(0\right) = 0 and {g}^{′}\left(1\right) \ne 0 .$ Let $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{| x |}g\left(x\right), & x \ne 0 \\ 0, & x = 0\end{cases}\right$ and $h\left(x\right) = {e}^{| x |}$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R} .$ Let $\left(foh\right) ( x )$ denote $f\left(h\left(x\right)\right)and ( hof ) ( x )$denote $h\left(f\left(x\right)\right)$ .Then which of the following is (are) true?
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}g\left(x\right) & x > 0 \\ 0 & x = 0 \\ - g\left(x\right) & x < 0\end{cases}\right$
$LHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}} ⁡ \left(- {g}^{′}\left(x\right)\right) = - \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}} ⁡ {g}^{′}\left(x\right) = - 0 = 0$
$RHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}} ⁡ {g}^{′}\left(x\right) = {g}^{′}\left({0}^{+}\right) = 0$
Hence $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable at $x = 0$
$h\left(x\right) = {e}^{\left|x\right|} = \left\{\begin{cases}{e}^{x} & x \ge 0 \\ {e}^{- x} & x < 0\end{cases}\right$
$LHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}} ⁡ \left(- {e}^{- x}\right) = - 1$
$RHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}} ⁡ \left({e}^{x}\right) = 1$
Hence $h\left(x\right)$ is not differentiable at $x = 0$
$f\left(h\left(x\right)\right) = \left\{\dfrac{{e}^{\left|x\right|}}{\left|{e}^{\left|x\right|}\right|}\rightg\left({e}^{\left|x\right|}\right)$
$f\left(h\left(x\right)\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}g\left({e}^{x}\right) & x \ge 0 \\ g\left({e}^{- x}\right) & x < 0\end{cases}\right$
$LHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}} ⁡ {g}^{′}\left({e}^{- x}\right) \times - {e}^{- x} = {g}^{′}\left(1\right) \times - 1 = - {g}^{′}\left(1\right)$
$RHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}} ⁡ {g}^{′}\left({e}^{x}\right) \times{e}^{x} = {g}^{′}\left(1\right)$
Hence foh is non-differentiable at $x = 0$
$h\left(f\left(x\right)\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}1 & x = 0 \\ {e}^{\left|\dfrac{x}{\left|x\right|}g\left(x\right)\right|} & x \ne 0\end{cases}\right$
$= \left\{\begin{cases}1 & x = 0 \\ {e}^{\left|g\left(x\right)\right|} & x \ne 0\end{cases}\right$
$LHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}} ⁡ {e}^{\left|g\left(x\right)\right|} \times \pm {g}^{′}\left(x\right) = {e}^{\left|g\left({0}^{-}\right)\right|} \times \pm \left({g}^{′}\left({0}^{-}\right)\right) = 0$
$RHD: \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}} ⁡ {e}^{\left|g\left(x\right)\right|} \times \pm {g}^{′}\left(x\right) = {e}^{\left|g\left({0}^{+}\right)\right|} \times \pm {g}^{′}\left({0}^{+}\right) = 0$

questions.q:
For every integer $n$, let $a_{n}$ and $b_{n}$ be real numbers. Let function $f: I R \rightarrow I R$ be given by

$f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lll}

a_{n}+\sin \pi x, & \text{ for } & x \in[2 n, 2 n+1] \\

b_{n}+\cos \pi x, & \text{ for } & x \in(2 n-1,2 n)

\end{array}\right.$

for all integers $n$. If $f$ is continuous, then which of the following hold $(s)$ for all $n$ ?
questions.solution:
Given : $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}a_{n}+\sin \pi x, & x \in[2 n, 2 n+1] \\ b_{n}+\cos \pi x, & x \in(2 n-1,2 n)\end{array}\right.$

$\because f$ is continuous for all $n$

$\therefore$ At $x=2 n, \mathrm{LHL}=\mathrm{RHL}=f(2 n)$

$\Rightarrow b_{n}+\cos 2 \pi n=a_{n}+\sin 2 \pi n=a_{n}+\sin 2 \pi n$

$\Rightarrow b_{n}+1=a_{n} \Rightarrow a_{n}-b_{n}=1, \therefore$ option (b) is correct.

Also at $x=2 n+1, \mathrm{LHL}=\mathrm{RHL}=f(2 n+1)$

$\Rightarrow \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} a_{n}+\sin \pi(2 n+1-h)$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} b_{n+1}+\cos \pi(2 n+1-h)=a_{n}+\sin (2 n+1) \pi$

$\Rightarrow a_{n}=b_{n+1}-1=a_{n} \Rightarrow a_{n}-b_{n+1}=-1$

$\therefore$ option (c) is incorrect.

$\Rightarrow a_{n-1}-b_{n}=-1, \therefore$ option (d) is correct.

questions.q: Let $\int(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{r}x^{2}\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{x}\right|, \quad x \neq 0 \\ 0, \quad x=0\end{array}, x \in R\right.$ then $\int$ is
options: differentiable at $x=0$ but not differentiable at $x=2$
not differentiable at $x=0$ but differentiable at $x=2$
questions.solution:
$f^{\prime}\left(0^{+}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0+h)-f(0)}{h}$

$\begin{aligned}

=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h^{2}\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{h}\right|}{h} &=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} h\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{h}\right| \\

&=0 \times \text{ some finite value }=0

\end{aligned}$

$\begin{array}{c}

=0 \times \text{ some finite value }=0 \\

\text{ and } f^{\prime}\left(0^{-}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(0-h)-f(0)}{-h}=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{h^{2}\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{-h}\right|}{-h} \\

=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}-h\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{h}\right|=0 \times \text{ some finite value }=0

\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l}

\because f^{\prime}\left(0^{+}\right)=f^{\prime}\left(0^{-}\right) \therefore f \text{ is differentiable at } x=0 \\

\text{ Now } f^{\prime}\left(2^{+}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(2+h)-f(2)}{h} \\

\quad=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2+h)^{2}\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{2+h}\right|-4\left|\cos \frac{\pi}{2}\right|}{h}

\end{array}$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2+h)^{2}\left(\cos \frac{\pi}{2+h}\right)}{h}$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2+h)^{2}}{h} \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{2+h}\right)$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2+h)^{2}}{h} \sin \left(\frac{\pi h}{2(2+h)}\right)$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2+h)^{2}}{h} \times \frac{\sin \left(\frac{\pi h}{2(2+h)}\right)}{\left(\frac{\pi h}{2(2+h)}\right)} \times \frac{\pi h}{2(2+h)}=\pi$

and $f^{\prime}\left(2^{-}\right)=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(2-h)-f(2)}{-h}$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2-h)^{2}\left|\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2-h}\right)\right|-0}{-h}$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{-(2-h)^{2} \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2-h}\right)}{-h}$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2-h)^{2} \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{2-h}\right)}{h}$

$=\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(2-h)^{2}}{h} \times \frac{\sin \left(\frac{-\pi h}{2(2-h)}\right)}{\left(\frac{-\pi h}{2(2-h)}\right)} \times\left(\frac{-\pi h}{2(2-h)}\right)=-\pi$

$\because f^{\prime}\left(2^{+}\right) \neq f^{\prime}\left(2^{-}\right), \therefore f$ is not differentiable at $x=2 .$

questions.q: If $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}-x-\frac{\pi}{2}, & x \leq-\frac{\pi}{2} \\ -\cos x, & -\frac{\pi}{2} < x \leq 0 \\ x-1, & 0 < x \leq 1 \\ \log x, & x>1\end{array}\right.$, then
options:
$f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$

$f(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=0$

$f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=1$

$f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=-\frac{3}{2}$
questions.solution:
$f(x)=\left\{$\begin{array}{cc}-x-$\frac{\pi}{2}$, & x \leq-$\frac{\pi}{2}$ \\ -$\cos x$, & -$\frac{\pi}{2}$ \lt  x \leq 0 \\ x-1, & 0 \lt  x \leq 1 \\ $\log x$, & x \gt 1\end{array}$\right.$
Continuity at $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$,

$\begin{aligned}$& f$\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=-\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-\frac{\pi}{2}=$0 \\
& $\mathrm{RHL} \Rightarrow \lim _{h \rightarrow 0}-\cos \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}+$h\right)=0
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ Continuous at $x=0$
Continuity at $x=0 \Rightarrow f(0)=-1\mathrm{RHL} \Rightarrow \lim _{h \rightarrow 0}(0+h)-1=-1\therefore$ Continuous at $x=0$
Continuity at $x=1 ; f(1)=0\mathrm{RHL} \Rightarrow \lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \log (1+h)=0\therefore$ Continuous at $x=1$
Here, $f^{\prime}(x)=\left\{$\begin{array}{cc}-1, & x \leq-$\frac{\pi}{2}$ \\ $\sin x$, & -$\frac{\pi}{2}$ \lt  x \leq 0 \\ 1, & 0 \lt  x \leq 1 \\ $\frac{1}{x}$, & x \gt 1\end{array}$\right.$
Differentiable at $x=0$, $\mathrm{LHD}=0, \mathrm{RHD}=1\therefore \quad$ Not differentiable at $x=0$

Differentiable at $x=1$, $\mathrm{LHD}=1, \mathrm{RHD}=1\therefore$ Differentiable at $x=1$
Also, for $x=-\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow f(x)=-x-\frac{3}{2}\therefore$ Differentiable at $x=-\frac{3}{2}$

questions.q: Let $f$ be a real-valued function defined on the interval $(0, \infty)$, by $f(x)=\ln x+\int_0^x \sqrt{1+\sin t} d t$. Then which of the following statement(s) is (are) true ?
options: $f^{\prime}(x)$ exists for all $x \in(0, \infty)$ and $f^{\prime}$ is continuous on $(0, \infty)$, but not differentiable on $(0, \infty)$
there exists $\alpha>1$ such that $\left|f^{\prime}(x)\right| < |f(x)|$ for all $x \in(\alpha, \infty)$
there exists $\beta>0$ such that $|f(x)|+\left|f^{\prime}(x)\right| \leq \beta \quad$ from all $x \in(0, \infty)$
questions.solution:
Here, $f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{x}+\sqrt{1+\sin x}, x>0$ but $f(x)$ is not differentiable in $(0, \infty)$ as $\sin x$ may be $-1$ and then $f^{\prime \prime}(x)=-\frac{1}{x^2}+\frac{\cos x}{2 \sqrt{1+\sin x}}$ will not exists.
$\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)$ is continuous for all $x \in(0, \infty)$ but $f^{\prime}(x)$ is not differentiable on $(0, \infty)$.
$\therefore$ Option (b) is true.
Also, $\quad f^{\prime}(x) \leq 3$, if $x>1$ and $\quad f(x)>3$, if $x>e^3$
$\therefore$ Let $\alpha=e^3$
$\Rightarrow$ Option (c) is true.
(d) is not possible as $f(x) \rightarrow \infty$ when $x \rightarrow \infty$.
Hence, (b, c) is the correct option.

questions.q:
Let $f$ and $g$ be real valued functions defined on interval $(-1,1)$ such that $g^{\prime \prime}(x)$ is continuous, $g(0) \neq 0, g^{\prime}(0)=0, g^{\prime \prime}(0) \neq 0$ and $f(x)=g(x) \sin x$.
Statement $1 \lim _{x \rightarrow 0}[g(x) \cos x-g(0) \operatorname{cosec} x]=f^{\prime \prime}(0)$.
Statement $2 f^{\prime}(0)=g(0)$.
options:
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.

Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.

Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.

Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true
questions.solution:
We have,

$\begin{aligned}$& $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{g(x) \cos x-g(0)}{\sin x}$\\
& =$\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{g^{\prime}(x) \cos x-g(x) \sin x}{\cos x}=$0
\end{aligned}

Since, $f(x)=g(x) \sin x \begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x) \sin x+g(x) \cos x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime \prime}(x)=g^{\prime \prime}(x) \sin x+2 g^{\prime}(x) \cos x-g(x) \sin x \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime \prime}(0)=0
\end{aligned}

Thus, $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}[g(x) \cos x-g(0) \operatorname{cosec} x]=0=f^{\prime \prime}(0)\Rightarrow$ Statement 1 is true.
Statement 2. $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x) \sin x+g(x) \cos x$
\Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(0)=g(0)

Statement 2 is not a correct explanation of Statement 1.

questions.q: In the following $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Match the functions in Column I with the properties Column II.
options:
A-p, r; B-p, q, s; C-p; D-q, r

A-p, s; B-p, r, s; C-p, s; D-q, r

A-p, q, r; B-p, s; C-r, s; D-p, q

A-r, s; B-q; C-p; D-p, q, s
questions.solution:
(A) $x|x|$ is continuous, differentiable and strictly increasing in $(-1,1)$.

The function is continuous and differentiable in $(-1,1)$.

questions.q:
The value of the definite integral
$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{1}{3^{\frac{x+3}{2}}}\, dx$
is
questions.solution:
Let $I = \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{1}{3^x + 3} dx$

Substitute $t = 3^x$, which gives $dt = 3^x \ln 3 dx \Rightarrow dx = \dfrac{dt}{t \ln 3}$.

When $x = 0$, $t = 1$.

When $x = 2$, $t = 9$.

The integral becomes:

$I = \int_{1}^{9} \dfrac{1}{t + 3} \dfrac{dt}{t \ln 3} = \dfrac{1}{\ln 3} \int_{1}^{9} \dfrac{1}{t(t + 3)} dt$

Using partial fractions:

$\dfrac{1}{t(t + 3)} = \dfrac{1}{3} \left( \dfrac{1}{t} - \dfrac{1}{t + 3} \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} \int_{1}^{9} \left( \dfrac{1}{t} - \dfrac{1}{t + 3} \right) dt$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} [\ln t - \ln(t + 3)]_{1}^{9}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} \left[ \ln\left(\dfrac{t}{t + 3}\right) \right]_{1}^{9}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{9}{12}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} \left( \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) \right)$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} \ln\left(\dfrac{3/4}{1/4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3 \ln 3} \ln 3$

$I = \dfrac{1}{3}$

questions.q:
If $\alpha=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2 \frac{\tan ^{-1} x}{2 x^2-3 x+2} d x$ 
then the value of $\sqrt{7} \tan \left(\frac{2 \alpha \sqrt{7}}{\pi}\right)$ is ____________.
(Here, the $inverse trigonometric function\tan ^{-1} x$ assumes values in $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.)
questions.solution:
$\alpha=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2 \frac{\tan ^{-1} x}{2 x^2-3 x+2} d x$ ....(i)
$\begin{aligned} & \text{ Let } x=\frac{1}{t} \\ & \qquad d x=-\frac{1}{t^2} d t \\ & \alpha=\int_2^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)}{\frac{2}{t^2}-\frac{3}{t}+2}\left(\frac{-1}{t^2}\right) d t\end{aligned} \alpha=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2 \frac{\cot ^{-1} \mathrm{t}}{2 \mathrm{t}^2-3 \mathrm{t}+2} \mathrm{dt}$ ....(ii)
Now by (i) + (ii)
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 \alpha=\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2 \frac{\frac{\pi}{2}}{2 x^2-3 x+2} d x \\
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{8} \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2 \frac{d x}{x^2-\frac{3 x}{2}+1} \\
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{8} \int_{\frac{1}{2}}^2\left(x-\frac{3}{4}\right)^2+\frac{7}{16} \\
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{8 \times \frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}}\left[\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x-\frac{3}{4}}{\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}}\right)\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^2
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{7}}\left[\tan ^{-1} \frac{4 x-3}{\sqrt{7}}\right]_{\frac{1}{2}}^2 \\
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{7}}\left[\tan ^{-1} \frac{5}{\sqrt{7}}-\tan ^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\right)\right] \\
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{7}} \tan ^{-1} \frac{\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt{7}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}\right)}{1-\frac{5}{7}} \\
& \alpha=\frac{\pi}{2 \sqrt{7}} \tan ^{-1}(3 \sqrt{7})
\end{aligned}$
Now $\sqrt{7} \tan \left(\frac{2 \sqrt{7} \alpha}{\pi}\right) \begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{7} \times \tan \left(\tan ^{-1}(3 \sqrt{7})\right) \\
& \sqrt{7} \times 3 \sqrt{7} \\
& =21
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{x\tan^{- 1}x}\dfrac{{e}^{\left(t - cost\right)}}{1 + {t}^{2023}}dt$

Now differentiating both side we get,

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{e}^{\left[x\tan^{- 1}x - cos\left(x\tan^{- 1}x\right)\right]}}{1 + {\left(x\tan^{- 1}x\right)}^{2023}} \times \left(\dfrac{x}{1 + {x}^{2}} + \tan^{- 1}x\right)$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = g\left(x\right) \cdot h\left(x\right)$

$\text{where}g\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{e}^{\left[x\tan^{- 1} ⁡ x - cos ⁡ \left(x\tan^{- 1} ⁡ x\right)\right]}}{1 + {\left(x\tan^{- 1} ⁡ x\right)}^{2023}} > 0∀x$

And $h\left(x\right) = \dfrac{x}{1 + {x}^{2}} + \tan^{- 1}x\text{which is}\left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0x > 0\end{array}\right$

$∴ f\left(x\right)$ has minimum at $x = 0$

And $f{\left(x\right)}_{min} = f\left(0\right) = 0$

questions.solution:

$= \left(\dfrac{16 + 5n - 3{n}^{2}}{4n + 3{n}^{2}} + 1\right) + \left(\dfrac{32 + n - 3{n}^{2}}{8n + 3{n}^{2}} + 1\right) + \ldots \ldots + \left(\dfrac{25n - 7{n}^{2}}{7{n}^{2}} + 1\right)$

i.e. $f\left(n\right) = \mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}\dfrac{9n + 16r}{4rn + 3{n}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{n}\mathop{∑}_{r = 1}^{n}\dfrac{9 + 16\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right)}{4\left(\dfrac{r}{n}\right) + 3}$

Consider the equation

${∫}_{1}^{e}\dfrac{{\left({\log}_{e}x\right)}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}}{x{\left(a - {\left({\log}_{e}x\right)}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)}^{2}}dx = 1, a \in \left(- \infty , 0\right) ∪ \left(1, \infty\right)$.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: No a satisfies the above equation
An integer a satisfies the above equation
An irrational number a satisfies the above equation
More than one a satisfy the above equation
questions.solution:
Let $I = {∫}_{1}^{e}\dfrac{{\left(lnx\right)}^{\dfrac{1}{2}}dx}{x{\left(a - {\left(lnx\right)}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}\right)}^{2}}$

Now put $a - \left(lnx\right)\dfrac{3}{2} = t$

$⇒ - \dfrac{3}{2}\left(lnx\right)\dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}dx = dt$

So, the integral becomes $I = {∫}_{a}^{a - 1}\dfrac{\left(- \dfrac{2}{3}\right)dt}{{t}^{2}}$

$⇒ I = \left(- \dfrac{2}{3}\right){\dfrac{{t}^{- 2 + 1}}{- 2 + 1}}_{a}^{a - 1}$

$⇒ I = {\dfrac{2}{3t}}_{a}^{a - 1}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{a - 1} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right)$

Now given $I = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\dfrac{1}{a\left(a - 1\right)} = 1$

$⇒ 2 = 3{a}^{2} - 3a$

$⇒ 3{a}^{2} - 3a - 2 = 0$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 4\left(3\right)\left(- 2\right)}}{6}$

So, $a = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{33}}{6}, \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{33}}{6}$

Let $f: \left[- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function such that $f\left(0\right) = 1$ and ${∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}f\left(t\right)dt = 0$

Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The equation $f\left(x\right) - 3cos3x = 0$ has at least one solution in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$
The equation $f\left(x\right) - 3sin3x = - \dfrac{6}{\pi}$ has at least one solution in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$
questions.solution:
(A) Let $g\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right) - 3cos3x$

Now

${∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}g\left(x\right)dx = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}f\left(x\right)dx - 3{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}cos3xdx$

$= 0 - {\left[sin3x\right]}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} = 0$

Hence $g\left(x\right) = 0$ has a root in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

(B) Let $h\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right) - 3sin3x + \dfrac{6}{\pi}$

Now

${∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}h\left(x\right)dx = {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}f\left(x\right)dx - 3{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}sin3xdx + {∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}\dfrac{6}{\pi}dx$

$= 0 - {\left[- cos3x\right]}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}} + {\left[\dfrac{6x}{\pi}\right]}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{3}}$

$= 0 - 2 + 2 = 0$

Hence $h\left(x\right) = 0$has a root in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$

(C) $\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{x{∫}_{0}^{x}f ( t ) dt}{1 - {e}^{{x}^{2}}}$

$= \lim_{x \to 0}\left(\mathop{\mathop{\left(\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{1 - {e}^{{x}^{2}}}\right) \times}_{⏟}}_{- 1}\mathop{\mathop{\left(\dfrac{{∫}_{0}^{x}f( t )dt}{x}\right)}_{⏟}}_{Apply{L}^{'}hospitalrule}\right)$

$= - 1\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{1} = - 1$

(D) $\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{( sinx ) {∫}_{0}^{x}f\left(t\right)dt}{{x}^{2}}$

$= \lim_{x \to 0}\left(\mathop{\mathop{\left(\dfrac{sinx}{x}\right)}_{⏟}}_{1} \times \mathop{\mathop{\left(\dfrac{{∫}_{0}^{x}f( t )dt}{x}\right)}_{⏟}}_{Apply{L}^{'}hospitalrule}\right)$

$= 1\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{1} = 1$

Let $g_{i}:\left[\frac{\pi}{8}, \frac{3 \pi}{8}\right] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, i=1,2$, and $f:\left[\frac{\pi}{8}, \frac{3 \pi}{8}\right] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be functions such that $g_{1}(x)=1, g_{2}(x)=|4 x-\pi|$ and $f(x)=\sin ^{2} x$, for all $x \in\left[\frac{\pi}{8}, \frac{3 \pi}{8}\right]$

Define

$$

S_{i}=\int_{\frac{\pi}{8}}^{\frac{3 \pi}{8}} f(x) \cdot g_{i}(x) d x, \quad i=1,2

$$

The value of $\dfrac{16{S}_{1}}{\pi}$ is ___.
questions.solution:
${S}_{1} = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{8}}^{\dfrac{3\pi}{8}}\sin^{2}x \cdot 1dx \ldots \ldots . . . \left(i\right)$

${S}_{1} = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{8}}^{\dfrac{3\pi}{8}}\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{8} + \dfrac{\pi}{8} - x\right)dx$

${S}_{1} = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{8}}^{\dfrac{3\pi}{8}}\cos^{2}xdx \ldots \ldots . . \left(ii\right)$

From (i) and (ii), we get

$2{S}_{1} = {∫}_{\dfrac{\pi}{8}}^{\dfrac{3\pi}{8}}1dx$

$2{S}_{1} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$\dfrac{16{S}_{1}}{\pi} = 2$

questions.q:
Let $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that its derivative ${f}^{'}$ is continuous and $f\left(\pi\right) = - 6$. If $F: \left[0, \pi\right] \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by $F\left(x\right) = {∫}_{0}^{x}f\left(t\right)dt,$ and if

${∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left({f}^{'}\left(x\right) + F\left(x\right)\right)cosxdx = 2$, then the value of $f\left(0\right)$ is_______
questions.solution:
$I = {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left({f}^{'}\left(x\right) \cdot cosx + F\left(x\right) \cdot cosx\right)dx = 2$

$= {∫}_{0}^{\pi}{f}^{'}\left(x\right) \cdot cosx \cdot dx + {∫}_{0}^{\pi}F\left(x\right)cosx \cdot dx = 2$

$= {\left(cosx \cdot f ( x )\right)}_{0}^{\pi} - {∫}_{0}^{\pi}\left(- sinx\right) \cdot f\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_{0}^{\pi}F\left(x\right) \cdot cosx \cdot dx = 2$

$⇒ \left(cos\pi . f\left(\pi\right) - cos0 . f\left(0\right)\right) + {∫}_{0}^{\pi}sinx \cdot f\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_{0}^{\pi}F\left(x\right) \cdot cosxdx = 2$

$⇒ \left(\left(- 1\right) \cdot \left(- 6\right) - f\left(0\right)\right) + {\left(sinx . F ( x )\right)}_{0}^{\pi} - {∫}_{0}^{\pi}cosx \cdot F\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_{0}^{\pi}F\left(x\right) \cdot cosx \cdot dx = 2$

$⇒ 6 - f\left(0\right) + \left(sin\pi \cdot F\left(\pi\right) - sin0 . F\left(0\right)\right) = 2$

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = 4$.

questions.q: Which of the following inequalities is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
We know that $cosx = 1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2 !} + \dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4 !} - \dfrac{{x}^{6}}{6 !} + \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots$

$⇒ cosx \ge 1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}$

$∴ {∫}_{0}^{1}xcosxdx \ge {∫}_{0}^{1}x\left(1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)dx = {\left(\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{{x}^{4}}{8}\right)}_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{3}{8}$

So, option $\left(A\right)$ is correct.

Now, we also know that $sinx = x - \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3 !} + \dfrac{{x}^{5}}{5 !} - \dfrac{{x}^{7}}{7 !} + \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots$

$⇒ sinx \ge x - \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3 !}, x \in \left[0, 1\right]

$∴ {∫}_{0}^{1}xsinxdx \ge {∫}_{0}^{1}x $\left(x - \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{6}\right)$dx = {$\left(\dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{{x}^{5}}{6 \times 5}\right)$}_{0}^{1} = $\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{9}{30} = \dfrac{3}{10}

So, option \left(B\right) is correct.

Now, ${∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}cosxdx \ge {∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}$\left(1 - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right)$dx = {$\left(\dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{{x}^{5}}{2 \times 5}\right)$}_{0}^{1} = $\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{7}{30}

Also, ${x}^{2}cosx \le {x}^{2}$

$⇒ {∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}cosxdx \le {∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}dx$

$⇒ {∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}cosxdx \le {$\left(\dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3}\right)$}_{0}^{1} = $\dfrac{1}{3}

So, \dfrac{7}{30}$ \le {∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}cosxdx \le $\dfrac{1}{3}$

So, option $\left(C\right)$ is incorrect.

Now, ${∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}sinxdx \ge {∫}_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\left(x - \dfrac{{x}^{3}}{3 !}\right)dx = {\left(\dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{{x}^{6}}{6 \times 6}\right)}_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{36} = \dfrac{8}{36} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

So, option $\left(D\right)$ is correct.

questions.q: The value of the integral $\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\pi / 2}\dfrac{3\sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta}}{{\left(\sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta} + \sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{5}}d\theta$ equals
questions.solution:
$I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{3\sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta}}{{\left(\sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta} + \sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{5}} . d\theta$ …(i)
$I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{3\sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta}}{{\left(\sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta} + \sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{5}} . d\theta$ …(ii) $using\mathop{∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(x\right) . dx = \mathop{∫}_{a}^{b}f\left(a + b - x\right) . dx$
(i) $+$ (ii)
$⇒ 2I = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{3\left(\sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta} + \sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta}\right)}{{\left(\sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta} + \sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{5}} . d\theta$
$⇒ 2I = 3\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{d\theta}{{\left(\sqrt{sin ⁡ \theta} + \sqrt{cos ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{4}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{2I}{3} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{{sec}^{2} ⁡ \theta .d\theta}{{\left(1 + \sqrt{tan ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{4}}$
Put $tan ⁡ \theta = {t}^{2}$
${sec}^{2} ⁡ \theta . d\theta = 2t . dt$
when
$\begin{cases}\theta \to 0, & t \to 0\end{cases}$
$\begin{cases}\theta \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}, & t \to \infty\end{cases}$
$⇒ \dfrac{2I}{3} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{2tdt}{{\left(1 + t\right)}^{4}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{I}{3} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\left(t + 1\right) - 1}{{\left(1 + t\right)}^{4}} . dt$
$\dfrac{I}{3} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{{\left(1 + t\right)}^{3}} - \dfrac{1}{{\left(1 + t\right)}^{4}} . dt$
$\dfrac{I}{3} = {\left[- \dfrac{1}{2{\left(1 + t\right)}^{2}} + \dfrac{1}{3{\left(1 + t\right)}^{3}}\right]}_{0}^{\infty}$
$\dfrac{I}{3} = \left[0 + 0 - \left(- \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right]$
$\dfrac{I}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6} ⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{2I}{3} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\dfrac{{sec}^{2} ⁡ \theta .d\theta}{{\left(1 + \sqrt{tan ⁡ \theta}\right)}^{4}}$
Put $tan ⁡ \theta = {t}^{2}$
${sec}^{2} ⁡ \theta . d\theta = 2t . dt$
when
$\begin{cases}\theta \to 0, & t \to 0\end{cases}$
$\begin{cases}\theta \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}, & t \to \infty\end{cases}$
$⇒ \dfrac{2I}{3} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{\infty}\dfrac{2tdt}{{\left(1 + t\right)}^{4}}$

$\dfrac{I}{3} = \left[0 + 0 - \left(- \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3}\right)\right]$
$\dfrac{I}{3} = \dfrac{1}{6} ⇒ I = \dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.q: If $I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{\pi}{4}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{dx}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(2 - cos2x\right)}$ then find $27{I}^{2}$ equals____
questions.solution:
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{- \dfrac{\pi}{4}}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{1}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(2 - cos2x\right)} ⋅ dx$
Using $\mathop{∫}_{- a}^{a}f\left(x\right) ⋅ dx = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{a}\left(f\left(x\right) + f\left(- x\right)\right) ⋅ dx$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(2 - cos2x\right)} + \dfrac{1}{\left(1 + {e}^{- sinx}\right)\left(2 - cos2x\right)}\right) ⋅ dx$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\left(1 + {e}^{sinx}\right)\left(2 - cos2x\right)} + \dfrac{{e}^{sinx}}{\left({e}^{sinx} + 1\right)\left(2 - cos2x\right)}\right) ⋅ dx$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{dx}{2 - cos2x}$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{dx}{2 - \dfrac{1 - \tan^{2}x}{1 + \tan^{2}x}} = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{\left(1 + \tan^{2}x\right)dx}{1 + 3\tan^{2}x}$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\dfrac{{sec}^{2}xdx}{1 + 3ta{n}^{2}x}$
Put $tanx = t$
${sec}^{2} ⁡ xdx = dt$
and when $x = 0 ⇒ t = 0$
$x = \dfrac{\pi}{4} ⇒ t = 1$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{1 + 3{t}^{2}}$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{1 + {\left(\sqrt{3}t\right)}^{2}}$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{\left[ta{n}^{- 1}\sqrt{3}t\right]}_{0}^{1}\left(∵ \mathop{∫}_{0}^{1}\dfrac{dx}{{a}^{2} + {x}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{a}\tan^{- 1}\dfrac{x}{a} + C\right)$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}\pi}\left[ta{n}^{- 1}\left(\sqrt{3}\right) - ta{n}^{- 1}\left(0\right)\right]$
$I = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}\pi} \times \dfrac{\pi}{3}$
$I = \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{3}}$
$27{I}^{2} = 27 \times \dfrac{4}{27} = 4$
