questions.q: Let $M$ and $N$ be two $3 \times 3$ non-singular skew-symmetric matrices such that $M N=N M$. If $P^T$ denotes the transpose of $P$, then $M^2 N^2\left(M^T N\right)^{-1}\left(M N^{-1}\right)^T$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $M^T=-M, N^T=-N$
and $\quad M N=N M$
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore$& M² N²$\left($M^T N\right)^{-1}$\left($M N^{-1}\right)^T \\
& =M² N² N^{-1}$\left($M^T\right)^{-1}$\left($N^{-1}\right)^T $\cdot$M^T \\
& =M² N$\left($N N^{-1}\right)(-M)^{-1}$\left($N^T\right)^{-1}(-M) \\
& =M² N$\left(-$M^{-1}\right)(-N)^{-1}(-M) \\
& =-M² N M^{-1} N^{-1} M \\
& =-M $\cdot($M N) M^{-1} N^{-1} M \\
& =-M(N M) M^{-1} N^{-1} M \\
& =-M N$\left($N M^{-1}\right) N^{-1} M \\
& =-M$\left($N N^{-1}\right) M=-M²
\end{aligned}

Note Here, non-singular word should not be used, since there is no non-singular $3 \times 3$ skew-symmetric matrix.

\Rightarrow & \quad \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{7}\right)^n \Rightarrow \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{6}{7}\right)^n \\

& =\frac{1}{1-\frac{6}{7}}=\frac{1}{1 / 7}=7
\end{array} $

Since, $A\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{array}\right]$ is linear equation in three variables and that could have only unique, no solution or infinitely many solution.

Hence, number of matrices $A$ is zero.

questions.q: Let $a and b$ be non-zero and real numbers. Then, the equation $\left(a x^2+b y^2+c\right)\left(x^2-5 x y+6 y^2\right)=0$ represents
options:
Four straight lines, when $c=0$ and $a, b$ are of the same sign

Two straight lines and a circle, when $a=b$ and $c$ is of sign opposite to that of $a$

Two straight lines and a hyperbola, when $a$ and $b$ are of the same sign and $c$ is of sign opposite to that of $a$

A circle and an ellipse, when $a$ and $b$ are of the same sign and $c$ is of sign opposite to that of $a$
questions.solution:
Let $a$ and $b$ be non- zero real numbers.
Therefore, the given equation $\left(a x^2+b y^2+c\right)\left(x^2-5 x y+6 y^2\right)=0$ implies either

$\begin{array}{rc}$& x²-5 x y+6 y²=0 \\
\Rightarrow & (x-2 y)(x-3 y)=0 \\
\Rightarrow & x=2 y $\text{ and }$x=3 y
\end{array}

represent two straight lines passing through origin.
Or $\quad a x^2+b y^2+c=0$
When $c=0$ and $a$ and $b$ are of same signs, then

$\begin{aligned}$& a x²+b y²+c=0 \\
\Rightarrow & x=0 $\text{ and }$y=0
\end{aligned}

which is a point specified as the origin.
When $a=b$ and $c$ is of sign opposite to that of $a, a x^2+b y^2+c=0$ represents a circle.
Hence, the given equation $\left(a x^2+b y^2+c\right)\left(x^2-5 x y+6 y^2\right)=0$
may represent two straight lines and a circle.

questions.q: Let $T$ be the tangent to the parabola $y^2 = 16x$ at the point $(64, 32)$. Let $L$ be the tangent to the same parabola at another point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the parabola. If $L$ and $T$ are perpendicular to each other, then the distance between the point $(x_1, y_1)$ and the focus of the parabola, is
questions.solution:
The equation of the parabola is $y^2 = 16x$. Comparing with $y^2 = 4ax$, we get $a = 4$.

Let the parametric coordinates of the point $(64, 32)$ be $(at_1^2, 2at_1)$.

$2at_1 = 32 \Rightarrow 8t_1 = 32 \Rightarrow t_1 = 4$

The slope of the tangent $T$ at $t_1$ is $m_1 = \dfrac{1}{t_1} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

Let the tangent $L$ be at the point $(x_1, y_1)$ with parameter $t_2$. Its slope is $m_2 = \dfrac{1}{t_2}$.

Since $T$ and $L$ are perpendicular, $m_1 m_2 = -1$.

$\dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{t_2} = -1 \Rightarrow t_2 = -\dfrac{1}{4}$

The $x$-coordinate of the point $(x_1, y_1)$ is $x_1 = at_2^2 = 4\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

The distance of a point $(x_1, y_1)$ on the parabola from the focus is given by its focal distance $x_1 + a$.

Distance $= \dfrac{1}{4} + 4 = \dfrac{17}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{17}{4}$

Let $R$ denote the region lying in the first quadrant, enclosed by the parabola $y^2=x$, the curve $S$, and the lines $x=1$ and $x=4$.
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & T=S_1 \\ & k y-\left(\frac{x+h}{2}\right)=k^2-h \\ & x-2 k y+2 k^2-h=0 \\ & k^2-h <0 \quad \Rightarrow h-k^2>0 \\ & \text{$ For $Area : interchange } x \& y \\ & y-2 k x+2 k^2-h=0 \& y=x^2 \\ & x^2-2 k x+\left(2 k^2-h\right)=0 <_\beta^\alpha \\ & |\alpha-\beta|=\sqrt{4 k^2-4\left(2 k^2-h\right)}=\sqrt{4 h-4 k^2} \\ & A=\int_\alpha^\beta\left(\left(2 k x+h-2 k^2\right)-x^2\right) d x \\ & A=\frac{\left(4 h-4 k^2\right)^{3 / 2}}{6}=\frac{4}{3} \\ & \left(4 h-4 k^2\right)^{3 / 2}=8 \quad \Rightarrow\left(4 h-4 k^2\right)=4\end{aligned} \mathrm{h}-\mathrm{k}^2=1 (4, \sqrt{3}) \in \mathrm{S}  \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{A}=\int_1^4(\sqrt{\mathrm{x}}-\sqrt{\mathrm{x}-1}) \mathrm{dx}=\frac{2}{3}\left(\mathrm{x}^{3 / 2}-(\mathrm{x}-1)^{3 / 2}\right)_1^4 \\ & \mathrm{ A}=\frac{2}{3}(8-3 \sqrt{3}-1)=\frac{2}{3}(7-3 \sqrt{3})=\frac{14}{3}-2 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A normal with slope $\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$ is drawn from the point $(0,-\alpha)$ to the parabola $x^2=-4 a y$, where $a>0$. Let $L$ be the line passing through $(0,-\alpha)$ and parallel to the directrix of the parabola. Suppose that $L$ intersects the parabola at two points $A$ and $B$. Let $r$ denote the length of the latus rectum and $s$ denote the square of the length of the line segment $A B$. If $r: s=1: 16$, then the value of 24ais ________.
questions.solution: $\frac{d y}{d x}=\left.\frac{x}{-2 a} \Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}\right|_N=-t$ Slope of normal $=\frac{1}{t}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \Rightarrow t=\sqrt{6}$ Now, $\frac{-\mathrm{at}^2+\alpha}{2 \mathrm{at}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{t}}\Rightarrow-\mathrm{at}^2+\alpha=2 \mathrm{a} \Rightarrow-6 \mathrm{a}+\alpha=2 \mathrm{a} \Rightarrow \alpha=8 \mathrm{a}$ For A and B $\begin{aligned} & x^2=-4 a(-8 a) \\ & \Rightarrow x^2=32 a^2 \Rightarrow x= \pm 4 \sqrt{2} a \\ & \therefore A(-4 \sqrt{2} a,-8 a), B(4 \sqrt{2} a,-8 a) \\ & \therefore A B^2=(8 \sqrt{2} a)^2=128 a^2=s\end{aligned} \therefore$ Length of LR $=\mathrm{r}=4 \mathrm{a} \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{4 \mathrm{a}}{128 \mathrm{a}^2}=\frac{1}{16} \\ & \therefore 32 \mathrm{a}=16 \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=\frac{1}{2} \\ & \therefore 24 \mathrm{a}=12 \text{ Ans. }\end{aligned}$

Parabola ${y}^{2} = 4ax$,

Now plotting the normal to parabola at point $P\left(a{m}^{2}, - 2am\right), we get

So, equation of normal at $P$\left(a{m}^{2}, - 2am\right)$ is $y = mx - 2am - a{m}^{3}$

questions.q: Consider the parabola ${y}^{2} = 4x$. Let $S$ be the focus of the parabola. A pair of tangents drawn to the parabola from the point $P = \left(- 2, 1\right)$ meet the parabola at ${P}_{1}$ and ${P}_{2}$. Let ${Q}_{1}$ and ${Q}_{2}$ be points on the lines $S{P}_{1}$ and $S{P}_{2}$ respectively such that $P{Q}_{1}$ is perpendicular to $S{P}_{1}$ and $P{Q}_{2}$ is perpendicular to $S{P}_{2}$. Then, which of the following is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
On plotting the diagram of the given value we have,

Now let ${P}_{1}\left({t}^{2}, 2t\right)$ then tangent at ${P}_{1}$ will be $ty = x + {t}^{2}$

Since it passes through $\left(- 2, 1\right)$

$⇒ {t}^{2} - t - 2 = 0$

$⇒ t = 2, - 1$

So, we get points ${P}_{1}\left(4, 4\right)$ and ${P}_{2}\left(1, - 2\right)$

Now finding the equation of $S{P}_{1}: 4x - 3y - 4 = 0$

And equation of $S{P}_{2}: x - 1 = 0$

Now finding the point by foot of point on line formula,

${Q}_{1}: \dfrac{{x}_{1} + 2}{4} = \dfrac{{y}_{1} - 1}{- 3} = \dfrac{- \left(- 8 - 3 - 4\right)}{25} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

We get ${x}_{1} = \dfrac{2}{5}, {y}_{1} = \dfrac{- 4}{5}$

Similarly for ${Q}_{2} = \left(1, 1\right)$

Now using the distance formula we get, $S{Q}_{1} = \sqrt{{\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{5}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)}^{2}} = 1$

${Q}_{1}{Q}_{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{9}{25} + \dfrac{81}{25}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{90}{25}} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{5}$

$P{Q}_{1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{144}{25} + \dfrac{81}{25}} = 3$

$S{Q}_{2} = 1$.

questions.q: Let $E$ denote the parabola ${y}^{2} = 8x .$ Let $P = \left(- 2, 4\right)$, and let $Q$ and ${Q}^{'}$ be two distinct points on $E$ such that the lines $PQ$ and $P{Q}^{'}$ are tangents to $E$. Let $F$ be the focus of $E$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The triangle $PFQ$ is a right-angled triangle
The triangle $QP{Q}^{'}$ is a right-angled triangle
$F$ lies on the line joining $Q$ and ${Q}^{'}$
questions.solution:
${y}^{2} = 8x$

$⇒ a = 2,$ Focus $F\left(2, 0\right),$ and Directrix $x = - 2$

$∵ P\left(- 2, 4\right)$ lies on directrix

$⇒ Q{Q}^{'}$ will be a focal chord and tangents are mutually perpendicular.

$⇒ \DeltaQP{Q}^{'}$ is right angled.

Also the portion between point of contact and directrix of parabola subtends right angle at the focus.

So, $△ PFQ$ is a right- angled triangle.

$PF = \sqrt{{\left(- 2 - 2\right)}^{2} + {\left(4 - 0\right)}^{2}} = 4\sqrt{2}$

questions.q: If a chord, which is not a tangent, of the parabola ${y}^{2} = 16x$ has the equation $2x + y = p$, and midpoint (h, k), then which of the following is (are) possible value(s) of $p, h$ and $k$?
questions.solution:
Equation of chord with mid point $( h, k )$:

$k . y - 16\left(\dfrac{x + h}{2}\right) = {k}^{2} - 16h$

$⇒ 8x - ky + {k}^{2} - 8h = 0$

Comparing with $2x + y - p = 0,$ we get

$k = - 4; 2h - p = 4$

Only $p = 2, h = 3, k = - 4$ satisfies above relation.

options: The x - intercept of the normal to the parabola at P is 6
The slope of the tangent to the circle at Q is $\dfrac{1}{2}$
questions.solution:
${y}^{2} = 4x$
Point P lies on normal to parabola passing through centre of circle
$y + tx = 2t + {t}^{3}$ ......(i)
$8 + 2t = 2t + {t}^{3}$
$t = 2$
$P\left(4, 4\right)$
$SP = \sqrt{{\left(4 - 2\right)}^{2} + {\left(4 - 8\right)}^{2}}$
$SP = 2\sqrt{5}$
$SQ = 2$
$⇒$ $PQ = 2\sqrt{5} - 2$
$\dfrac{SQ}{QP} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5} - 1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5} + 1}{4}$
To find $x$ intercept
Put $y = 0$ in (i)
$⇒$ $x = 2 + {t}^{2}$
$x = 6$
$∵$ Slope of common normal $= - t = - 2$
$∴$ Slope of tangent $= \dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.solution: Given parabola $y^{2}=8 x$ and circle $x^{2}+y^{2}-2 x-4 y=0$ pass through the origin $\therefore$ One end of common chord PQ is origin. Say $\mathrm{P}(0,0)$ Let $\mathrm{Q}$ be the point $\left(2 t^{2}, 4 t\right)$, then it will satisfy the equation of circle. $\therefore \quad 4 t^{4}+16 t^{2}-4 t^{2}-16 t=0 \Rightarrow t^{4}+3 t^{2}-4 t=0 \Rightarrow t\left(t^{3}+3 t-4\right)=0 \Rightarrow t(t-1)\left(t^{2}+t-4\right)=0 \Rightarrow t=0$ or 1 For $t=0$, we get point $P$, therefore $t=1$ gives point $Q$ as $(2,4)$. questions.q: The tangent $P T$ and the normal $P N$ to the parabola $y^2=4 a x$ at a point $P$ on
options:
vertex is $\left(\frac{2 a}{3}, 0\right)$ it meet its axis at points $T$ and $N$,

directrix is $x=0$ respectively. The locus of the centroid of $\triangle P T N$ is a parabola whose

latusrectum is $\frac{2 a}{3}$

focus is $(a, 0)$
questions.solution:
Equation of tangent and normal at point $P\left(a t^2, 2 a t\right)$ is $t y=x=a t^2$ and $y=-t x+2 a t+a t^2$ Let centroid of $\triangle P T N$ is $R(h, k)$. $\therefore \quad h=\frac{a t^2+\left(-a t^2\right)+2 a+a t^2}{3}$ and $k=\frac{2 a t}{3}$
$$ \begin{array}{rlrl} & \Rightarrow & 3 h & =2 a+a \cdot\left(\frac{3 k}{2 a}\right)^2 \\ \Rightarrow & & 3 h & =2 a+\frac{9 k^2}{4 a} \\ \Rightarrow & 9 k^2 & =4 a(3 h-2 a) \end{array} $$ $\therefore$ Locus of centroid is $$ y^2=\frac{4 a}{3}\left(x-\frac{2 a}{3}\right) $$ $\therefore \operatorname{Vertex}\left(\frac{2 a}{3}, 0\right)$; directrix $$ x-\frac{2 a}{3}=-\frac{a}{3} \Rightarrow x=\frac{a}{3} $$ Latusrectum $=\frac{4 a}{3}$ $\therefore$ Focus $\left(\frac{a}{3}+\frac{2 a}{3}, 0\right)$ i.e. $(a, 0)$

questions.q: Equation of common tangent of $y=x^2, y=-x^2+4 x-4$ is
questions.solution:
The equation of tangent to $y=x^2$, be $y=m x-\frac{m^2}{4}$, putting in $y=-x^2+4 x-4$, we should only get one value of $x$ i.e. Discriminate must be zero.
$ \begin{array}{rrr}
\therefore & m x-\frac{m^2}{4} & =-x^2+4 x-4 \\
\Rightarrow & x^2+x(m-4)+4-\frac{m^2}{4} & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & m(m-4) & =0 \\
& \therefore y=0 & \text{ or } m=0,4
\end{array}  $
\therefore y=0 $\text{$ and } y=4(x-1) $\text{$ are tangents. }

questions.explanation:
The equation of tangent to $y=x^2$, be $y=m x-\frac{m^2}{4}$, putting in $y=-x^2+4 x-4$, we should only get one value of $x$ i.e. Discriminate must be zero.
$ \begin{array}{rrr}
\therefore & m x-\frac{m^2}{4} & =-x^2+4 x-4 \\
\Rightarrow & x^2+x(m-4)+4-\frac{m^2}{4} & =0 \\
\Rightarrow & m(m-4) & =0 \\
& \therefore y=0 & \text{ or } m=0,4
\end{array}  $
\therefore y=0 $\text{$ and } y=4(x-1) $\text{$ are tangents. }

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of ways to distribute $10$ identical red pens and $14$ identical blue pens among four persons such that each person gets $6$ pens, is _____________.
questions.solution:
Let $r_i$ and $b_i$ be the number of red and blue pens given to the $i$-th person, where $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$.

Given that each person receives exactly $6$ pens, we have:
$r_i + b_i = 6 \Rightarrow b_i = 6 - r_i$

Since the number of blue pens must be non-negative ($b_i \ge 0$), we get $r_i \le 6$. Also, $r_i \ge 0$.

The total number of red pens is $10$, so:
$r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4 = 10$

The number of ways to distribute the pens is the number of non-negative integer solutions to this equation subject to $0 \le r_i \le 6$.

This is equivalent to finding the coefficient of $x^{10}$ in the expansion of $(1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^6)^4$.

$(1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^6)^4 = \left( \dfrac{1 - x^7}{1 - x} \right)^4 = (1 - x^7)^4 (1 - x)^{-4}$

Expanding both terms:
$(1 - x^7)^4 = 1 - 4x^7 + 6x^{14} - \dots$
$(1 - x)^{-4} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} {}^{k+3}C_{3} x^k$

We need the coefficient of $x^{10}$ in the product $(1 - 4x^7 + \dots) \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} {}^{k+3}C_{3} x^k$.

Coefficient of $x^{10} = 1 \times (\text{coefficient of } x^{10} \text{ in } (1-x)^{-4}) - 4 \times (\text{coefficient of } x^3 \text{ in } (1-x)^{-4})$

$= {}^{10+3}C_{3} - 4 \times {}^{3+3}C_{3}$

$= {}^{13}C_{3} - 4 \times {}^{6}C_{3}$

$= \dfrac{13 \times 12 \times 11}{3 \times 2 \times 1} - 4 \times \dfrac{6 \times 5 \times 4}{3 \times 2 \times 1}$

$= 286 - 4 \times 20$

$= 286 - 80 = 206$

Answer: $206$

questions.q: A bookshelf contains $6$ distinct books of Mathematics and $5$ distinct books of Physics. From these $11$ books, $6$ books are chosen at random. Let $X$ be the absolute value of the difference between the number of Mathematics books chosen and the number of Physics books chosen. If $\alpha$ is the mean of the random variable $X$, then the value of $77\alpha$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
Total number of ways to choose $6$ books from $11$ books is $^{11}C_{6} = 462$.

Let $M$ and $P$ be the number of Mathematics and Physics books chosen respectively. Since $6$ books are chosen, $M + P = 6$.

The random variable $X$ is given by $X = |M - P| = |2M - 6|$.

The possible selections of $(M, P)$, the corresponding values of $X$, and the number of ways are as follows:

For $M=1, P=5$: $X = |1 - 5| = 4$, Number of ways $= ^{6}C_{1} \times ^{5}C_{5} = 6 \times 1 = 6$

For $M=2, P=4$: $X = |2 - 4| = 2$, Number of ways $= ^{6}C_{2} \times ^{5}C_{4} = 15 \times 5 = 75$

For $M=3, P=3$: $X = |3 - 3| = 0$, Number of ways $= ^{6}C_{3} \times ^{5}C_{3} = 20 \times 10 = 200$

For $M=4, P=2$: $X = |4 - 2| = 2$, Number of ways $= ^{6}C_{4} \times ^{5}C_{2} = 15 \times 10 = 150$

For $M=5, P=1$: $X = |5 - 1| = 4$, Number of ways $= ^{6}C_{5} \times ^{5}C_{1} = 6 \times 5 = 30$

For $M=6, P=0$: $X = |6 - 0| = 6$, Number of ways $= ^{6}C_{6} \times ^{5}C_{0} = 1 \times 1 = 1$

The mean $\alpha$ of the random variable $X$ is given by:

$\alpha = \dfrac{\sum X_i f_i}{\sum f_i}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{4(6) + 2(75) + 0(200) + 2(150) + 4(30) + 6(1)}{462}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{24 + 150 + 0 + 300 + 120 + 6}{462}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{600}{462} = \dfrac{100}{77}$

Therefore, the value of $77\alpha$ is:

$77\alpha = 77 \times \dfrac{100}{77} = 100$

Answer: $100$

questions.q:
Let $S$ be the set of all seven-digit numbers that can be formed using the digits 0,1 and 2 . For example, 2210222 is in $S$, but 0210222 is NOT in $S$.
Then the number of elements $x$ in $S$ such that at least one the digits 0 and 1 appears exactly twice in $x$, is equal to ______.
questions.solution:
Let $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow$ " 0 " appear exactly twice.
and $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow " 1 "$ appear exactly twice.
$\therefore \mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B} \rightarrow$ " 0 " and " 1 " both appears exactly twice.
$\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A})=-\underbrace{-------} ={ }_{\text{placing zero }^6 \mathrm{C}_2(1)(2)^5=\frac{6 \times 5}{2} \times 2^5=480$ for $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{B})$
C-I : $1$ at first place
$\underline{1}\underbrace{-------} \text{ Number$ of $ways }=\underset{\text{ placing } 1}{} \mathrm{}^6{C}_1(1)(2)^5=192$
C-II : 2 at first place
$\underline{2}\underbrace{-------}$
Number of ways $=\underset{\text{ placing } 1}{{ }^6 \mathrm{C}_2(1)(2)^4}=\frac{6 \times 5}{2} \times 2^4=240 n(B)=240+192$
for $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}) \underline{}\underbrace{-------}$
for $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B})=\underset{\text{ placing zero }}{{ }^6 \mathrm{C}_2(1)} \times \underset{\text{ placing } 1}{{ }^5 \mathrm{C}_2(1)} \times \underset{\text{ 2at rest places } 1}{(1)} =\frac{6 \times 5}{2} \times \frac{5 \times 4}{2}=150 \begin{aligned} & \therefore \mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{B})=\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A})+\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{B})-\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B}) \\ & =480+(192+240)-150 \\ & =762\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $X$ be the set of all five digit numbers formed using $1, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 0$. For example, $22240$ is in $X$ while $02244$ and $44422$ are not in $X$. Suppose that each element of $X$ has an equal chance of being chosen. Let $p$ be the conditional probability that an element chosen at random is a multiple of $20$ given that it is a multiple of $5$. Then the value of $38p$ is equal to
questions.solution:
First we will find the sample space in which the number of five-digit numbers are divisible by $5$,

So, fixing zero at the last place we get,

$\mathop{- - - - 0}_{⏟}$

Now in first four place following number can take place,

$2224 \to \dfrac{4 !}{3 !} = 4\text{ways}$

$2244 \to \dfrac{4 !}{2 ! 2 !} = 6\text{ways}$

$2221 \to \dfrac{4 !}{3 !} = 4\text{ways}$

$2241 \to \dfrac{4 !}{2 !} = 12\text{ways}$

$2441 \to \dfrac{4 !}{2 !} = 12\text{ways}$

So, total sample space will be $4 + 6 + 4 + 12 + 12 = 38$

Now finding the number of favourable outcomes,

So, Number of five-digit numbers divisible by $5$ but 'not' by $20$

Now fixing $10$ in last two places, we get

$\mathop{- - - 1 0}_{⏟}$

So, the first three places can be occupied by,

$222 \to 1\text{ways}$

$224 \to 3\text{ways}$

$244 \to 3\text{ways}$

So, total number of numbers which are divisible by $5$ but not $20$ will be, $1 + 3 + 3 = 7$

So, favourable number of five-digit numbers that are divisible by $5$ and $20 = 38 - 7 = 31$

Hence, probability is given by, $p = \dfrac{31}{38}$

$⇒ 38p = 31$

questions.q: Consider $4$ boxes, where each box contains $3$ red balls and $2$ blue balls. Assume that all $20$ balls are distinct. In how many different ways can $10$ balls be chosen from these $4$ boxes so that from each box at least one red ball and one blue ball are chosen?
questions.solution:
Let the four boxes be Box-1, Box-2, Box-3 and Box-4. Each of the box has $3$ red balls and $2$ blue balls.

$10$ balls can be chosen in:

Case I - When exactly one box gives four balls

Case II - When exactly two boxes gives three balls

Required number of ways$=$ Number of ways in Case I $+$ Number of ways in Case II.

$= C1 4 \left[C1 2 + C1 3\right]{\left(C1 3 C1 2\right)}^{3} + C2 4 {\left[C2 3 C1 2 + C1 3 C2 2\right]}^{2}{\left[C1 3 C1 2\right]}^{2}$

$= 4\left(5\right){\left(6\right)}^{3} + 6{\left(3 \times 2 + 3\right)}^{2}{\left(6\right)}^{2}$

$= 4320 + 17496 = 21816$

questions.q: The number of $4$-digit integers in the closed interval $\left[2022, 4482\right]$ formed by using the digits $0, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7$ is ______.
questions.solution:
Given the number to be formed by using the digits $0, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7$

Now assuming counting integers starting from $2$

Case-I: if zero on ${2}^{nd}$ place

(i) $202_$, now here at unit place $5$ number can take place except zero {as $2020 < 2022$}, so $5$ possible way.

(ii) $20__$, now here at ten's place $4$ number $\left\{3, 4, 6, 7\right\}$ can take place and at unit place all $6$ number can take place so total $4 \times 6 = 24$ possible way

Case-II: If non-zero number on ${2}^{nd}$ place

i.e $2\mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{5}\mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6}\mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6}$, here at hundredth place $5$ possibility will be there and at unit and ten's place $6 \text{ and } 6$ possibility will be there, so in total $5 \times 6 \times 6 = 180$ possible cases,

Case -III when counting integers starting from $3$

$\begin{cases}3 & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6} & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6} & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6}\end{cases}$ here total $6 \times 6 \times 6 = 216$ possible cases

Case -IV when counting integers starting from $4$

(i) If $0, 2 or 3$ on ${2}^{nd}$ place

i.e., $\begin{cases}4 & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{3} & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6} & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6}\end{cases}$ here total $3 \times 6 \times 6 = 108$ possible cases

(ii) If $4$ on ${2}^{nd}$ place

i.e., $\begin{cases}3 & 4 & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6} & \mathop{\mathop{_}_{⏟}}_{6}\end{cases}$ here total $6 \times 6 = 36$ possible cases

So, total possible cases will be $5 + 24 + 180 + 216 + 108 + 36 = 569$ numbers

questions.q:
In a high school, a committee has to be formed from a group of $6$ boys
${M}_{1}, {M}_{2}, {M}_{3}, {M}_{4}, {M}_{5}, {M}_{6}$ and $5$ girls ${G}_{1}, {G}_{2}, {G}_{3}, {G}_{4}, {G}_{5}$.
(i) Let ${\alpha}_{1}$ be the total number of ways in which the committee can be formed such that the committee has $5$ members, having exactly $3$ boys and $2$ girls.
(ii) Let ${\alpha}_{2}$ be the total number of ways in which the committee can be formed such that the committee has at least $2$ members, and having an equal number of boys and girls.
(iii) Let ${\alpha}_{3}$ be the total number of ways in which the committee can be formed such that the committee has $5$ members, at least $2$ of them being girls.
(iv) Let ${\alpha}_{4}$ be the total number of ways in which the committee can be formed such that the committee has $4$ members, having at least $2$ girls and such that both ${M}_{1}$ and ${G}_{1}$ are NOT in the committee together.
LIST-I LIST-II
A. The value of ${\alpha}_{1}$ is P. $136$
B. The value of ${\alpha}_{2}$ is Q. $189$
C. The value of ${\alpha}_{3}$ is R. $192$
D. The value of ${\alpha}_{4}$ is S. $200$
T. $381$
U. $461$
The correct option is:
questions.solution:
$\left(1\right)$ ${\alpha}_{1} = \left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 3\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 2\end{array}\right) = 200$
So $P \to 4$
$\left(2\right)$ ${\alpha}_{2} = \left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 1\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 2\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 2\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 3\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}2 \\ 3\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 4\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 4\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 5\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 5\end{array}\right)$
$= \left(\begin{array}{ll}11 \\ 5\end{array}\right) - 1 = 461$
So $Q \to 6$
$\left(3\right)$ ${\alpha}_{3} = \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 2\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 3\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 3\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 2\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 4\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 1\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 5\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 0\end{array}\right)$
$= \left(\begin{array}{ll}11 \\ 5\end{array}\right) - \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 0\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 5\end{array}\right) - \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 4\end{array}\right) = 381$
So $R \to 5$
$\left(4\right)$ ${\alpha}_{2} = \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 2\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 2\end{array}\right) - \left(\begin{array}{ll}4 \\ 1\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 1\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 3\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}6 \\ 1\end{array}\right) - \left(\begin{array}{ll}4 \\ 2\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 1\end{array}\right) + \left(\begin{array}{ll}5 \\ 4\end{array}\right) = 189$
So $S \to 2$

questions.solution:
$x =$number of ways in which$10$ letter word can be formed using the given ten distinct letters.

$x = 10 !$

$y =$ number of ways, in which$10$ letter words can be formed, in which exactly $1$ letter is repeated twice and remaining $8$ letters are distinct.

$\dfrac{y}{9x} = \dfrac{5 \times 9 \times 10 !}{9 \times 10 !} = 5$

questions.q:
Six cards and six envelopes are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and cards are to be placed in envelopes so that

each envelope contains exactly one card and no card is placed in the envelope bearing the same number and

more over the card numbered 1 is always placed in envelope numbered 2. Then the number of ways it can

be done is
questions.solution:
Total number of placements of 6 cards into 6 envelopes when no card is placed in the envelope bearing the same number.
$= 6 ! ( 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 !} + \dfrac{1}{2 !} - \dfrac{1}{3 !} + \dfrac{1}{4 !} - \dfrac{1}{5 !} + \dfrac{1}{6 !} )$
$= 6 ! ( \dfrac{1}{2 !} - \dfrac{1}{3 !} + \dfrac{1}{4 !} - \dfrac{1}{5 !} + \dfrac{1}{6 !} )$
$= 360 - 120 + 30 - 6 + 5 = 265$
Number of ways the card numbered 1 is placed among the above placements = 5 (envelope number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
So the required number of ways when card 1 is placed in the envelope numbered 2 = 265 / 5 = 53

questions.q: Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. Take n distinct points on a circle and join each pair of points by a line segment. Colour the line segment joining every pair of adjacent points by blue and the rest by red. If the number of red and blue line segments are equal, then the value of n is ________
questions.solution:
Number of red lines $= n{C}_{2} - n$
Number of blue lines = n
Hence, $n{C}_{2} - n = n$
$n{C}_{2} = 2n$
$\dfrac{n\left(n - 1\right)}{2} = 2n$
$n - 1 = 4 ⇒ n = 5 .$

questions.q:
Suppose that Box I contains $6$ red balls and $9$ green balls, and Box II contains $8$ red balls and $12$ green balls. All the balls of Box I and Box II are mixed together and a ball is chosen at random from them. Let $E_1$ be the event that the ball chosen belonged to Box I and let $E_2$ be the event that the ball chosen belonged to Box II. Let $F_1$ be the event that the ball chosen is red and let $F_2$ be the event that the ball chosen is green.

Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The conditional probability $P(F_1 \mid E_1)$ is equal to the conditional probability $P(F_1 \mid E_2)$
The conditional probability $P(F_1 \mid E_1)$ is greater than the conditional probability $P(F_2 \mid E_2)$
questions.solution:
Total balls in Box I $= 6 + 9 = 15$
Total balls in Box II $= 8 + 12 = 20$
Total balls in the mixture $= 15 + 20 = 35$
Total red balls $= 6 + 8 = 14$
Total green balls $= 9 + 12 = 21$

The probabilities of the given events are:
$P(E_1) = \dfrac{15}{35} = \dfrac{3}{7}$
$P(E_2) = \dfrac{20}{35} = \dfrac{4}{7}$
$P(F_1) = \dfrac{14}{35} = \dfrac{2}{5}$
$P(F_2) = \dfrac{21}{35} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

The joint probabilities are:
$P(E_1 \cap F_1) = \dfrac{6}{35}$
$P(E_2 \cap F_2) = \dfrac{12}{35}$

For statement (A):
$P(E_1) P(F_1) = \dfrac{3}{7} \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{35} = P(E_1 \cap F_1)$
Thus, $E_1$ and $F_1$ are independent. Statement (A) is TRUE.

For statement (B):
$P(E_2) P(F_2) = \dfrac{4}{7} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{12}{35} = P(E_2 \cap F_2)$
Thus, $E_2$ and $F_2$ are independent. Statement (B) is FALSE.

For statement (C):
$P(F_1 \mid E_1) = \dfrac{P(E_1 \cap F_1)}{P(E_1)} = \dfrac{6/35}{15/35} = \dfrac{2}{5}$
$P(F_1 \mid E_2) = \dfrac{P(E_2 \cap F_1)}{P(E_2)} = \dfrac{8/35}{20/35} = \dfrac{2}{5}$
Since $P(F_1 \mid E_1) = P(F_1 \mid E_2)$, statement (C) is TRUE.

For statement (D):
$P(F_2 \mid E_2) = \dfrac{P(E_2 \cap F_2)}{P(E_2)} = \dfrac{12/35}{20/35} = \dfrac{3}{5}$
Since $\dfrac{2}{5} < \dfrac{3}{5}$, $P(F_1 \mid E_1)$ is not greater than $P(F_2 \mid E_2)$. Statement (D) is FALSE.

Answer: The events $E_1$ and $F_1$ are independent; The conditional probability $P(F_1 \mid E_1)$ is equal to the conditional probability $P(F_1 \mid E_2)$

$V: S_1$ can solve the problem, given that neither $\mathrm{S}_2$ nor $\mathrm{S}_3$ can solve the problem,
$W: S_2$ can solve the problem and $S_3$ cannot solve the problem,
$T: S_3$ can solve the problem.
For any event $E$, let $P(E)$ denote the probability of $E$.
If $P(U)=\frac{1}{2}, P(V)=\frac{1}{10}$ and $P(W)=\frac{1}{12}$, then $P(T)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{U})=1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_1^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{S}_2^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{S}_3^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_1^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{S}_2^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{S}_3^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{2} ; \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_1^{\prime}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2^{\prime}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \\
& \Rightarrow\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_1\right)\right)\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)\right)\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)\right)=\frac{1}{2} \quad \ldots(1)
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{V})=\frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_1 \cap \mathrm{ S}_2^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{S}_3^{\prime}\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_2^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{S}_3^{\prime}\right)}=\frac{1}{10} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_1\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_2^{\prime}\right) \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_3^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{10} \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_2^{\prime}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_3^{\prime}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{S}_1\right)=\frac{1}{10}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{ W})=\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2 \cap \mathrm{ S}_3^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{12} \\
& \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3^{\prime}\right)=\frac{1}{12} \\
& \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)\right)=\frac{1}{12}...(2)
\end{aligned}$
Eq. (1)
$\left(1-\frac{1}{10}\right)\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)\right)\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)\right)=\frac{1}{2} \left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)\right)\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)\right)=\frac{5}{9}....(3) \begin{aligned}
& \frac{\text{ Eq. }(2)}{\text{ Eq. }(3)} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)}{1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)}=\frac{1}{12} \times \frac{9}{5} \\
& \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_2\right)=\frac{3}{23}
\end{aligned}$
Put in Eq. (2)
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{3}{23}\left(1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)\right)=\frac{1}{12} \\
& 1-\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)=\frac{23}{36} \\
& \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{ S}_3\right)=\frac{13}{36} \\
& \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{ T})=\frac{13}{36}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
A factory has a total of three manufacturing units, $M_1, M_2$, and $M_3$, which produce bulbs independent of each other. The units $M_1, M_2$, and $M_3$ produce bulbs in the proportions of 2:2:1, respectively. It is known that $20 \%$ of the bulbs produced in the factory are defective. It is also known that, of all the bulbs produced by $M_1, 15 \%$ are defective. Suppose that, if a randomly chosen bulb produced in the factory is found to be defective, the probability that it was produced by $M_2$ is $\frac{2}{5}$.
If a bulb is chosen randomly from the bulbs produced by $M_3$, then the probability that it is defective is ____.
questions.solution:
Now given probability
$\begin{aligned}
& P\left(\frac{\text{ Produced by } \mathrm{M}_2}{\text{ defective }}\right)=\frac{\frac{40}{100} \times \frac{14-\mathrm{x}}{40}}{\frac{20}{100}}=\frac{2}{5} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{14-\mathrm{x}}{40}=\frac{1}{5} \\
& \Rightarrow 14-\mathrm{x}=8 \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=6
\end{aligned}So,$ the required probability =$\frac{6}{20}=$0.3

questions.q: A bag contains $N$ balls out of which 3 balls are white, 6 balls are green, and the remaining balls are blue. Assume that the balls are identical otherwise. Three balls are drawn randomly one after the other without replacement. For $i=1,2,3$, let $W_i, G_i$, and $B_i$ denote the events that the ball drawn in the $i^{\text{th }}$ draw is a white ball, green ball, and blue ball, respectively. If the probability $P\left(W_1 \cap G_2 \cap B_3\right)=\frac{2}{5 N}$ and the conditional probability $P\left(B_3 \mid W_1 \cap G_2\right)=\frac{2}{9}$, then $N$ equals ________.
questions.solution: Given $\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{W}_1 \cap \mathrm{G}_2 \cap \mathrm{B}_3\right)=\frac{2}{5 \mathrm{~N}}$ and $\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{B}_3 \mid \mathrm{W}_1 \cap \mathrm{G}_2\right)=\frac{2}{9} \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{B}_3 \cap \mathrm{W}_1 \cap \mathrm{G}_2\right)}{\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{W}_1 \cap \mathrm{G}_2\right)}=\frac{2}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2}{5 \mathrm{~N}} \times \frac{\mathrm{N} \times(\mathrm{N}-1)}{3 \times 6}=\frac{2}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{N}=11\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A student appears for a quiz consisting of only true-false type questions and answers all the questions. The student knows the answers of some questions and guesses the answers for the remaining questions. Whenever the student knows the answer of a question, he gives the correct answer. Assume that the probability of the student giving the correct answer for a question, given that he has guessed it, is $\frac{1}{2}$. Also assume that the probability of the answer for a question being guessed, given that the student's answer is correct, is $\frac{1}{6}$. Then the probability that the student knows the answer of a randomly chosen question is
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{C} \rightarrow$ Correct
$\mathrm{G} \rightarrow$ Guess
$\mathrm{K} \rightarrow$ Knows
$\begin{array}{ll}\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{G}}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \quad, \quad \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{K}}\right)=1 \\\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{C}}\right)=\frac{1}{6}\end{array} \begin{aligned} & \text{ Let required probability }=\mathrm{x} \\ & \therefore \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{G}}{\mathrm{C}}\right)=\frac{(1-\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{G}}\right)}{(1-\mathrm{x}) \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{G}}\right)+\mathrm{x} \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{K}}\right)} \\ & \frac{1}{6}=\frac{(1-\mathrm{x})\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{(1-\mathrm{x})\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+(\mathrm{x})(1)} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\frac{5}{7} \Rightarrow \text{ Option (3) is correct. }\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Consider an experiment of tossing a coin repeatedly until the outcomes of two consecutive tosses are same. If the probability of a random toss resulting in head is $\dfrac{1}{3}$, then the probability that the experiment stops with head is
questions.solution:
Given,

$P ( H ) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

So, $P ( T ) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Now probability of the event is given by,

$P ( E ) = P ( HH ) + P ( THH ) + P ( HTHH ) + P ( THTHH ) + P ( HTHTHH ) + P ( THTHTHH ) + \ldots$

$⇒ P ( E ) = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{4}{{3}^{5}} + \dfrac{4}{{3}^{6}} + \dfrac{8}{{3}^{7}} + \dfrac{8}{{3}^{8}} + \ldots$

$⇒ P ( E ) = \dfrac{1}{{3}^{2}} + \dfrac{2}{{3}^{3}} + \dfrac{2}{{3}^{4}} + \dfrac{4}{{3}^{5}} + \dfrac{4}{{3}^{6}} + \dfrac{8}{{3}^{7}} + \dfrac{8}{{3}^{8}} + \ldots$

$⇒ P ( E ) = \left(\dfrac{1}{{3}^{2}} + \dfrac{2}{{3}^{4}} + \dfrac{4}{{3}^{6}} + \ldots .\right) + \left(\dfrac{2}{{3}^{3}} + \dfrac{4}{{3}^{5}} + \dfrac{8}{{3}^{7}} + \ldots .\right)$

$⇒ P ( E ) = \left(\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{{3}^{2}}}{\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{{3}^{2}}\right)}\right) + \left(\dfrac{\dfrac{2}{{3}^{3}}}{\left(1 - \dfrac{2}{{3}^{2}}\right)}\right)$

$⇒ P ( E ) = \dfrac{1}{7} + \dfrac{2}{21} = \dfrac{5}{21}$

questions.q: Let $X = \left\{\left(x, y\right) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}: \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{8} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{20} < 1and{y}^{2} < 5x\right\}$. Three distinct point $P, Q$ and $R$ are randomly chosen from $X$. Then the probability that $P, Q$ and $R$ form a triangle whose area is a positive integer, is
questions.solution:
Given,

Equation of ellipse $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{8} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{20} = 1$

And equation of parabola ${y}^{2} = 5x$

Now intersection point of ellipse and parabola will be $\left(2, \sqrt{10}\right) \text{ and } \left(2, - \sqrt{10}\right)$

Now plotting the region $\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{8} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{20} < 1and{y}^{2} < 5x$ we get,

Now randomly chosen points will be between origin and the intersecting point,

So, the integer points inside region are $\left\{\left(2, 1\right), \left(2, - 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left(2, - 2\right), \left(2, 3\right), \left(2, - 3\right), \left(2, 0\right), \left(1, 1\right), \left(1, - 1\right), \left(1, 2\right), \left(1, - 2\right), \left(1, 0\right)\right\}$

Total number of ways to select three points $= C3 12 = 220$

Required number of triangle $= 4 \times C1 7 + 9 \times C1 5 = 73$

{Note: Points are taken such a way that distance between two points are multiple of $2$ for example if we take points on line $x = 1$ we can take following points $\left\{\left(1, 2\right) \text{ and } \left(1, 0\right), \left(1, 0\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 2\right), \left(1, 1\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 1\right), \left(1, 2\right) \text{ and } \left(1, - 2\right)\right\}$

so there will be $4$ pairs from line $x = 1$ and will chose another point from $x = 2$ line so triangle will have a positive area. Also note that height of the triangle will always be $1$}

Hence, probability will be $= \dfrac{73}{220}$

Suppose that
Box-I contains $8$ red, $3$ blue and $5$ green balls,
Box-ll contains $24$ red, $9$ blue and $15$ green balls,
Box-III contains $1$ blue, $12$ green and $3$ yellow balls,
Box-IV contains $10$ green, $16$ orange and $6$ white balls.
A ball is chosen randomly from Box-l; call this ball $b$. If $b$ is red then a ball is chosen randomly from Box-ll, if $b$ is blue then a ball is chosen randomly from Box-III, and if $b$ is green then a ball is chosen randomly from Box-IV. The conditional probability of the event 'one of the chosen balls is white' given that the event 'at least one of the chosen balls is green' has happened, is equal to
questions.solution:
$P\left(\text{Red from Box}I\right) = \dfrac{8}{16} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$P\left(\text{Blue from Box}I\right) = \dfrac{3}{16}$

$P\left(\text{Green from Box}I\right) = \dfrac{10}{32} = \dfrac{5}{16}$

Now,

$P\left(\text{Green from Box}II\right) = \dfrac{15}{48}$

$P\left(\text{Green from Box}III\right) = \dfrac{12}{16} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$P\left(\text{White from Box}IV\right) = \dfrac{6}{32} = \dfrac{3}{16}$

Event $A$ : One of the chosen ball is white
$B:$ At least one of the chosen ball is green

$P\left(\dfrac{A}{B}\right) = \dfrac{P\left(A ∩ B\right)}{P\left(B\right)}$

$= \dfrac{\dfrac{5}{16} \times \dfrac{3}{16}}{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{15}{48} + \dfrac{3}{16} \times \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{5}{16} \times 1}$

$= \dfrac{5}{52}$

questions.q:
Two players, ${P}_{1} and {P}_{2}$, play a game against each other. In every round of the game, each player rolls a fair die once, where the six faces of the die have six distinct numbers. Let $x and y$ denote the readings on the die rolled by ${P}_{1} and {P}_{2}$, respectively. If $x > y$, then ${P}_{1}$ scores $5$ points and ${P}_{2}$ scores $0$ point. If $x = y$, then each player scores $2$ points. If $x < y$, then ${P}_{1}$ scores $0$ point and ${P}_{2}$ scores $5$ points. Let ${X}_{i} and {Y}_{i}$ be the total scores of ${P}_{1} and {P}_{2}$, respectively, after playing the ${i}^{th}$ round.

List-$I$ List-$II$
$\left(I\right)$ Probability of $\left({X}_{2} \ge {Y}_{2}\right)$ is $\left(P\right)$ $\dfrac{3}{8}$
$\left(II\right)$ Probability of $\left({X}_{2} > {Y}_{2}\right)$ is $\left(Q\right)$ $\dfrac{11}{16}$
$\left(III\right)$ Probability of $\left({X}_{3} = {Y}_{3}\right)$ is $\left(R\right)$ $\dfrac{5}{16}$
$\left(IV\right)$ Probability of $\left({X}_{3} > {Y}_{3}\right)$ is $\left(S\right)$ $\dfrac{355}{864}$
$\left(T\right)$ $\dfrac{77}{432}$

The correct option is:
questions.solution:
Given,

$P$(draw in $1$ round)$= \dfrac{6}{36} = \dfrac{1}{6}$

$P$(win in $1$ round) $= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{6}\right) = \dfrac{5}{12}$

$P$(loss in $1$ round) $= \dfrac{5}{12}$

Now finding the probability of all we get,$P\left({X}_{2} > {Y}_{2}\right) = P\left(10, 0\right) + P\left(7, 2\right) = \dfrac{5}{12} \times \dfrac{5}{12} + \dfrac{5}{12} \times \dfrac{1}{6} \times 2 = \dfrac{45}{144} = \dfrac{5}{16} \to R$

$P\left({X}_{2} = {Y}_{2}\right) = P\left(5, 5\right) + P\left(4, 4\right) = \dfrac{5}{12} \times \dfrac{5}{12} \times 2 + \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{25 + 2}{72} = \dfrac{3}{8}$

$P\left({X}_{2} \ge {Y}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{16} + \dfrac{3}{8} = \dfrac{11}{16} \to Q$

$P\left({X}_{3} = {Y}_{3}\right) = P\left(6, 6\right) + P\left(7, 7\right) = \dfrac{1}{6 \times 6 \times 6} + \dfrac{5}{12} \times \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{12} \times 6 = \dfrac{2}{432} + \dfrac{75}{432} = \dfrac{77}{432} \to T$

$P\left({X}_{3} > {Y}_{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \dfrac{77}{432}\right) = \dfrac{355}{864} \to S$

questions.q:
Consider three sets ${E}_{1} = { 1, 2, 3 } , {F}_{1} = { 1, 3, 4 }$ and ${G}_{1} = { 2, 3, 4, 5 }$. Two elements are chosen at random, without replacement, from the set ${E}_{1}$, and let ${S}_{1}$ denote the set of these chosen elements. Let ${E}_{2} = {E}_{1} - {S}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2} = {F}_{1} ∪ {S}_{1}$. Now two elements are chosen at random, without replacement, from the set ${F}_{2}$ and let ${S}_{2}$ denote the set of these chosen elements.

Let ${G}_{2} = {G}_{1} ∪ {S}_{2}$. Finally, two elements are chosen at random, without replacement, from the set ${G}_{2}$ and let ${S}_{3}$ denote the set of these chosen elements.
Let ${E}_{3} = {E}_{2} ∪ {S}_{3}$. Given that ${E}_{1} = {E}_{3}$, let $p$ be the conditional probability of the event ${S}_{1} = { 1, 2 }$. Then the value of $p$ is
questions.solution:
We need to find $p$, the conditional probability of the event ${S}_{1} = { 1, 2 }$, given ${E}_{1} = {E}_{3}$.

So, $p = \dfrac{P\left({S}_{1} ∩ \left({E}_{1} = {E}_{3}\right)\right)}{P\left({E}_{1} = {E}_{3}\right)} = \dfrac{P\left({B}_{1, 2}\right)}{P ( B )}$

$P ( B ) = P\left({B}_{1, 2}\right) + P\left({B}_{1, 3}\right) + P\left({B}_{2, 3}\right)$

$P\left({B}_{1, 2}\right) \to$ If ${ 1, 2 }$ chosen in the beginning

$P\left({B}_{1, 3}\right) \to$If ${ 1, 3 }$ chosen in the beginning

$P\left({B}_{2, 3}\right) \to$If ${ 2, 3 }$ chosen in the beginning

(i) If ${ 1, 2 }$ is chosen in the begining, then ${F}_{2} = { 1, 2, 3, 4 }$ and ${S}_{2}$ must contain $\left\{1\right\}$ and ${S}_{3} = \left\{1, 2\right\}$ from ${G}_{2} = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }$

So, $P\left({B}_{1, 2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1 \times C1 3}{C2 4} \times \dfrac{1}{C2 5} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{10}$

(ii) If ${ 1, 3 }$ is chosen in the begining, then ${F}_{2} = { 1, 3, 4 }$ and ${S}_{2}$ must contain $\left\{1\right\}$ and ${S}_{3} = \left\{1, 3\right\}$ from ${G}_{2} =$${ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 }$

So, $P\left({B}_{1, 3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1 \times C1 2}{C2 3} \times \dfrac{1}{C2 5} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{10}$

(iii) If ${ 2, 3 }$ is chosen in the begining, then ${F}_{2} = { 1, 2, 3, 4 }$, then two cases are possible

1. ${S}_{2}$ may contain $\left\{1\right\}$ and getting ${S}_{3} = ( 2, 3 )$ from ${G}_{2} = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 )$

2. ${S}_{2}$ does not contain $\left\{1\right\}$ and getting $( 2, 3 )$ from ${G}_{2} = { 2, 3, 4, 5 ]$

So, $P\left({B}_{2, 3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \left[\dfrac{C2 3 \times 1}{C2 4} \times \dfrac{1}{C2 4} + \dfrac{1 \times C1 3}{C2 4} \times \dfrac{1}{C2 5}\right] = \dfrac{1}{3} \times \left[\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{10}\right]$

Now, $p = \dfrac{P\left({B}_{1, 2}\right)}{P\left({B}_{1, 2}\right) + P\left({B}_{1, 3}\right) + P\left({B}_{2, 3}\right)}$

$= \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{10}}{\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{3} \times \left[\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{10}\right]} = \dfrac{1}{5}$

Three numbers are chosen at random, one after another with replacement, from the set $S=\{1,2,3, \ldots, 100\}$. Let $p_{1}$ be the probability that the maximum of chosen numbers is at least 81 and $p_{2}$ be the probability that the minimum of chosen numbers is at most 40 .
The value of $\dfrac{625}{4}{p}_{1}$ is
questions.solution:
Maximum of the chosen numbers is at least $81$

It means we have to choose at least one number from $81$ to $100$

Total number of possible selections $= 100 \times 100 \times 100 = {100}^{3}$

Favourable cases $=$ Total $-$ unfavourable cases

Unfavourable cases are those in which we have selected all the three numbers form $1$ to $80$ $= 80 \times 80 \times 80 = {80}^{3}$

Total number of favourable cases $= {100}^{3} - {80}^{3}$

So, ${p}_{1} = \dfrac{{100}^{3} - {80}^{3}}{{100}^{3}}$

$= \dfrac{{20}^{3}\left({5}^{3} - {4}^{3}\right)}{{20}^{3} \times {5}^{3}} = \dfrac{125 - 64}{125} = \dfrac{61}{125}$

Hence, $\dfrac{625}{4}{p}_{1} = \dfrac{625}{4} \times \dfrac{61}{125} = 76 . 25$

questions.q: The probability that a missile hits a target successfully is $0 . 75 .$ In order to destroy the target completely, at least three successful hits are required. Then the minimum number of missiles that have to be fired so that the probability of completely destroying the target is not less than $0 . 95,$ is ___________
questions.solution:
Let the number of missiles be $n$,

$P$ (of destroying the target) $\ge 0 . 95$

$C3 n \cdot {\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{3} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{n - 3} + C4 n {\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{4}{\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{n - 4} + \ldots . . + Cn n {\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{n} \ge 0 . 95$

$1 - \left\{C0 n {\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{0} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{n} + C1 n {\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{1} \cdot {\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{n - 1} + C2 n {\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}^{2}{\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}^{n - 2}\right\} \ge 0 . 95$

$1 - \dfrac{95}{100} \ge \dfrac{1}{{4}^{n}} + \dfrac{3n}{{4}^{n}} + \dfrac{n\left(n - 1\right)}{2} \cdot \dfrac{9}{{4}^{n}}$

$\dfrac{{4}^{n}}{20} \ge \dfrac{2 + 6n + 9{n}^{2} - 9n}{2}$

$\dfrac{{2}^{2n - 1}}{5} \ge 9{n}^{2} - 3n + 2$

${2}^{2n - 1} \ge 5\left(9{n}^{2} - 3n + 2\right)$

$n = 3 ⇒ 32 \ge 5 \times 74$ (not true)

$n = 4 ⇒ 128 \ge 5 \times 134$ (not true)

$n = 5 ⇒ 512 \ge 5 \times 212$ (not true)

$n = 6 ⇒ 2048 \ge 5 \times 308$ (true)

So, $n = 6$.

questions.q: Two fair dice, each with faces numbered $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$, are rolled together and the sum of the numbers on the faces is observed. This process is repeated till the sum is either a prime number or a perfect square. Suppose the sum turns out to be a perfect square before it turns out to be a prime number. If $p$ is the probability that this perfect square is an odd number, then the value of $14p$ is_____
questions.solution:
Perfect Square can be $4$ or $9$, which can be obtained by $\left(1, 3\right), \left(3, 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left(6, 3\right)\left(3, 6\right), \left(5, 4\right), \left(4, 5\right)$.

Prime Number can be $2$ or $3$ or $5$ or $7$ or $11$, which can be obtained by

$\left(1, 1\right), \left(1, 2\right), \left(2, 1\right), \left(1, 4\right), \left(4, 1\right), \left(2, 3\right), \left(3, 2\right), \left(1, 6\right), \left(6, 1\right), \left(5, 2\right), \left(2, 5\right), \left(3, 4\right), \left(4, 3\right), \left(6, 5\right), \left(5, 6\right)$

$P$(square or prime)$= \dfrac{22}{36}$

$P\left(\dfrac{\text{Perfect square is odd}}{\text{perfect square before prime}}\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{36} + \dfrac{14}{36} . \dfrac{4}{36} + \dfrac{14}{36} . \dfrac{14}{36} . \dfrac{4}{36} + . . . .}{\dfrac{7}{36} + \dfrac{14}{36} . \dfrac{7}{36} + \dfrac{14}{36} . \dfrac{14}{36} . \dfrac{7}{36} + . . . . . .}$

$= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{4}{36}}{1 - \dfrac{14}{36}}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{7}{36}}{1 - \dfrac{14}{36}}\right)} = \dfrac{4}{7} = P$

$⇒ 14P = 8$

questions.q: Let ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{2}$ be two biased coins such that the probabilities of getting head in a single toss are $\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{1}{3}$, respectively. Suppose $\alpha$ is the number of heads that appear when ${C}_{1}$ is tossed twice, independently, and suppose $\beta$ is the number of heads that appear when ${C}_{2}$ is tossed twice, independently. Then the probability that the roots of the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2} - \alphax + \beta$ are real and equal, is
questions.solution:
For tossing two coins independently, maximum and minimum heads that can appear will be $2 \text{ and } 0$ respectively.

Roots of equation ${x}^{2} - \alphax + \beta = 0$ are real and equal, then discriminant $D = 0$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{2} - 4\beta = 0 ⇒ {\alpha}^{2} = 4\beta$

$⇒ \left(\alpha = 0, \beta = 0\right)$ or $\left(\alpha = 2, \beta = 1\right)$

Thus, the required probability

$= C0 2 {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{0}{\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)}^{2} . C0 2 {\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)}^{0}{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{2} + C2 2 {\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{2}{\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)}^{0} . C1 2 {\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)}^{1}{\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)}^{1}$

$= \dfrac{1}{9} \times \dfrac{4}{9} + \dfrac{4}{9} \times \dfrac{4}{9} = \dfrac{20}{81}$

$\begin{cases}\left|S\right|\left|A ∩ B\right| = \left|A\right| \cdot \left|B\right| & \left(∴ \left|x\right| = numberofelementinset\right)\end{cases}$
$\left|S\right| = 6$
$6\left|A ∩ B\right| = \left|A\right|\left|B\right|$
$\begin{cases}6n\left(A ∩ B\right) = n\left(A\right)n\left(B\right) & \left(set\left|x\right| = n\left(x\right)\right)\end{cases}$
Case $I:$
$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 1$
$⇒ n\left(A\right)n\left(B\right) = 6$
$\left(a\right)\begin{cases}n\left(A\right) = 6, n\left(B\right) = 1 & Numberofways = C6 6 \times C1 6 = 6\end{cases}$

$\left(b\right)n\left(A\right) = 3, n\left(B\right) = 1Numberofways = C3 6 \times C1 3 \times C2 5 = 180$

$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 2$
$⇒ n\left(A\right)n\left(B\right) = 12$
$\begin{cases}\left(a\right)n\left(A\right) = 6 & n\left(B\right) = 2 & Numberofways\end{cases} = {C}_{6} 6 {C}_{2} 6 = 15$
$\begin{cases}\left(b\right)n\left(A\right) = 4 & n\left(B\right) = 3 & Numberofways =\end{cases} C4 6 \times C2 4 \times C1 2 = 180$

$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 3$
$⇒ n\left(A\right)n\left(B\right) = 18$
$\left(a\right)\begin{cases}n\left(A\right) = 6, & n\left(B\right) = 3Numberofways ⇒ & C6 6 \times C3 6 = 20\end{cases}$
Case $IV:$
$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 4$
$⇒ n\left(A\right)n\left(B\right) = 24$
$\begin{cases}\left(a\right)n\left(A\right) = 6 & n\left(B\right) = 4Numberofways ⇒ & C6 6 \times C4 6 = 15\end{cases}$

$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = 5$
$⇒ 1n\left(A\right)n\left(B\right) = 30$
$\begin{cases}\left(a\right)n\left(A\right) = 6 & n\left(B\right) = 5Numberofways ⇒ & C6 6 C5 6 = 6\end{cases}$
Total ordered pairs $= 422$

questions.q: There are three bags ${B}_{1}, {B}_{2}$ and ${B}_{3} .$ The bag ${B}_{1}$ contains $5$ red and $5$ green balls, ${B}_{2}$ contains $3$ red and $5$ green balls, and ${B}_{3}$ contains $5$ red and $3$ green balls, Bags ${B}_{1}, {B}_{2}$ and ${B}_{3}$ have probabilities $\dfrac{3}{10}, \dfrac{3}{10}$ and $\dfrac{4}{10}$ respectively of being chosen. A bag is selected at random and a ball is chosen at random from the bag. Then which of the following options is/are correct?
options: Probability that the selected bag is  ${B}_{3}$  and the chosen ball is green equals  $\dfrac{3}{10}$
Probability that the chosen ball is green equals  $\dfrac{39}{80}$
Probability that the chosen ball is green, given that the selected bag is  ${B}_{3},$  equals  $\dfrac{3}{8}$
Probability that the selected bag is  ${B}_{3},$  given that the chosen balls is green, equals  $\dfrac{5}{13}$
questions.solution:
Let us define following events
${B}_{1}$ : Event of selection of bag $1$ ( $5$ Red, $5$ Green)
${B}_{2}$ : Event of selection of bag $2$ ( $3$ Red, $5$ Green)
${B}_{3}$ : Event of selection of bag $3$ ( $5$ Red, $3$ Green)
$R =$ Event of selection of Red ball
$G =$ Event of selection of Green ball
Option $( C )$ :
$P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{3}}\right) = \dfrac{3}{8}$ (as bag $3$ has been selected now total balls in bag $3 = 8,$ green ball $= 3$ )
Option $( B )$ :
$P\left(G\right) = P\left({B}_{1}\right)P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{1}}\right) + P\left({B}_{2}\right)P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{2}}\right) + P\left({B}_{3}\right)P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{3}}\right)$
$= \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{5}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{5}{8} + \dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{8}$
$= \dfrac{39}{80}$
Option $( D )$ :
$P\left(\dfrac{{B}_{3}}{G}\right) = \dfrac{P\left({B}_{3} ∩ G\right)}{P\left(G\right)}$
$= \dfrac{P\left({B}_{3}\right)P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{3}}\right)}{P ( G )}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{8}}{\dfrac{35}{80}}\left(∴ P\left(G\right) = \dfrac{39}{80}\right)$
$= \dfrac{4}{13}$
Option $( A )$ :
$P\left({B}_{3} ∩ G\right) = P\left({B}_{3}\right)P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{3}}\right)$
$P\left({B}_{3} ∩ G\right) = P\left({B}_{3}\right)P\left(\dfrac{G}{{B}_{3}}\right)$
$= \dfrac{3}{20}$

Let $S$ be the sample space of all $3 \times 3$ matrices with entries from the set $\left\{0, 1\right\} .$ Let the events ${E}_{1} and {E}_{2}$ be given by
${E}_{1} = \left\{A \in S: detA = 0\right\} and
${E}_{2} = { A \in S:$ sum of entries of A$ is $7 } .
If a matrix is chosen at random from $S,$ then the conditional probability $P$\left({E}_{1}{E}_{2}\right)$ equals____
questions.solution:
For sum to be seven, we need seven $1s$ and two $0s$
Number of different possible matrices= $= \dfrac{9}{7 2} = 36$
Eg. $\left[\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{cases}\right]$ {arrangement of seven $1s$ and two $0s$ }
Now, for determined of matrix to be zero, both the zero must be in same row or in same column.
Eg. $\left[\begin{cases}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{cases}\right]$ Now, arrangement of 0s and $1s = \mathop{6}_{\begin{array}{ll}Selectionof \\ acolumn / row\end{array}} \times \mathop{3}_{\begin{array}{ll}arrangement \\ oftwo0s \\ andone1in \\ arow / column\end{array}} = 18$
Hence, required probability $= \dfrac{18}{36} = \dfrac{1}{2}$
(Note: If two zero's lies on different row/column then $\left|\begin{cases}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{cases}\right| = + 1 \ne 0$ )

Paragraph: There are five students ${S}_{1}, {S}_{2}, {S}_{3}, {S}_{4}$ and ${S}_{5}$ in a music class and for them there are five seats ${R}_{1}, {R}_{2}, {R}_{3}, {R}_{4}$ and ${R}_{5}$ arranged in a row, where initially the seat ${R}_{i}$ is allotted to the student ${S}_{i}, i = 1,2, 3,4, 5 .$ But, on the examination day, the five students are randomly allotted the five seats
Question : The probability that, on the examination day, the student ${S}_{1}$ gets the previously allotted seat ${R}_{1},$ and NONE of the remaining students gets the seat previously allotted to him/her is
questions.solution: Required probability $= \dfrac{4 ! \left(\dfrac{1}{2 !} - \dfrac{1}{3 !} + \dfrac{1}{4 !}\right)}{5 !} = \dfrac{9}{120} = \dfrac{3}{40}$

questions.q: Three randomly chosen non negative integers $x, y, z$ are found to satisfy the equation $x + y + z = 10$ . Then the probability that $z$ is even, is
questions.solution:
Let $z = 2k,$ where $k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$

$∴ x + y = 10 - 2k$

Number of non negative integral solutions

$\mathop{∑}_{k = 0}^{5}{}^{11 - 2k}{C}_{1} = ∑ 11 - 2k = 36$

Total cases $= {}^{10 + 3 - 1}{C}_{3 - 1} = 66$

Required probability $= \dfrac{36}{66} = \dfrac{6}{11}$

questions.q: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two events such that $P\left(X\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$, $P\left(XY\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $P\left(Y | X\right) = \dfrac{2}{5} .$ Then
questions.solution:
Using formula $P\left(X | Y\right) = \dfrac{P( X ∩ Y )}{P( Y )}$ and $P\left(Y | X\right) = \dfrac{P( Y ∩ X )}{P( X )}$
$P\left(X\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}; \dfrac{P\left(X ∩ Y\right)}{P\left(Y\right)} = \dfrac{1}{2}; \dfrac{P\left(Y ∩ X\right)}{P\left(X\right)} = \dfrac{2}{5}$
From this information, we get
$P\left(X ∩ Y\right) = \dfrac{2}{15}; P\left(Y\right) = \dfrac{4}{15}$
Using formula $P ( X ∪ Y ) = P ( X ) + P ( Y ) - P ( X ∩ Y )$
$∴ P\left(X ∪ Y\right) = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{4}{15} - \dfrac{2}{15} = \dfrac{7}{15}$
$P\left(\overset{¯}{X} | Y\right) = \dfrac{P\left(\overset{-}{X} ∩ Y\right)}{P\left(Y\right)} = \dfrac{P\left(Y\right) - P\left(X ∩ Y\right)}{P\left(Y\right)}$
$⇒ P\left(\overset{¯}{X} | Y\right) = 1 - \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{15}}{\dfrac{4}{15}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

The probabilities of $T_{1}$ winning, drawing and losing a game against $T_{2}$ are $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{6}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$, respectively. Each team gets $3$ points for a win, $1$ point for a draw and $0$ point for a loss in a game. Let $X$ and $Y$ denote the total points scored by teams $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, respectively, after two games.
Question: $P(X>Y)$ is
questions.solution:
$P\left(X > Y\right) = P\left({T}_{1}win\right)P\left({T}_{1}win\right) + P\left({T}_{1}win\right)P\left(matchdraw\right) + P\left(matchdraw\right) . P\left({T}_{1}win\right)$
$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5}{12}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
A computer producing factory has only two plants ${T}_{1}$ and ${T}_{2}$. Plant ${T}_{1}$ produces $20 %$ and plant ${T}_{2}$ produces $80 %$ of the total computers produced. $7 %$ of computers produced in the factory turn out to be defective. It is known that,

$P$(computer turns out to be defective given that it is produced in plant ${T}_{1}$)

$= 10P$(computer turns out to be defective given that it is produced in plant ${T}_{2}$).

Where, $P\left(E\right)$ denotes the probability of an event $E .$ A computer produced in the factory is randomly selected and it does not turn out to be defective. Then the probability that it is produced in plant ${T}_{2}$ is
questions.solution:
$P\left({T}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{20}{100}$

$P\left({T}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{80}{100}$

Let, $P\left(\dfrac{D}{{T}_{2}}\right) = x$ (where, $D$ represents defective units)

$P\left(\dfrac{D}{{T}_{1}}\right) = 10x$

$P\left(D\right) = \dfrac{7}{100}$ (given)

$P\left({T}_{1}\right)P\left(\dfrac{D}{{T}_{1}}\right) + P\left({T}_{2}\right)P\left(\dfrac{D}{{T}_{2}}\right) = \dfrac{7}{100}$

$\dfrac{20}{100} \times 10x + \dfrac{80}{100} \times x = \dfrac{7}{100}$

$x = \dfrac{1}{40}$

$P\left(\dfrac{D}{{T}_{2}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{40}$

$⇒ P\left(\overset{-}{D}{T}_{2}\right) = \dfrac{39}{40} =$Probability of not defective, given that it is produced in plant ${T}_{2}$

$P\left(\dfrac{D}{{T}_{1}}\right) = \dfrac{10}{40} ⇒ P\left(\overset{-}{D}{T}_{1}\right) = \dfrac{30}{40}$

Now using Bayes' theorem

Probability of computer from ${T}_{2}$ given that it is not defective :

$P\left({T}_{2}\overset{-}{D}\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{80}{100} \times \dfrac{39}{40}}{\dfrac{20}{100} \times \dfrac{30}{40} + \dfrac{80}{100} \times \dfrac{39}{40}} = \dfrac{78}{93}$

questions.q:
Let ${n}_{1}and{n}_{2}$ be the number of red and black balls, respectively, in box I. Let ${n}_{3}and{n}_{4}$ be the number of red and black balls, respectively, in box II.
One of the two boxes, box I and box II, was selected at random and a ball was drawn randomly out of this box. The balls was found to be red. If the probability that this red ball was drawn from box II is $\dfrac{1}{3}$ , then the correct option(s) with the possible values of ${n}_{1}, {n}_{2}, {n}_{3}and{n}_{4}$ is(are)
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{{n}_{3}}{{n}_{3} + {n}_{4}}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{{n}_{1}}{{n}_{1} + {n}_{2}} + \dfrac{{n}_{3}}{{n}_{3} + {n}_{4}}\right)}$
$\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{{n}_{3}}{{n}_{3} + {n}_{4}}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{{n}_{1}}{{n}_{1} + {n}_{2}} + \dfrac{{n}_{3}}{{n}_{3} + {n}_{4}}\right)}$
(i) $RHS\dfrac{\dfrac{5}{20}}{\dfrac{5}{20} + \dfrac{3}{6}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4}}{\dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{4}}{\dfrac{1 + 2}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
(ii) $RHS\dfrac{\dfrac{10}{60}}{\dfrac{10}{60} + \dfrac{3}{9}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{6}}{\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{6}}{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
(iii) $\dfrac{\dfrac{5}{25}}{\dfrac{8}{14} + \dfrac{5}{25}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{5}}{\dfrac{4}{7} + \dfrac{1}{5}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{5}}{\dfrac{20 + 7}{35}} = \dfrac{7}{27}$
(iv) $\dfrac{\dfrac{5}{25}}{\dfrac{6}{18} + \dfrac{5}{25}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{5}}{\dfrac{5 + 3}{15}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{5}}{\dfrac{8}{15}} = \dfrac{1}{5} \times \dfrac{15}{8} = \dfrac{3}{8}$ .

questions.q: The minimum number of times a fair coin needs to be tossed so that the probability of getting at least two heads is at least $0 . 96$, is
questions.solution:
$P\left(2\right) + P\left(3\right) \ldots \ge 0 .96$
$1 - P\left(0\right) - P\left(1\right) \ge 0 .96$
$1 - 0 .96 {\ge}^{n}{C}_{0}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n}{+}^{n}{C}_{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{n}$
$⇒ \left(0 .04\right){2}^{n} \ge 1 + n$
$⇒ 4{.2}^{n} \ge \left(n + 1\right)100$
$⇒ {2}^{n + 2} \ge \left(n + 1\right)100$
As, ${2}^{10} \ge 900$
$⇒ n = 8$

questions.q:
Paragraph: Box $1$ contains three cards bearing numbers $1,2,3$; box $2$ contains five cards bearing numbers $1,2,3,4,5$; and box $3$ contains seven cards bearing numbers $1,2,3,4,5,6,7$. A card is drawn from each of the boxes. Let $x_{i}$ be the number on the card drawn from the $i^{t h}$ box, $i=1,2,3$.
Question: The probability that $x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}$ is odd, is
questions.solution:
Case I: One odd, 2 even
Total number of ways $= 2 \times 2 \times 3 + 1 \times 3 \times 3 + 1 \times 2 \times 4 = 29$
Case II: All 3 odd
Number of ways $= 2 \times 3 \times 4 = 24$
Favourable ways = 53
Required probability $= \dfrac{53}{3 \times 5 \times 7} = \dfrac{53}{105}$

questions.solution:
Let $A:$ one ball is white and other is red
${E}_{1}:$ both balls are from box ${B}_{1}$
${E}_{2}:$ both ball are from box ${B}_{2}$
${E}_{3}:$ both ball are from box ${B}_{3}$
Hence, $\text{P}\left(\text{required}\right) = \text{P}\left(\dfrac{{\text{E}}_{2}}{\text{A}}\right)$
$= \dfrac{\text{P} \left(\dfrac{\text{A}}{{\text{E}}_{2}}\right) \cdot \text{P} \left({\text{E}}_{2}\right)}{\text{P} \left(\dfrac{\text{A}}{{\text{E}}_{1}}\right) \cdot \text{P} \left({\text{E}}_{1}\right) + \text{P} \left(\dfrac{\text{A}}{{\text{E}}_{2}}\right) \cdot \text{P} \left({\text{E}}_{2}\right) + \text{P} \left(\dfrac{\text{A}}{{\text{E}}_{3}}\right) \cdot \text{P} \left({\text{E}}_{3}\right)}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{{}^{2} {\text{C}}_{1} \times {}^{3} {\text{C}}_{1}}{{}^{9} {\text{C}}_{2}} \times \dfrac{1}{3}}{\dfrac{{}^{1} {\text{C}}_{1} \times {}^{3} {\text{C}}_{1}}{{}^{6} {\text{C}}_{2}} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{{}^{2} {\text{C}}_{1} \times {}^{3} {\text{C}}_{1}}{{}^{9} {\text{C}}_{2}} \times \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{{}^{3} {\text{C}}_{1} \times {}^{4} {\text{C}}_{1}}{{}^{1 2} {\text{C}}_{2}} \times \dfrac{1}{3}}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{6}}{\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{2}{1 1}}$
$= \dfrac{5 5}{1 8 1}$

questions.q: Four fair dice $D_{1}, D_{2}, D_{3}$ and $D_{4}$; each having six faces numbered $1,2,3,4,5$ and 6 are rolled simultaneously. The probability that $D_{4}$ shows a number appearing on one of $D_{1}, D_{2}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{3}$ is
questions.solution:
$D_{4}$ can show a number appearing on one of $D_{1}, D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$ in the following cases.

Case $\mathbf{I}: D_{4}$ shows a number which is shown by exactly one of $D_{1}, D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$.

$D_{4}$ shows a number in ${ }^{6} C_{1}$ ways.

One out of $D_{1}, D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$ can be selected in ${ }^{3} C_{1}$ ways.

[The selected die shows the same number as on $D_{4}$ in one way and rest two dice show the different number in 5 ways each, ]

$\therefore$ Number of ways

$={ }^{6} C_{1} \times{ }^{3} C_{1} \times 1 \times 5 \times 5=450$

Case II : $D_{4}$ shows a number which is shown by exactly two of $D_{1}, D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$.

Number of ways

$={ }^{6} C_{1} \times{ }^{3} C_{2} \times 1 \times 1 \times 5=90$

Case III : $D_{4}$ shows a number which is shown by all three dice $D_{1}, D_{2}$ and $D_{3}$.

Number of ways

$={ }^{6} C_{1} \times{ }^{3} C_{3} \times 1 \times 1 \times 1=6$

$\therefore$ Total number of favourable ways $=450+90+6=546$ Total ways $=6 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6$

$\therefore$ Required Probability $=\frac{546}{6 \times 6 \times 6 \times 6}=\frac{91}{216}$

questions.q: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two events such that $P(X \mid Y)=\frac{1}{2}$, $P(Y / X)=\frac{1}{3}$ and $P(X \cap Y)=\frac{1}{6}$. Which of the following is (are) correct?
questions.solution:
$\because P(X / Y)=\frac{P(X \cap Y)}{P(Y)} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1 / 6}{P(Y)} \Rightarrow P(Y)=\frac{1}{3}$

Similarly, $\mathrm{P}(Y / X)=\frac{P(X \cap Y)}{P(X)}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1 / 6}{P(X)} \Rightarrow P(X)=\frac{1}{2}$

(a) $P(X \cup Y)=P(X)+P(Y)-P(X \cap Y)=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{6}=\frac{2}{3}$

$\therefore$ (a) is true.

(b) $\because P(X \cap Y)=P(X) P(Y)$

$\Rightarrow X$ and $Y$ are independent events.

$\therefore$ (b) is true.

But (c) is not true.

(d) $\mathrm{P}\left(X^{C} \cap Y\right)=P\left(X^{C}\right) \times P(Y)=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{6}$

$\therefore$ (d) is not true.

questions.q: A ship is fitted with three engines $E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$. The engines function independently of each other with respective probabilities $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$. For the ship to be operational at least two of its engines must function. Let $X$ denote the event that the ship is operational and let $X_{1}, X_{2}$ and $X_{3}$ denote respectively the events that the engines $E_{1}, E_{2}$ and $E_{3}$ are functioning. Which of the following is(are) true?
options: $P$ [Exactly two engines of the ship are functioning $[X]=\frac{7}{8}$
questions.solution:
Given that $P\left(X_{1}\right)=\frac{1}{2}, \mathrm{P}\left(X_{2}\right)=\frac{1}{4}, \mathrm{P}\left(X_{3}\right)=\frac{1}{4} P(X)=P$ (at least 2 engines are functioning)

$\begin{aligned}=P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2}\right.&\left.\cap X_{3}^{C}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2}^{C} \cap X_{3}\right) \\ &+P\left(X_{1}^{C} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right) \end{aligned} =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{4}$

(a) $P\left(X_{1}^{C} / X\right)=\frac{P\left(X_{1}^{C} \cap X\right)}{P(X)}=\frac{P\left(X_{1}^{C} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right)}{P(X)} =\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{8} \therefore$ (a) is not true.

(b) $P$ [Exactly two engines are functioning $/ X] =\frac{P[(\text{ Exactly two engines are functioning }) \cap X]}{P(X)} =\frac{P\left(X_{1}^{C} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2}^{C} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}^{C}\right)}{P(X)} =\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{7}{8} \therefore$ (b) is true.

(c) $P\left(X / X_{2}\right)=\frac{P\left(X \cap X_{2}\right)}{P\left(X_{2}\right)} =\frac{P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1}^{C} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}^{C}\right)}{P\left(X_{2}\right)} =\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{5}{8} \therefore$ (c) is not true.

(d) $P\left(X / X_{1}\right)=\frac{P\left(X \cap X_{1}\right)}{P\left(X_{1}\right)} =\frac{P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2}^{C} \cap X_{3}\right)+P\left(X_{1} \cap X_{2} \cap X_{3}^{C}\right)}{P\left(X_{1}\right)} =\frac{\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{7}{16} \therefore$ (d) is true.

questions.q: An experiment has 10 equally likely outcomes. Let $A$ and $B$ be two non-empty events of the experiment. If $A$ consists of 4 outcomes, the number of outcomes that $B$ must have so that $A$ and $B$ are independent, is
questions.solution:
$P(A)=\frac{2}{5}$
For independent events,

$\begin{aligned}$& P(A \cap B)=P(A) P(B) \Rightarrow P(A \cap B) \leq $\frac{2}{5}$\\
& \Rightarrow P(A \cap B)=$\frac{1}{10}, \frac{2}{10}, \frac{3}{10}, \frac{4}{10}$\\
& $\text{ (i) }$P(A \cap B)=$\frac{1}{10}$\\
& \Rightarrow P(A) $\cdot$P(B)=$\frac{1}{10}$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad P(B)=$\frac{1}{10} \times \frac{5}{2}=\frac{1}{4}, \text{ not possible. }$\\
& $\text{ (ii) }$P(A \cap B)=$\frac{2}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{5} \times$P(B)=$\frac{2}{10}$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad P(B)=$\frac{5}{10}, \text{ outcomes$ of }B=5
\end{aligned}$\text{ (iii) } \begin{aligned}$& P(A \cap B)=$\frac{3}{10} \Rightarrow$P(A) $\cdot$P(B)=$\frac{3}{10}$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad $\frac{2}{5} \times$P(B)=$\frac{3}{10}$\\
& P(B)=$\frac{3}{4}, \text{ not possible }
\end{aligned}

\text{ (iv) } \begin{aligned}$& P(A \cap B)=$\frac{4}{10}$\\
\Rightarrow & P(A) $\cdot$P(B)=$\frac{4}{10}$\\
\Rightarrow & P(B)=1, $\text{ outcomes$ of }B=10 .
\end{aligned}

questions.q:
Let $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ be mutually exclusive events with $P\left(H_i\right)>0, i=1,2, \ldots, n$. Let $E$ be any other event with $0 < P(E) < 1$.
Statement I $P\left(H_i / E\right)>P\left(E / H_i\right) P\left(H_i\right)$ for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$.
Statement II $\sum_{i=1}^n P\left(H_i\right)=1$
options:
Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is a correct explanation for Statement I

Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is not a correct explanation for Statement II

Statement I is true, Statement II is false

Statement I is false, Statement II is true
questions.solution:
Statement : I If $P\left(H_i \cap E\right)=0$ for some $i$, then

P$\left(\frac{H_i}{E}\right)=$P$\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right)=$0

If $P\left(H_i \cap E\right) \neq 0$ for $\forall i=1,2, \ldots . n$, then

$\begin{aligned}$P$\left(\frac{H_i}{E}\right)$& =$\frac{P\left(H_i \cap E\right)}{P\left(H_i\right)} \times \frac{P\left(H_i\right)}{P(E)}$\\
& $\left.=\frac{P\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right) \times P\left(H_i\right)}{P(E)}$>P$\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right) \cdot$P$\left(H_i\right) \quad \text{ [as }0$< P(E) < 1\right]
\end{aligned}

Hence, Statement I may not always be true.
Statement II
Clearly, $H_1 \cup H_2 \cup \ldots . \cup H_n=S$ (sample space)

\Rightarrow \quad P$\left(H_1\right)$+P$\left(H_2\right)$+\ldots+P$\left(H_n\right)$=1 .

Hence, Statement II is true.

Let $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ be mutually exclusive events with $P\left(H_i\right)>0, i=1,2, \ldots, n$. Let $E$ be any other event with $0 < P(E) < 1$.
Statement I $P\left(H_i / E\right)>P\left(E / H_i\right) P\left(H_i\right)$ for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$.
Statement II $\sum_{i=1}^n P\left(H_i\right)=1$
questions.explanation:
Statement : I If $P\left(H_i \cap E\right)=0$ for some $i$, then
$$
P\left(\frac{H_i}{E}\right)=P\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right)=0
$$
If $P\left(H_i \cap E\right) \neq 0$ for $\forall i=1,2, \ldots . n$, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
P\left(\frac{H_i}{E}\right) & =\frac{P\left(H_i \cap E\right)}{P\left(H_i\right)} \times \frac{P\left(H_i\right)}{P(E)} \\
& \left.=\frac{P\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right) \times P\left(H_i\right)}{P(E)}>P\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right) \cdot P\left(H_i\right) \quad \text{ [as } 0 < P(E) < 1\right]
\end{aligned}
$$
Hence, Statement I may not always be true.
Statement II
Clearly, $H_1 \cup H_2 \cup \ldots . \cup H_n=S$ (sample space)
$$
\Rightarrow \quad P\left(H_1\right)+P\left(H_2\right)+\ldots+P\left(H_n\right)=1 .
$$
Hence, Statement II is true.

questions.q: Let $ABC$ be the triangle with $AB = 1, AC = 3$ and $∠ BAC = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. If a circle of radius $r > 0$ touches the sides $AB, AC$ and also touches internally the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$, then the value of $r$ is ______. (round-off the value to two decimal place)
questions.solution:
Let $A$ be the origin $B$ on $x -$axis, $C$ on $y -$axis,

So on plotting the diagram we get,

Now equation of circumcircle is given by

${\left(x - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left(y - \dfrac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} = {\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{5}{2} ⋯ \left(1\right)$

Required equation of circle touches $AB$ and $AC$ and have radius $r$ so its equation is given by,

${\left(x - r\right)}^{2} + {\left(y - r\right)}^{2} = {r}^{2} ⋯ \left(2\right)$

Now given circle in equation $\left(2\right)$ touches circumcircle internally, so by property distance between the centre will be equal to modulus of difference of radii,

So, ${d}_{{c}_{1}{c}_{2}} = \left|{r}_{1} - {r}_{2}\right|$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - r\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{3}{2} - r\right)}^{2} = {\left(\left|\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}} - r\right|\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{4} + {r}^{2} - r + \dfrac{9}{4} + {r}^{2} - 3r = {\left(\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}} - r\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ 2{r}^{2} - 4r + \dfrac{5}{2} = \dfrac{5}{2} + {r}^{2} - \sqrt{10}r$

$⇒ r = 0$ or $r = 4 - \sqrt{10} = 0 . 837$

So, $r = 0 . 84$ (on rounding off)

questions.q: Consider a triangle $PQR$ having sides of lengths $p, q$ and $r$ opposite to the angles $P, Q$ and $R$, respectively. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: If $p < q$ and $p < r,$ then $cosQ > \dfrac{p}{r}$ and $cosR > \dfrac{p}{q}$
questions.solution:
(A) Applying cosine rule

$cosP = \dfrac{{q}^{2} + {r}^{2} - {p}^{2}}{2qr}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{q}{r} + \dfrac{r}{q}\right) - \dfrac{{p}^{2}}{2qr}$

We know, using $A . M . \ge G . M .$

$\left(\dfrac{q}{r} + \dfrac{r}{q}\right) \ge 2$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{q}{r} + \dfrac{r}{q}\right) \ge 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{q}{r} + \dfrac{r}{q}\right)\dfrac{- {p}^{2}}{2qr} \ge 1 - \dfrac{{p}^{2}}{2qr}$

$⇒ cosP \ge 1 - \dfrac{{p}^{2}}{2qr}$

(B) $\left(p + q\right)cosR \ge \left(q - r\right)cosP + \left(p - r\right)cosQ$

$\left(pcosR + rcosP\right) + \left(qcosR + rcosQ\right) \ge \left(qcosP + pcosQ\right)$

using projection formula

$q + p \ge r$

Which is true as sum of two sides of triangles is greater than third side.

(C) $\dfrac{q + r}{p} < \dfrac{2\sqrt{sinQsinR}}{sinP}$

$\dfrac{q + r}{p} < 2\sqrt{\dfrac{sinQsinR}{\sin^{2}P}}$

Applying sine rule

$⇒ \dfrac{q + r}{p} < 2\sqrt{\dfrac{qr}{{p}^{2}}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{q + r}{2p} < \sqrt{\dfrac{qr}{{p}^{2}}}$

Applying $A . M . \ge G . M .$

$\dfrac{\dfrac{q}{p} + \dfrac{r}{p}}{2} \ge \sqrt{\dfrac{qr}{{p}^{2}}}$

So, (C) is not true

$⇒ \dfrac{q + r}{2p} \ge \sqrt{\dfrac{qr}{{p}^{2}}}$

(D) $p < q$ & $p < r$

$⇒ p$ is smallest side

Let $cosQ > \dfrac{p}{r}$ and $cosR > \dfrac{p}{q}$ is true

$⇒ p < rcosQ$

$p < qcosR$

adding both inequalities

$⇒ 2p < rcosQ + qcosR$

using projection formula

$⇒ 2p < p$

$2 < 1$

Which is not correct.

questions.q: In a triangle $ABC$, let $AB = \sqrt{23}, BC = 3$ and $CA = 4$. Then the value of $\dfrac{cotA + cotC}{cotB}$ is
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{cotA + cotC}{cotB} = \dfrac{\dfrac{cosA}{sinA} + \dfrac{cosC}{sinC}}{\dfrac{cosB}{sinB}}$

$= \dfrac{cosAsinC + cosCsinA}{sinAsinC} \cdot \dfrac{sinB}{cosB}$

$= \dfrac{sin ( A + C )}{sinAsinC} \cdot \dfrac{sinB}{cosB}$

$= \dfrac{sin ( \pi - B )}{sinAsinC} \cdot \dfrac{sinB}{cosB}$

$= \dfrac{\sin^{2}B}{sinAsinCcosB}$

Let, $AB = c, BC = a, CA = b$

By using sine rule, we get

$= \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{accosB}$

$= \dfrac{{b}^{2}}{ac\left(\dfrac{{a}^{2} + {c}^{2} - {b}^{2}}{2ac}\right)}$

$= \dfrac{2{b}^{2}}{{a}^{2} + {c}^{2} - {b}^{2}}$

$= \dfrac{32}{9 + 23 - 16}$

$= \dfrac{32}{16} = 2$

questions.q: Let $x, y$ and $z$ be positive real numbers. Suppose $x, y$ and $z$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle opposite to its angles $X, Y$ and $Z$ respectively. If $tan\dfrac{X}{2} + tan\dfrac{Z}{2} = \dfrac{2y}{x + y + z}$, then which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
We have, $tan\dfrac{X}{2} + tan\dfrac{Z}{2} = \dfrac{2y}{x + y + z} \text{ and } s = x + y + z =$perimeter of a triangle

Apply half-angle formula and $x + y + z = s$ then,

$⇒ \dfrac{∆}{s\left(s - x\right)} + \dfrac{∆}{s\left(s - z\right)} = \dfrac{y}{s} ⇒ ∆ = \left(s - x\right)\left(s - z\right)$

$⇒ {∆}^{2} = s\left(s - x\right)\left(s - y\right)\left(s - z\right) = {\left(s - x\right)}^{2}{\left(s - z\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ {y}^{2} = {x}^{2} + {z}^{2} ⇒ ∠ Y = 90 °$

$⇒ ∠ Y = ∠ X + ∠ Z$

An option $\left(B\right)$ is correct.

Now, $\dfrac{x}{y + z} = \dfrac{sinX}{sinY + sinZ} = \dfrac{sinX}{1 + sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - X\right)} = \dfrac{2sin\dfrac{X}{2}cos\dfrac{X}{2}}{2\cos^{2}\dfrac{X}{2}} = tan\dfrac{X}{2}$

An Option $\left(C\right)$ is correct.
