questions.q: In a non-right-angled triangle $\DeltaPQR,$ let $p, q, r$ denote the lengths of the sides opposite to the angles at $P, Q, R$ respectively. The median from $R$ meets the side $PQ$ at $S,$ the perpendicular from $P$ meets the side $QR$ at $E$, and $RS$ and $PE$ intersect at $0 .$ If $p = \sqrt{3}, q = 1,$ and the radius of the circumcircle of the $\DeltaPQR$ equals $1,$ then which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution: By sine rule in $PQR$ $\dfrac{p}{sinP} = \dfrac{q}{sinQ} = \dfrac{r}{sinR} = 2R$ $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{sinP} = \dfrac{1}{sinQ} = \dfrac{1}{sinR} = 2\left(1\right)$ $sinP = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $sinQ = sinR = \dfrac{1}{2}$ $P = {60}^{°}$ or ${120}^{°}, Q = {30}^{°}$ and ${150}^{°}$ $⇒$ As $PQR$ is not a right angle triangle Only possibility is $P = {120}^{°}, Q = R = {30}^{°}$ $⇒ PQR$ is an isosceles triangle, hence, $PE$ is also a median and $‘O’$ will be centroid. ( $∆ PQE$ and $∆ PRE$ are congruent and $E$ is mid point of $QR$ ) $⇒ r = q = 1, P = \sqrt{3}$ Option $\left(A\right):$ Length of median from $R$ $RS = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2{p}^{2} + 2{q}^{2} - {r}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2{\left(\sqrt{3}\right)}^{2} + 2 ( 1 ) - 1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}$ Option $\left(B\right):$ Now, area of $\DeltaSEF = \dfrac{1}{4}\DeltaPQR$   ...$\left(i\right)$ and area of $\DeltaSOE = \dfrac{1}{3}\DeltaSEF$ ...$\left(ii\right)$ from $\left(i\right)$ and $\left(ii\right)$ $\DeltaSOE = \dfrac{1}{12}\DeltaPQR$ ...$\left(iii\right)$ $\DeltaPQR = \dfrac{1}{2}pqsinR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \sqrt{3} \times 1 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ $\DeltaSOE = \dfrac{1}{12}\DeltaPQR = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{48}$ Option $\left(D\right):$ Length of $OE$ As $O$ is centroid $OE$ will be $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of $PE$ $PE = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2{q}^{2} + 2{r}^{2} - {p}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 + 2 - 3}$ $= \dfrac{1}{2}$ $OE = \dfrac{1}{3}PE = \dfrac{1}{6}$ Option $\left(C\right):$ Radius of incircle $= \dfrac{\Delta}{S}\left(i . e . \dfrac{area}{semi - perimeter}\right)$ $= \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}}{\left(\dfrac{1 + 1 + \sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}$ $= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)}$ $= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)$

questions.explanation: By sine rule in $PQR$ $\dfrac{p}{sinP} = \dfrac{q}{sinQ} = \dfrac{r}{sinR} = 2R$ $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{sinP} = \dfrac{1}{sinQ} = \dfrac{1}{sinR} = 2\left(1\right)$ $sinP = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $sinQ = sinR = \dfrac{1}{2}$ $P = {60}^{°}$ or ${120}^{°}, Q = {30}^{°}$ and ${150}^{°}$ $⇒$ As $PQR$ is not a right angle triangle Only possibility is $P = {120}^{°}, Q = R = {30}^{°}$ $⇒ PQR$ is an isosceles triangle, hence, $PE$ is also a median and $‘O’$ will be centroid. ( $∆ PQE$ and $∆ PRE$ are congruent and $E$ is mid point of $QR$ ) $⇒ r = q = 1, P = \sqrt{3}$ Option $\left(A\right):$ Length of median from $R$ $RS = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2{p}^{2} + 2{q}^{2} - {r}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2{\left(\sqrt{3}\right)}^{2} + 2 ( 1 ) - 1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}$ Option $\left(B\right):$ Now, area of $\DeltaSEF = \dfrac{1}{4}\DeltaPQR$   ...$\left(i\right)$ and area of $\DeltaSOE = \dfrac{1}{3}\DeltaSEF$ ...$\left(ii\right)$ from $\left(i\right)$ and $\left(ii\right)$ $\DeltaSOE = \dfrac{1}{12}\DeltaPQR$ ...$\left(iii\right)$ $\DeltaPQR = \dfrac{1}{2}pqsinR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \sqrt{3} \times 1 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ $\DeltaSOE = \dfrac{1}{12}\DeltaPQR = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{48}$ Option $\left(D\right):$ Length of $OE$ As $O$ is centroid $OE$ will be $\dfrac{1}{3}$ of $PE$ $PE = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2{q}^{2} + 2{r}^{2} - {p}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 + 2 - 3}$ $= \dfrac{1}{2}$ $OE = \dfrac{1}{3}PE = \dfrac{1}{6}$ Option $\left(C\right):$ Radius of incircle $= \dfrac{\Delta}{S}\left(i . e . \dfrac{area}{semi - perimeter}\right)$ $= \dfrac{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}}{\left(\dfrac{1 + 1 + \sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}$ $= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)}$ $= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)$

questions.q: In a triangle $PQR, let∠PQR = {30}^{o}$ and the sides $PQandQR$ have lengths $10\sqrt{3}and10$ , respectively. Then, which of the following statement(s) is (are) TRUE?
options: The radius of the in circle of the triangle $PQRis10\sqrt{3} - 15$
The area of the circumcircle of the triangle $PQRis100\pi$
questions.solution:
$cos ⁡ {30}^{o} = \dfrac{{\left(10\sqrt{3}\right)}^{2} + {\left(10\right)}^{2} - {\left(PR\right)}^{2}}{2 \times 10\sqrt{3} \times 10}$
$⇒ PR = 10$
$∵ QR = PR ⇒ ∠PQR = ∠QPR$
$∠QPR = {30}^{o}$
$\left(B\right)$ Area of $∆ PQR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10\sqrt{3} \times 10 \times sin ⁡ {30}^{o} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10\sqrt{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2}$
$= 25\sqrt{3}$
$∠QRP = {180}^{o} - \left({30}^{o} + {30}^{o}\right) = {120}^{o}$
$\left(C\right) r = \dfrac{∆}{S} = \dfrac{25\sqrt{3}}{\left(\dfrac{10 + 10 + 10\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{25\sqrt{3}}{10 + 5\sqrt{3}}$
$= 5\sqrt{3} . \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right) = 10\sqrt{3} - 15$
$\left(D\right) R = \dfrac{a}{2sin ⁡ A} = \dfrac{10}{2sin ⁡ {30}^{o}} = 10$
$∴ Area = \pi{R}^{2} = 100\pi$

Paragraph: Let $O$ be the origin, and $\overrightarrow{O X}, \overrightarrow{O Y}, \overrightarrow{O Z}$ be three unit vectors in the directions of the sides $\overrightarrow{Q R}, \overrightarrow{R P}$, $\overrightarrow{P Q}$, respectively, of a triangle $P Q R$.
Question: If the triangle $P Q R$ varies, then the minimum value of $\cos (P+Q)+\cos (Q+R)+\cos (R+P)$ is
questions.solution:
$cos\left(P + Q\right) + cos\left(Q + R\right) + cos\left(R + P\right)$

$= cos\left(180 - R\right) + cos\left(180 - P\right) + cos\left(180 - Q\right)$

$= - \left[cosP + cosQ + cosR\right]$

In any $\DeltaPQR$, $cosP + cosQ + cosR \le \dfrac{3}{2}$

$⇒ - \left(cosP + cosQ + cosR\right) \ge - \dfrac{3}{2}$

questions.q: In a $∆ XYZ$ let $x, y, z$,  be the lengths of sides opposite to the angles, $X, Y, Z$, respectively and $2s = x + y + z .$ If $\dfrac{s - x}{4} = \dfrac{s - y}{3} = \dfrac{s - z}{2}$ and area of incircle of the triangle XYZ is $\dfrac{8\pi}{3},$ then
options: Area of the triangle XYZ is $6\sqrt{6}$
The radius of circumcircle of the triangle XYZ is $\dfrac{35}{6}\sqrt{6}$
questions.solution:
Let $\dfrac{s - x}{4} = \dfrac{s - y}{3} = \dfrac{s - z}{2} = k( K \ne 0 )$
$s - x = 4k$
$s - y = 3k$
$s - z = 2k$
$Adding this, we get$
$3s - \left(x + y + z\right) = 9k$
$⟹ s = 9k$
$⇒x = 5k, y = 6k, z = 7k$

$⇒\pir^{2} = \dfrac{8\pi}{3}$
$\pi{\left(\dfrac{\Delta}{s}\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{8\pi}{3}$
$∆ = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}}.$s
$\sqrt{s\left(s - x\right)\left(s - y\right)\left(s - z\right)} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}} . s$
$\sqrt{9k . 4k . 3k . 2k} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}}9k$
$\sqrt{24.9}k^{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}} . 9k⇒ 3 \times 2\sqrt{6}K = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}9$
$⇒ K\dfrac{2\sqrt{2}.9}{6\sqrt{6}\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{2}} = 1$
$k = 1$
$⇒x = 5, y = 6, z = 7$
$\Delta = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}} . 9k = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3}} . 9 = 6\sqrt{6}$
R = circumradius $= \dfrac{xyz}{4\Delta} = \dfrac{5 . 6 . 7}{4 . . 6\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{35}{4\sqrt{6}}$
Using formula $sin ⁡ \dfrac{X}{2}sin ⁡ \dfrac{Y}{2}sin ⁡ \dfrac{Z}{2} = \dfrac{r}{4R} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\Delta}{s}}{\dfrac{xyz}{\Delta}} = \dfrac{{\Delta}^{2}}{s . xyz} = \dfrac{36.6}{9.5 . 6.7} = \dfrac{4}{35}$
$cos ⁡ Z =\dfrac{x^{2} + y^{2} - z^{2}}{2xy} = \dfrac{25 + 36 - 49}{2.5 . 6} = \dfrac{1}{5}$
${sin}^{2} ⁡ \left(\dfrac{X + Y}{2}\right){= cos}^{2} ⁡ \dfrac{Z}{2} = \dfrac{1 + cos ⁡ Z}{2} = \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{5}}{2} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

$\frac{2 \sin P-\sin 2 P}{2 \sin P+\sin 2 P}=\frac{2 \sin P-2 \sin P \cos P}{2 \sin P+2 \sin P \cos P}=\frac{1-\cos P}{1-\sin P}$

$=\frac{2 \sin ^{2} \frac{P}{2}}{2 \cos ^{2} \frac{P}{2}}=\tan ^{2} \frac{P}{2}=\frac{(s-b)(s-c)}{s(s-a)}$ where $s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}$

$=\frac{(s-b)^{2}(s-c)^{2}}{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}=\frac{(a+c-b)^{2}(a+b-c)^{2}}{16 . \Delta^{2}}$

$=\frac{\left(2+\frac{5}{2}-\frac{7}{2}\right)^{2}\left(2+\frac{7}{2}-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}}{16 \Delta^{2}}=\frac{1 \times 9}{16 \Delta^{2}}=\left(\frac{3}{4 \Delta}\right)^{2}$

questions.solution:
Using, $\cos C=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2 a b}$
$\begin{gathered} \Rightarrow\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{\left(x^2+x+1\right)^2+\left(x^2-1\right)^2-(2 x+1)^2}{2\left(x^2+x+1\right) \left($ x^2-1\right)}$\\ \Rightarrow(x+2)(x+1)(x-1) x+\left(x^2-1\right)^2 \\ =\sqrt{3}\left(x^2+x+1\right)\left(x^2-1\right) \\ \Rightarrow x^2+2 x+\left(x^2-1\right)=\sqrt{3}\left(x^2+x+1\right) \\ \Rightarrow(2-\sqrt{3})x^2+(2-\sqrt{3})x-(\sqrt{3}+1)=0 \end{gathered} ⇒ x=-(2+\sqrt{3}) and x=1+\sqrt{3} But, x=-(2+\sqrt{3}) \Rightarrow$ c$ is negative. $\therefore \quad x=1+\sqrt{3}$ is the only solution. questions.q: Let $A B C$ and $A B C^{\prime}$ be two non-congruent triangles with sides $A B=4$, $A C=A C^{\prime}=2 \sqrt{2}$ and angle $B=30^{\circ}$. The absolute value of the difference between the areas of these triangles is
questions.solution: In $\triangle A B C$, by sine rule, $\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{\sin 30^{{}^{\circ}}}=\frac{4}{\sin C}$\\ \Rightarrow \quad & C=45^{{}^{\circ}}, C^{\prime}=135^{{}^{\circ}} \\ \Rightarrow & A=180^{{}^{\circ}}-$\left($45^{{}^{\circ}}+30^{{}^{\circ}}\right)=105^{{}^{\circ}} \end{aligned} $$ \\ When $\quad C^{\prime}=135^{{}^{\circ}}$, then $\begin{aligned}$& \quad A=180^{{}^{\circ}}-$\left($135^{{}^{\circ}}+30^{{}^{\circ}}\right)=15^{{}^{\circ}} \\ & $\text{ Area of } \triangle$A B C=$\frac{1}{2}$A B $\times$A C \sin A \\ & =$\frac{1}{2} \times$4 $\times$2 $\sqrt{2} \sin \left($105^{{}^{\circ}}\right) \\ & =4 $\sqrt{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2 \sqrt{2}}=$2($\sqrt{3}+$1) \\ & $\text{ Area of } \triangle$A B C^{\prime}=$\frac{1}{2}$A B $\times$A C \sin A \\ & =$\frac{1}{2} \times$4 $\times$2 $\sqrt{2} \sin \left($15^{{}^{\circ}}\right)=2($\sqrt{3}-$1) \end{aligned} Difference of areas of triangles =|2($\sqrt{3}+$1)-2($\sqrt{3}-$1)|=4 $$ \\ A D=2, D C=2 Difference of areas of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A B C^{\prime}\begin{aligned}$& =$\text{ Area of } \triangle$A C C^{\prime} \\ & =$\frac{1}{2}$A D $\times$C C^{\prime}=$\frac{1}{2} \times$2 $\times$4=4 \end{aligned}

questions.explanation:
In $\triangle A B C$, by sine rule, $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=\frac{4}{\sin C} \\ \Rightarrow \quad & C=45^{\circ}, C^{\prime}=135^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow & A=180^{\circ}-\left(45^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\right)=105^{\circ} \end{aligned} $$
When $\quad C^{\prime}=135^{\circ}$, then $$ \begin{aligned} & \quad A=180^{\circ}-\left(135^{\circ}+30^{\circ}\right)=15^{\circ} \\ & \text{ Area of } \triangle A B C=\frac{1}{2} A B \times A C \sin A \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 2 \sqrt{2} \sin \left(105^{\circ}\right) \\ & =4 \sqrt{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2 \sqrt{2}}=2(\sqrt{3}+1) \\ & \text{ Area of } \triangle A B C^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2} A B \times A C \sin A \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 2 \sqrt{2} \sin \left(15^{\circ}\right)=2(\sqrt{3}-1) \end{aligned} $$ Difference of areas of triangles $$ =|2(\sqrt{3}+1)-2(\sqrt{3}-1)|=4 $$
$$ A D=2, D C=2 $$ Difference of areas of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A B C^{\prime} $ \begin{aligned} & =$\text{ Area$ of } \triangle A C C^{\prime} \\ & =$\frac{1}{2}$ A D \times C C^{\prime}=$\frac{1}{2}$ \times 2 \times 4=4 \end{aligned} $$

questions.q: In a $\triangle A B C$ with fixed base $B C$, the vertex $A$ moves such that $\cos B+\cos C=4 \sin ^2 \frac{A}{2}$. If $a, b$ and $c$ denote the lengths of the sides of the triangle opposite to the angles $A, B$ and $C$ respectively, then
options:
$b+c=4 a$

$b+c=2 a$

locus of point $A$ is an ellipse

locus of point $A$ is a pair of straight line
questions.solution: Given, $\cos B+\cos C=4 \sin ^2 \frac{A}{2} \begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow 2 \cos $\left(\frac{B+C}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{B-C}{2}\right)=$4 \sin ^2 $\frac{A}{2}$\\ & \Rightarrow 2 \sin $\frac{A}{2}\left[\cos \left(\frac{B-C}{2}\right)-$2 \sin $\frac{A}{2}\right]=$0 \\ & \Rightarrow \cos $\left(\frac{B-C}{2}\right)-$2 \cos $\left(\frac{B+C}{2}\right)=$0 \\ & \Rightarrow-\cos $\frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{C}{2}+$3 \sin $\frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}=$0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \tan $\frac{B}{2} \tan \frac{C}{2}=\frac{1}{3}$\\ & \Rightarrow \quad $\sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-c)}{s(s-b)} \cdot \frac{(s-b)(s-a)}{s(s-c)}}=\frac{1}{3}$\\ & \Rightarrow \quad $\frac{s-a}{s}=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow$2 s=3 a \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b+c=2 a \end{aligned} $$ \\ $\therefore$ Locus of $A$ is an ellipse.
questions.question: In a $\triangle A B C$ with fixed base $B C$, the vertex $A$ moves such that $\cos B+\cos C=4 \sin ^2 \frac{A}{2}$. If $a, b$ and $c$ denote the lengths of the sides of the triangle opposite to the angles $A, B$ and $C$ respectively, then
questions.explanation:
Given, $\cos B+\cos C=4 \sin ^2 \frac{A}{2}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2 \cos \left(\frac{B+C}{2}\right) \cos \left(\frac{B-C}{2}\right)=4 \sin ^2 \frac{A}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow 2 \sin \frac{A}{2}\left[\cos \left(\frac{B-C}{2}\right)-2 \sin \frac{A}{2}\right]=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \cos \left(\frac{B-C}{2}\right)-2 \cos \left(\frac{B+C}{2}\right)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow-\cos \frac{B}{2} \cos \frac{C}{2}+3 \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \tan \frac{B}{2} \tan \frac{C}{2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \sqrt{\frac{(s-a)(s-c)}{s(s-b)} \cdot \frac{(s-b)(s-a)}{s(s-c)}}=\frac{1}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \frac{s-a}{s}=\frac{1}{3} \Rightarrow 2 s=3 a \\ & \Rightarrow \quad b+c=2 a \end{aligned} $$
$\therefore$ Locus of $A$ is an ellipse.

questions.q:
Match each entry in List-I to the correct entry in List-II and choose the correct option.
List-IList-II
(P) If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$, then the quadratic equation with roots $\dfrac{1}{(\alpha+1)^{2026}}$ and $\dfrac{1}{(\beta+1)^{2026}}$ is(1) $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$
(Q) If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$, then the quadratic equation with roots $\dfrac{1}{(\alpha+1)^{2027}}$ and $\dfrac{1}{(\beta+1)^{2027}}$ is(2) $x^2 - x + 1 = 0$
(R) If $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2 - x + 1 = 0$, then the value of $\dfrac{1}{(\gamma-1)^{2026}} + \dfrac{1}{(\delta-1)^{2026}}$ is(3) $x^2 + x - 1 = 0$
(S) If $p$ and $r$ are the distinct roots of the equation $x^2 + x - 1 = 0$, then the value of $\dfrac{1}{(p+1)^3} + \dfrac{1}{(r+1)^3}$ is(4) $-1$
(5) $-4$
questions.solution:
For (P):
Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$, we have $\alpha^2 + \alpha + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha + 1 = -\alpha^2$ and $\alpha^3 = 1$.
$\dfrac{1}{(\alpha+1)^{2026}} = \dfrac{1}{(-\alpha^2)^{2026}} = \dfrac{1}{\alpha^{4052}}$
Since $4052 = 3 \times 1350 + 2$, $\alpha^{4052} = (\alpha^3)^{1350} \cdot \alpha^2 = \alpha^2$.
Thus, $\dfrac{1}{\alpha^2} = \dfrac{\alpha^3}{\alpha^2} = \alpha$.
Similarly, $\dfrac{1}{(\beta+1)^{2026}} = \beta$.
The quadratic equation with roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is the original equation $x^2 + x + 1 = 0$.
So, (P) $\rightarrow$ (1).

For (Q):
$\dfrac{1}{(\alpha+1)^{2027}} = \dfrac{1}{(-\alpha^2)^{2027}} = -\dfrac{1}{\alpha^{4054}}$
Since $4054 = 3 \times 1351 + 1$, $\alpha^{4054} = \alpha$.
Thus, $-\dfrac{1}{\alpha} = -\beta$.
Similarly, the other root is $-\alpha$.
Sum of roots $= -\alpha - \beta = -(\alpha + \beta) = -(-1) = 1$.
Product of roots $= (-\alpha)(-\beta) = \alpha\beta = 1$.
The quadratic equation is $x^2 - x + 1 = 0$.
So, (Q) $\rightarrow$ (2).

For (R):
Since $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are roots of $x^2 - x + 1 = 0$, we have $\gamma^2 - \gamma + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \gamma - 1 = \gamma^2$ and $\gamma^3 = -1$.
$\dfrac{1}{(\gamma-1)^{2026}} = \dfrac{1}{(\gamma^2)^{2026}} = \dfrac{1}{\gamma^{4052}}$
$\gamma^{4052} = (\gamma^3)^{1350} \cdot \gamma^2 = (-1)^{1350} \cdot \gamma^2 = \gamma^2$.
Thus, $\dfrac{1}{\gamma^2} = \dfrac{\gamma}{\gamma^3} = -\gamma$.
Similarly, the second term is $-\delta$.
The sum is $-\gamma - \delta = -(\gamma + \delta) = -(1) = -1$.
So, (R) $\rightarrow$ (4).

For (S):
Since $p$ and $r$ are roots of $x^2 + x - 1 = 0$, we have $x^2 + x = 1 \Rightarrow x(x+1) = 1 \Rightarrow x+1 = \dfrac{1}{x}$.
$\dfrac{1}{(p+1)^3} + \dfrac{1}{(r+1)^3} = p^3 + r^3$
We know $p+r = -1$ and $pr = -1$.
$p^3 + r^3 = (p+r)^3 - 3pr(p+r) = (-1)^3 - 3(-1)(-1) = -1 - 3 = -4$.
So, (S) $\rightarrow$ (5).

Answer: (P) $\rightarrow$ (1), (Q) $\rightarrow$ (2), (R) $\rightarrow$ (4), (S) $\rightarrow$ (5)

questions.q:
Let $a, b, c$ be positive integers in arithmetic progression such that the equation
$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$
has only integer solutions.
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE ?
options: $c - b$ is an integer multiple of $a$
Both the roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are odd integers
If $b = 8$, then $x = 3$ is a root of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$
questions.solution:
Given $a, b, c$ are in arithmetic progression, we have $2b = a + c$.

Let the integer roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ be $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

Sum of the roots is $\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac{b}{a}$ and product of the roots is $\alpha \beta = \dfrac{c}{a}$.

Dividing the arithmetic progression condition by $a$, we get:

$\dfrac{2b}{a} = 1 + \dfrac{c}{a}$

Substituting the sum and product of the roots:

$-2(\alpha + \beta) = 1 + \alpha \beta$

$\alpha \beta + 2\alpha + 2\beta + 1 = 0$

Adding $3$ to both sides to factorize:

$\alpha \beta + 2\alpha + 2\beta + 4 = 3$

$(\alpha + 2)(\beta + 2) = 3$

Since $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are integers, $(\alpha + 2)$ and $(\beta + 2)$ must be integer factors of $3$. The possible pairs are $(1, 3)$, $(3, 1)$, $(-1, -3)$, and $(-3, -1)$.

If $(\alpha + 2, \beta + 2) = (1, 3)$ or $(3, 1)$, the roots are $-1$ and $1$. The sum of the roots is $0$, which implies $b = 0$. This is rejected because $b$ is a positive integer.

If $(\alpha + 2, \beta + 2) = (-1, -3)$ or $(-3, -1)$, the roots are $-3$ and $-5$. The sum of the roots is $-8$, which implies $-\dfrac{b}{a} = -8 \Rightarrow b = 8a$.

The product of the roots is $15$, which implies $\dfrac{c}{a} = 15 \Rightarrow c = 15a$.

Since $a$ is a positive integer, $b = 8a$ and $c = 15a$ are also positive integers. The roots of the equation are always $-3$ and $-5$.

Evaluating the given statements:

$c - b = 15a - 8a = 7a$, which is an integer multiple of $a$.

The roots are $-3$ and $-5$, both of which are odd integers.

If $c = 15$, then $15a = 15 \Rightarrow a = 1$. Consequently, $b = 8(1) = 8$. Thus, $ab = 1 \times 8 = 8$.

If $b = 8$, then $8a = 8 \Rightarrow a = 1$. The roots are $-3$ and $-5$, so $x = 3$ is not a root.

Answer: $c - b$ is an integer multiple of $a$; Both the roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are odd integers; If $c = 15$, then $ab = 8$

If $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$, and $\alpha_4$ are all the roots of the equation $f(x)=0$, then $\left|\alpha_1\right|^2+\left|\alpha_2\right|^2+\left|\alpha_3\right|^2+\left|\alpha_4\right|^2$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution:
$f(1)=1+a+b+c=-9 \quad \Rightarrow \quad a+b+c=-10.....(1)$
$4 x^3+3 a x^2+2 b x=0$ roots are $\sqrt{3} i,-\sqrt{3} i, 0$
$\Rightarrow4 x^2+3 a x+2 b=0 < ^{\sqrt{3i}}_{-{\sqrt{3i}}}$
$\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{a}=0 ~\&~ \frac{2 \mathrm{~b}}{4}=(\sqrt{3} \mathrm{i})(-\sqrt{3} \mathrm{i})$
$\mathrm{b}=6$ use $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}$ in (1) $\Rightarrow \mathrm{c}=-16$
$\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})=\mathrm{x}^4+6 \mathrm{x}^2-16=0 \\ & \left(\mathrm{x}^2+8\right)\left(\mathrm{x}^2-2\right)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & \mathrm{x}= \pm \sqrt{8} \mathrm{i}, \pm \sqrt{2}\end{array}$
$\Rightarrow \quad\left|\alpha_1\right|^2+\left|\alpha_2\right|^2+\left|\alpha_3\right|^2+\left|\alpha_4\right|^2=20$

questions.q: For $x \in R$, the number of real roots of the equation $3{x}^{2} - 4\left|{x}^{2} - 1\right| + x - 1 = 0$ is
questions.solution:
$\left|{x}^{2} - 1\right| = \left\{$\begin{array}{ll}{x}^{2} - 1, {x}^{2} \ge 1 \\ - $\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)${x}^{2} < 1\end{array}\right

Case 1

${x}^{2} - 1 < 0 ⇒ x \in ( - 1, 1 )$

$3{x}^{2} + 4\left({x}^{2} - 1\right) + x - 1 = 0$

$7{x}^{2} + x - 5 = 0$

$x = \dfrac{- 1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 140}}{2 \times 7} = \dfrac{- 1 + \sqrt{141}}{14}, \dfrac{- 1 - \sqrt{141}}{14}$

We know, $\sqrt{141} \approx 11 . 5$

So, both roots lie in the interval $\left(- 1, 1\right)$

Case 2

${x}^{2} - 1 \ge 0 ⇒ x \in ( - \infty , - 1 ] ∪ [ 1, \infty )$

$3{x}^{2} - 4\left({x}^{2} - 1\right) + x - 1 = 0$

$- {x}^{2} + 4 + x - 1 = 0$

${x}^{2} - x - 3 = 0$

$x = \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 12}}{2} = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{13}}{2}, \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{13}}{2}$

We know, $3 < \sqrt{13} < 4$

So, both roots lie in the interval $( - \infty , - 1 ] ∪ [ 1, \infty )$

Hence, $4$ real roots.

questions.q: Suppose $a, b$ denote the distinct real roots of the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2} + 20x - 2020$ and suppose $c, d$ denote the distinct complex roots of the quadratic polynomial ${x}^{2} - 20x + 2020$. Then the value of $ac\left(a - c\right) + ad\left(a - d\right) + bc\left(b - c\right) + bd\left(b - d\right)$
questions.solution:
Finding the sum and product of roots of the two given quadratic equations i.e.

$a + b = - 20 \text{ and } ab = - 2020 . . . . . . . . . . . \left(i\right)$

$c + d = 20 \text{ and } cd = 2020 . . . . . . . . . . . \left(ii\right)$

Now, $ac\left(a - c\right) + ad\left(a - d\right) + bc\left(b - c\right) + bd\left(b - d\right)$

$= {a}^{2}\left(c + d\right) - a\left({c}^{2} + {d}^{2}\right) + {b}^{2}\left(c + d\right) - b\left({c}^{2} + {d}^{2}\right)$

$= \left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2}\right)\left(c + d\right) - \left(a + b\right)\left({c}^{2} + {d}^{2}\right)$

$= \left\{{\left(a + b\right)}^{2} - 2ab\right\}\left(c + d\right) - \left(a + b\right)\left\{{\left(c + d\right)}^{2} - 2cd\right\}$

$= \left\{{\left(- 20\right)}^{2} - 2\left(- 2020\right)\right\}\left(20\right) - \left(- 20\right)\left\{{\left(20\right)}^{2} - 2\left(2020\right)\right\}$ (using equations $\left(i\right) \text{ and } \left(ii\right)$)

$= 16000$

Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of ${x}^{2} - x - 1 = 0,$ with $\alpha > \beta .$ For all positive integers $n,$ define
${a}_{n} = \dfrac{{\alpha}^{n} - {\beta}^{n}}{\alpha - \beta}, n \ge 1$
${b}_{1} = 1$ and ${b}_{n} = {a}_{n - 1} + {a}_{n + 1}, n \ge 2 .$
Then which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Given, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of ${x}^{2} - x - 1 = 0$

${a}_{k + 2} - {a}_{k} = \dfrac{\left({\alpha}^{k + 2} - {\beta}^{k + 2}\right) - \left({\alpha}^{k} - {\beta}^{k}\right)}{\alpha - \beta} = \dfrac{\left({\alpha}^{k + 2} - {\alpha}^{k}\right) - \left({\beta}^{k + 2} - {\beta}^{k}\right)}{\alpha - \beta}$

$= \dfrac{{\alpha}^{k}\left({\alpha}^{2} - 1\right) - {\beta}^{k}\left({\beta}^{2} - 1\right)}{\alpha - \beta} = {a}_{k + 1}$

$⇒ {a}_{k + 2} - {a}_{k} = {a}_{k + 1} ⇒ {a}_{k + 2} - {a}_{k + 1} = {a}_{k}$

$\mathop{∑ {a}_{k}}_{k = 1}^{n} = {a}_{k + 2} - {a}_{2} = {a}_{k + 2} - \dfrac{{\alpha}^{2} - {\beta}^{2}}{\alpha - \beta} = {a}_{k + 2} - \left(\alpha + \beta\right)$

$= {a}_{k + 2} - 1$

$⇒ {a}_{1} + {a}_{2} + {a}_{3} + . . . . . + {a}_{n} = {a}_{n + 2} - 1$
Option $( B )$
$\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}\dfrac{{a}_{n}}{{10}^{n}} = \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}\dfrac{{\alpha}^{n} - {\beta}^{n}}{( \alpha - \beta ) {10}^{n}}$
$= \dfrac{1}{\alpha - \beta}\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}\left({\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{10}\right)}^{n} - {\left(\dfrac{\beta}{10}\right)}^{n}\right)$
$= \dfrac{1}{\alpha - \beta}\left[\dfrac{\dfrac{\alpha}{10}}{1 - \dfrac{\alpha}{10}} - \dfrac{\dfrac{\beta}{10}}{1 - \dfrac{\beta}{10}}\right]$
$= \dfrac{1}{\alpha - \beta}\left[\dfrac{\alpha}{10 - \alpha} - \dfrac{\beta}{10 - \beta}\right]$
$= \dfrac{1}{\alpha - \beta}\left[\dfrac{10\alpha - 10\beta}{\left(10 - \alpha\right)\left(10 - \beta\right)}\right]$
$= \dfrac{1}{\alpha - \beta}\left[\dfrac{10\left(\alpha - \beta\right)}{100 - 10\left(\alpha + \beta\right) + \alpha\beta}\right]$
$= \dfrac{10}{100 - 10 - 1} = \dfrac{10}{89}$
Option $( C ) :$
$\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}\dfrac{{b}_{n}}{{10}^{n}} = \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}\dfrac{{\alpha}^{n} + {\beta}^{n}}{{10}^{n}} = \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{\infty}{\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{10}\right)}^{n} + {\left(\dfrac{\beta}{10}\right)}^{n}$
$= \dfrac{\dfrac{\alpha}{10}}{1 - \dfrac{\alpha}{10}} + \dfrac{\dfrac{\beta}{10}}{1 - \dfrac{\beta}{10}}$
apply sum of infinite G.P. with $\left(a = \dfrac{\alpha}{10}andr = \dfrac{\alpha}{10}\right)$
$= \dfrac{10\left(\alpha + \beta\right) - 2\alpha\beta}{\left(10 - \alpha\right)\left(10 - \beta\right)}$
$= \dfrac{10 ( 1 ) - 2 ( - 1 )}{100 + \alpha\beta - 10 ( \alpha + \beta )} = \dfrac{12}{100 - 1 - 10} = \dfrac{12}{89}$
Option $( D ) :$
As given ${b}_{n} = {a}_{n - 1} + {a}_{n + 1}$
${b}_{n} = \dfrac{{\alpha}^{n - 1} - {\beta}^{n - 1}}{\alpha - \beta} + \dfrac{{\alpha}^{n + 1} - {\beta}^{n + 1}}{\alpha - \beta}$
$∵ \alpha - \beta = 1$
${b}_{n} = \left({\alpha}^{n - 1} - {\beta}^{n - 1}\right) + \left({\alpha}^{n + 1} - {\beta}^{n + 1}\right)$
Now, as $\alpha\beta = 1$
$∴ {\alpha}^{n}\beta = - {\alpha}^{n - 1}$
$∴ \alpha{\beta}^{n} = - {\beta}^{n - 1}$
${b}_{n} = {\alpha}^{n}\left(\alpha - \beta\right) + {\beta}^{n}\left(\alpha - \beta\right)$
${b}_{n} = {\alpha}^{n} + {\beta}^{n}$

Paragraph: Let $p, q$ be integers and let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of the equation, $x^{2}-x-1=0$, where $\alpha \neq \beta$. For $n=0,1,2, \ldots$, let $a_{n}=p \alpha^{n}+q \beta^{n}$ FACT: If $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers and $a+b \sqrt{5}=0$, then $a=0=b$.
Question: If $a_{4}=28$, then $p+2 q=$
questions.solution:
${\alpha}^{2} = \alpha + 1$
$⇒ {\alpha}^{4} = {( {\alpha}^{2} )}^{2}$
$⇒ {\alpha}^{4} = {( \alpha + 1 )}^{2}$
$⇒ {\alpha}^{4} = {\alpha}^{2} + 2\alpha + 1$
$⇒ {\alpha}^{4} = \alpha + 1 + 2\alpha + 1$
$⇒ {\alpha}^{4} = 3\alpha + 2$

$Also\alpha + \beta = 1$

$∴ {a}_{4} = 28 ⇒ p{\alpha}^{4} + q{\beta}^{4} = p\left(3\alpha + 2\right) + q\left(3\beta + 2\right) = 28$

$⇒ p\left(3\alpha + 2\right) + q\left(3 - 3\alpha + 2\right) = 28$

$⇒ \alpha\left(3p - 3q\right) + 2p + 5q = 28$ (as $\alpha \in {Q}^{c}$) (as it is root of quadratic equation)

$⇒ p = q, 2p + 5q = 28 ⇒ p = q = 4$

$∴ p + 2q = 12$

questions.q: Let S be the set of all non - zero real numbers $\alpha$ such that the quadratic equation $\alpha{x}^{2} - x + \alpha = 0$ has two distinct real roots ${x}_{1}and{x}_{2}$ satisfying the inequality $\left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right| < 1 .$ Which of the following intervals is(are) a subset(s) of S?
questions.solution:
$\alpha{x}^{2} - x + \alpha = 0$
$\left|{x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right| < 0$
$\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - 4{\alpha}^{2}}}{\alpha}\right| < 1$
$\sqrt{1 - 4{\alpha}^{2}} < | \alpha |$
$1 - 4{\alpha}^{2} < {\alpha}^{2}$
${\alpha}^{2} - \dfrac{1}{5} > 0$
$\alpha \in \left(- \infty, - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right) ∪ \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \infty\right)$
Also, $1 - 4{\alpha}^{2} > 0$
${\alpha}^{2} - \dfrac{1}{4} < 0$
$\left(\alpha - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\left(\alpha + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) < 0$
$\alpha \in \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$
Taking intersection
$\alpha \in \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\right) ∪ \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

questions.q:
The value of

$6+\log _{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}}} \cdots}}\right) \text{$ is }
questions.solution:
Let $x=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}}}}} \ldots \ldots \Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{2}} \sqrt{4-x} \Rightarrow \quad 3 \sqrt{2} x=\sqrt{4-x} \begin{array}{l}

\Rightarrow \quad 18 x^{2}=4-x \\

\Rightarrow \quad 18 x^{2}+x-4=0 \\

\Rightarrow \quad(9 x-4)(2 x+1)=0 \\

\Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{4}{9} \text{ or } x=-\frac{1}{2}

\end{array}$

(Not possible because log is not define for -ve value)

$\begin{aligned}

\therefore \quad & 6+\log _{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\frac{4}{9}\right)=6+\log _{\frac{3}{2}}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{-2} \\

&=6-2=4

\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The value of $b$ for which the equations $x^2+b x-1=0, x^2+x+b=0$ have one root in common is
questions.solution:
If $\quad a_1 x^2+b_1 x+c_1=0$
and $a_2 x^2+b_2 x+c_2=0$
have a common real root, then

$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad\left($ a_1 c_2-a_2 c_1\right)^2=$\left($ b_1 c_2-\right. & $\left.$ b_2 c_1\right) \\
& $\left($ a_1 b_2-a_2 b_1\right)
\end{aligned}

$\left.\therefore \begin{array}{l}x^2+b x-1=0 \\ x^2+x+b=0\end{array}\right\}$ have a common root.
$\Rightarrow \quad(1+b)^2=\left(b^2+1\right)(1-b)\Rightarrow b^2+2 b+1=b^2-b^3+1-b\Rightarrow \quad b^3+3 b=0 \Rightarrow b\left(b^2+3\right)=0\Rightarrow \quad b=0, \pm \sqrt{3} i$
questions.question: The value of $b$ for which the equations $x^2+b x-1=0, x^2+x+b=0$ have one root in common is
questions.explanation:
If $\quad a_1 x^2+b_1 x+c_1=0$
and $a_2 x^2+b_2 x+c_2=0$
have a common real root, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow \quad\left(a_1 c_2-a_2 c_1\right)^2=\left(b_1 c_2-\right. & \left.b_2 c_1\right) \\
& \left(a_1 b_2-a_2 b_1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$
$\left.\therefore \begin{array}{l}x^2+b x-1=0 \\ x^2+x+b=0\end{array}\right\}$ have a common root.
$\Rightarrow \quad(1+b)^2=\left(b^2+1\right)(1-b)$
$\Rightarrow b^2+2 b+1=b^2-b^3+1-b$
$\Rightarrow \quad b^3+3 b=0 \Rightarrow b\left(b^2+3\right)=0$
$\Rightarrow \quad b=0, \pm \sqrt{3} i$

questions.q: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^2-6 x-2=0$ with $\alpha>\beta$. If $a_n=\alpha^n-\beta^n$ for $n \geq 1$, then the value of $\frac{a_{10}-2 a_8}{2 a_9}$ is
questions.solution:
$\frac{a_{10}-2 a_8}{2 a_9}=\frac{\left(\alpha^{10}-\beta^{10}\right)-2\left(\alpha^8-\beta^8\right)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}$ $=\frac{\alpha^8\left(\alpha^2-2\right)-\beta^8\left(\beta^2-2\right)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}$ $\left[\because \alpha\right.$ is root of $x^2-6 x-2=0$ $\left.\alpha^2-2=6 \alpha\right]$
Also, $\beta$ is root of $x^2-6 x-2=0$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \beta^2-2=6 \beta \\
& =\frac{\alpha^8(6 \alpha)-\beta^8(6 \beta)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}=\frac{6\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}=3
\end{aligned}
$$
questions.question: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be the roots of $x^2-6 x-2=0$ with $\alpha>\beta$. If $a_n=\alpha^n-\beta^n$ for $n \geq 1$, then the value of $\frac{a_{10}-2 a_8}{2 a_9}$ is
questions.explanation:
$\frac{a_{10}-2 a_8}{2 a_9}=\frac{\left(\alpha^{10}-\beta^{10}\right)-2\left(\alpha^8-\beta^8\right)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}$ $=\frac{\alpha^8\left(\alpha^2-2\right)-\beta^8\left(\beta^2-2\right)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}$ $\left[\because \alpha\right.$ is root of $x^2-6 x-2=0$ $\left.\alpha^2-2=6 \alpha\right]$
Also, $\beta$ is root of $x^2-6 x-2=0$
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad \beta^2-2=6 \beta \\
& =\frac{\alpha^8(6 \alpha)-\beta^8(6 \beta)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}=\frac{6\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}{2\left(\alpha^9-\beta^9\right)}=3
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.q: Let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-p x+r=0$ and $\frac{\alpha}{2}, 2 \beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2-q x+r=0$. Then, the value of $r$ is
questions.solution:
The equation $x^2-p x+r=0$ has roots $(\alpha, \beta)$ and the equation $x^2-q x+r=0$ has roots
$ \begin{array}{ll}
\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}, 2 \beta\right) . & \\
\Rightarrow & r=\alpha \beta \text{ and } \alpha+\beta=p \text{ and } \frac{\alpha}{2}+2 \beta=q \\
\Rightarrow & \beta=\frac{2 q-p}{3} \text{ and } \alpha=\frac{2(2 p-q)}{3} \\
\Rightarrow & \alpha \beta=r=\frac{2}{9}(2 q-p)(2 p-q)
\end{array} $

questions.q: If $x^2-10 a x-11 b=0$ have roots $c$ and $d$ and $x^2-10 c x-11 d=0$ have roots $a$ and $b$, then, find $a+b+c+d$.
questions.solution:
Here, $a+b=10 c$
c+d=10 a

On subtracting Eq. (ii) from Eq. (i), we get, $\quad(a-c)+(b-d)=10(c-a)\Rightarrow \quad(b-d)=11(c-a)$
Since, $c$ is the root of $x^2-10 a x+11 b=0$
\Rightarrow \quad c²-10 a c-11 b=0

Similarly, $a$ is the root of

$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow$& x²-10 c x+11 d=0 \\
& a²-10 c a-11 d=0
\end{aligned}

On subtracting Eq. (v) from Eq. (iv), we get

$\begin{aligned}$& $\left($c^2-a²\right)=11(b-d) \\
& \therefore \quad(c+a)(c-a)=11 $\times$11(c-a) \quad\{$\text{ from (i) \& (ii) }$\\
& \Rightarrow \quad c+a=121 . \\
& \therefore \quad a+b+c+d=10 c+10 a \\
& =10(c+a)=1210 \\
&
\end{aligned}

questions.q:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function such that $f(x)>0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f(x+y)=f(x) f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
Let the real numbers $\mathrm{a}_1, \mathrm{a}_2 \ldots, \mathrm{a}_{50}$ be in an arithmetic progression. If $f\left(\mathrm{a}_{31}\right)=64 f\left(\mathrm{a}_{25}\right)$, and $\sum_{i=1}^{50} f\left(a_i\right)=3\left(2^{25}+1\right)$ then the value of $\sum_{i=6}^{30} f\left(a_i\right)$ is ________
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \because f(x+y)=f(x) \cdot f(y) \\ & \Rightarrow f(x)=k^x \quad(f(x)>0 \forall x \in R) \\ & \because f\left(a_{31}\right)=64 f\left(a_{25}\right)\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}^{(\mathrm{a}+30 \mathrm{ d})}=64 \cdot \mathrm{k}^{(\mathrm{a}+24 \mathrm{ d})} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}^{6 \mathrm{ d}}=64 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{d}}=2\end{aligned} \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{50} \mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)=\mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{a}_1\right)+\mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{a}_2\right)+\ldots \ldots+\mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{a}_{50}\right) \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}}+\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{d}}+\ldots+\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}+49 \mathrm{ d}}=\frac{\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}}\left(\mathrm{k}^{50 \mathrm{ d}}-1\right)}{\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{d}}-1} \\ & =\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}}\left(2^{50}-1\right)=3\left(2^{25}+1\right)(\text{ Given }) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{3}{2^{25}-1}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \therefore \sum_{\mathrm{i}=6}^{30} \mathrm{f}\left(\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)=\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}+5 \mathrm{ d}}+\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}+6 \mathrm{ d}}+\ldots+\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}+29 \mathrm{ d}} \\ & \quad=\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}+5 \mathrm{ d}} \frac{\left(\mathrm{k}^{25 \mathrm{ d}}-1\right)}{\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{d}}-1}=\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{a}} \cdot\left(\mathrm{k}^{\mathrm{d}}\right)^5\left(2^{25}-1\right) \\ & \quad=\frac{3}{2^{25}-1} \cdot 2^5\left(2^{25}-1\right)=96\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Let $\overset{r}{7\overset{⏞}{5 \ldots 5}7}$ denote the $\left(r + 2\right)$ digit number where the first and the last digits are $7$ and the remaining $r$ digits are $5$. Consider the sum $S = 77 + 757 + 7557 + \ldots + \overset{98}{7\overset{⏞}{5 \ldots 5}7}$. If $S = \dfrac{7\overset{99}{\overset{⏞}{5 \ldots 5}}7 + m}{n}$, where $m and n$ are natural numbers less than $3000$, then the value of $m + n$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

$S = 77 + 757 + 7557 + \ldots + \overset{98}{7\overset{⏞}{5 \ldots 5}7}$

$⇒ S = 7 \times 10 + 7 + 7 \times 100 + 5 \times 10 + 7 + 7 \times 1000 + 5 \times 100 + 5 \times 10 + 7 \ldots + \overset{98}{7\overset{⏞}{5 \ldots 5}7}$

$⇒ S = 7\left(10 + {10}^{2} + \ldots + {10}^{99}\right) + 50\left(1 + 11 + \ldots + \overset{98}{\overset{⏞}{111 \ldots 1}}\right) + 7 \times 99$

$⇒ S = 70\left(\dfrac{{10}^{99} - 1}{9}\right) + \dfrac{50}{9}\left[\left(10 - 1\right) + \left({10}^{2} - 1\right) + \ldots + \left({10}^{98} - 1\right)\right] + 7 \times 99$

$⇒ S = 70\left(\dfrac{{10}^{99} - 1}{9}\right) + \dfrac{50}{9}\left[10\left(\dfrac{{10}^{98} - 1}{9}\right) - 98\right] + 7 \times 99$

$⇒ S = \dfrac{7 \times {10}^{100}}{9} - \dfrac{70}{9} + \dfrac{50}{9}\left[\dfrac{{10}^{99} - 1 - 9}{9} - 98\right] + 7 \times 99$

$⇒ S = \dfrac{7 \times {10}^{100}}{9} - \dfrac{70}{9} + \dfrac{50}{9}\left[\overset{99}{\overset{⏞}{111 \ldots 1}} - 99\right] + 7 \times 99$

$⇒ S = \dfrac{7 \times {10}^{100} - 70 + \overset{99}{\overset{⏞}{555 \ldots 5}}0}{9} - 550 + 693$

$⇒ S = \dfrac{7\overset{99}{\overset{⏞}{555 \ldots . 5}} - 70 + 143 \times 9}{9}$

$⇒ S = \dfrac{7\overset{99}{\overset{⏞}{55 \ldots 5}}7 + 1210}{9}$

So, on comparing we get, $m + n = 1210 + 9 = 1219$

questions.q: Let ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}, {a}_{3}, \ldots$ be an arithmetic progression with ${a}_{1} = 7$ and common difference $8$. Let ${T}_{1}, {T}_{2}, {T}_{3}, \ldots$ be such that ${T}_{1} = 3$ and ${T}_{n + 1} - {T}_{n} = {a}_{n}$ fo $n \ge 1$. Then, which of the following is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Given,

${a}_{n} = 7 + \left(n - 1\right)8$ and ${T}_{1} = 3$

Also ${T}_{n + 1} = {T}_{n} + {a}_{n}$

Now ${T}_{n} = {T}_{n - 1} + {a}_{n - 1}$

Putting $n = 1$ we get,

${T}_{2} = {T}_{1} + {a}_{1}$

Now putting $n = 2$ we get,

${T}_{3} = {T}_{2} + {a}_{2} ⇒ {T}_{3} = {T}_{1} + {a}_{1} + {a}_{2}$

And so on we get,

$⇒ {T}_{n + 1} = {T}_{1} + {a}_{1} + {a}_{2} + \ldots + {a}_{n}$

$⇒ {T}_{n + 1} = {T}_{1} + \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2\left(7\right) + \left(n - 1\right)8\right]$

$⇒ {T}_{n + 1} = {T}_{1} + n\left(4n + 3\right) ⋯ \left(1\right)$

Now for $n = 19$ we get,

${T}_{20} = 3 + \left(19\right)\left(79\right) = 1504$

And for $n = 29$ we get,

${T}_{30} = 3 + \left(29\right)\left(119\right) = 3454$ {option C is correct}

Now finding sum we get,

$\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{20}{T}_{k} = 3 + \mathop{∑}_{k = 2}^{20}{T}_{k} = 3 + \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{19}\left(3 + 4{n}^{2} + 3n\right)$

$= 3 + 3\left(19\right) + \dfrac{3\left(19\right)\left(20\right)}{2} + \dfrac{4\left(19\right)\left(20\right)\left(39\right)}{6}$

$= 3 + 10507 = 10510$ {option B is correct}

And Similarly $\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{30}{T}_{k} = 3 + \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{29}\left(4{n}^{2} + 3n + 3\right) = 35615$

questions.q: Let $AP\left(a; d\right)$ denote the set of all the terms of an infinite arithmetic progression with first term a and common difference $d > 0 .$ If $AP\left(1; 3\right) ∩ AP\left(2; 5\right) ∩ AP\left(3; 7\right) = AP\left(a; d\right)$ then $a + d$ equals ____
questions.solution:
Let ${T}_{\left(1, m\right)}: {m}^{th}$ term of ${1}^{st}$ series $A\left(1; 3\right)$
${T}_{\left(2, n\right)}: {n}^{th}$ term of ${2}^{nd}$ series $A\left(2; 5\right)$
${T}_{\left(3, r\right)}: {r}^{th}$ term of ${3}^{rd}$ series $A ( 3; 7 )$
For common terms
${T}_{( 1, m )} = {T}_{( 2, n )} = {T}_{( 3, r )}$
$1 + 3\left(m - 1\right) = 2 + 5\left(n - 1\right) = 3 + 7\left(r - 1\right)$
$3m - 2 = 5n - 3 = 7r - 4$
$⇒ m = \dfrac{5n - 1}{3}andr = \dfrac{5n + 1}{7}$
For $‘m’$ to be a natural number $n = 2,5, 11, \ldots$
And for $‘r’$ to be a natural number $n = 4,11, \ldots$
When $n = 11, m = 18 and r = 8$
$⇒$ For ${1}^{st}$ common term of three series $A ( a, d )$
$a = {1}^{st}$ term of $A ( 1,3 )$
$a = 1 + ( 181 ) 3 = 52$
$⇒$ Common difference of $A\left(a, d\right) = LCM$ of common difference of $\left(A\left(1; 3\right), A\left(2; 5\right), A\left(3; 7\right)\right)$
$d = LCM ( 3, 5, 7 )$
$d = 105$
Hence, $a + d = 52 + 105 = 157$

questions.q: Let $X$ be the set consisting of the first $2018$ terms of the arithmetic progression $1,6, 11, \ldots ,$ and $Y$ be the set consisting of the first $2018$ terms of the arithmetic progression $9,16,23, \ldots$ . Then, the number of elements in the set $X ∪ Y$ is___.
questions.solution:
$X: 1, 6, 11, \ldots , 10086$
$Y: 9, 16, 23, \ldots . , 14128$
$X ∩ Y: 16, 51, 86, \ldots . .$
Let $m = n\left(X ∩ Y\right)$
$∴ 16 + \left(m - 1\right) \times 35 \le 10086$
$⇒ m \le 288.71$
$⇒ m = 288$
$∴ n\left(X ∪ Y\right) = n\left(X\right) + n\left(Y\right) - n\left(X ∩ Y\right)$
$= 2018 + 2018 - 288 = 3748$

questions.q: The sides of a right-angled triangle are in arithmetic progression. If the triangle has area 24 square units, then what is the length of its smallest side?
questions.solution:
Let three sides of triangle be: $a - d, a, a + d$.

Where, $d > 0, a > 0$.

$⇒$  length of smallest side $= a - d$ units

Now,  ${( a + d )}^{2} = {a}^{2} + {( a - d )}^{2}$

$⇒ a\left(a - 4d\right) = 0$

$∴ a = 4d$        .....(i)

(As $a = 0$ is rejected)

Also,    $\dfrac{1}{2}a . \left(a - d\right) = 24$

$⇒ a\left(a - d\right) = 48$        .....(ii)

$∴$     From (i) and (ii), we get  $a = 8, d = 2$

Hence, length of smallest side is

$\left(a - d\right) = \left(8 - 2\right) = 6$units

questions.solution:
Let $\dfrac{\pi}{4} + ( K - 1 )\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \theta$
$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{13} \dfrac{1}{sin\thetasin( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} )} = \dfrac{1}{sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}} \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{13} \dfrac{sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}}{sin\thetasin( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} )}$
$= 2 \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{13} \dfrac{sin( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} - \theta )}{sin\thetasin( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} )} = 2 \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{13} \dfrac{sin( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} )cos\theta - cos( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} )sin\theta}{sin\thetasin( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} )}$
$= 2 \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{13} ( cot\theta - cot( \theta + \dfrac{\pi}{6} ) ) = 2 \mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{13} ( cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + ( k - 1 )\dfrac{\pi}{6} ) - cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{k\pi}{6} ) )$
$= 2( cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} - cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{6} ) + cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{\pi}{6} ) - cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{2\pi}{6} ) + - - - - - cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{12\pi}{6} ) - cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{13\pi}{6} ) )$
$= 2[ cot\dfrac{\pi}{4} - cot( \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{13\pi}{6} ) ] = 2[ 1 - cot\dfrac{29\pi}{12} ] = 2[ 1 - cot{75}^{ο} ] = 2[ 1 - ( 2 - \sqrt{3} ) ] = 2( \sqrt{3 - 1} )$

Column I Column II
$( A )$ In ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ , if the magnitude of the projection vector of the vector $\alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j}$ on $\sqrt{3}\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}$ is $\sqrt{3}$ and if $\alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3}\beta,$ then possible value (s) of $| \alpha |$ is (are) $\left(P\right)$ 1
$( B )$ Let a and b be real numbers such that the function $f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}- 3a{x}^{2} - 2, & x < 1 \\ bx + {a}^{2}, & x \ge 1\end{cases}\right$ is differentiable for all $x \in \mathbb{R} .$ Then possible value (s) of a is (are) $\left(Q\right)$ 2
$( C )$ Let $\omega \ne 1$ be a complex cube roots of unity. If ${\left(3 - 3\omega + 2{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3} + {\left(2 + 3\omega - 3{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3} + {\left(- 3 + 2\omega + 3{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3} = 0$ then possible value (s) of n is (are) $\left(R\right)$ 3
$( D )$ Let the harmonic mean of two positive real numbers a and b 4. If q is a positive real number such that a, 5, q, b is an arithmetic progression, then the value (s) of |q – a| is (are) $\left(S\right)$ 4
$(T)$ 5
questions.solution:
$\left(A\right)$ As $\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\alpha + \beta}{2}\right| = \sqrt{3} ⇒ \left|\sqrt{3}\alpha + \beta\right| = 2\sqrt{3}$ ...(i)
And, also $\alpha = 2 + \sqrt{3}\beta$ ...(ii)
Solving (i) & (ii), we get
$⇒ 2\sqrt{3} + 4\beta = \pm 2\sqrt{3}$
$⇒ \beta = 0, - \sqrt{3}$
So, $\alpha = 2$ and $- 1$
i.e, $\left|\alpha\right| = 2, 1$
$( B )$ Here $- 3a - 2 = b + {a}^{2}$ ...(i)
And $- 6a = b$ ...(ii)
Solving (i) and (ii),
$- 3a - 2 = - 6a + {a}^{2}$
$⇒ {a}^{2} - 3a + 2 = 0$
$⇒ a = 1, 2$
$\left(C\right)$ Here, ${\left(3 - 3\omega + 2{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3}\left\{1 + {\omega}^{4n + 3} + {\left({\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3}\right\}$
$⇒ {\left(3 - 3\omega + 2{\omega}^{2}\right)}^{4n + 3}\left\{1 + {\omega}^{4n} + {\omega}^{8n}\right\} = 0$
So, $n = 1, 2, 4, 5$
$\left(D\right)$ $q - a = 2d$
Let $q - q = \alpha, d = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}$
$a = 5 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}, b = a + \dfrac{3\alpha}{2} = 5 + \alpha$
Now, $\dfrac{ab}{a + b} = 2$
$⇒ \dfrac{\left(5 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)\left(5 + \alpha\right)}{5 - \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + 5 + \alpha} = 2$
$⇒ \alpha = 5, - 2$
$\left|\alpha\right| = 5, 2$

questions.q: Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots . .$ be in harmonic progression with $a_{1}=5$ and $a_{20}=25$. The least positive integer $n$ for which $a_{n} < 0$ is
questions.solution:
$\because a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots \ldots$ are in H.P.

$\begin{array}{l}

\therefore \frac{1}{a_{1}}, \frac{1}{a_{2}}, \frac{1}{a_{3}} \ldots \ldots \text{ are in A.P. } \\

\therefore \quad \frac{1}{a_{1}}=\frac{1}{5} \text{ and } \frac{1}{a_{20}}=\frac{1}{25} \\

\frac{1}{a_{1}}+19 d=\frac{1}{a_{20}} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{5}+19 d=\frac{1}{25} \Rightarrow d=\frac{-4}{475} \\

\text{ Now } \frac{1}{a_{n}}=\frac{1}{5}+(n-1)\left(\frac{-4}{475}\right) \\

\text{ Clearly } a_{n} < 0, \text{ if } \frac{1}{a_{n}} < 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{5}-\frac{4 n}{475}+\frac{4}{475} < 0 \\

\Rightarrow \quad-4 n < -99 \text{ or } n>\frac{99}{4}=24 \frac{3}{4} \quad \therefore n \geq 25 \\

\therefore \quad \text{ Least value of } n \text{ is } 25 .

\end{array}$

questions.q: Let $S_k, k=1,2, \ldots, 100$, denote the sum of the infinite geometric series whose first term is $\frac{k-1}{k !}$ and the common ratio is $\frac{1}{k}$. Then the value of $\frac{100^2}{100 !}+\sum_{k=1}^{100}\left|\left(k^2-3 k+1\right) S_k\right|$ is
questions.solution:
We have, $S_k=\frac{\frac{k-1}{k !}}{1-\frac{1}{k}}=\frac{1}{(k-1) !}$
Now,

$\begin{aligned}$& $\left($k^2-3 k+1\right) S_k=\{(k-2)(k-1)-1\} \\
& =$\frac{1}{(k-3) !}-\frac{1}{(k-1) !}$\\
& \Rightarrow \sum_{k=1}^{100}$\left|\left($k^2-3 k+1\right) S_k\right| \\
& =1+1+2-$\left(\frac{1}{99 !}+\frac{1}{98 !}\right)=$4-$\frac{100^2}{100 !}
\end{aligned}

\Rightarrow \quad \frac{100^2}{100 !}+\sum_{k=1}^{100}\left|\left($k^2-3 k+1\right) S_k\right|=4

questions.q: If the sum of first $n$ terms of an $\mathrm{AP}$ is $\mathrm{cn}^2$, then the sum of squares of these $n$ terms is
options:
$\frac{n\left(4 n^2-1\right) c^2}{6}$

$\frac{n\left(4 n^2+1\right) c^2}{3}$

$\frac{n\left(4 n^2-1\right) c^2}{3}$

$\frac{n\left(4 n^2+1\right) c^2}{6}$
questions.solution:
Let $S_n=c^2\begin{aligned}$& S_{n-1}=c(n-1)^2=c n²+c-2 c n \\
& \therefore T_n=2 c n-c \quad$\left(\because$T_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\right) \\
& T_n^2=(2 c n-c)^2=4 c² n²+c²-4 c² n \\
& \therefore $\text{ Sum }=\Sigma$T_n^2=$\frac{4 c^2 \cdot n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}$\\
& =$\frac{2 c^2 n(n+1)(2 n+1)+3 n c^2-6 c^2 n(n+1)}{3}$\\
& =$\frac{n c^2\left[4 n^2+6 n+2+3-6 n-6\right]}{3}$\\
& =$\frac{n c^2\left(4 n^2-1\right)}{3}
\end{aligned}$

$B_n=1-A_n > A_n \Rightarrow A_n <  \frac{1}{2}$ Now, $A_n=\frac{\frac{3}{4}\left(1-\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)^n\right)}{1+\frac{3}{4}} <  \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) > -\frac{1}{6}$

n & =5, & $\frac{243}{1024}$ & >$\frac{1}{6}
\end{aligned}$ which is true for $n=7$.
Obviously, $n_0=7$

questions.q:
Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 10\}$. Consider the set
$X = \{R : R$ is an equivalence relation on the set $S$ such that $R$ has exactly $42$ elements$\}$.

Then the number of elements in $X$ is _____________.
questions.solution:
An equivalence relation on a set $S$ corresponds to a partition of $S$ into disjoint equivalence classes. Let the sizes of these equivalence classes be $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$.

The number of elements in the equivalence relation $R$ is given by the sum of the squares of the sizes of its equivalence classes:
$\sum_{i=1}^k a_i^2 = 42$

Since the total number of elements in $S$ is $10$, we also have:
$\sum_{i=1}^k a_i = 10$

We need to find all possible partitions of $10$ such that the sum of their squares is $42$. Let's check the possible sizes of the largest equivalence class, $a_1$:

Case 1: $a_1 = 6$
$a_1^2 = 36$. The remaining sum of squares is $42 - 36 = 6$, and the remaining sum of elements is $10 - 6 = 4$.
The only way to partition $4$ such that the sum of squares is $6$ is $2, 1, 1$ (since $2^2 + 1^2 + 1^2 = 6$).
Thus, one valid partition is $\{6, 2, 1, 1\}$.

Case 2: $a_1 = 5$
$a_1^2 = 25$. The remaining sum of squares is $42 - 25 = 17$, and the remaining sum of elements is $10 - 5 = 5$.
The only way to partition $5$ such that the sum of squares is $17$ is $4, 1$ (since $4^2 + 1^2 = 17$).
Thus, another valid partition is $\{5, 4, 1\}$.

Case 3: $a_1 \le 4$
The maximum possible sum of squares would be for the partition $\{4, 4, 2\}$, which gives $4^2 + 4^2 + 2^2 = 36 < 42$. No other partitions can yield a sum of $42$.

Now, we calculate the number of ways to form these partitions from the $10$ elements of $S$.

For the partition $\{6, 2, 1, 1\}$:
The number of ways to divide $10$ elements into groups of sizes $6, 2, 1, 1$ is:
$\dfrac{10!}{6! \times 2! \times 1! \times 1! \times 2!} = \dfrac{3628800}{720 \times 2 \times 1 \times 1 \times 2} = \dfrac{3628800}{2880} = 1260$
(Note: We divide by $2!$ because there are two groups of identical size $1$).

For the partition $\{5, 4, 1\}$:
The number of ways to divide $10$ elements into groups of sizes $5, 4, 1$ is:
$\dfrac{10!}{5! \times 4! \times 1!} = \dfrac{3628800}{120 \times 24 \times 1} = \dfrac{3628800}{2880} = 1260$

Total number of equivalence relations in $X$ is:
$1260 + 1260 = 2520$

Answer: $2520$

questions.q:
In a study about a pandemic, data of $900$ persons was collected. It was found that

$190$ persons had symptom of fever,

$220$ persons had symptom of cough,

$220$ persons had symptom of breathing problem,

$330$ persons had symptom of fever or cough or both,

$350$ persons had symptom of cough or breathing problem or both,

$340$ persons had symptom of fever or breathing problem or both,

$30$ persons had all three symptoms (fever, cough and breathing problem).

If a person is chosen randomly from these $900$ persons, then the probability that the person has at most one symptom is ______.
questions.solution:
We denote the set of people having symptoms of fever, cough and breathing problem by $F, C$ and $B$ respectively

Given that $n\left(F\right) = 190, n\left(B\right) = 220$ and $n\left(C\right) = 220$

Also given, $n\left(F ∪ C\right) = 330, n\left(B ∪ C\right) = 350,$ $n\left(F ∪ B\right) = 340$ and $n\left(F ∩ C ∩ B\right) = 30$

So $n\left(F ∩ C\right) = n\left(F\right) + n\left(C\right) - n\left(F ∪ C\right)$

$= 80$

Similarly, $n\left(F ∩ B\right) = n\left(F\right) + n\left(B\right) - n\left(F ∪ B\right) = 70$ and $n\left(C ∩ B\right) = n\left(C\right) + n\left(B\right) - n\left(B ∪ C\right) = 90$

Putting the data in Venn diagram

Number of people having at most one symptom$=$Number of people having zero symptom or one symptom

$= 70 + 80 + 90 + 480 = 720$

Required probability $= \dfrac{720}{900} = 0 . 8$

questions.q: Consider a data consisting of $10$ observations $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{10}$, whose mean is $5$ and variance is $7$. If the mean and the variance of the first $8$ observations $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_8$ are $4$ and $3.5$, respectively, and $x_9 < x_{10}$, then the value of $3x_9 + 2x_{10}$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
Given $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i}{10} = 5 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i = 50$

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i^2}{10} - 5^2 = 7 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i^2 = 320$

For the first $8$ observations:

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i}{8} = 4 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 32$

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2}{8} - 4^2 = 3.5 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 8(3.5 + 16) = 156$

Subtracting the sums, we get:

$x_9 + x_{10} = 50 - 32 = 18$

$x_9^2 + x_{10}^2 = 320 - 156 = 164$

Using $(x_9 + x_{10})^2 = x_9^2 + x_{10}^2 + 2x_9 x_{10}$:

$18^2 = 164 + 2x_9 x_{10} \Rightarrow 2x_9 x_{10} = 324 - 164 = 160 \Rightarrow x_9 x_{10} = 80$

The numbers $x_9$ and $x_{10}$ are roots of the equation $t^2 - 18t + 80 = 0$.

$(t - 8)(t - 10) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 8, 10$

Since $x_9 < x_{10}$, we have $x_9 = 8$ and $x_{10} = 10$.

Therefore, $3x_9 + 2x_{10} = 3(8) + 2(10) = 24 + 20 = 44$.

Answer: $44$

Given $\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i}{10} = 5 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i = 50$

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i^2}{10} - 5^2 = 7 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{10} x_i^2 = 320$

For the first $8$ observations:

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i}{8} = 4 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i = 32$

$\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2}{8} - 4^2 = 3.5 \Rightarrow \sum_{i=1}^{8} x_i^2 = 8(3.5 + 16) = 156$

Subtracting the sums, we get:

$x_9 + x_{10} = 50 - 32 = 18$

$x_9^2 + x_{10}^2 = 320 - 156 = 164$

Using $(x_9 + x_{10})^2 = x_9^2 + x_{10}^2 + 2x_9 x_{10}$:

$18^2 = 164 + 2x_9 x_{10} \Rightarrow 2x_9 x_{10} = 324 - 164 = 160 \Rightarrow x_9 x_{10} = 80$

The numbers $x_9$ and $x_{10}$ are roots of the equation $t^2 - 18t + 80 = 0$.

$(t - 8)(t - 10) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 8, 10$

Since $x_9 < x_{10}$, we have $x_9 = 8$ and $x_{10} = 10$.

Therefore, $3x_9 + 2x_{10} = 3(8) + 2(10) = 24 + 20 = 44$.

Answer: $44$

questions.q: Let $X$ be a random variable, and let $P(X=x)$ denote the probability that $X$ takes the value $x$. Suppose that the points $(x, P(X=x)), x=0,1,2,3,4$, lie on a fixed straight line in the $x y$-plane, and $P(X=x)=0$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}-\{0,1,2,3,4\}$. If the mean of $X$ is $\frac{5}{2}$, and the variance of $X$ is $\alpha$, then the value of $24 \alpha$ is ___
questions.solution:
Let equation of line is y = mx + c
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \mathrm{x} & 0 & \mathrm{l} & 2 & 3 & 4 & \mathrm{R}-\{0,1,2,3,4\} \\
\hline \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{x}) & \mathrm{c} & \mathrm{m}+\mathrm{c} & 2 \mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{c} & 3 \mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{c} & 4 \mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{c} & 0 \\
\hline
\end{array}$
$\sum_{x=0}^4(m x+c)=1 \Rightarrow 10 m+5 c=1 \Rightarrow 2 m+c=\frac{1}{5}...(1)$
$\begin{aligned} & \text{ mean }=\sum x_i P_i=\sum_{\mathrm{i}=0}^4\left(\mathrm{mx}_{\mathrm{i}}+\mathrm{c}\right) \cdot \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}=30 \mathrm{~m}+10 \mathrm{c}=\frac{5}{2} \\ & \therefore 3 \mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{c}=\frac{1}{4} \ldots(2)\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned} & \Sigma \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}^2=\sum_{\mathrm{i}=0}^4\left(\mathrm{mx}_{\mathrm{i}}+\mathrm{c}\right) \mathrm{x}_1^2 \\ & =\sum_{\mathrm{i}=0}^4\left(\mathrm{mx}_{\mathrm{i}}^3+\mathrm{cx}_{\mathrm{i}}^2\right) \Rightarrow 100 \mathrm{~m}+30 \mathrm{c} \text{ (Now putting } \mathrm{m} \text{ and } \mathrm{c} \text{ ) } \\ & \Rightarrow \Sigma \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}^2=5+3=8 \\ & \text{ Variance }=\Sigma \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}^2-\left(\Sigma \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}\right)^2=8-\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^2=\frac{7}{4} \\ & \therefore 24 \alpha=42\end{aligned}$

Consider the given data with frequency distribution

$\begin{cases}{x}_{i} & 3 & 8 & 11 & 10 & 5 & 4 \\ {f}_{i} & 5 & 2 & 3 & 2 & 4 & 4\end{cases}$

Match each entry in List-I to the correct entries in List-II.

List-I List-II
$\left(P\right)$ The mean of the above data is $\left(1\right)$ $2 . 5$
$\left(Q\right)$ The median of the above data is $\left(2\right)$ $5$
$\left(R\right)$ The mean deviation about the
mean of the above data is		 $\left(3\right)$ $6$
$\left(S\right)$ The mean deviation about the
median of the above data is		 $\left(4\right)$ $2 . 7$
$\left(5\right)$ $2 . 4$

The correct option is
questions.solution:
Arranging the given data in ascending order

we get,

$\begin{cases}{x}_{i} & 3 & 4 & 5 & 8 & 10 & 11 \\ {f}_{i} & 5 & 4 & 4 & 2 & 2 & 3\end{cases}$

Now finding the mean of the above data we get,

Mean $= \dfrac{3 \times 5 + 8 \times 2 + 11 \times 3 + 10 \times 2 + 5 \times 4 + 4 \times 4}{5 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 4}$

$= \dfrac{15 + 16 + 33 + 20 + 20 + 16}{20} = \dfrac{120}{20} = 6$

Now, median $= \dfrac{1}{2}\left({10}^{th} + {11}^{th}observation\right)$

$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(5 + 5\right) = 5$

Hence, Mean deviation about mean will be,

$= \dfrac{3 \times 5 + 2 \times 4 + 1 \times 4 + 2 \times 2 + 4 \times 2 + 5 \times 3}{20}$

$= \dfrac{54}{20} = 2 . 7$

And Mean deviation about median

$= \dfrac{2 \times 5 + 1 \times 4 + 0 + 3 \times 2 + 5 \times 2 + 6 \times 3}{20}$

$= \dfrac{4 . 8}{20} = 2 . 4$

$P \to 3; Q \to 2; R \to 4; S \to 5$

$∴$ Option A is correct.

questions.q:
Let $\mathbb{R}^2$ denote $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}. Let $S=$\left\{(a, b, c): a, b, c \in \mathbb{R} \text{$ and } a x^2+2 b x y+c y^2>0 $\text{ for $all }(x, y) \in$\mathbb{R}^2-$\{(0,0)\}\right\} .$
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?$
options:
For any given $(a, b, c) \in S$, the system of linear equations
$\begin{aligned}& a x+b y=1 \\& b x+c y=-1\end{aligned}$ 
has a unique solution.

For any given $(a, b, c) \in S$, the system of linear equations
$\begin{aligned}& (a+1) x+b y=0 \\& b x+(c+1) y=0\end{aligned}$
has a unique solution.
questions.solution:
\(\begin{aligned}
& a x^2+2 b x y+c y^2>0 \\
& y, x \in \mathbb{R}-\{(0,0)\} \\
& \Rightarrow c\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2+2 b\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+a>0 \\
& 4 b^2-4 a c<0 \\
& \Rightarrow b^2<a c
\end{aligned}\)
(A) \(\left(2, \frac{7}{2}, 6\right)\)
\(\left(\frac{7}{2}\right)^2>2 \times 6\)
\(\therefore\) option A is incorrect
\(\begin{aligned}
& \text{(B) if }\left(3, b, \frac{1}{12}\right) \in S \\
& \Rightarrow b^2<3 \cdot \frac{1}{12} \\
& \Rightarrow b^2<\frac{1}{4} \\
& \Rightarrow 4 b^2<1 \\
& \Rightarrow|2 b|<1 \text{ option } B \text{ is correct }
\end{aligned}\)
\(\begin{aligned}
& \text{(C) } a x+b y=1 \\
& b x+c y=-1 \\
& D=\left|\begin{array}{ll}
a & b \\
b & c
\end{array}\right|=a c-b^2 \neq 0
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore\) unique solution option C is correct.
\(\begin{aligned}
& \text{(D) }(a+1) \mathrm{x}+\mathrm{by}=0 \\
& \mathrm{bx}+(\mathrm{c}+1) \mathrm{y}=0 \\
& D=\left|\begin{array}{cc}
(a+1) & b \\
b & (c+1)
\end{array}\right| \\
& =(a+1)(c+1)-b^2 \\
& \Rightarrow a c-b^2+a+c+1 \\
& b^2<a c \Rightarrow a c \text{ is +ve } \\
& \Rightarrow a \text{ and care positive then }\left(a c-b^2\right)+a+c+1>0
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore\) unique solution
\(\therefore\) option D is correct.

questions.q: Consider a triangle $\Delta$ whose two sides lie on the $x$-axis and the line $x + y + 1 = 0$. If the orthocenter of $\Delta$ is $( 1, 1 )$, then the equation of the circle passing through the vertices of the triangle $\Delta$ is
questions.solution: Let A$ is the point of intersection of the given lines $y = 0, x + y + 1 = 0$ Their point of intersection A$ is $\left(- 1, 0\right)$ Let $B$ is the other point on the line $x + y + 1 = 0$, Now, the perpendicular from $B$ on the $x$-axis will pass through the orthocenter. So, the equation of perpendicular from $B$ on the $x$-axis is $x = 1$ Thus, the coordinates of $B$ are $\left(1, - 2\right)$ Let the third vertex is $\left(h, k\right)$ Slope of the line perpendicular to $x + y + 1 = 0$ is $1$ So, the perpendicular from $\left(h, k\right)$ to line $x + y + 1 = 0$ has slope $1$ and passes through the orthocenter $\left(1, 1\right)$ Thus, its equation is $y = x$ Now, $y = x and x$-axis intersects at the origin. Hence, the vertices of the triangle are $( - 1, 0 ) , ( 1, - 2 ) \text{$ and } ( 0, 0 ) Let the equation of the circle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2gx + 2fy = 0 ( 0, 0 ) \to c = 0 ( - 1, 0 ) \to 1 - 2g = 0 ⇒ g = \dfrac{1}{2} ( 1, - 2 ) \to 5 + 1 - 4f = 0 ⇒ f = \dfrac{3}{2}$ Hence, the equation of the circumcircle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + x + 3y = 0$. Aliter We know, the image of the orthocentre about the sides of a triangle lies on circumcircle. The image of $( 1, 1 )$ about $y = 0$ is $( 1, - 1 )$ The image of $\left(1, 1\right)$ about $x + y + 1 = 0$ is $( - 2, - 2 )$ & intersection of $y = 0, x + y + 1 = 0$ is $( - 1, 0 ) .$ Let the equation of circle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ All the three points $( 1, - 1 ) , \left(- 2, - 2\right) \text{$ and } $\left(- 1, 0\right)$ lies on this circle $( 1, - 1 ) \to 2 + 2g - 2f + c = 0 . . . \left(i\right) ( - 1, 0 ) \to 1 - 2g + c = 0 . . . \left(ii\right)$ ( - 2, - 2 ) \to 8 - 4g - 4f + c = 0 . . . $\left(iii\right)$ By using the equations $\left(i\right)$, $\left(ii\right)\text{$ and } $\left(iii\right)$, we get $g = \dfrac{1}{2},$f = $\dfrac{3}{2}, c = 0$ Hence, the equation of the circle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + x + 3y = 0$

The image of $( 1, 1 )$ about $y = 0$ is $( 1, - 1 )$ The image of $\left(1, 1\right)$ about $x + y + 1 = 0$ is $( - 2, - 2 )$ & intersection of $y = 0, x + y + 1 = 0$ is $( - 1, 0 ) .$ Let the equation of circle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ All the three points $( 1, - 1 ) , \left(- 2, - 2\right) \text{$ and } $\left(- 1, 0\right)$ lies on this circle $( 1, - 1 ) \to 2 + 2g - 2f + c = 0 . . . \left(i\right) ( - 1, 0 ) \to 1 - 2g + c = 0 . . . \left(ii\right)$ ( - 2, - 2 ) \to 8 - 4g - 4f + c = 0 . . . $\left(iii\right)$ By using the equations $\left(i\right)$, $\left(ii\right)\text{$ and } $\left(iii\right)$, we get $g = \dfrac{1}{2},$f = $\dfrac{3}{2}, c = 0$ Hence, the equation of the circle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + x + 3y = 0$

The line $y=2 x+1$ meets $C$ at two points $R$ and $S$, where the distance between $R$ and $S$ is $\sqrt{270}$. \\ Let the perpendicular bisector of $R S$ meet $C$ at two distinct points $R^{\prime}$ and $S^{\prime}$. Let $D$ be the square of the distance between $R^{\prime}$ and $S^{\prime}$.

The value of ${λ}^{2}$ is
questions.solution:
Let the point $P$ is $\left(h, k\right)$

Distance of $P$ from ${L}_{1} = \left|\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} + k - 1}{\sqrt{( \sqrt{2}{)}^{2} + {1}^{2}}}\right|

$= $\left|\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} + k - 1}{\sqrt{3}}\right|$

Distance of $P$ from ${L}_{2} = \left|\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} - k + 1}{\sqrt{( \sqrt{2}{)}^{2} + {1}^{2}}}\right|

$= $\left|\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} - k + 1}{\sqrt{3}}\right|$

$∴$ The equation of the locus of $P$ is

$\left|\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} + k - 1}{\sqrt{3}}\right| \times \left|\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} - k + 1}{\sqrt{3}}\right| = {\lambda}^{2}$

$\left|\left(\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} + k - 1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\dfrac{h\sqrt{2} - k + 1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right| = {\lambda}^{2}$

$⇒ \left|2{h}^{2} - ( k - 1{)}^{2}\right| = 3{\lambda}^{2}$

Hence, the equation of the locus is $\left|2{x}^{2} - ( y - 1{)}^{2}\right| = 3{\lambda}^{2}$

The line is $y = 2x + 1 or y - 1 = 2x$

By substituting the value of $y$ in the equation of the curve $C$, we get

$\left|2{x}^{2} - ( y - 1{)}^{2}\right| = 3{\lambda}^{2}$

$⇒ \left|2{x}^{2} - ( 2x{)}^{2}\right| = 3{\lambda}^{2}$

$⇒ 2{x}^{2} = 3{\lambda}^{2}$

$⇒ x = \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}\lambda$

$⇒ {x}_{2} - {x}_{1} = | \sqrt{6}\lambda |$

Also, $y - 1 = 2x$

$⇒ {y}_{2} - 1 = 2{x}_{2} and {y}_{1} - 1 = 2{x}_{1}$

$⇒ {y}_{2} - {y}_{1} = 2\left({x}_{2} - {x}_{1}\right)$

$⇒ {y}_{2} - {y}_{1} = | 2\sqrt{6}\lambda |$

Given $RS = \sqrt{270}$

$⇒ \sqrt{{\left({x}_{2} - {x}_{1}\right)}^{2} + {\left({y}_{2} - {y}_{1}\right)}^{2}} = \sqrt{270}$

$⇒ ( \sqrt{6}\lambda{)}^{2} + ( 2\sqrt{6}\lambda{)}^{2} = 270$

$30{\lambda}^{2} = 270$

${\lambda}^{2} = 9$

questions.q: Let $O$ be the center of the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} = {r}^{2},$ where $r > \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} .$ Suppose $PQ$ is a chord of this circle and the equation of the line passing through $P$ and $Q$ is  $2x + 4y = 5$. If the center of the circumcircle of the triangle $OPQ$ lies on the line $x + 2y = 4,$ then the value of $r$ is ______
questions.solution:
Circumcenter $C$ of $\DeltaOPQ$ lies on $x + 2y = 4$

Let $C ≡ \left(4 - 2\alpha, \alpha\right)$

$∵ OC ⊥ PQ ⇒ \left(slopeofOC\right) \cdot \left(slopeofPQ\right) = - 1$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{\alpha}{4 - 2\alpha}\right)\left(- \dfrac{2}{4}\right) = - 1 ⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{8}{5} ⇒ C\left(\dfrac{4}{5}, \dfrac{8}{5}\right)$

$OM = \dfrac{| 0 + 0 - 5 |}{\sqrt{{2}^{2} + {4}^{2}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$

$CM = \dfrac{\left|2\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right) + 4\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right) - 5\right|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2} + {4}^{2}}} = \dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{5}}$

$OC = PC = \sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)}^{2} + {\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{5}}$

Now, $P{M}^{2} = O{P}^{2} - O{M}^{2} = P{C}^{2} - C{M}^{2} ⇒ {r}^{2} - \dfrac{5}{4} = \dfrac{16}{5} - \dfrac{9}{20} ⇒ r = 2$

questions.q: Let the point $B$ be the reflection of the point $A\left(2, 3\right)$ with respect to the line $8x - 6y - 23 = 0 .$ Let ${T}_{A}$ and ${T}_{B}$ be circle of radii $2$ and $1$ with centres $A$ and $B$ respectively. Let $T$ be a common tangent to the circle ${T}_{A}$ and ${T}_{B}$ such that both the circle are on the same side of $T .$ If $C$ is the point of intersection of $T$ and the line passing through $A$ and $B,$ then the length of the line segment $AC$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
Clearly,$ACP$ and $BCQ$ are similar triangles.
Hence,
$\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{{r}_{1}}{{r}_{2}}$
$\dfrac{AC}{BC} = 2$
$AC = 2BC$ ...(i)

Now, since $B$ , is image of $A$ in line $8x - 6y = 23$
$AD = BD$
$AB = 2AD$ ...(ii)
$AD =$ distance of $A$ from line
$8x - 6y = 23$
$AD = \left|\dfrac{16 - 16 - 23}{10}\right| = \dfrac{5}{2}$
Now as $AC = 2BC$
$⇒ AC = 2 ( AC - AB )$
$⇒ AC = 2AB$
$⇒ AC = 4AD$ (from (ii))
$AC = 4 \times \dfrac{5}{2}$
$AC = 10$

$\dfrac{{x}^{2}}{9} + \dfrac{{y}^{2}}{8} = 1$
${F}_{1} ( - 1, 0 ), {F}_{2} ( 1, 0 )$

questions.explanation:
$2 \le {d}_{1}\left(p\right) + {d}_{2}\left(p\right) \le 4$
For $P\left(\alpha, \beta\right), \alpha > \beta$
$⇒$ $2\sqrt{2} \le 2\alpha \le 4\sqrt{2}$
$\sqrt{2} \le \alpha \le 2\sqrt{2}$

questions.q: For a > b > c > 0, the distance between (1, 1) and the point of intersection of the lines ax + by + c = 0 and bx + ay + c = 0 is less than $2 \sqrt{2}$.Then
questions.solution:
$\left(\text{a} - \text{b}\right) \text{x} + \left(\text{b} - \text{a}\right) \text{y} = 0$
$⇒ \text{x} = \text{y}$
$⇒ \text{Point$ of $intersection} \left(\dfrac{- \text{c}}{\text{a} + \text{b}} \text{,} \dfrac{- \text{c}}{\text{a} + \text{b}}\right)$
Now using distance formula between two points $d = \sqrt{{\left({x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left({y}_{1} - {y}_{2}\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \sqrt{{\left(1 + \dfrac{\text{c}}{\text{a} + \text{b}}\right)}^{2} + {\left(1 + \dfrac{\text{c}}{\text{a} + \text{b}}\right)}^{2}} < 2\sqrt{2}$
$⇒ \sqrt{2}\left(\left|\dfrac{\text{a} + \text{b} + \text{c}}{\text{a} + \text{b}}\right|\right) < 2\sqrt{2}$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{\text{a} + \text{b} + \text{c}}{\text{a} + \text{b}}\right) < 2$

$\text{⇒a} + \text{b} + \text{c} < 2\left(\text{a} + \text{b}\right)$
$⇒ \text{a} + \text{b} - \text{c} > 0$

questions.solution:
$$ \text{ Equation of } A B \text{ is } $$
$$ \begin{aligned} y-0 & =\frac{\frac{8}{5}}{-\frac{9}{5}-3}(x-3)=\frac{8}{-24}(x-3) \\ \Rightarrow \quad y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-3) \\ \Rightarrow \quad x & +3 y=3 \end{aligned} $$ Equation of the straight line perpendicular to A B$ through $P$ is $3 x-y=5$. Equation of $P A$ is $x-3=0$. The equation of straight line perpendicular to $P A$ through $B$\left(\frac{-9}{5}, \frac{8}{5}\right)$. is $y=\frac{8}{5}$. Hence, the orthocentre is $\left(\frac{11}{5}, \frac{8}{5}\right)$.

options:

(i) and (ii), we get C\{p q,(1+p)(1+q)\} $\therefore$ Equation of altitude $C M$ passing through $C$ and perpendicular to $A B$ is x=p q $\because$ Slope of line (ii) is $\left(\frac{1+q}{q}\right)$. $\therefore$ Slope of altitude $B N$ (as shown in figure) is $\frac{-q}{1+q}$. $$ \\ $\therefore$ Equation of $B N$ is $y-0=\frac{-q}{1+q}(x+p)$ \Rightarrow \quad y=$\frac{-q}{(1+q)}($x+p) Let orthocentre of triangle be $H(h, k)$, which is the point of intersection of Eqs. questions.q: Consider three points $P=(-\sin (\beta-\alpha),-\cos \beta), Q=(\cos (\beta-\alpha), \sin \beta)$ and $R=(\cos (\beta-\alpha+\theta), \sin (\beta-\theta)$, where $0 < \alpha, \beta, \theta < \frac{\pi}{4}$. Then,
options:
$P$ lies on the line segment $R Q$

$Q$ lies on the line segment $P R$

$R$ lies on the line segment $Q P$

$P, Q, R$ are non- collinear
questions.solution:
For collinear points

$\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
-\sin (\beta-\alpha)$& -\cos $\beta$& 1 \\
\cos ($\beta-\alpha)$& \sin $\beta$& 1 \\
\cos ($\beta-\alpha+\theta)$& \sin ($\beta-\theta)$& 1
\end{array}\right|

Clearly, $\Delta \neq 0$ for any value of $\alpha, \beta, \theta$, hence points are non-collinear.

questions.q:
Consider $L_1: 2 x+3 y+p-3=0 ; L_2: 2 x+3 y+p+3=0$ where $p$ is a real number and $C: x^2+y^2+6 x-10 y+30=0$.
Statement 1 If line $L_1$ is a chord of circle $C$, then line $L_2$ is not always a diameter of circle $C$.
Statement 2 If line $L_1$ is a diameter of circle $C$, then line $L_2$ is not a chord of circle $C$.
options:
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.

Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.

Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.

Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true
questions.solution:
Equation of circle $C$ is

$\begin{aligned}
($x+3)^2+(y-5)^2 & =9+25-30=4 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \quad(x+3)^2+(y-5)^2 & =2^2 \\
$\text{ Centre }$& =(3,-5)
\end{aligned}

If $L_1$ is diameter, then $2(3)+3(-5)+p-3=0 \Rightarrow p=12\therefore \quad L_1$ is $2 x+3 y+9=0 and L_2$ is $2 x+3 y+15=0$
Distance of centre of circle from $L_2=\left|\frac{2(3)+3(-5)+15}{\sqrt{2^2+3^2}}\right|=\frac{6}{\sqrt{13}} \lt  2 \quad$ [radius of circle]
$\therefore L_2$ is a chord of circle $C$.
Statement 2 is false.

questions.q: A straight line through the vertex $P$ of a $\triangle P Q R$ intersects the side $Q R$ at the point $S$ and the circumcircle of the $\triangle P Q R$ at the point $T$. If $S$ is not the centre of the circumcircle, then
questions.solution:
Let a straight line through the vertex $P$ of a given $\triangle P Q R$ intersects the side $Q R$ at the point $S$ and the circumcircle of $\triangle P Q R$ at the point $T$.
Points $P, Q, R, T$ are concyclic, hence
$ \begin{array}{rlrl}
P S \cdot S T & =Q S \cdot S R & & \\
\Rightarrow \quad P_1 & \geq 2 \sqrt{P S \cdot S T} & \\
& \text{ Now, } \frac{P S+S T}{2} & \geq \sqrt{P S \cdot S T} & {[\because \mathrm{AM} \geq \mathrm{GM}]}
\end{array} $

and $\quad \frac{1}{P S}+\frac{1}{S T} \geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{P S \cdot S T}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{Q S \cdot S R}}$
Also, $\quad \frac{S Q+Q R}{2} \geq \sqrt{S Q \cdot S R} \Rightarrow \quad \frac{Q R}{2} \geq \sqrt{S Q \cdot S R} \begin{array}{ll}
\Rightarrow & \frac{1}{\sqrt{S Q \cdot S R}} \geq \frac{2}{Q R} \Rightarrow \frac{2}{\sqrt{S Q \cdot S R}} \geq \frac{4}{Q R} \\
\text{ Hence, } & \frac{1}{P S}+\frac{1}{S T} \geq \frac{2}{\sqrt{Q S \cdot S R}} \geq \frac{4}{Q R} .
\end{array} $

questions.q: Paragraph: A circle $C$ of radius 1 is inscribed in an equilateral $\triangle P Q R$. The points of contact of $C$ with the sides $P Q, Q R, R P$ are $D, E, F$ respectively. The line $P Q$ is given by the equation $\sqrt{3} x+y-6=0$ and the point $D$ is $\left(\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{3}{2}\right)$. Further, it is given that the origin and the centre of $C$ are on the same side of the line $P Q$.Question: Points $E and F$ are given by
questions.solution:
Slope of line joining centre of circle to point $D$ $$ =\frac{\frac{3}{2}-1}{\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2}-\sqrt{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} $$ [makes an angle $30^{\circ}$ with $X$-axis] $\therefore$ Points $E$ and $F$ will make angle $150^{\circ}$ and $-90^{\circ}$ with $X$-axis.
$\therefore E$ and $F$ are given by and $\therefore$ $$ \begin{aligned} \frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{\cos 150^{\circ}} & =\frac{y-1}{\sin 150^{\circ}}=1 \\ \frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{\cos \left(-90^{\circ}\right)} & =\frac{y-1}{\sin \left(-90^{\circ}\right)}=1 \\ E & =\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{3}{2}\right) \\ and F & =(\sqrt{3}, 0) \end{aligned} $$

questions.q:
Let $P$ be the plane such that it contains the straight line $\dfrac{x-1}{2} = \dfrac{y-3}{3} = \dfrac{z+2}{1}$ and is perpendicular to the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 4$. Let $P_1$ be the plane which passes through the point $(4, 2, 2)$ and is parallel to $P$.

Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The equation of the plane $P$ is $7x - 5y + z = -10$
The distance between the planes $P$ and $P_1$ is $30$
The distance of the plane $P$ from the origin is $2\sqrt{3}$
The acute angle between the plane $P$ and the plane $2x + 2y + z = 3$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let the normal vector to the plane $P$ be $\vec{n}$.

Since the plane $P$ contains the line $\dfrac{x-1}{2} = \dfrac{y-3}{3} = \dfrac{z+2}{1}$, its normal vector $\vec{n}$ is perpendicular to the line's direction vector $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}$.

Since $P$ is perpendicular to the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 4$, $\vec{n}$ is perpendicular to its normal vector $\vec{n}_1 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$.

$\vec{n} = (2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}) \times (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}) = \hat{i}(9-2) - \hat{j}(6-1) + \hat{k}(4-3) = 7\hat{i} - 5\hat{j} + \hat{k}$

Plane $P$ passes through the point $(1, 3, -2)$ which lies on the given line.

Equation of plane $P$ is $7(x-1) - 5(y-3) + 1(z+2) = 0 \Rightarrow 7x - 5y + z = -10$

Statement (1) is TRUE.

The plane $P_1$ is parallel to $P$ and passes through $(4, 2, 2)$.

Equation of plane $P_1$ is $7(x-4) - 5(y-2) + 1(z-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 7x - 5y + z = 20$

Distance between parallel planes $P$ and $P_1$ is $d = \dfrac{|20 - (-10)|}{\sqrt{7^2 + (-5)^2 + 1^2}} = \dfrac{30}{\sqrt{75}} = 2\sqrt{3}$. Statement (2) is FALSE.

Distance of plane $P$ from the origin is $d_0 = \dfrac{|-10|}{\sqrt{75}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. Statement (3) is FALSE.

Angle $\theta$ between the planes $7x - 5y + z + 10 = 0$ and $2x + 2y + z - 3 = 0$ is given by:

$\cos\theta = \dfrac{|7(2) + (-5)(2) + 1(1)|}{\sqrt{7^2+(-5)^2+1^2} \sqrt{2^2+2^2+1^2}} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{75} \sqrt{9}} = \dfrac{5}{15\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$

$\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)$. Statement (4) is TRUE.

questions.q:
Let $L$ be the straight line joining the points $P(1, 2, -1)$ and $Q(2, 3, 1)$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $R(4, -1, 5)$ to the line $L$. Another line passing through $R$ intersects $L$ at a point $T$ such that the point $S$ divides the line segment $PT$ internally in the ratio $|PS| : |ST| = 1 : 2$, where $|PS|$ and $|ST|$ are the lengths of the line segments $PS$ and $ST$, respectively.
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE ?
options: The orthocentre of the triangle $PRT$ is $\left(\dfrac{23}{5}, -4, \dfrac{31}{5}\right)$
The orthocentre of the triangle $PRT$ is $(4, 3, 5)$
The area of the triangle $PRT$ is $6\sqrt{5}$
The area of the triangle $PRT$ is $18\sqrt{5}$
questions.solution:
The direction ratios of line $L$ passing through $P(1, 2, -1)$ and $Q(2, 3, 1)$ are $(2-1, 3-2, 1-(-1)) = (1, 1, 2)$.

The equation of line $L$ is $\dfrac{x-1}{1} = \dfrac{y-2}{1} = \dfrac{z+1}{2} = \lambda$.

Any point on $L$ can be written as $S(\lambda+1, \lambda+2, 2\lambda-1)$.

Since $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $R(4, -1, 5)$ to $L$, the direction ratios of $RS$ are $(\lambda-3, \lambda+3, 2\lambda-6)$.

As $RS \perp L$, the dot product of their direction ratios is zero:

$1(\lambda-3) + 1(\lambda+3) + 2(2\lambda-6) = 0$

$6\lambda - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$

Thus, the coordinates of $S$ are $(3, 4, 3)$.

The length of $PS$ is $\sqrt{(3-1)^2 + (4-2)^2 + (3-(-1))^2} = \sqrt{4+4+16} = 2\sqrt{6}$.

The length of the altitude $RS$ is $\sqrt{(3-4)^2 + (4-(-1))^2 + (3-5)^2} = \sqrt{1+25+4} = \sqrt{30}$.

Since $S$ divides $PT$ internally in the ratio $1:2$, we have:

$S = \dfrac{T + 2P}{3} \Rightarrow T = 3S - 2P$

$T = 3(3, 4, 3) - 2(1, 2, -1) = (7, 8, 11)$

The length of the base $PT$ is $3|PS| = 6\sqrt{6}$.

The area of $\triangle PRT$ is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times |PT| \times |RS| = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6\sqrt{6} \times \sqrt{30} = 18\sqrt{5}$.

The orthocentre $H$ lies on the altitude $RS$. The line $RS$ passes through $S(3, 4, 3)$ and has direction ratios proportional to $R-S = (1, -5, 2)$.

Let the coordinates of $H$ be $(3+t, 4-5t, 3+2t)$.

Since $H$ is the orthocentre, $PH \perp RT$.

The direction ratios of $RT$ are $(7-4, 8-(-1), 11-5) = (3, 9, 6)$, which is proportional to $(1, 3, 2)$.

The direction ratios of $PH$ are $(3+t-1, 4-5t-2, 3+2t-(-1)) = (t+2, 2-5t, 2t+4)$.

Taking the dot product of $PH$ and $RT$:

$1(t+2) + 3(2-5t) + 2(2t+4) = 0$

$t + 2 + 6 - 15t + 4t + 8 = 0$

$16 - 10t = 0 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{8}{5}$

Substituting $t = \dfrac{8}{5}$ into the coordinates of $H$, we get:

$H = \left(3 + \dfrac{8}{5}, 4 - 5\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right), 3 + 2\left(\dfrac{8}{5}\right)\right) = \left(\dfrac{23}{5}, -4, \dfrac{31}{5}\right)$

Answer: The orthocentre of the triangle $PRT$ is $\left(\dfrac{23}{5}, -4, \dfrac{31}{5}\right)$; The area of the triangle $PRT$ is $18\sqrt{5}$

questions.q:
Let $L_1$ be the line of intersection of the planes given by the equation- $2 x+3 y+z=4 \text{ and } x+2 y+z=5 .$
Let $L_2$ be the line passing through the point $P(2,-1,3)$ and parallel to $L_1$. Let $M$ denote the plane given by the equation- $2 x+y-2 z=6$
Suppose that the line $L_2$ meets the plane $M$ at the point $Q$. Let $R$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from $P$ to the plane $M$.
Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The length of the line segment $P Q$ is $9 \sqrt{3}$
The length of the line segment $Q R$ is 15
The area of $\triangle P Q R$ is $\frac{3}{2} \sqrt{234}$
The acute angle between the line segments $P Q$ and $P R$ is $\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{3}}\right)$
questions.solution:
Let $L_1: \vec{r}=\vec{a}+t \vec{b} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\hat{\mathrm{i}} & \hat{\mathrm{j}} & \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{array}\right|=\hat{\mathrm{i}}(1)-\hat{\mathrm{j}}(1)+\hat{\mathrm{k}}(1)$ Dr's of $L_1: <1,-1,1> \begin{aligned} & L_1: \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y-0}{-1}=\frac{z-6}{1} \\ & \& L_2: \frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-3}{1}=\lambda \\ & M: 2 x+y-2 z-6=0 \end{aligned}$ Let point on $\mathrm{L}_2(\lambda+2,-\lambda-1, \lambda+3) \begin{aligned} & 2(\lambda+2)-\lambda-1-2 \lambda-6-6=0 \\ & 2 \lambda+4-3 \lambda-13=0 \\ & \lambda=-9 \\ & \therefore Q(-7,8,-6) \end{aligned}$
Line PR: $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-3}{-2}=\mu \mathrm{R}(2 \mu+2, \mu-1,-2 \mu+3)$ Put in plane $\begin{aligned} & 2(2 \mu+2)+\mu-1-2(-2 \mu+3)-6=0 \\ & 4 \mu+4+\mu-1+4 \mu-6-6=0 \\ & 9 \mu-9=0 \Rightarrow \mu=1 \\ & \mathrm{R}(4,0,1) \\ & \mathrm{P}(2,-1,3) \& \mathrm{Q}(-7,8,-6) \\ & \mathrm{PQ}=\sqrt{81+81+81}=9 \sqrt{3} \\ & \mathrm{Q}(-7,8,-6) \& \mathrm{R}(4,0,1) \end{aligned} \mathrm{QR}=\sqrt{121+64+49}=\sqrt{234}$ Area ( $\triangle \mathrm{PQR}$ ) $\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{QP}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{QR}}| \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{\mathrm{i}} & \hat{\mathrm{j}} & \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ 9 & -9 & 9 \\ 11 & -8 & 7 \end{array}\right| \\ & =\frac{3}{2} \sqrt{234} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}}=-9 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+9 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-9 \hat{\mathrm{k}}=-9(\hat{\mathrm{i}}-\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}}) \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PR}}=2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}-2 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \cos \theta=\left|\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{PQ}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PR}}}{\mathrm{PQ} \cdot \mathrm{PR}}\right| \\ & =\frac{9}{9 \sqrt{3} \times 3}=\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{3}} \\ & \theta=\cos ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3 \sqrt{3}}\right)\end{aligned}$
