Let $P$ be the plane $\sqrt{3}x + 2y + 3z = 16$ and let
$S = \left\{\alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j} + \gamma\overset{^}{k}: {\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} + {\gamma}^{2} = 1\right$ and the distance of $\left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right)$ from the plane $P$ is $\dfrac{7}{2} }$.
Let $\overset{\to}{u}, \overset{\to}{v}$ and $\overset{\to}{w}$ be three distinct vectors in $S$ such that $\left|\overset{\to}{u} - \overset{\to}{v}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{v} - \overset{\to}{w}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{w} - \overset{\to}{u}\right|$. Let $V$ be the volume of the parallelepiped determined by vectors $\overset{\to}{u}, \overset{\to}{v}$ and $\overset{\to}{w}$. Then the value of $\dfrac{80}{\sqrt{3}}V$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

Equation of plane,

$P: \sqrt{3}x + 2y + 3z = 16$

And $S = \alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j} + \gamma\overset{^}{k}: {\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} + {γ}^{2} = 1$ which is equation of sphere,

Also distance, $d \left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right) from $ P = $\dfrac{7}{2}

And relation between distinct vector is given by,\left|\overset{→}{u} - \overset{→}{v}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{v} - \overset{→}{w}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{w} - \overset{→}{u}\right|

Now $ V$ : volume of parallelepiped by vectors \overset{→}{u}, \overset{→}{v}, \overset{→}{w}$

So, using formula of distance $d \left(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\right)$ from $P = \dfrac{7}{2}$ we get,

$⇒ \left|\sqrt{3}\alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma - 16\right|\sqrt{3 + 4 + 9} = \dfrac{7}{2}$

$⇒ \left|\sqrt{3}\alpha + 2\beta + 3\gamma - 16\right|4 = \dfrac{7}{2}$

$⇒ \left|\sqrt{3}\alpha ++2\beta ++3\gamma -16\right| = 14.... \left(i\right)$

Also, ${\alpha}^{2} + {\beta}^{2} + {γ}^{2} = 1....... \left(ii\right)$

Now we know that,

Volume of parallelepiped by vector, \overset{→}{u}, \overset{→}{v}, \overset{→}{w}$ is given by,

$V = $\left[\overset{→}{u}\overset{→}{v}\overset{→}{w}\right]

$= \overset{→}{u} \cdot $\left(v \times$ w\right)...... $\left(iii\right)$

$\left|\overset{→}{u}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{v}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{w}\right| =1$ (As they lie on sphere of unit radius) $...... \left(iv\right)$

$\left|\overset{→}{u} - \overset{→}{v}\right| =\left|\overset{→}{v} - \overset{→}{w}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{w} - \overset{→}{u}\right|$ (Given)

Now squaring, we get,

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{u} - \overset{→}{v}\right|2 = \left|\overset{→}{v} - \overset{→}{w}\right|2 = \left|\overset{→}{w} - \overset{→}{u}\right|2$

$⇒ \mathop{u^{2} + v^{2} - 2\overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{v}}_{A} = \mathop{v^{2} + w^{2} - 2\overset{→}{v} \cdot \overset{→}{w}}_{B} = \mathop{w^{2} + u^{2} - 2\overset{→}{w} \cdot \overset{→}{u}⏟}_{C}$

Now from $\left(A\right)$ and $\left(B\right)$ we get,

$⇒ u^{2} + v^{2} - 2\overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{v} =$ v^{2} + w^{2} - 2\overset{→}{v} $\cdot \overset{→}{w}

$⇒ u^{2} - w^{2} = 2\overset{→}{u} $\cdot \overset{→}{v} -2\overset{→}{v} $\cdot \overset{→}{w} $\left[∵ \left|\overset{→}{u}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{w}\right| =$=1$\left(Given\right)\right]$

$⇒ \overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{v} = \overset{→}{v} \cdot \overset{→}{w}

Hence, by using \left(B\right)$ and $\left(C\right)$ also, we will get

\overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{v} = \overset{→}{v} \cdot \overset{→}{w} = \overset{→}{w} \cdot \overset{→}{u} =m $\left(say\right)....... \left(v\right)$

$⇒ \overset{→}{u}, \overset{→}{v}, \overset{→}{w}$ are the vectors of an equilateral triangle (say $∆ ABC$)

d$\left(O, P\right) =\dfrac{16}{3 + 4 + 9}= \dfrac{16}{4}=4$ units

\overset{→}{OA} = \overset{→}{u}, \overset{→}{OB} = \overset{→}{v}, \overset{→}{OC} = \overset{→}{w}$

\left|\overset{→}{OA}\right| =\left|\overset{→}{OB}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{OC}\right| =1$ (Given)

In an equilateral triangle, circumcentre, orthrocentre and centroid coincide.

Let $D$ be the circumcentre of $∆ ABC$, then

$∠ ADB = {120}^{∘}$

$⇒ cos ∠ ADB = \dfrac{DA^{2} + DB^{2} - AB^{2}}{2 \left(DA\right)\cdot\left(DB\right)$}$...... \left(vi\right)$

$OE = OD + DE= OD + AF$

$⇒ 4 = OD + \dfrac{7}{2}

$⇒ OD = 4 - $\dfrac{7}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ DA = $\sqrt{OA^{2} - OD^{2}}= \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}}

$⇒ DA = $\dfrac{3}{2}

$⇒ DA = DB = $\dfrac{3}{2}..... \left(vii\right)$

From $\left(vi\right)$ and $\left(vii\right)$ we get,

$- \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} - AB^{2}}{2\dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{2}}$

$- \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{2} - AB^{2}}{32}$

$⇒ - \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} -$ AB^{2}$

$⇒ AB^{2} = $\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{3}{4}$

$⇒ AB^{2} = \dfrac{9}{4}$

$⇒ AB = \dfrac{3}{2} = \left|\overset{→}{u} - \overset{→}{v}\right|$

$⇒ AB^{2} = \dfrac{9}{4} =$ u^{2} + v^{2} - 2\overset{→}{u} $\cdot \overset{→}{v}

$⇒ $\dfrac{9}{4} =1 + 1 - 2m$

$⇒ 2m = 2 - \dfrac{9}{4} = - \dfrac{1}{4}$

$⇒ m = - \dfrac{1}{8}......\left(viii\right)$

Volume of parallelepiped,

$V = \left|\left[\overset{→}{u}\overset{→}{v}\overset{→}{w}\right]\right|

\left|\overset{→}{u}\overset{→}{v}\overset{→}{w}\right|2 = \left|\begin{cases}1 & \overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{v}& \overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{w}\\ \overset{→}{u} \cdot \overset{→}{v}& 1 & \overset{→}{v} \cdot \overset{→}{w}\\ \overset{→}{w} \cdot \overset{→}{u}& \overset{→}{w} \cdot \overset{→}{v}& 1\end{cases}\right|$

$= \left|\begin{cases}1 & m & m \\ m & 1 & m \\ m & m & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$= 1 \left(1 - m^{2}\right) - m \left(m - m^{2}\right) + m\left(m^{2} - m\right)$

$= 1 - m^{2} - m^{2} + m^{3} + m^{3} - m^{2}$

$= 1 - 3m^{2} + 2m^{3}$

$\left|\begin{cases}\overset{→}{u}& \overset{→}{v} & \overset{→}{w}\end{cases}\right|2 = 2m^{3} - 3m^{2} + 1$

$= \left(m - 1\right) \left[2m^{2} - m - 1\right]$

$= \left(m - 1\right) \left[2m^{2} - 2m + m - 1\right]$

$= \left(m - 1\right)\left(m - 1\right) \left(2m + 1\right)$

$= \left(m - 1\right)^{2} \left(2m + 1\right)$

$⇒ \left|\left[\begin{cases}\overset{→}{u}& \overset{→}{v} & \overset{→}{w}\end{cases}\right]\right| = \left(m - 1\right)\sqrt{\left(2m + 1\right)$}

$⇒ V = \left|\left(- \dfrac{1}{8} -1\right)\sqrt{2 \times - \dfrac{1}{8} +1}\right|$

$⇒ V = \dfrac{9}{8} \times \dfrac{3}{2}

Hence, \dfrac{80}{3}$ V = $\dfrac{80}{3} \times \dfrac{9}{8} \times \dfrac{3}{2}=45$

$\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} = \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} = m\left(say\right) . . . . . . . \left(v\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{u}, \overset{\to}{v}, \overset{\to}{w}$ are the vectors of an equilateral triangle (say $∆ ABC$)

$d\left(O, P\right) = \dfrac{16}{\sqrt{3 + 4 + 9}}$$= \dfrac{16}{4}$$= 4$ units

$\overset{\to}{OA} = \overset{\to}{u}, \overset{\to}{OB} = \overset{\to}{v}, \overset{\to}{OC} = \overset{\to}{w}$

$\left|\overset{\to}{OA}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{OB}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{OC}\right| = 1$ (Given)

In an equilateral triangle, circumcentre, orthrocentre and centroid coincide.

Let $D$ be the circumcentre of $∆ ABC$, then

$∠ ADB = {120}^{∘}$

$⇒ cos ∠ ADB = \dfrac{D{A}^{2} + D{B}^{2} - A{B}^{2}}{2\left(DA\right) \cdot \left(DB\right)} . . . . . . \left(vi\right)$

$OE = OD + DE$$= OD + AF$

$⇒ 4 = OD + \dfrac{7}{2}$

$⇒ OD = 4 - \dfrac{7}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ DA = \sqrt{O{A}^{2} - O{D}^{2}}$$= \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}}$

$⇒ DA = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$⇒ DA = DB = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} . . . . . \left(vii\right)$

From $\left(vi\right)$ and $\left(vii\right)$ we get,

$- \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} - A{B}^{2}}{2\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}$

$- \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{2} - A{B}^{2}}{\dfrac{3}{2}}$

$⇒ - \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} - A{B}^{2}$

$⇒ A{B}^{2} = \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{3}{4}$

$⇒ A{B}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{4}$

$⇒ AB = \dfrac{3}{2} = \left|\overset{\to}{u} - \overset{\to}{v}\right|$

$⇒ A{B}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{4} = {u}^{2} + {v}^{2} - 2\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v}$

$⇒ \dfrac{9}{4} = 1 + 1 - 2m$

$⇒ 2m = 2 - \dfrac{9}{4} = - \dfrac{1}{4}$

$⇒ m = - \dfrac{1}{8} . . . . . . \left(viii\right)$

Volume of parallelepiped,

$V = \left|\left[\overset{\to}{u}\overset{\to}{v}\overset{\to}{w}\right]\right|$

${\left|\overset{\to}{u}\overset{\to}{v}\overset{\to}{w}\right|}^{2} = \left|\begin{cases}1 & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} \\ \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & 1 & \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} \\ \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$= \left|\begin{cases}1 & m & m \\ m & 1 & m \\ m & m & 1\end{cases}\right|$

$= 1\left(1 - {m}^{2}\right) - m\left(m - {m}^{2}\right) + m\left({m}^{2} - m\right)$

$= 1 - {m}^{2} - {m}^{2} + {m}^{3} + {m}^{3} - {m}^{2}$

$= 1 - 3{m}^{2} + 2{m}^{3}$

Hence, $\dfrac{80}{\sqrt{3}}V = \dfrac{80}{\sqrt{3}} \times \dfrac{9}{8} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$= 45$

questions.q:
Let $\overset{^}{i}, \overset{^}{j}$ and $\overset{^}{k}$ be the unit vectors along the three positive coordinate axes. Let

$\overset{\to}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{b} = \overset{^}{i} + {b}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {b}_{3}\overset{^}{k}, {b}_{2}, {b}_{3} \in \mathbb{R}$

$\overset{\to}{c} = {c}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {c}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{3}\overset{^}{k}, {c}_{1}, {c}_{2}, {c}_{3} \in \mathbb{R}$

be three vectors such that ${b}_{2}{b}_{3} > 0, \overset{\to}{a} \cdot \overset{\to}{b} = 0$ and $\left(\begin{cases}0 & - {c}_{3} & {c}_{2} \\ {c}_{3} & 0 & - {c}_{1} \\ - {c}_{2} & {c}_{1} & 0\end{cases}\right)\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{3}\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ll}3 - {c}_{1} \\ 1 - {c}_{2} \\ - 1 - {c}_{3}\end{array}$\right) .$ Then, which of the following is/are TRUE?

$
questions.solution:
Given,

$\overset{\to}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{b} = \overset{^}{i} + {b}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {b}_{3}\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{c} = {c}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {c}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{3}\overset{^}{k}$

$\left[\begin{cases}0 & - {c}_{3} & {c}_{2} \\ {c}_{3} & 0 & - {c}_{1} \\ - {c}_{2} & {c}_{1} & 0\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ {b}_{2} \\ {b}_{3}\end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{ll}3 - {c}_{1} \\ 1 - {c}_{2} \\ - 1 - {c}_{3}\end{array}\right]$

Now multiply and compare we get,

${b}_{2}{c}_{3} - {b}_{3}{c}_{2} = {c}_{1} - 3 . . . . . . . \left(1\right)$

${c}_{3} - {b}_{3}{c}_{1} = 1 - {c}_{2} . . . . . . . . . . . \left(2\right)$

${c}_{2} - {b}_{2}{c}_{1} = 1 + {c}_{3} . . . . . . . . . . . \left(3\right)$

Now applying operation $\text{equation}\left(1\right)\overset{^}{i} - \left(2\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left(3\right)\overset{^}{k}$ we get,

$\overset{^}{i}\left({b}_{2}{c}_{3} - {c}_{2}{b}_{3}\right) - \overset{^}{j}\left({c}_{3} - {b}_{3}{c}_{1}\right) + \overset{^}{k}\left({c}_{2} - {b}_{2}{c}_{1}\right) = {c}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {c}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {c}_{3}\overset{^}{k} - 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{b} \times \overset{\to}{c} = \overset{\to}{c} - \overset{\to}{a} . . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ \left(\overset{\to}{b} \times \overset{\to}{c}\right) \cdot \overset{\to}{b} = \overset{\to}{c} \cdot \overset{\to}{b} - \overset{\to}{a} \cdot \overset{\to}{b}$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{b} \cdot \overset{\to}{c} = 0$ $\left\{\text{given}\overset{\to}{a}\text{.}\overset{\to}{b}\text{=0}\right\}$

Again from (i)

$\left(\overset{\to}{c} \times \overset{\to}{b}\right) \cdot \overset{\to}{c} = \overset{\to}{a} \cdot \overset{\to}{c} - {\left|\overset{\to}{c}\right|}^{2} = 0$

$⇒ {\left|\overset{\to}{c}\right|}^{2} = \left|\overset{\to}{a}\right|\left|\overset{\to}{c}\right|cos\theta$, where $\theta = \overset{\to}{a} ∧\overset{\to}{c}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{\to}{c}\right| \ge \left|\overset{\to}{a}\right| ⇒ \left|\overset{\to}{c}\right| \ge \sqrt{11}$

Given that $\overset{\to}{a} \cdot \overset{\to}{b} = 0 ⇒ {b}_{2} - {b}_{3} + 3 = 0$

$⇒ {b}_{3} - {b}_{2} = 3$

Also ${b}_{2} - {b}_{3} > 0$

Now $\left|\overset{\to}{b}\right| = 1 + {b}_{2}^{2} + {b}_{3}^{2}$

$= 1 + {\left({b}_{3} - {b}_{2}\right)}^{2} + 2{b}_{2}{b}_{3}$

$= 10 + 2{b}_{2}{b}_{3}$

$⇒ {\left|\overset{\to}{b}\right|}^{2} > 10 ⇒ \left|\overset{\to}{b}\right| > \sqrt{10}$

$⇒ \left|\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\left(\overset{\to}{OA} \times \overset{\to}{OB}\right)\right| = \dfrac{9}{2} . . . \left(1\right)$

now, $\overset{\to}{OA} \times \overset{\to}{OB} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & - 2 & 2\end{cases}\right|$

$= 6\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} - 6\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{\to}{OA} \times \overset{\to}{OB}\right| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 36} = 9 . . . \left(2\right)$

Put in (1) $\left|\dfrac{\lambda}{2} \times 9\right| = \dfrac{9}{2}$

$⇒ \left|\lambda\right| = 1$

$⇒ \lambda = \pm 1\left(∵ \lambda > 0\right)$

$⇒ \lambda = 1$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{OC} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\overset{\to}{OB} - \overset{\to}{OA}\right)$

(A)

Projection of $\overset{\to}{OC}$ on $\overset{\to}{OA}$

$= \dfrac{\overset{\to}{OC} ⋅ \overset{\to}{OA}}{\left|\overset{\to}{OA}\right|}$

$= 6\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} - 6\overset{^}{k}$

Let $\overset{\to}{u}, \overset{\to}{v}$ and $\overset{\to}{w}$ be vectors in three-dimensional space, where $\overset{\to}{u}$ and $\overset{\to}{v}$ are unit vectors which are not perpendicular to each other and $\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = 1, \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = 1, \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = 4$.
If the volume of the parallelopiped, whose adjacent sides are represented by the vectors $\overset{\to}{u}, \overset{\to}{v}$ and $\overset{\to}{w}$, is $\sqrt{2}$, then the value of $| 3\overset{\to}{u} + 5\overset{\to}{v} |$ is
questions.solution:
Volume of the parallelopiped is $\left[\overset{\to}{u}\overset{\to}{v}\overset{\to}{w}\right] = \sqrt{2}$

$⇒ {\left[\overset{\to}{u}\overset{\to}{v}\overset{\to}{w}\right]}^{2} = 2$

$⇒ \left|\begin{cases}\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot v & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} \\ \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} \\ \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{w}\end{cases}\right| = 2$

Using $\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = 1, \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = 1, \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} = 4$, we get

$\left|\begin{cases}\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot v & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} \\ \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{w} \\ \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & \overset{\to}{w} \cdot \overset{\to}{w}\end{cases}\right| = \left|\begin{cases}1 & \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} & 1 \\ \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{cases}\right| = 2$

$⇒ 3 - \left(\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v}\right)\left(4\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} - 1\right) + \overset{\to}{v} \cdot \overset{\to}{u} - 1 = 2$

$⇒ \left(\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v}\right) ( 1 - 4\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} + 1 ) = 0$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} = \dfrac{1}{2} ( ∵ \overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v} \ne 0 )$

Also, $\left|\overset{\to}{u}\right| = 1, \left|\overset{\to}{v}\right| = 1$

So, $| 3\overset{\to}{u} + 5\overset{\to}{v} | = \sqrt{{\left(| 3\overset{\to}{u} + 5\overset{\to}{v} |\right)}^{2}}$

$= \sqrt{9{\left|\overset{\to}{u}\right|}^{2} + 25{\left|\overset{\to}{v}\right|}^{2} + 30\overset{\to}{u} \cdot \overset{\to}{v}}$

$= 7$

questions.q: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Suppose $\overset{\to}{PQ} = a\overset{^}{i} + b\overset{^}{j}$ and $\overset{\to}{PS} = a\overset{^}{i} - b\overset{^}{j}$ are adjacent sides of a parallelogram $PQRS .$ Let $\overset{\to}{u}$ and $\overset{\to}{v}$ be the projection vectors of $\overset{\to}{w} = \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}$ along $\overset{\to}{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to}{PS}$, respectively. If $| \overset{\to}{u} | + \left|\overset{\to}{v}\right| = \left|\overset{\to}{w}\right|$ and if the area of the parallelogram $PQRS$ is $8,$ then which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: The length of the diagonal $PR$ of the parallelogram $PQRS$ is 4
$\overset{\to}{w}$ is an angle bisector of the vectors $\overset{\to}{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to}{PS}$
questions.solution:
Projection of $\overset{\to}{a}along\overset{\to}{b} = \dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} . \overset{\to}{b}}{\left|\overset{\to}{b}\right|} \cdot \overset{^}{b}$

$\overset{\to}{u} = \left\{\left(\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}\right) \cdot \dfrac{a\overset{^}{i} + b\overset{^}{j}}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}\right\}\dfrac{a\overset{^}{i} + b\overset{^}{j}}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}} = \dfrac{\left(a + b\right)}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}} \cdot \dfrac{a\overset{^}{i} + b\overset{^}{j}}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}$

$\overset{\to}{v} = \left\{\left(\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}\right) \cdot \dfrac{a\overset{^}{i} - b\overset{^}{j}}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}\right\}\dfrac{a\overset{^}{i} - b\overset{^}{j}}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}} = \dfrac{\left(a - b\right)}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}} \cdot \dfrac{a\overset{^}{i} - b\overset{^}{j}}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}$

given $\left|\begin{cases}i & j & k \\ a & b & 0 \\ a & - b & 0\end{cases}\right| = 8$

$\left|\overset{^}{k}\left(- ab - ab\right)\right| = 8$

$ab = 4$

Given $\left|\overset{\to}{u}\right| + | \overset{\to}{v} | = \overset{\to}{w}$

$\dfrac{a + b}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}}\dfrac{\left|a - b\right|}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}} = \sqrt{2}$

For $a > b$,

$2a = \sqrt{2}\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}$

$2{a}^{2} = {a}^{2} + {b}^{2}$

${a}^{2} = {b}^{2} ⇒ a = b = 2$

Similarly, for $b > a, a = b = 2$

$a + b = 4$

$a - b = 0$

Length of diagonal $\overset{\to}{\left|PR\right|} = \left|\overset{\to}{PS} + \overset{\to}{PQ}\right| = \left|2a\overset{^}{i}\right| = 2a = 4$.

questions.solution:
$\overset{\to}{a} + \overset{\to}{b} + \overset{\to}{c} = 0$

$∵ \dfrac{\overset{\to}{a} . \left(\overset{\to}{c} - \overset{\to}{b}\right)}{\overset{\to}{c} . \left(\overset{\to}{a} - \overset{\to}{b}\right)} = \dfrac{\left|\overset{\to}{a}\right|}{\left|\overset{\to}{a}\right| + \left|\overset{\to}{b}\right|}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{\left|\overset{\to}{c}\right|}^{2} - {\left|\overset{\to}{b}\right|}^{2}}{{\left|\overset{\to}{a}\right|}^{2} - {\left|\overset{\to}{b}\right|}^{2}} = \dfrac{3}{3 + 4} = \dfrac{3}{7}$

$⇒ {\left|\overset{\to}{c}\right|}^{2} = 13$

$⇒ 9 + 16 + 2\left(\overset{\to}{a} . \overset{\to}{b}\right) = 13$

questions.q: Consider the cube in the first octant with sides $OP, OQ$ and OR of length $1$, along the x-axis, y-axis and z-axis, respectively, where $O ( 0, 0, 0 )$ is the origin. Let $S\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ be the centre of the cube and $T$ be the vertex of the cube opposite to the origin $O$ such that $S$ lies on the diagonal $OT$. If $\overset{\to}{p} = \overset{\to}{SP}, \overset{\to}{q} = \overset{\to}{SQ}, \overset{\to}{r} = \overset{\to}{SR}$ and $\overset{\to}{t} = \overset{\to}{ST}$, then the value of $\left|\left(\overset{\to}{p} \times \overset{\to}{q}\right) \times \left(\overset{\to}{r} \times \overset{\to}{t}\right)\right|$ is ______.
questions.solution:
$\overset{\to}{p} = \overset{\to}{SP} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, - \dfrac{1}{2}, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right)$
$\overset{\to}{q} = \overset{\to}{SQ} = \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(- \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right)$
$\overset{\to}{r} = \overset{\to}{SR} = \left(- \dfrac{1}{2}, - \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(- \overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}\right)$
$\overset{\to}{t} = \overset{\to}{ST} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}\right)$
$\left|\left(\overset{\to}{p} \times \overset{\to}{q}\right) \times \left(\overset{\to}{r} \times \overset{\to}{t}\right)\right| = \left|\dfrac{1}{4}\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & 1 & - 1\end{cases}\right| \times \dfrac{1}{4}\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ - 1 & - 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{cases}\right|\right|$
$= \dfrac{1}{16}\left|\left(2\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j}\right) \times \left(- 2\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j}\right)\right| = \left|\dfrac{\overset{^}{k}}{2}\right| = \dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.solution:

${u}_{2}{v}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}, - u{}_{1}{v}_{3} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} ⇒ \left|{u}_{1}\right| = \left|{u}_{2}\right|$

$⇒$ $2\left|{u}_{3}\right| = \left|{u}_{1}\right|$

$⇒$ $p = r = - q$

questions.solution:
Given that $\vec{a} \times(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})=(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k}) \times \vec{b}$ $\Rightarrow(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \times(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})=\overrightarrow{0}$

But $\vec{a}+\vec{b} \neq 0$ and $2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k} \neq 0$

$\therefore(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \|(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})$.

Let $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=\lambda(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})$

Also given that $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|=\sqrt{29} \Rightarrow \lambda=\pm 1$

$\therefore \vec{a}+\vec{b}=\pm(2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{j}+4 \hat{k})$

So, $(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) \cdot(-7 \hat{i}+2 \hat{i}+3 \hat{k})=\pm 4$

questions.q: If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are unit vectors satisfying $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9$, then $|2 \vec{a}+5 \vec{b}+5 \vec{c}|$ is
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{l}

\because|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=1 \\

|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9 \\

\Rightarrow 2\left(|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}\right)-2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a})=9 \\

\Rightarrow \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=\frac{-3}{2}

\end{array}$

Also,

$\begin{array}{l}

|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}) \\

=1+1+1+2 \times\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=0 \\

\Rightarrow \vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=0 \Rightarrow(\vec{b}+\vec{c})=-\vec{a} \\

\therefore|2 \vec{a}+5(\vec{b}+\vec{c})|=|2 \vec{a}-5 \vec{a}|=|-3 \vec{a}|=3

\end{array}$

If $\mathbf{r}$ is a vector such that $\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{a}=0$, then the value of $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$& $\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{b}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{c}) \times \mathbf{b}=0 \Rightarrow \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{c}+\lambda \mathbf{b} \\
 \text{$ or $} \quad \mathbf{r}=\mathbf{c}+\lambda \mathbf{b}\\
&
\end{aligned}

Given, \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{a}=0$, taking dot product with a for Eq. (i).
Now, $\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{a}=\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}+\lambda \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}\therefore \quad \lambda=\frac{-\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}}{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}} \quad[\because \vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0] \ldots$ (i)
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get

$\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{c}-\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}} \mathbf{b}$ Taking dot with $\mathbf{b}$, we get

$\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b}-\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}(\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b})$ where, $\left[$\begin{array}{l}$\mathbf{a}=$-\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-\hat{$\mathbf{k}$} \\ $\mathbf{b}=$-\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+\hat{$\mathbf{j}$} \\ $\mathbf{c}=$\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+2 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+3 \hat{$\mathbf{k}$}\end{array}$\right]$
=(-1+2)-$\frac{(-1-3)}{(1)}$(1+1)=1+8=9

questions.question: Let $\mathbf{a}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}, \mathbf{b}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ and $\mathbf{c}=\hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ be three vectors. questions.explanation:
Let $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{a}+\lambda \mathbf{b}$
$$
\mathbf{v}=(1+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(1-\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+(1+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{k}}
$$
Projection of $\mathbf{v}$ on $\mathbf{c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$
$$
\begin{array}{lc}
\Rightarrow & \frac{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{c}}{|\mathbf{c}|}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\
\Rightarrow & \frac{(1+\lambda)-(1-\lambda)-(1+\lambda)}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\
\Rightarrow & 1+\lambda-1+\lambda-1-\lambda=1 \\
\Rightarrow & \lambda-1=1 \Rightarrow \lambda=2 \\
\therefore & \mathbf{v}=3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}
\end{array}
$$

The side $A D$ is rotated by an acute angle $\alpha$ in the plane of the parallelogram so that $A D$ becomes $A D^{\prime}$. If $A D^{\prime}$ makes a right angle with the side $A B$, then the cosine of the angle $\alpha$ is given by
questions.solution:
$$ \overrightarrow{\mathbf{A B}}=2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+10 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+11 \hat{\mathbf{k}} $$
$$ \overrightarrow{\mathbf{A D}}=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}} $$ Angle ' $\theta$ ' between $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{A B}}$ and $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{A D}}$ is $$ \begin{aligned} & \cos (\theta)=\left|\begin{array}{l} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{A B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{A D}} \\ \mid \overrightarrow{\mathbf{A B}}\|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{A D}}\| \end{array}\right| \\ & =\left|\frac{-2+20+22}{(15)(3)}\right|=\frac{8}{9} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \sin (\theta)=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{9} \\ & \text { Since, } \quad \alpha+\theta=90^{\circ} \\ & \therefore \quad \cos (\alpha)=\cos \left(90^{\circ}-\theta\right) \\ & =\sin (\theta)=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{9} \\ & \end{aligned} $$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{x}{a}=\frac{y}{b}=\frac{z}{c} \\
& \therefore \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
2 & 1 & -1 \\
1 & -2 & 1 \\
a & b & c
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a(-1)-b(3)+c(-5)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad-a-3 b-5 c=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a+3 b+5 c=0 \\
& \text{ Also, } \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\frac{8}{3} & -3 & 1 \\
2 & -1 & 1 \\
a & b & c
\end{array}\right|=0
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad a(-2)-b\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)+c\left(\frac{10}{3}\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2 a+\frac{2 b}{3}-\frac{10 c}{3}=0 \\
& 3 a+b-5 c=0 \\
&
\end{aligned}
$$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii),
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a}{-20} & =\frac{b}{20}=\frac{c}{-8} \\
\frac{a}{5} & =\frac{b}{-5}=\frac{c}{4}
\end{aligned}
$$
Equation of line is
$$
\frac{x}{5}=\frac{y}{-5}=\frac{z}{4}=\lambda \text{ (say) }
$$
Also, $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+1}{1}=k_1$ (say)
Now, $\frac{x-\frac{8}{3}}{2}=\frac{y+3}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{1}=k_2$ (say)
Point on (iii) is $(5 \lambda,-5 \lambda,+4 \lambda)$ Point on (iv) is

$$
\left(2+k_1, 1-2 k_1,-1+k_1\right)
$$
Point on $(\mathrm{v})$ is
$$
\left(\frac{8}{3}+2 k_2,-3-k_2, 1+k_2\right)
$$
On solving, $2+k_1+1-2 k_1=0$
$$
-k_1+3=0
$$
$$
\begin{aligned}
k_1 & =3 \\
P & \equiv(5,-5,2)
\end{aligned}
$$
Again, for $Q$
$$
\begin{array}{r}
\frac{8}{3}+2 k_2-3-k_2=0 \\
k_2-\frac{1}{3}=0 \\
k_2=\frac{1}{3} \\
Q \equiv\left(\frac{10}{3}, \frac{-10}{3}, \frac{4}{3}\right)
\end{array}
$$
$$
\text{ Now, } \begin{aligned}
P Q & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2} \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{54}}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P Q^2=d^2=\frac{54}{9}=6
$$

$$
\begin{array}{rlrl}
\Rightarrow & & \frac{6}{x^2-8} & =\frac{3}{4} \\
\Rightarrow & & 3 x^2 & =48 \\
\Rightarrow & x & =\pm 4
\end{array}
$$
(C)
$$
\begin{aligned}
& (\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}-\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}) \cdot\left(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}-\mu \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}}{4}\right)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}-\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}) \cdot(4 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}-\mu \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}})=0 \\
& \text{ Also, } 2\left|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}+\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}-\mu \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}}{4}\right|=|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}-\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}| \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 2\left|\frac{(4-\mu) \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}^2-\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}^2=0}{4}\right|=|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}-\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}|
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \frac{(4-\mu)^2 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}^2}{4}+\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}^2}{4}=\overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}^2+\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}^2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{3 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}^2}{4}=\frac{(4-\mu)^2-4}{4} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}^2 \\
& 3 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}^2=C(4-\mu)^2-4 \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}^2
\end{aligned}
$$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii)
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 3(4-\mu)=(4-\mu)^2-4 \\
& (4-\mu)^2-3(4-\mu)-4=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \mu=0,5 \\
& \mu=5 \text{ is not admissible. }
\end{aligned}
$$
(D) $f(0)=9$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& f(x)=\frac{\sin \left(\frac{9 x}{2}\right)}{\sin \frac{x}{2}} \\
& =\left(3-4 \sin ^2 \frac{x}{2}\right)\left(3-4 \sin ^2 \frac{3 x}{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =9-12 \sin ^2 \frac{x}{2}-12 \sin ^2 \frac{3 x}{2} \\
& \quad+16 \sin ^2 \frac{x}{2} \cdot \sin ^2 \frac{3 x}{2} \\
& =9-6(1-\cos x)-6(1-\cos 3 x) \\
& \quad+4(1-\cos x)(1-\cos 3 x) \\
& =1+6 \cos x+6 \cos 3 x-4 \cos x \\
& \quad-4 \cos 3 x+4 \cos x \cos 3 x \\
& \text{ Let } \quad I=\frac{2}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^\pi \frac{\sin \frac{9 x}{2}}{2} d x \\
& =\frac{4}{\pi} \int_0^\pi 1+2 \cos x+2 \cos 3 x \\
& =\frac{4}{\pi} \times \pi \quad+2(\cos 4 x+\cos x) d x \\
& =4
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.q: If $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ are the unit vectors such that $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}=\frac{1}{2}$, then
options:
$\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are non-coplanar

$\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{d}$ are non-parallel

$\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{d}$ are non-coplanar

a, d are parallel and $\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are parallel
questions.solution:
Let angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be $\theta_1, \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ be $\theta_2$ and $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}$ be $\theta$. Since, $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1\Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta_1 \cdot \sin \theta_2 \cdot \cos \theta=1\Rightarrow \theta_1=90^{{}^{\circ}}, \theta_2=90^{{}^{\circ}}, \theta=0^{{}^{\circ}}\Rightarrow \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \perp \mathbf{d},(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \|(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})$ So, $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})$ and $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})\Rightarrow \quad(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}) \cdot \mathbf{c} and (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{d}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}) \cdot \mathbf{d}\Rightarrow\left[$\begin{array}{lll}$\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{c}$\end{array}$\right]=0$ and $\left[$\begin{array}{lll}$\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{d}$\end{array}$\right]=0\Rightarrow \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{d}$ are coplanar vectors, so options (a) and (b) are incorrect. Let $\quad \mathbf{b} \| \mathbf{d} \Rightarrow \mathbf{b}=\pm \mathbf{d}$ As $\quad(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{b})=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad[\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c} \mathbf{b}]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad[\mathbf{c} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{c} \cdot[\mathbf{b} \times(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{c} \cdot[\mathbf{a}-(\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \mathbf{b}]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}=\pm 1 \quad[\because \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=0]$ which is a contradiction, so option (c) is correct.

Let two non-collinear unit vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ form an acute angle.
A point $P$ moves so that at any time $t$ the position vector $\mathbf{O P}$ (where, $O$ is the origin) is given by $\mathbf{a} \cos t+\hat{\mathbf{b}} \sin t$. When $P$ is farthest from origin $O$, let $M$ be the length of $\mathbf{O P}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ be the unit vector along $\mathbf{O P}$. Then,
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{O P}=\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cos t+\hat{\mathbf{b}} \sin t 
\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad|\mathbf{O P}|=\sqrt{\left(\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cos ^2 t+\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \sin ^2 t+2 \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \sin t \cos t\right)} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad|\mathbf{O P}|=\sqrt{1+2 \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \sin t \cos t} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad|\mathbf{O P}|=\sqrt{1+\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \sin 2 t} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad|\mathbf{O P}|_{\max }=\sqrt{1+\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}} \text{ at } \sin 2 t=1 \Rightarrow t=\frac{\pi}{4} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathbf{O P}\left(\text{ at } t=\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}+\hat{\mathbf{b}}) \\
&
\end{aligned}
$ \therefore$ Unit vector along  \mathbf{O P}  at \left(t=\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{a}}+\hat{\mathbf{b}}}{|\hat{\mathbf{a}}+\hat{\mathbf{b}}|}$

questions.q: The edges of a parallelopiped are of unit length and are parallel to non-coplanar unit vectors $\hat{\mathbf{a}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}, \hat{\mathbf{c}}$ such that $\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{c}}=\hat{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}=\frac{1}{2}$. Then, the volume of the parallelopiped is
options:
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{cu}$ units

$\frac{1}{2 \sqrt{2}}$ cu units

$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ cu units

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \mathrm{cu}$ units
questions.solution:
The volume of the parallelopiped with coterminus edges as $\hat{\mathbf{a}}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}, \hat{\mathbf{c}}$ is given by $[\hat{\mathbf{a}} \hat{\mathbf{b}} \hat{\mathbf{c}}]=\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \times \hat{\mathbf{c}})$
$\begin{aligned}& \text{ Now, }[\hat{\mathbf{a}} \hat{\mathbf{b}} \hat{\mathbf{c}}]^2=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}& \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}& \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{c}}\\ \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}& \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}& \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{c}}\\ \hat{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}& \hat{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}& \hat{\mathbf{c}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{c}} \end{array}\right|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 1 / 2 & 1 / 2 \\ 1 / 2 & 1 & 1 / 2 \\ 1 / 2 & 1 / 2 & 1 \end{array}$\right|=$\frac{1}{2}\\ & \Rightarrow \quad[\hat{\mathbf{a}}$\hat{$\mathbf{b}} \hat{\mathbf{c}}]$^2=$\frac{1}{2}\\ & \end{aligned} Thus,$ the $required volume of the parallelopiped =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\mathrm{cu} units$

questions.q: Let $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ be unit vectors such that $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}$. Which one of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
Since $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are unit vectors and $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}$ $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ represent an equilateral triangle.
$$
\therefore \quad \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0} .
$$

questions.q: Consider a circuit consisting of a capacitor of capacitance $C$ and a coil with $N$ turns per unit length, cross sectional area $S$ and length $d$, where $d^2 \gg S$. There is another coil of length $d/2$, cross sectional area $S/2$ and $2N$ turns per unit length completely inside the larger coil, as shown in the figure. The ends of this smaller coil are connected with each other by an insulated conducting wire. The self-inductance of the larger coil is $L$. Neglecting edge effects and all the Ohmic resistances, the resonant frequency of the circuit is:
questions.solution:
Let the larger coil be coil 1 and the smaller coil be coil 2.

The self-inductance of the larger coil is given by:
$L_1 = \mu_0 n_1^2 A_1 l_1 = \mu_0 N^2 S d = L$

The self-inductance of the smaller coil is:
$L_2 = \mu_0 n_2^2 A_2 l_2 = \mu_0 (2N)^2 \left(\dfrac{S}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = \mu_0 (4N^2) \left(\dfrac{Sd}{4}\right) = \mu_0 N^2 S d = L$

The mutual inductance between the two coils is:
$M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 A_{\text{common}} l_{\text{common}}$
Since the smaller coil is completely inside the larger coil, the common area is $S/2$ and the common length is $d/2$.
$M = \mu_0 (N) (2N) \left(\dfrac{S}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu_0 N^2 S d = \dfrac{L}{2}$

Let $i_1$ be the current in the larger coil and $i_2$ be the current in the smaller coil. The voltage across the larger coil is:
$V = L_1 \dfrac{di_1}{dt} + M \dfrac{di_2}{dt}$

Since the smaller coil is short-circuited, the net voltage across it is zero:
$0 = L_2 \dfrac{di_2}{dt} + M \dfrac{di_1}{dt} \Rightarrow \dfrac{di_2}{dt} = -\dfrac{M}{L_2} \dfrac{di_1}{dt}$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get the effective inductance $L_{\text{eq}}$:
$V = L_1 \dfrac{di_1}{dt} - \dfrac{M^2}{L_2} \dfrac{di_1}{dt} = \left( L_1 - \dfrac{M^2}{L_2} \right) \dfrac{di_1}{dt}$
$L_{\text{eq}} = L_1 - \dfrac{M^2}{L_2} = L - \dfrac{(L/2)^2}{L} = L - \dfrac{L}{4} = \dfrac{3L}{4}$

The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is:
$\omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{L_{\text{eq}} C}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\dfrac{3L}{4} C}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3LC}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3\, LC}}$

questions.q:
A circuit with an electrical load having impedance $Z$ is connected with an AC source as shown in the diagram. The source voltage varies in time as $V(t)=300 \sin (400 t) \mathrm{V}$, where $t$ is time in s. List-I shows various options for the load. The possible currents $i(t)$ in the circuit as a function of time are given in List-II.

Choose the option that describes the correct match between the entries in List-I to those in List-II.
List-I List-II
$(P)$
$(1)$
$(Q)$
$(2)$
$(R)$
$(3)$
$(S)$
$(4)$
$(5)$
questions.solution:
For P
$i=\frac{V}{R}=10 \sin 400 t \Rightarrow(3)$
For Q
$\begin{aligned} & X_L=\omega L=400 \times 100 \times 10^{-3}=40 \Omega \\ & \therefore Z=50 \Omega \\ & \left.\therefore i=\frac{300}{50} \sin \left(400 t-53^{\circ}\right) \text{ [current will lag by } \tan ^{-1} \frac{X_L}{R}\right] \Rightarrow(5)\end{aligned}$
For R
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{10^6}{400 \times 50} \Omega=50 \Omega \text{ and } \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=400 \times 25 \times 10^{-3}=10 \Omega \\ & \therefore \mathrm{Z}=50 \Omega \\ & \therefore \mathrm{i}=\frac{300}{50} \sin \left(400 \mathrm{t}+53^{\circ}\right) \quad\left[\text{ Current will lead by } \tan ^{-1} \frac{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}-\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mathrm{R}}\right] \Rightarrow(2)\end{aligned}$
For $S \therefore \mathrm{i}=\frac{300}{60} \sin (400 \mathrm{t}) \quad \mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}} \Rightarrow$ Resonance $\Rightarrow(1)$

questions.q: The circuit shown in the figure contains an inductor $L$, a capacitor $C_0$, a resistor $R_0$ and an ideal battery. The circuit also contains two keys $\mathrm{K}_1$ and $\mathrm{K}_2$. Initially, both the keys are open and there is no charge on the capacitor. At an instant, key $K_1$ is closed and immediately after this the current in $R_0$ is found to be $I_1$. After a long time, the current attains a steady state value $I_2$. Thereafter, $\mathrm{K}_2$ is closed and simultaneously $\mathrm{K}_1$ is opened and the voltage across $C_0$ oscillates with amplitude $V_0$ and angular frequency $\omega_0$. Match the quantities mentioned in List-I with their values in List-II and choose the correct option.
questions.solution:
(P) When $K_1$ is closed current in $R_0$ is $I_1$ At $\mathrm{t}=0$; circuit will be

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_1=0 \\ & \mathrm{P} \rightarrow(1)\end{aligned}$
(Q) After long time inductor behave as a wire so $\mathrm{I}_2 \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}_2=\frac{20}{5}=4 \mathrm{ A} \\ & \mathrm{Q} \rightarrow(3)\end{aligned}$
(R) When $\mathrm{K}_2$ is closed and $\mathrm{K}_1$ open

$\begin{aligned} & \omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{LC}}} \\ & \omega_0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{25 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 \times 10^{-6}}}=\frac{1}{5 \times 10^{-4}} \\ & \omega_0=2 \times 10^3 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s} \\ & \omega_0=2 \text{ kilo-radian } / \mathrm{s} \\ & \mathrm{R} \rightarrow(2)\end{aligned}$
(S) Now $\mathrm{K}_2$ is closed and $\mathrm{K}_1$ open

$\begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{LI}_2^2=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{CV}_0^2 \\ & 25 \times 10^{-3} \times(4)^2=10 \times 10^{-6} \times \mathrm{V}_0^2 \\ & \mathrm{ V}_0^2=2500 \times 16 \\ & \mathrm{ V}_0=50 \times 4=200 \mathrm{ V} \\ & \mathrm{ S} \rightarrow(5)\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
In a circuit shown in the figure, the capacitor $C$ is initially uncharged and the key $K$ is open. In this condition, a current of $1A$ flows through the $1Ω$ resistor. The key is closed at time $t = {t}_{0}$. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?

[Given : ${e}^{– 1} = 0 . 36$]
options: The value of the resistance $R$ is $3Ω$
For $t < {t}_{0}$, the value of current ${I}_{1}$ is $2A$
At $t = {t}_{0} + 7 . 2\mus$, the current in the capacitor is $0 . 6A$
For $t \to \infty$, the charge on the capacitor is $12\muC$
questions.solution:
From second branch, we can see the potential drop across the branch is $5 + \left(1 \times 1\right) = 6V$.

Now for the first branch, we can write

$15 - IR = 6 . . . \left(1\right)$ and from third branch, we can write

${I}_{1} \times 3 = 6$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = 2A$

Now from Kirchoff's junction rule,

$I = {I}_{1} + 1 = 3$

Now, from equation(1), we can write

$15 - 3R = 6$

$⇒ R = 3Ω$

All three branches are in parallel, therefore we can write equivalent resistance as:

$\dfrac{1}{{R}_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} + 1$

$⇒ {R}_{eq} = \dfrac{3}{5}Ω = 0 . 6Ω$

As all branches are in parallel with the capacitor branch, potential drop across all three branches will be the same. Therefore,

${E}_{eq} = 6V$.

Now, current variation in the circuit due to charging will be $\dfrac{6}{\left(\dfrac{3}{5} + 3\right)}e\dfrac{- \left(t - {t}_{0}\right)}{CR}$

At, $t = {t}_{0} + 7 . 2\mu s$, we get

$i = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{18}{e}^{- \dfrac{\left(7 . 2 \times {10}^{- 6}\right)}{\left(2 \times {10}^{- 6}\right) \times \left(3 . 6\right)}}$

$= \dfrac{30}{18} \times {e}^{- 1} = \dfrac{30}{18} \times 0 . 36$

$= 0 . 6A$

At steady state, voltage across capacitor $= 6V$.

$Q = 6 \times 2 = 12\muC$.

questions.q:
A series LCR circuit is connected to a $45sin ( \omegat )$ Volt source. The resonant angular frequency of the circuit is ${10}^{5}rad{s}^{- 1}$ and current amplitude at resonance is ${I}_{0}$. When the angular frequency of the source is $\omega = 8 \times {10}^{4}rad{s}^{- 1}$, the current amplitude in the circuit is $0 . 05{I}_{0}$. If $L = 50mH$, match each entry in List-$I$ with an appropriate value from List-$II$ and choose the correct option.

List-$I$ List-$II$
$P$ ${I}_{0}$ in $mA$ $1$ $44 . 4$
$Q$ The quality factor of the circuit $2$ $18$
$R$ The bandwidth of the circuit in $rad{s}^{- 1}$ $3$ $400$
$S$ The peak power dissipated at resonance in Watt $4$ $2250$
$5$ $500$
questions.solution:
Resonant angular frequency is given by, $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = {10}^{5}$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(50 \times {10}^{- 3}\right)C}} = {10}^{5} ⇒ C = 2 \times {10}^{- 9}F$

Given: $V = 45sin\left(\omegat\right)$. Therefore, ${V}_{0} = 45$.

Now, ${I}_{0} = \dfrac{{V}_{0}}{R} = \dfrac{45}{R} . . . \left(ii\right)$

Inductive reactance, ${X}_{L} = \omegaL = \left(8 \times {10}^{4}\right) \times \left(50 \times {10}^{- 3}\right) = 4000Ω$.

and capacitive reactance, ${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omegaC} = \dfrac{1}{\left(8 \times {10}^{4}\right) \times \left(2 \times {10}^{- 9}\right)} = 6250Ω$.

For new current amplitude, we can write

$0 . 05{I}_{0} = \dfrac{45}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{L} - {X}_{C}\right)}^{2}}} ⇒ 0 . 05{I}_{0} = \dfrac{45}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(6250 - 4000\right)}^{2}}} ⇒ 0 . 05 \times \dfrac{45}{R} = \dfrac{45}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(6250 - 4000\right)}^{2}}} ⇒ {R}^{2} + {\left(6250 - 4000\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{{\left(0 . 05\right)}^{2}} ⇒ {R}^{2} + {\left(2250\right)}^{2} = 400{R}^{2} ⇒ R = \dfrac{2250}{\sqrt{399}} = 112 . 67Ω$

Where ${X}_{{L}_{0}} = {X}_{{C}_{0}}$ are at resonant frequencies

On solving, $⇒ {I}_{0} = \dfrac{45}{R} ≃ 400mA$

Quality factor $Q = \dfrac{{X}_{L}}{R} ≃ 44 . 44$

Now, $Q = \dfrac{{\omega}_{0}}{∆ \omega} ⇒ ∆ \omega ≃ 2250rad{s}^{- 1}$.

Peak power $= 45 \times \dfrac{400}{1000}W = 18W$

Therefore, $P \to 3, Q \to 1, R \to 4, S \to 2$.

questions.q: Consider an $LC$ circuit, with inductance $L = 0 . 1H$ and capacitance $C = {10}^{- 3}F$, kept on a plane. The area of the circuit is $1{m}^{2}$. It is placed in a constant magnetic field of strength ${B}_{0}$ which is perpendicular to the plane of the circuit. At time $t = 0$, the magnetic field strength starts increasing linearly as $B = {B}_{0} + \betat$ with $\beta = 0 . 04T{s}^{- 1}$. The maximum magnitude of the current in the circuit is____$mA$.
questions.solution:
Emf induced in the circuit is

$\left|E\right| = \left|\dfrac{dϕ}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\left({B}_{0} + \betat\right)A\right]$

$= \beta \times A$

$= 0 . 04V$

So the circuit can be rearranged as

Using Kirchhoff's law we can write

$E = L\dfrac{di}{dt} + \dfrac{q}{C}$

$L\dfrac{di}{dt} = E - \dfrac{q}{C}$

For maximum current, $\dfrac{d i}{d t} = 0$,

Or $q = CE$

Using work energy theorem,

$qE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}^{2} + \dfrac{{q}^{2}}{2C}$

At ${i}_{max}$, $CEE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}_{max}^{2} + \dfrac{{E}^{2}{C}^{2}}{2C}$

Or, ${i}_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{C}{L}}E$

So, ${i}_{max} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{10}^{- 3} \times 0 . 04}{0 . 1 \times {10}^{- 3}}}$$= 4mA$

$\left|E\right| = \left|\dfrac{dϕ}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[\left({B}_{0} + \betat\right)A\right]$

$= \beta \times A$

$= 0 . 04V$

So the circuit can be rearranged as

Using Kirchhoff's law we can write

$E = L\dfrac{di}{dt} + \dfrac{q}{C}$

$L\dfrac{di}{dt} = E - \dfrac{q}{C}$

For maximum current, $\dfrac{d i}{d t} = 0$,

Or $q = CE$

Using work energy theorem,

$qE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}^{2} + \dfrac{{q}^{2}}{2C}$

At ${i}_{max}$, $CEE = \dfrac{1}{2}L{i}_{max}^{2} + \dfrac{{E}^{2}{C}^{2}}{2C}$

questions.q:
In a circuit, a metal filament lamp is connected in series with a capacitor of capacitance $\mathrm{C} \mu F$ across a $200 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz}$ supply. The power consumed by the lamp is $500 \mathrm{~W}$ while the voltage drop across it is $100 \mathrm{~V}$. Assume that there is no inductive load in the circuit. Take $r m s$ values of the voltages. The magnitude of the phaseangle (in degrees) between the current and the supply voltage is $\varphi$. Assume, $\pi \sqrt{3} \approx 5$.
The value of $C$ is ____.
questions.solution:
Given,

$P = 500W$

${V}_{R} = 100V$

$f = 50Hz$

${V}_{rms} = 200V$

$P = \dfrac{{{V}_{R}}^{2}}{R} ⇒ R = \dfrac{{{V}_{R}}^{2}}{P} ⇒ R = \dfrac{{\left(100\right)}^{2}}{500}$

$∴ R = 20Ω$

Now current in the circuit,

$i = {i}_{rms} = \dfrac{voltageacrossresistor}{resistance}i = \dfrac{100}{20}i = 5A$

Phasor diagram of the given circuit for voltage,

Now,

${V}^{2} = {{V}_{C}}^{2} + {{V}_{R}}^{2} ⇒ {200}^{2} = {{V}_{C}}^{2} + {100}^{2} ⇒ {V}_{C} = 100\sqrt{3}V$

Now,

${V}_{C} = 100\sqrt{3}V = I{X}_{C} ⇒ {X}_{C} = \dfrac{100\sqrt{3}}{5} = 20\sqrt{3}Ω$

and

${X}_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\left(2\pif\right)C} ⇒ 20\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{1}{\left(2\pi \times 100\right)C} ⇒ C = 100\mu F$

From the phasor diagram,

$tan\left(ϕ\right) = \dfrac{{X}_{C}}{R} = \dfrac{20\sqrt{3}}{20} = \sqrt{3} ⇒ ϕ = 60 °$

In the circuit shown, initially there is no charge on capacitors and keys ${S}_{1}$ and ${S}_{2}$ are open. The values of the capacitors are ${C}_{1} = 10\muF, {C}_{2} = 30\muF$ and ${C}_{3} = {C}_{4} = 80\muF .$

Which of the statement(s) is/are correct?
options: If key  ${S}_{1}$  is kept closed for long time such that capacitors are fully charged, the voltage difference between points  $P$  and  $Q$  will be  $10V .$

The keys  ${S}_{1}$  is kept closed for long time such that capacitors are fully charged. Now key  ${S}_{2}$  is closed, at this time, the instantaneous current across  $30Ω$  resistor (between points  $P$  and  $Q$ ) will be  $0.2A$  (round off to  ${1}^{st}$  decimal place).
At time  $t = 0,$  the key  ${S}_{1}$  is closed, the instantaneous current in the closed circuit will be  $25mA .$
If key  ${S}_{1}$  is kept closed for long time such that capacitors are fully charged, the voltage across the capacitors  ${C}_{1}$  will be  $4V .$
questions.solution:
For option $( C )$ , refer circuit diagram below

Just after closing of switch charge on all the capacitors $\left({C}_{1}, {C}_{3}and{C}_{4}\right) = 0$
$∴$ Replace all capacitors with wire, then circuit will get reduced as shown below.

$i = \dfrac{5}{70 + 100 + 30} = \dfrac{5}{200} = 25mA ⇒ ( C )$ is correct
Now ${S}_{1}$ is kept closed for long time circuit is in steady state

$⇒$ Apply KVL in loop, start from battery
$+ 5 - \dfrac{2}{80} - \dfrac{2}{10} - \dfrac{2}{80} = 0$
$⇒ \dfrac{10.2}{80} = 5$
$⇒ 2 = 40\muC$
$⇒$ Potential difference across ${C}_{1}$
$\Delta{V}_{{C}_{1}} = \dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{40}{10} = 4volt$
$⇒ ( D )$ is correct.
For option $( B ) ⇒$ Now just after closing of ${S}_{2}$ charge on each capacitor remain same,
Refer circuit below -

KVL in left loop, starting from battery of $10$ volts,
$10 - 30x - \dfrac{40}{10} - 70y = 0$
$⇒ 30x + 70y = 6$ ...(i)
Now, apply KVL in right loop starting from $80\muF$ capacitor
$⇒ - \dfrac{40}{80} + 5 + \left(x - y\right)30 - \dfrac{40}{80} + \left(x - y\right) \times 100 - 10 + x \times 30 = 0$
$⇒ 160x - 130y - 6 = 0$ ...(ii)
Now, solving equation (i) and (ii) we get,
$y = \dfrac{96}{1510}$
and $x = 0.05amp . ⇒ ( B )$ is incorrect.

questions.q:
The instantaneous voltages at three terminals marked $X, Y$ and $Z$ are given by
${V}_{X} = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \omegat$
${V}_{Y} = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \left(\omegat + \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ and
${V}_{Z} = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \left(\omegat + \dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) .$
An ideal voltmeter is configured to read rms value of the potential difference between its terminals. It is connected between points $X$ and $Y$ and then between $Y$ and $Z$ . The reading(s) of the voltmeter will be
options: Independent of the choice of the terminals
questions.solution:
Potential difference between $XandY = {V}_{X} - {V}_{Y}$

Potential difference between $YandZ = {V}_{Y} - {V}_{Z}$

Phasor of the voltages:

From phasor diagram the peak value of ${V}_{x} - {V}_{y}$ can be calculated from parallelogram law

${\left({V}_{x} - {V}_{y}\right)}_{peak} = \sqrt{{V}_{X}^{2} + {V}_{Y}^{2} + 2{V}_{X}{V}_{Y}cos\left(60\right)} = \sqrt{{V}_{0}^{2} + {V}_{0}^{2} + 2{V}_{0}{V}_{0} \times \dfrac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{3}{V}_{0}$

$∴ {\left({V}_{X} - {V}_{Y}\right)}_{peak} = \sqrt{3}{V}_{0}$

${\left({V}_{x} - {V}_{y}\right)}_{rms} = {V}_{XY}^{rms} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}{V}_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$

Similarly  ${\left({V}_{y} - {V}_{z}\right)}_{rms} = {V}_{XY}^{rms} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}{V}_{0}}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.q: In the circuit shown, $L = 1\text{\mu}H, C = 1\text{\mu}FandR = 1kΩ .$ They are connected in series with an a.c. source $V = {V}_{0}sin ⁡ \text{\omega}t$ as shown. Which of the following options is/are correct?
options: At  $\omega ≫ {10}^{6}rad{sec}^{- 1} ⁡$ the circuit behaves as a capacitor
The frequency at which the current will be in phase with the voltage is independent of $R$
The current will be in phase with the voltage if  $\omega = {10}^{4}rad{sec}^{- 1} ⁡$
At $ω ~ 0$ the current flowing through the circuit becomes nearly zero
questions.solution:
The current will be in phase with voltage when phase angle is zero,

$∴ tan ⁡ \text{ϕ} = \dfrac{\text{\omega}L - \dfrac{1}{\text{\omega}C}}{R} = 0$

Where $\text{\omega}, L, C, R$ are the angular frequency, inductance, capacitance and resistance respectively.

$⇒ \text{\omega} = {\text{\omega}}_{0} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$

$⇒ {\text{\omega}}_{\text{ο}}$is independent of $R$

$⇒ ( resonantfrequency ) {\text{\omega}}_{0} = {10}^{6}rad / s$

Current in the circuit is given by,

${i}_{0} = \dfrac{{V}_{0}}{\sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left(\text{\omega}L - \dfrac{1}{\text{\omega}C}\right)}^{2}}}$

When $\text{\omega} \to 0, {i}_{0} \to 0$

For $\text{\omega} ≫ {\text{\omega}}_{0}$ circuit behaves as inductor.

questions.q: In the circuit shown below, the key is pressed at time t = 0. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) true?
options: The voltmeter displays -5V as soon as the key is pressed, and displays +5V after a long time
The voltmeter will display 0 V at time t = ln 2 seconds
The current in the ammeter becomes 1/e of the initial value after 1 second
The current in the ammeter becomes zero after a long time
questions.solution:
(i) At t = 0, capacitor acts as short - circuit

The the reading of voltmeter will be -5 V
At $t \to \infty,$ capacitor acts as open circuit and no current flows through voltmeter.

If it is ideal voltmeter then its resistance is infinite & therefore it will read +5V
(ii)

The Charge on the capacitor is given by
$q = {q}_{0} ( 1 - {e}^{- t / RC} )$
as q0 = RC is the max charge stored

For C1=2C=40 $\mu$F, R1=R=25 k${q}_{x} = 2CV\left(1 - e\dfrac{- t}{2CR}\right)$

The current through resistance of R=25 k is 

$x = \dfrac{V}{R}e\dfrac{- t}{2CR}$

For C2=C=20 $\mu$F, R2=2R=50 k
${q}_{y} = CV\left(1 - e\dfrac{- t}{2CR}\right)$

The current through resistance of 2R=50k is 

$y = \dfrac{V}{2R}e\dfrac{- t}{2CR}$

Reading of voltmeter ($∆$V) = Voltage across 2C - Voltage across 2R

$∆ V = \dfrac{{q}_{x}}{2C} - y ( 2R ) = V\left[1 - 2e\dfrac{- t}{2CR}\right] = 0$


(iii)

$τ = 2RC = 2 \times 25 \times {10}^{3} \times 40 \times {10}^{- 6} = 1sec$
Now Current is given by$i = {i}_{0}{e}^{\left(- \dfrac{t}{τ}\right)}$

at t= 1 sec, Current $i = \dfrac{{i}_{o}}{e}$


(iv) After long time no current flows since capacitor act as a open circuit and voltmeter acts as an ideal it's resistance is infinite, therefore current does not allow.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two inductors ${L}_{i}$ (inductance $1mH$, internal resistance $3Ω$ ) and ${L}_{2}$ (inductance $2mH$, internal resistance $4Ω$ ), and a resistor $R$(resistance $12Ω$ ) are all connected in parallel across a $5V$ battery. The circuit is switched on at time $t = 0$. The ratio of the maximum current $\left(\dfrac{{I}_{max}}{{I}_{min}}\right)$ drawn from the battery is:
questions.solution:
Initally, the inductances will offer infinite resistance and the current will be maximum.

${I}_{max} = \dfrac{ε}{R} = \dfrac{5}{12}A$ (Initially at t = 0)

Upon reaching steady state, the inductances will act as pure resistors and hence the current will be minimum.
${I}_{min} = \dfrac{ε}{{R}_{eq}} = ε\left(\dfrac{1}{{r}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{r}_{2}} + \dfrac{1}{R}\right)$ (Finally in steady state)
$= 5\left(\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{12}\right)$
$= \dfrac{10}{3}A$
$\dfrac{{I}_{max}}{{I}_{min}} = 8$

questions.q: At time t = 0, terminal A in the circuit shown in the figure is connected to B by a key and an alternating current $I\left(t\right) = {I}_{0}cos ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)$ , with ${I}_{0} = 1A$ and $\omega = 500$ rad/s starts flowing in it with the initial direction shown in the figure. At $t = \dfrac{7\pi}{6\omega}$ , the key is switched from B to D. Now onwards only A and D are connected. A total charge Q flows from the battery to charge the capacitor fully. If $C = 20\muF, R = 10Ω$ and the battery is ideal with of 50V, identify the correct statement(s).
options: Magnitude of the maximum charge on the capacitor before  $t = \dfrac{7\pi}{6\omega}$  is  $1 \times {10}^{- 3}C$ .
The current in the left part of the circuit just before  $t = \dfrac{7\pi}{6\omega}$  is clockwise.
Immediately after A is connected to D, the current in R is 10 A.
questions.solution:
$Given, I = {I}_{0}cos\left(\omega t\right), Peakormaximumcurrent{I}_{0} = 1Aangularfrequency, \omega = 500rad{s}^{- 1}capacitanceC = 20\mu FresistanceR = 10ΩbatteryvoltageV = 50V$If q represent the charge on capacitor’s upper plate:
$I\left(t\right) = {I}_{0}cos ⁡ ( \omegat )$
$⇒ q\left(t\right) = \dfrac{{I}_{0}}{\omega}sin ⁡ \left(\omegat\right)$
$∴$ Max charge $\left({q}_{max}\right) = \dfrac{1A}{500\dfrac{Rad}{s}} = 2 \times {10}^{- 3}C$

questions.q:
Paragraph: A thermal power plant produces electric power of $600 \mathrm{~kW}$ at $4000 \mathrm{~V}$, which is to be transported to a place $20 \mathrm{~km}$ away from the power plant for consumers' usage. It can be transported either directly with a cable of large current carrying capacity or by using a combination of step-up and step-down transformers at the two ends. The drawback of the direct transmission is the large energy dissipation. In the method using transformers, the dissipation is much smaller. In this method, a step-up transformer is used at the plant side so that the current is reduced to a smaller value. At the consumers' end, a step-down transformer is used to supply power to the consumers at the specified lower voltage. It is reasonable to assume that the power cable is purely resistive and the transformers are ideal with a power factor unity. All the currents and voltages mentioned are rms values.
Question: In the method using the transformers, assume that the ratio of the number of turns in the primary to that in the secondary in the step-up transformer is $1: 10$. If the power to the consumers has to be supplied at $200 \mathrm{~V}$, the ratio of the number of turns in the primary to that in the secondary in the step-down transformer is
questions.solution: $\dfrac{{\text{N}}_{\text{p}}}{{\text{N}}_{\text{s}}} = \dfrac{\text{40,000}}{2 0 0} = \dfrac{2 0 0}{1}$

questions.q: At time $t=0$, a battery of $10 \mathrm{~V}$ is connected across points $A$ and $B$ in the given circuit. If the capacitors have no charge initially, at what time (in second) does the voltage across them become $4 \mathrm{~V}$ ? [Take $: \ln 5=1.6, \ln 3=1.1]$
questions.solution:
Voltage across the capacitors will increase from 0 to $10 \mathrm{~V}$ exponentially. The voltage at time $t$ will be given by

$\begin{aligned}$& V=10$\left($1-e^{-t / \tau} $\mathrm{C}\right)$\\
& $\text{ Here } \tau_$c=C_{$\text{net }$} R_{$\text{net }$} \\
& =$\left($1 $\times$10^6\right)$\left($4 $\times$10^{-6}\right)=4 $\mathrm{~s}$\\
& \therefore \quad V=10$\left($1-e^{-t / 4}\right) \\
&
\end{aligned}

Substituting $V=4$ volt we have,

4=10$\left($1-e^{-t / 4}\right)

Substituting $V=4$ volt we have,

4=10$\left($1-e^{-t / 4}\right)

or $e^{-t / 4}=0.6=\frac{3}{5}$
Taking $\log$ both sides we have,

-$\frac{t}{4}=\ln$3-\ln 5

or $\quad t=4(\ln 5-\ln 3)=2 \mathrm{~s}$.
Hence, the answer is 2 .

Comparing the LC oscillations with normal SHM, we get

$\frac{d^2 Q}{d t^2}=-\omega^$2 Q

Here,

Q & =-L C $\frac{d^2 Q}{d t^2}

\therefore \quad$Q=-L C $\frac{d^2 Q}{d t^2}$

questions.q: Consider a hydrogen atom with $v_k$, $r_k$, and $K_k$ denoting the velocity, orbital radius and kinetic energy of the electron in the $k^{\text{th}}$ orbit, respectively. The electron undergoes a transition from the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit, emitting radiation corresponding to the Lyman series. Considering $h$ to be the Planck's constant and $\epsilon_0$ the permittivity of the free space, the correct statement(s) is/are:
options: Magnitude of change in kinetic energy of electron can be expressed as $\dfrac{h}{4\pi}\left|\dfrac{n v_n}{r_n} - \dfrac{v_1}{r_1}\right|$.
Magnitude of change in de Broglie wavelength of the electron can be expressed as $\dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0}\left|\dfrac{1}{K_n} - \dfrac{1}{K_1}\right|$.
Frequency of the radiation emitted can be expressed as $\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 h}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_n}\right)$.
Magnitude of change in total energy of the electron can be expressed as $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\left|\dfrac{v_1}{r_1} - \dfrac{n v_n}{r_n}\right|$.
questions.solution:
From Bohr's quantization condition, the angular momentum of an electron in the $k^{\text{th}}$ orbit is given by:

$m v_k r_k = \dfrac{k h}{2\pi}$

The kinetic energy of the electron in the $k^{\text{th}}$ orbit is:

$K_k = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_k^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} (m v_k r_k) \dfrac{v_k}{r_k}$

Substituting the value of angular momentum:

$K_k = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( \dfrac{k h}{2\pi} \right) \dfrac{v_k}{r_k} = \dfrac{k h v_k}{4\pi r_k}$

The magnitude of change in kinetic energy for a transition from the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit to the $1^{\text{st}}$ orbit is:

$|\Delta K| = |K_n - K_1| = \dfrac{h}{4\pi} \left| \dfrac{n v_n}{r_n} - \dfrac{v_1}{r_1} \right|$

This makes statement (A) correct.

Since the total energy $E_k = -K_k$, the magnitude of change in total energy is equal to the magnitude of change in kinetic energy:

$|\Delta E| = |\Delta K| = \dfrac{h}{4\pi} \left| \dfrac{n v_n}{r_n} - \dfrac{v_1}{r_1} \right|$

This makes statement (D) incorrect.

The electrostatic force provides the necessary centripetal force:

$\dfrac{m v_k^2}{r_k} = \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_k^2} \Rightarrow K_k = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_k^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 r_k}$

The total energy is $E_k = -K_k = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 r_k}$. The energy of the emitted photon during the transition is:

$\Delta E = E_n - E_1 = -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 r_n} - \left( -\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 r_1} \right) = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_n} \right)$

The frequency of the emitted radiation is $\nu = \dfrac{\Delta E}{h}$:

$\nu = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 h} \left( \dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_n} \right)$

This makes statement (C) correct.

The de Broglie wavelength of the electron is $\lambda_k = \dfrac{h}{m v_k}$. Using Bohr's quantization $m v_k = \dfrac{k h}{2\pi r_k}$, we get:

$\lambda_k = \dfrac{2\pi r_k}{k}$

From the kinetic energy relation $r_k = \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 K_k}$, substituting $r_k$ gives:

$\lambda_k = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} \left( \dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 K_k} \right) = \dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0 k K_k}$

The magnitude of change in de Broglie wavelength is:

$|\Delta \lambda| = |\lambda_n - \lambda_1| = \dfrac{e^2}{4\epsilon_0} \left| \dfrac{1}{n K_n} - \dfrac{1}{K_1} \right|$

This makes statement (B) incorrect.

Answer: Magnitude of change in kinetic energy of electron can be expressed as $\dfrac{h}{4\pi}\left|\dfrac{n v_n}{r_n} - \dfrac{v_1}{r_1}\right|$.; Frequency of the radiation emitted can be expressed as $\dfrac{e^2}{8\pi\epsilon_0 h}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_n}\right)$.

questions.q: Consider an electron in the $n=3$ orbit of a hydrogen-like atom with atomic number $Z$. At absolute temperature $T$, a neutron having thermal energy $k_{\mathrm{B}} T$ has the same de Broglie wavelength as that of this electron. If this temperature is given by $T=\frac{Z^2 h^2}{\alpha \pi^2 a_0^2 m_N k_B}$, (where $h$ is the Planck's constant, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, $m_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the mass of the neutron and $a_0$ is the first Bohr radius of hydrogen atom) then the value of $\alpha$ is ________
questions.solution:
$\frac{\mathrm{mv}^2}{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{\mathrm{KZe}^2}{\mathrm{r}^2} \mathrm{mv}^2 \mathrm{r}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \mathrm{Ze}^2 \mathrm{mvr}=\frac{\mathrm{nh}}{2 \pi}$
(1)/(2) gives
$\mathrm{v}=\frac{\frac{\mathrm{Ze}^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0}}{\frac{\mathrm{nh}}{2 \pi}}=\frac{\mathrm{Ze}^2}{2 \epsilon_0 \mathrm{nh}} \begin{aligned} & \frac{h}{m v}=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m_N \cdot K_B T}} \\ & T=\frac{m^2 Z^2 e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 n^2 h^2 m_N K_B} \\ & n=3 \Rightarrow T=\frac{m^2 Z^2 e^4}{72 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 m_N K_B} \\ & \frac{(1)}{(2)^2} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{m r}=\frac{\frac{Z e^2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0}}{\frac{n^2 h^2}{4 \pi^2}}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{r}=\frac{\mathrm{n}^2 \mathrm{~h}^2 \epsilon_0}{\pi \mathrm{Ze}^2 \cdot \mathrm{~m}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}_0=\frac{\mathrm{h}^2 \epsilon_0}{\pi \mathrm{e}^2 \mathrm{~m}} \\ & \mathrm{a}_0^2=\frac{\mathrm{h}^4 \epsilon_0^2}{\pi^2 \mathrm{e}^4 \mathrm{~m}^2} \\ & \mathrm{Ta}_0^2=\frac{\mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{Z}^2 \mathrm{e}^4}{72 \epsilon_0 \mathrm{~h}^2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{h}^4 \epsilon_0^2}{\pi^2 \mathrm{e}^4 \mathrm{~m}^2} \\ & \mathrm{~T}=\frac{\mathrm{h}^2 \mathrm{Z}^2}{72 \pi^2 \mathrm{a}_0^2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{N}} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}} \Rightarrow \alpha=72\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
List-I shows various functional dependencies of energy $(E)$ on the atomic number $(Z)$. Energies associated with certain phenomena are given in List-II.\nChoose the option that describes the correct match between the entries in List-I to those in List-II.
List-I List-II
$(P)$ $E \\propto Z^2$ $(1)$ energy of characteristic x-rays
$(Q)$ $E \\propto(Z-1)^2$ $(2)$ electrostatic part of the nuclear binding energy for stable nuclei with mass numbers in the range 30 to 170
$(R)$ $E \\propto Z(Z-1)$ $(3)$ energy of continuous x-rays
$(S)$ $E$ is practically independent of $Z$ $(4)$ average nuclear binding energy per nucleon for stable nuclei with mass number in the range 30 to 170
$(5)$ energy of radiation due to electronic transitions from hydrogen-like atoms
questions.solution:
(P) Energy of H -like atom is
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}=-13.6 \frac{\mathrm{Z}^2}{\mathrm{n}^2} \text{ So } \\ & \mathrm{E} \propto \mathrm{Z}^2 \\ & \mathrm{P} \rightarrow(5)\end{aligned}$
(Q) Energy of characteristic X-ray by moseley's correction
$\begin{aligned} & E=-13.6(Z-1)^2\left[\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right] \text{ So } \\ & E \propto(Z-1)^2 \\ & Q \rightarrow(1)\end{aligned}$
(R) Electrostatics binding energy is proportional to $Z(Z-1) R \rightarrow(2)$
(S) For stable nuclei with mass no. in range 30 to 170 . Binding energy per nucleon is constant \& graph is straight line
$S \rightarrow(4)$
Ans. (C) is correct

questions.q: A hydrogen atom, initially at rest in its ground state, absorbs a photon of frequency $v_1$ and ejects the electron with a kinetic energy of 10 eV . The electron then combines with a positron at rest to form a positronium atom in its ground state and simultaneously emits a photon of frequency $v_2$. The center of mass of the resulting positronium atom moves with a kinetic energy of 5 eV . It is given that positron has the same mass as that of electron and the positronium atom can be considered as a Bohr atom, in which the electron and the positron orbit around their center of mass. Considering no other energy loss during the whole process, the difference between the two photon energies (in eV ) is $\qquad$
questions.solution: $\mathrm{h} v_1=13.6+10=23.6 \mathrm{eV} \qquad ....(1)$ Energy of positronium in ground state $\begin{aligned} & =-13.6 \frac{\mu}{m}\left(\frac{z}{n}\right)^2 \mathrm{eV} \\ & =-13.6 \times \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{eV}=-6.8 \mathrm{eV}\end{aligned}$ So to make positronium 6.8 eV must release \& 5 eV is the KE of COM . So total energy of photon released $\left(h v_2\right)$ will be : $\mathrm{h} v_2=(10-5)+6.8=11.8 \mathrm{eV} \qquad ....(2) \therefore \quad$ Difference in energy $=23.6-11.8=11.8 \mathrm{eV}$

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is moving in a circular orbit under the influence of the central force $F(r)=-k r$, corresponding to the potential energy $V(r)=k r^2 / 2$, where $k$ is a positive force constant and $r$ is the radial distance from the origin. According to the Bohr's quantization rule, the angular momentum of the particle is given by $L=n \hbar$, where $\hbar=h /(2 \pi), h$ is the Planck's constant, and $n$ a positive integer. If $v$ and $E$ are the speed and total energy of the particle, respectively, then which of the following expression(s) is(are) correct?
questions.solution:
The central force will provide necessary centripetal force
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{kr}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}^2}{\mathrm{r}}$
or, $\mathrm{kr}^2=\mathrm{mv}^2$    ...(1)
By quantisation rule
$\mathrm{n} \hbar=\mathrm{mvr}$
or, $\frac{\mathrm{n} \hbar}{\mathrm{r}}=\mathrm{mv}$  ...(2)
$\begin{aligned} & \frac{(1)}{(2)^2} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{kr}^2}{\frac{\mathrm{n}^2 \hbar^2}{\mathrm{r}^2}}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}^2}{\mathrm{~m}^2 \mathrm{v}^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{n}^2 \hbar^2} \mathrm{r}^4=\frac{1}{\mathrm{~m}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{n}^2 \hbar^2}{\mathrm{~km}}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{r}^2=\frac{\mathrm{n} \hbar}{\sqrt{\mathrm{mk}}}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \text{(2) Using (1), } \mathrm{K} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{n} \hbar}{\sqrt{\mathrm{mk}}}=\mathrm{mv}^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}^2=\mathrm{n} \hbar \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}^3}}\end{aligned}$
(3) $\frac{\mathrm{L}}{\mathrm{mr}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{mvr}}{\mathrm{mr}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}}}$ from (1)
$\begin{aligned} & \text{(4) } \mathrm{E}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{kr}^2=\frac{\mathrm{n} \hbar}{2} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}}}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{k} \frac{\mathrm{n} \hbar}{\sqrt{\mathrm{mk}}} \\ & \mathrm{E}=\mathrm{n} \hbar \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{m}}}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Which of the following statement(s) is (are) correct about the spectrum of hydrogen atom?
options: The ratio of the longest wavelength to the shortest wavelength in Balmer series is $\dfrac{9}{5}$.
There is an overlap between the wavelength ranges of Balmer and Paschen series.
The wavelengths of Lyman series are given by $\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{{m}^{2}}\right){\lambda}_{0}$, where ${\lambda}_{0}$ is the shortest wavelength of Lyman series and $m$ is an integer.
The wavelength ranges of Lyman and Balmer series do not overlap.
questions.solution:
For Balmer Series:

Shortest wavelength, $\dfrac{{E}_{o}}{4} = \dfrac{hc}{{\lambda}_{s}}$

Longest wavelength, $\left(\dfrac{{E}_{o}}{4} - \dfrac{{E}_{0}}{9}\right) = \dfrac{hc}{{\lambda}_{l}} = \dfrac{5{E}_{o}}{36}$

$∴ \dfrac{{\lambda}_{l}}{{\lambda}_{s}} = \dfrac{9}{5}$

Range of energy level in Balmer series,

$\left(\dfrac{5{E}_{0}}{36}, \dfrac{{E}_{0}}{4}\right)$

Range of energy level in Paschen series,

$\left(\dfrac{7{E}_{0}}{144}, \dfrac{{E}_{0}}{9}\right)$

Hence, no overlap.

For Lyman series:

For shortest wavelength,

${E}_{0} = \dfrac{hc}{{\lambda}_{0}}$

For general wavelength,

$\left({E}_{0} - \dfrac{{E}_{0}}{{n}^{2}}\right) = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{{n}^{2}}\right)} = \dfrac{\lambda}{{\lambda}_{0}}$

$∴ \lambda = \left(\dfrac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2} - 1}\right){\lambda}_{0}$

or $\lambda = \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{{n}^{2} - 1}\right){\lambda}_{0}= \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{{m}^{2}}\right){\lambda}_{0}$

as $m$ should be an integer.

Range of energy level in Lyman series, $\left(\dfrac{3{E}_{0}}{4}, {E}_{0}\right)$

$⇒$ Lyman and Balmer series wavelengths do not overlap.

A free hydrogen atom after absorbing a photon of wavelength ${\lambda}_{a}$ gets excited from the state $n = 1$ to the state $n = 4 .$ Immediately after that the electron jumps to $n = m$ state by emitting a photon of wavelength ${\lambda}_{e} .$ Let the change in momentum of atom due to the absorption and the emission are $\Delta{p}_{a}$ and $\Delta{p}_{e},$ respectively. If $\dfrac{{\lambda}_{a}}{{\lambda}_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{5} .$ Which of the option(s) is/are correct?
[Use $hc = 1242eVnm, 1nm = {10}^{- 9}m,$ $h$ and $c$ are Planck's constant and speed of light, respectively]
options: The ratio of kinetic energy of the electron in the state $n = m$ to the state $n = 1$ is $\dfrac{1}{4}$
questions.solution:
Energy for transition of electron from one orbit to other is given by-
${E}_{2} - {E}_{1} = \left(13.6\right){Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{n}_{1}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{n}_{2}^{2}}\right) = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$
$⇒ \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{13.6}{hc} . {Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{n}_{1}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{n}_{2}^{2}}\right)$
Now as per question
$\dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{a}} = \dfrac{13.6}{hc} . {Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{1}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{4}^{2}}\right)$
and $\dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{e}} = \dfrac{13.6}{hc} . {Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{m}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{{4}^{2}}\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{{\lambda}_{e}}{{\lambda}_{a}} = \dfrac{\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{16}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{{m}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{\left(15\right){m}^{2}}{16 - {m}^{2}}$
But $\dfrac{{\lambda}_{a}}{{\lambda}_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{5}\left(given\right)$
$⇒ \dfrac{16 - {m}^{2}}{15{m}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{5} ⇒ 16 - {m}^{2} = 3{m}^{2}$
$⇒ {m}^{2} = 4$
$⇒ m = 2 ⇒ \left(C\right)$ is correct
Now,
$\dfrac{1}{{\lambda}_{e}} = \dfrac{13.6}{hc} . {Z}^{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{{m}^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right)$
$= \dfrac{13.6}{1242} \times 1\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right)\left(ashc = 1242andz = 1\right)$
$⇒ {\lambda}_{e} = \dfrac{1242}{13.6} \times \dfrac{16}{3} = 487nm ⇒ \left(A\right)$ is incorrect
Now, kinetic energy of electron
$K ∝ \dfrac{1}{{n}^{2}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{K}_{2}}{{K}_{1}} = \dfrac{{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4} ⇒ \left(B\right)$ is correct
Also, $∆ P = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$
$⇒ \dfrac{∆ {P}_{a}}{∆ {P}_{e}} = \dfrac{{\lambda}_{e}}{{\lambda}_{a}} = 5$
$⇒ \left(D\right)$ is incorrect.

questions.q: Highly excited states for hydrogen like atoms (also called Rydberg states) with nuclear charge Ze are defined by their principal quantum number n, where n >> 1. Which of the following statement(s) is (are) true?
options: Relative change in the radii of two consecutive orbitals does not depend on Z
Relative change in the radii of two consecutive oribitals varies as 1/n
Relative change in the energy of two consecutive orbitals varies as 1/ ${n}^{3}$
Relative change in the angular momenta of two consecutive orbitals varies as 1/n
questions.solution:
As radius $r ∝ \dfrac{{n}^{2}}{z}0$
$⇒ \dfrac{∆ r}{r} = \dfrac{{\left(\dfrac{n + 1}{z}\right)}^{2} - {\left(\dfrac{n}{z}\right)}^{2}}{{\left(\dfrac{n}{z}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{2n + 1}{{n}^{2}} \approx \dfrac{2}{n} ∝ \dfrac{1}{n}$
As energy $E ∝ \dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{∆ E}{E} = \dfrac{\dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{n}^{2}} - \dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{\left(n + 1\right)}^{2}}}{\dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{\left(n + 1\right)}^{2}}} = \dfrac{{\left(n + 1\right)}^{2} - {n}^{2}}{{n}^{2} . {\left(n + 1\right)}^{2}} . {\left(n + 1\right)}^{2}$
$⇒ \dfrac{∆ E}{E} = \dfrac{2n + 1}{{n}^{2}} ≃ \dfrac{2n}{{n}^{2}} ∝ \dfrac{1}{n}$
As angular momentum $L = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$
$⇒ \dfrac{∆ L}{L} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\left(n + 1\right)h}{2\pi} - \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}}{\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}} = \dfrac{1}{n} ∝ \dfrac{1}{n}$

questions.q: Paragraph: When a particle is restricted to move along $x$-axis between $x=0$ and $x=a$, where $a$ is of nanometer dimension, its energy can take only certain specific values. The allowed energies of the particle moving in such a restricted region, correspond to the formation of standing waves with nodes at its ends $x=0$ and $x=a$. The wavelength of this standing wave is related to the liner momentum $p$ of the particle according to the de Broglie relation. The energy of the particle of mass $m$ is related to its linear momentum as $E=\frac{p^2}{2 m}$. questions.q: If the wavelength of the $n^{\text{th }}$ line of Lyman series is equal to the de-Broglie wavelength of electron in initial orbit of a hydrogen like element $(Z=11)$. Find the value of $n$.
questions.solution:
$n^{\text{th }}$ line of Lyman series means transition from $(n+1)$ th state to first state.

$\begin{aligned}$& $\frac{1}{\lambda}=$R Z²$\left[$1-$\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}\right]$\\
& $\text{ de-Broglie wavelength, } \quad \lambda=\frac{h}{m v}=\frac{h r}{m v r}=\frac{(2 \pi)(h r)}{(n+1) h}=\frac{2 \pi r}{(n+1)}$\\
& $\frac{1}{\lambda}=\frac{(n+1)}{2 \pi r}$\\
&
\end{aligned}

or
Equating (i) and (ii), we get

$\left(\frac{n+1}{2 \pi r}\right)=$R Z²$\left[\frac{n(n+2)}{(n+1)^2}\right]$Now, as

$\begin{aligned}$& r \propto $\frac{n^2}{Z}$\\
& r=$\frac{(n+1)^2}{11}$r_0
\end{aligned}

\therefore \quad r=$\frac{(n+1)^2}{11}$r_0

Substituting in equations (iii), we get

$\frac{11}{2 \pi r_0}=\frac{R(11)^2(n)(n+2)}{(n+1)}$or

(n+1)=$\left($1.09 $\times$10^7\right)(11)(2 $\pi) \times\left($0.529 $\times$10^{-10}\right)$\left($n^2+2 n\right)

Solving this equation we get, $n=24$

questions.explanation:
$n^{\text{th }}$ line of Lyman series means transition from $(n+1)$ th state to first state.
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{\lambda}=R Z^2\left[1-\frac{1}{(n+1)^2}\right] \\
& \text{ de-Broglie wavelength, } \quad \lambda=\frac{h}{m v}=\frac{h r}{m v r}=\frac{(2 \pi)(h r)}{(n+1) h}=\frac{2 \pi r}{(n+1)} \\
& \frac{1}{\lambda}=\frac{(n+1)}{2 \pi r} \\
&
\end{aligned}
$$
or
Equating (i) and (ii), we get
$$
\left(\frac{n+1}{2 \pi r}\right)=R Z^2\left[\frac{n(n+2)}{(n+1)^2}\right]
$$
Now, as
$$
\begin{aligned}
& r \propto \frac{n^2}{Z} \\
& r=\frac{(n+1)^2}{11} r_0
\end{aligned}
 
\therefore \quad r=\frac{(n+1)^2}{11} r_0
$$

$$
