questions.q:
A planet of mass M, has two natural satellites with masses ${m}_{1}and{m}_{2}$ . The radii of their circular orbits are ${R}_{1}and{R}_{2}$ respectively. Ignore the gravitational force between the satellites. Define ${v}_{1}, {L}_{1}, {K}_{1}and{T}_{1}$ to be, respectively, the orbital speed, angular momentum, kinetic energy and time period of revolution of satellite $1; and{v}_{2}, {L}_{2}, {K}_{2}and{T}_{2}$ and to be the corresponding quantities of satellite 2. Given ${m}_{1} / {m}_{2} = 2and{R}_{1} / {R}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ , match the ratios in List-I to the numbers in List-II.
LIST -I LIST-II
A) $\dfrac{{v}_{1}}{{v}_{2}}$ P) $\dfrac{1}{8}$
B) $\dfrac{{L}_{1}}{{L}_{2}}$ Q) 1
C) $\dfrac{{K}_{1}}{{K}_{2}}$ R) 2
D) $\dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}}$ S) 8
questions.solution:
$\left\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{{m}_{1}}{{m}_{2}} = 2 \\ \dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}\end{array}\right\}$ given
$\dfrac{GM{m}_{1}}{{R}_{1}^{2}} = \dfrac{{m}_{1}{V}_{1}^{1}}{{R}_{1}}$
${v}_{1}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{{R}_{1}}, {v}_{2}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{{R}_{2}}$
$\dfrac{{v}_{1}^{2}}{{v}_{2}^{2}} = \dfrac{{R}_{2}}{{R}_{1}} = 4$
$\left(i\right)$ $\dfrac{{v}_{1}}{{v}_{2}} = 2$
$\left(ii\right)$ $L = mvR$
$\dfrac{{L}_{1}}{{L}_{2}} = \dfrac{{m}_{1}{v}_{1}{R}_{1}}{{m}_{2}{v}_{2}{R}_{2}} = 2 \times 2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} = 1$
$\left(iii\right)$ $K = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$
$\dfrac{{K}_{1}}{{K}_{2}} = \dfrac{{m}_{1}{v}_{1}^{2}}{{m}_{2}{v}_{2}^{2}} = 2 \times {\left(2\right)}^{2} = 8$
$( iv )$ $T = 2\piR / V$
$\dfrac{{T}_{1}}{{T}_{2}} = \dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{v}_{1}} \times \dfrac{{v}_{2}}{{R}_{2}} = \dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{2}} \times \dfrac{{v}_{2}}{{v}_{1}} = \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

questions.q:
A rocket is launched normal to the surface of the Earth, away from the Sun, along the line joining the Sun and the Earth. The Sun is $3 \times {10}^{5}$ times heavier than the Earth and is at a distance $2.5 \times {10}^{4}$ times larger than the radius of the Earth. The escape velocity from Earth's gravitational field is ${v}_{e} = 11.2km{s}^{- 1}$ . The minimum initial velocity $\left({v}_{s}\right)$ required for the rocket to be able to leave the Sun-Earth system is closest to
(Ignore the rotation and revolution of the Earth and the presence of any other planet)
questions.solution:
Given ${v}_{e} = 11.2km / sec = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}}}$

$\dfrac{1}{2}m{v}_{s}^{2} - \dfrac{G{M}_{s}m}{r} - \dfrac{G{M}_{e}m}{{R}_{e}} = 0 - 0$ where r = distance of rocket from Sun

$\to {v}_{s} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}} + \dfrac{2G{M}_{s}}{r}}$

Given ${M}_{s} = 3 × {10}^{5}{M}_{e}$ and $r = 2.5 × {10}^{4}{R}_{e}$

$\to {v}_{s} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}} + \dfrac{2G3 × {10}^{5}{M}_{e}}{2.5 × {10}^{4}{R}_{e}}}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}}\left(1 + \dfrac{3 × {10}^{5}}{2.5 × {10}^{4}}\right)}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{2G{M}_{e}}{{R}_{e}} × 13}$

$\to {v}_{s} = 42km / s$

questions.q: A large spherical mass $M$ is fixed at one position and two identical point masses $m$ are kept on a line passing through the centre of $M$ (see figure). The point masses are connected by a rigid massless rod of length $l$ and this assembly is free to move along the line connecting them. All three masses interact only through their mutual gravitational interaction. When the point mass nearer to $M$ is at a distance $r = 3l$ from $M$ , the tension in the rod is zero for $m = k\left(\dfrac{M}{288}\right)$ . The value of $k$ is
questions.solution:
Due to gravitational interaction connected masses have some acceleration.
Let both small masses are moving with acceleration 'a' towards larger mass M



Force equation for mass nearer to larger mass
$\dfrac{GMm}{{\left(3l\right)}^{2}} - \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{l}^{2}} = ma$ ...(i)
Force equation for mass away from larger mass
$\dfrac{GMm}{{\left(4l\right)}^{2}} + \dfrac{G{m}^{2}}{{l}^{2}} = ma$ ...(ii)
From equation (i) & (ii)
$\dfrac{GM}{9{l}^{2}} - \dfrac{Gm}{{l}^{2}} = \dfrac{GM}{16{l}^{2}} + \dfrac{Gm}{{l}^{2}}$
$⇒ \dfrac{M}{9} - \dfrac{M}{16} = m + m$
$\dfrac{7M}{144} = 2m$
$⇒ m = \dfrac{7M}{288} = k\left(\dfrac{M}{288}\right)$
$⇒ K = 7$

questions.q: A bullet is fired vertically upwards with velocity $υ$ from the surface of a spherical planet. When it reaches its maximum height, its acceleration due to the planet's gravity is $\dfrac{1}{{4}^{th}}$ of its value at the surface of the planet. If the escape velocity from the planet is ${υ}_{esc} = υ\sqrt{N}$ , then the value of N is (ignore energy loss due to atmosphere)
questions.solution:
${g}^{′} = \dfrac{g}{{\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{g}{4}$
$1 + \dfrac{h}{R} = 2$
$h = R$ ...(i)
So velocity of particle becomes zero at $h = R$
Given ${v}_{esc} = v\sqrt{N}$
So $\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = v\sqrt{N}$ ...(ii)
Applying conservation of energy
$\dfrac{- GMm}{R} + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = - \dfrac{GMm}{2R} + 0$
On solving
${v}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{R}$
So $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}}$ putting in equation (ii)
$\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = v\sqrt{N}$
Comparing $N = 2$

questions.q: Two bodies, each of mass $M$, are kept fixed with a separation of $2L$. A particle of mass $m$ is projected from the midpoint of the line joining their centers, perpendicular to the line. The gravitational constant is $G$. The correct statement (s) is (are) :
options: The minimum initial velocity of the mass $m$ to escape the gravitational field of the two bodies is $4\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{L}}$.
The minimum initial velocity of the mass $m$ to escape the gravitational field of the two bodies is $2\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{L}}$.
The minimum initial velocity of the mass $m$ to escape the gravitational field of the two bodies is $\sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{L}}$.
The energy of the mass $m$ remains constant.
questions.solution:
Applying mechanical energy conservation,

${U}_{i} + K{E}_{i} = {U}_{f} + K{E}_{f}$
$- \dfrac{GMm}{L} \times 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2} = 0 + 0$
$⇒ v\text{=}\sqrt{\dfrac{4GM}{L}}$

$⇒ v\text{=}2\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{L}}$

questions.q: Two spherical planets $P and Q$ have the same uniform density $\rho$, masses $M_{P} and M_{Q}$ and surface areas $A$ and 4A respectively. A spherical planet $R$ also has uniform density $\rho$ and its mass is $\left(M_{P}+M_{Q}\right)$. The escape velocities from the planets $P, Q and R$ are $V_{P}, V_{Q} and V_{R}$, respectively. Then
questions.solution:
Here Planets $P$ and $Q$ have the same uniform density ' $\rho$ ' and surface areas $A$ and $4 A$ respectively. Let the mass of $P, M_{P}$ be $m$.

Then $m=\rho \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3}=\rho \times \frac{4}{3} \pi\left[\frac{A}{4 \pi}\right]^{3 / 2}$

The mass of $M_{Q}=\rho \times \frac{4}{3} \pi\left[\frac{4 A}{4 \pi}\right]^{3 / 2}=8 \mathrm{~m}$

$\therefore \quad$ The mass of Planet $R=8 \mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{m}=9 \mathrm{~m}$

If the radius of $P=r$

Then the radius of $Q=2 r$

$\left[\because r_{Q}=\left(\frac{4 A}{4 \pi}\right)^{3 / 2}=2\left(\frac{A}{4 \pi}\right)^{3 / 2}\right]$

and radius of $R=9^{1 / 3} r$

$\left[\begin{array}{l}

\because M_{R}=M_{P}+M_{Q} \\

r_{R}^{3}=r^{3}+(2 r)^{3}=9 r^{3}

\end{array}\right]$

As we know, escape velocity from the planet

$\begin{aligned} V_{e}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M}{R}} & \therefore v_{P}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M_{P}}{R_{p}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G m}{r}} \\ v_{Q} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 G M_{Q}}{R_{Q}}}=\sqrt{\frac{2 G(8 \mathrm{~m})}{2 r}}=2 v_{P} \\ v_{R} &=\sqrt{\frac{2 G(9 \mathrm{~m})}{9^{1 / 3} r}}=9^{1 / 3} v_{P} \end{aligned}$

questions.q: A satellite is moving with a constant speed $v$ in a circular orbit about the earth. An object of mass $m$ is ejected from the satellite such that it just escapes from the gravitational pull of the earth. At the time of its ejection, the kinetic energy of the object is
questions.solution:
In circular orbit of a satellite, potential energy

$\begin{aligned}$& =-2 $\times(\text{ kinetic energy) }$\\
& =-2 $\times \frac{1}{2}$m v²=-m v²
\end{aligned}

Just$ to escape from the gravitational pull, its total mechanical energy should be zero. Therefore, its kinetic energy should be+m v^2$.
$\therefore$ Correct answer is (b).
Analysis of Question
(i) Question is moderately difficult.
(ii) In circular orbit of satellite $U=-\frac{G M m}{r} and K=\frac{G M m}{2 r} or U=-2 K$
Here, $U$ is potential energy and $K$ is kinetic energy.

questions.q: A thin uniform annular disc (see figure) of mass $M$ has outer radius $4 R$ and inner radius $3 R$. The work required to take a unit mass from point $P$ on its axis to infinity is
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned}$W=$\Delta$U & =U_f-U_i=U_{$\infty$}-U_p \\ & =-U_P \\ & =-m V_P \\ & =-V_P \quad($\text{ as }$m=1) \end{aligned} Potential at point $P$ will be obtained by integration as given below $$ \\ Let $d M$ be the mass of small ring as shown $\begin{aligned}$d M & =$\frac{M}{\pi(4 R)^2-\pi(3 R)^2}($2 $\pi$r) d r \\ & =$\frac{2 M r d r}{7 R^2}$\\ d V_P & =-$\frac{G \cdot d M}{\sqrt{16 R^2+r^2}}$\\ & =-$\frac{2 G M}{7 R^2} \int_{3 R}^{4 R} \frac{r}{\sqrt{16 R^2+r^2}} \cdot$d r \\ & =-$\frac{2 G M}{7 R}($4 $\sqrt{2}-$5) \\ \therefore \quad W & =+$\frac{2 G M}{7 R}($4 $\sqrt{2}-$5) \end{aligned} $\therefore$ correct option is (a).
questions.question: A thin uniform annular disc (see figure) of mass $M$ has outer radius $4 R$ and inner radius $3 R$. The work required to take a unit mass from point $P$ on its axis to infinity is
questions.explanation:
$$ \text{ } \begin{aligned} W=\Delta U & =U_f-U_i=U_{\infty}-U_p \\ & =-U_P \\ & =-m V_P \\ & =-V_P \quad(\text{ as } m=1) \end{aligned} $$ Potential at point $P$ will be obtained by integration as given below
Let $d M$ be the mass of small ring as shown $$ \begin{aligned} d M & =\frac{M}{\pi(4 R)^2-\pi(3 R)^2}(2 \pi r) d r \\ & =\frac{2 M r d r}{7 R^2} \\ d V_P & =-\frac{G \cdot d M}{\sqrt{16 R^2+r^2}} \\ & =-\frac{2 G M}{7 R^2} \int_{3 R}^{4 R} \frac{r}{\sqrt{16 R^2+r^2}} \cdot d r \\ & =-\frac{2 G M}{7 R}(4 \sqrt{2}-5) \\ \therefore \quad W & =+\frac{2 G M}{7 R}(4 \sqrt{2}-5) \end{aligned} $$ $\therefore$ correct option is (a).

questions.q: A binary star consists of two stars $A$ (mass $2.2 M_S$ ) and $B$ (mass $11 M_s$ ), where $M_S$ is the mass of the sun. They are separated by distance $d$ and are rotating about their centre of mass, which is stationary. The ratio of the total angular momentum of the binary star to the angular momentum of $\operatorname{star} B$ about the centre of mass is
questions.solution:
$\frac{L_{\text{Total }}}{L_B}=\frac{\left(I_A+I_B\right) \omega}{I_B \cdot \omega}$ (as $\omega$ will be same in both cases)

$\begin{aligned}$& =$\frac{I_A}{I_B}+$1=$\frac{m_A r_A^2}{m_B r_B^2}+$1 \\
& $\left.=\frac{r_A}{r_B}+$1 \quad \quad $\text{ (as }$m_A r_A=m_B r_B\right) \\
& =$\frac{11}{2.2}+$1 \quad \quad$\left(\text{ as })$r \propto $\frac{1}{m}\right)$\\
& =6
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ The correct answer is 6 .

The average mass density of the planet is $\frac{2}{3}$ times that of the earth. If the escape speed on the surface of the earth is taken to be 11 $\mathrm{kms}^{-1}$, the escape speed on the surface of the planet in $\mathrm{kms}^{-1}$ will be
questions.solution:
$g=\frac{G M}{R^2}=\frac{G\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3\right) \rho}{R^2}$

questions.q:
A spherically symmetric gravitational system of particles has a mass density
$$
\rho=\left\{$\begin{array}{l}
\rho_0 \text{ for } r \leq R \\
0 \text{ for } r>R
\end{array}$\right.
$$
where $\rho_0$ is a constant. A test mass can undergo circular motion under the influence of the gravitational field of particles. Its speed $v$ as a function of distance $r(0 < r < \infty)$ from the centre of the system is represented by
questions.solution:
For $r \leq R$ :

$\frac{m v^2}{r}=\frac{G \cdot m m^{\prime}}{r^2}$Here, $m^{\prime}=\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi r^3\right) \rho_0$
Substituting in Eq. (i) we get, $v \propto r$
i.e., $v-r$ graph is a straight line passing through origin.
For $r \gt R$ :

$\frac{m v^2}{r}=\frac{G \cdot m\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi R^3\right) \rho_0}{r^2}$or $\quad V \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}$
The corresponding $v-r$ graph will be as shown in option (c).
$\therefore$ correct option is (c).

$\dfrac{{\text{ρ}}_{\text{A}}}{{\text{ρ}}_{\text{B}}} = \dfrac{{\text{M}}_{\text{A}} / \text{v}}{{\text{M}}_{\text{B}} / \text{v}} = \dfrac{{\text{n}}_{\text{A}} {m}_{\text{A}}}{{\text{n}}_{\text{B}} {\text{m}}_{\text{B}}}$
$= \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{9}$.

questions.q: A person sitting inside an elevator performs a weighing experiment with an object of mass 50 kg . Suppose that the variation of the height $y$ (in m ) of the elevator, from the ground, with time $t$ (in s ) is given by $y=8\left[1+\sin \left(\frac{2 \pi t}{T}\right)\right]$, where $T=40 \pi \mathrm{~s}$. Taking acceleration due to gravity, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$, the maximum variation of the object's weight (in N ) as observed in the experiment is _______ .
questions.solution:
$y=8+8 \sin \frac{2 \pi t}{T}$
With respect to elevator, variation in weight will be
$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{m}(\Delta \mathrm{a})_{\max } \\ & \Delta \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{m} \times 2 \omega^2 \mathrm{~A}\end{aligned}$
Here elevator is performing SHM
$\begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{W}=2 \mathrm{~m} \times\left(\frac{2 \pi}{\mathrm{~T}}\right)^2 \times \mathrm{A} \mathrm{N} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{W}=2 \times 50 \times\left(\frac{2 \pi}{40 \pi}\right)^2 \times 8 \mathrm{~N} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{~W}=2 \times 50 \times \frac{1}{400} \times 8 \mathrm{~N} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{~W}=\frac{800}{400} \mathrm{~N}=2 \mathrm{~N}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: One end of a horizontal uniform beam of weight $W$ and length $L$ is hinged on a vertical wall at point $O$ and its other end is supported by a light inextensible rope. The other end of the rope is fixed at point $Q$, at a height $L$ above the hinge at point $O$. A block of weight $\alphaW$ is attached at the point $P$ of the beam, as shown in the figure (not to scale). The rope can sustain a maximum tension of $\left(2\sqrt{2}\right)W$. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
options: The vertical component of reaction force at $O$ does not depend on $\alpha$.
The horizontal component of reaction force at $O$ is equal to $W$ for $\alpha = 0 . 5$.
The tension in the rope is $2W$ for $\alpha = 0 . 5$.
questions.solution:
$∵$ Rod is in equilibrium, net torque on the rod about $O$ will be zero.

$W\left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right) + \alphaW\left(l\right) = \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}}l$

$⇒ \dfrac{W}{2} + \alphaW = \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}} ⇒ T = \sqrt{2}W\left(\alpha + 0 . 5\right) . . . \left(1\right)$

Now checking options-

(A)

Force balance on rod,

${N}_{v} + \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}} = W + \alphaW$

$⇒ {N}_{v} = \left(W + \alphaW\right) - \left(\dfrac{W}{2} + \alphaW\right)$

$⇒ {N}_{v} = \dfrac{W}{2}$

Hence, option (A) is correct.

(B) Write horizontal force equation,

${N}_{H} = \dfrac{T}{\sqrt{2}} ⇒ {N}_{H} = W\left(\alpha + 0 . 5\right)$

If $\alpha = 0 . 5$, then,

${N}_{H} = W$ and $T = \sqrt{2}W$

Hence, option (B) is correct.

(D) $∴$ Maximum Tension of string $= 2\sqrt{2}W$

So, to break.

$T > 2\sqrt{2}W ⇒ \sqrt{2}W\left(\alpha + 0 . 5\right) > 2\sqrt{2}W ⇒ \alpha > 1 . 5$

So, string will break.

option (D) correct.

questions.q:
A block of mass $2M$ is attached to a massless spring with spring-constant $k .$ This block is connected to two other blocks of masses $M$ and $2M$ using two massless pulleys and strings. The accelerations of the blocks are ${a}_{1}, {a}_{2}$ and ${a}_{3}$ as shown in figure. The system is released from rest with the spring in its unstretched state. The maximum extension of the spring is ${x}_{0} .$ Which of the following option(s) is/are correct?
[ $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. Neglect friction]
options: When spring achieves an extension of $\dfrac{{x}_{0}}{2}$ for the first time, the speed of the block connected to the spring is $3g\sqrt{\dfrac{M}{5k}}$
At an extension of $\dfrac{{x}_{0}}{4}$ of the spring, the magnitude of acceleration of the block connected to the spring is $\dfrac{3g}{10}$
questions.solution:
Using string constraint
${a}_{1} = \dfrac{{a}_{2} + {a}_{3}}{2}$
$⇒ 2{a}_{1} = {a}_{2} + {a}_{3}$
${a}_{1} - {a}_{3} = {a}_{2} - {a}_{1} ⇒ \left(C\right)$ is correct.
for other options use $m$ equivalent

Equivalent mass
Or Reduced mass
${m}_{eq} = \dfrac{2{m}_{1} \times {m}_{2}}{{m}_{1} + {m}_{2}}$ (for a two-mass system)
$= \dfrac{2\left(2m\right) \times m}{2m + m} = \dfrac{4m}{3}$
$⇒ T = \left(\dfrac{4m}{3}\right) . g$
$∴ 2T = 2 . \dfrac{4mg}{3} = \left(\dfrac{8m}{3}\right)g$
$⇒ {m}_{eq} = \dfrac{8m}{3}$

Using mechanical energy conservation
$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2}k{x}_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{8mg}{3}{x}_{0}$
${x}_{0} = \dfrac{16mg}{3k} ⇒ \left(A\right)$ is incorrect
Option $\left(B\right) ⇒ {V}_{\dfrac{{x}_{0}}{2}} = {V}_{max} = \dfrac{{x}_{0}}{2}\omega = \dfrac{{x}_{0}}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{k}{2m + \dfrac{8m}{3}}} = \dfrac{{x}_{0}}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{3k}{14m}} = g\sqrt{\dfrac{32}{21k}}$
Option $\left(D\right) ⇒ {a}_{\dfrac{{x}_{0}}{4}} = \dfrac{{x}_{0}}{4}{\omega}^{2} = \dfrac{{x}_{0}}{4}\dfrac{3k}{14m} = \dfrac{3k{x}_{0}}{42m} = \dfrac{8g}{21}$
For a simple harmonic motion ${x}_{0} ⇒$ maximum displacement from extreme to extreme
$⇒ {x}_{0} = 2A ⇒ A = \dfrac{{x}_{0}}{2}$
and $\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3k}{14m}}$
$∴ {v}_{max} = A . \omega$
and $a = {\omega}^{2} . x$

questions.q: A particle of mass $m$ is initially at rest at the origin. It is subjected to a force and starts moving along the x - axis. Its kinetic energy changes with time as $dK / dt = \gammat,$ where $\gamma$ is a positive constant of appropriate dimensions. Which of the following statements is (are) true?
options: The force applied on the particle is constant
The speed of the particle is proportional to time
The distance of the particle from the origin increases linearly with time
Since force is constant, it is conservative.
questions.solution:
Given the change in kinetic energy$\dfrac{dk}{dt} = \gammat$.

Kinetic energy is expressed as $k = \dfrac{1}{2}m{v}^{2}$.
$∴ \dfrac{dk}{dt} = mv\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \gammat$
Integrating the above relation,

$m{∫}_{0}^{v}vdv = \gamma{∫}_{0}^{t}tdt$
$\dfrac{m{v}^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{\gamma{t}^{2}}{2}$
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma}{m}}t; υ ∝ t$ ... (i)
$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma}{m}} = constant$
Since $F = ma$
$∴ F = m\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma}{m}} = \sqrt{\gammam} = constant$

questions.q: A solid horizontal surface is covered with a thin layer of oil. A rectangular block of mass $m = 0.4kg$ is at rest on this surface. An impulse of $1.0Ns$ is applied to the block at time $t = 0$ so that it starts moving along the x-axis with a velocity $v\left(t\right) = {v}_{0}{e}^{- \dfrac{t}{τ}}$ , where ${v}_{0}$ is a constant and $τ = 4$ . The displacement of the block, in meter, at $t = τ$ is __________. Take ${e}^{- 1} = 0.37$
questions.solution:
$v = {v}_{0}{e}^{- \dfrac{t}{τ}}$
${v}_{0} = \dfrac{J}{m} = 2.5m / s$
$v = {v}_{0}{e}^{- \dfrac{t}{τ}}$
$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = {v}_{0}{e}^{- \dfrac{t}{τ}}$
${∫}_{0}^{x}dx = {v}_{0}{∫}_{0}^{τ}{e}^{- \dfrac{t}{τ}}dt$
$∫ {e}^{- x}dx = \dfrac{{e}^{- x}}{- 1}$
$x = {v}_{0}{\left[\dfrac{{e}^{- \dfrac{t}{τ}}}{- \dfrac{1}{τ}}\right]}_{0}^{τ}$
$x = 2.5\left(- 4\right)\left({e}^{- 1} - {e}^{0}\right)$
$x = 25\left(- 4\right)\left(0.37 - 1\right)$
$x = 6.30$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle, of mass ${10}^{- 3}kg$ and charge $1.0C$, is initially at rest. At time $t = 0$, the particle comes under the influence of an electric field $\overset{\to}{E}\left(t\right) = {E}_{0}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{i}$ where ${E}_{0} = 1.0N{C}^{- 1}$ and $\omega = {10}^{3}rad{s}^{- 1}$. Consider the effect of only the electrical force on the particle. Then the maximum speed, in $m{s}^{- 1}$, attained by the particle at subsequent times is ____________.
questions.solution:
$m = {10}^{- 3}kg, q = 1C, t = 0$
Force on particle will be
$F = qE = q{E}_{0}sin\left(\omegat\right)$
At ${v}_{max}, F = 0$ $⇒ q{E}_{0}sin ⁡ \omega{t}_{o} = 0$
$⇒ \omega{t}_{o} = \pi$
$F = q{E}_{0}sin ⁡ \omegat$
$\dfrac{dv}{dt} = q\dfrac{{E}_{0}}{m}sin\left(\omegat\right)$
${∫}_{0}^{v}dv = {∫}_{0}^{\pi ∕ \omega}\dfrac{q{E}_{0}}{m}sin\left(\omegat\right)dt$
$v - 0 = \dfrac{q{E}_{0}}{m\omega}{\left[- cos\left(\omegat\right)\right]}_{0}^{\pi ∕ \omega}$
$v - 0 = \dfrac{q{E}_{0}}{m\omega}\left[\left(- cos\left(\pi\right)\right) - \left(- cos\left(0\right)\right)\right]$
$v = \dfrac{1 \times 1}{m\omega} \times 2 = 2 m {s}^{- 1}$

questions.q:
Paragraph: A frame of reference that is accelerated with respect to an inertial frame of reference is called a non-inertial frame of reference. A coordinate system fixed on a circular disc rotating about a fixed axis with a constant angular velocity $\omega$ is an example of a non-inertial frame of reference. The relationship between the force $\vec{F}_{\text{rot }}$ experienced by a particle of mass $m$ moving on the rotating disc and the force $\vec{F}_{\text{in }}$ experienced by the particle in an inertial frame of reference is $\vec{F}_{\mathrm{rot}}=\vec{F}_{\mathrm{in}}+2 m\left(\vec{v}_{\mathrm{rot}} \times \vec{\omega}\right)+m(\vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}) \times \vec{\omega}$, where $\vec{v}_{\text{rot }}$ is the velocity of the particle in the rotating frame of reference and $\vec{r}$ is the position vector of the particle with respect to the centre of the disc. Now consider a smooth slot along a diameter of a disc of radius $R$ rotating counter-clockwise with a constant angular speed $\omega$ about its vertical axis through its center. We assign a coordinate system with the origin at the center of the disc, the $x$-axis along the slot, the $y$-axis perpendicular to the slot and the $z$-axis along the rotation axis $(\vec{\omega}=\omega \hat{k}) .$ A small block of mass $m$ is gently placed in the slot at $\vec{r}=(R / 2) \hat{i}$ at $t=0$ and is constrained to move only along the slot.

Question: The distance $r$ of the block at time $t$ is
questions.solution:
Force on block along slot $= m{\omega}^{2}r = ma = m\left(\dfrac{vdv}{dr}\right)$
$\mathop{∫}_{0}^{v}vdv = \mathop{∫}_{\dfrac{R}{2}}^{r}{\omega}^{2}rdr$
$\dfrac{{v}^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{{\omega}^{2}}{2}\left({r}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}\right) ⇒ v = \omega\sqrt{{r}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}} = \dfrac{dr}{dt}$
$⇒ \mathop{∫}_{\dfrac{R}{4}}^{r}\dfrac{dr}{\sqrt{{r}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}}} = \mathop{∫}_{0}^{t}\omegadt$
$ln\left(\dfrac{r + \sqrt{{r}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}}}{\dfrac{R}{2}}\right) - ln\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{R}{2} + \sqrt{\dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}}}{\dfrac{R}{2}}\right) = \omegat$
$⇒ r + \sqrt{{r}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}} = \dfrac{R}{2}e ^ \omegat$
$⇒ {r}^{2} - \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4} = \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}{e}^{2\omegat} + {r}^{2} - 2r\dfrac{R}{2}{e}^{\omegat}$
$⇒ r = \dfrac{\dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}{e}^{2\omegat} + \dfrac{{R}^{2}}{4}}{R{e}^{\omegat}} = \dfrac{R}{4}\left({e}^{\omegat} + {e}^{- \omegat}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform wooden stick of mass 1.6 kg and length $l$ rests in an inclined manner on a smooth, vertical wall of height h $\left(< l\right)$ such that a small portion of the stick extends beyond the wall. The reaction force of the wall on the stick is perpendicular to the stick. The stick makes an angle of ${30}^{o}$ with the wall and the bottom of the stick is on a rough floor. The reaction of the wall on the stick is equal in magnitude to the reaction of the floor on the stick. The ratio h/ $l$ and the frictional force f at the bottom of the stick are: $\left(g = 10m{s}^{- 2}\right)$
questions.solution:
Force equation in x-direction,
${N}_{1}cos ⁡ {30}^{o} - f = 0$ ....(i)
Force equation in y-direction,
${N}_{1}sin ⁡ {30}^{o} + {N}_{2} - mg = 0$ ....(ii)
Torque equation about O,
$mg\dfrac{l}{2}cos ⁡ {60}^{o} - {N}_{1}\dfrac{h}{cos ⁡ {30}^{o}} = 0$ ...(iii)
Also, given ${N}_{1} = {N}_{2}$ .....(iv)
[Note taking reaction from floor as normal reaction only]
Solving (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) we have
$\dfrac{h}{l} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16}$ and $f = \dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3}$

questions.q:
A person in a lift is holding a water jar, which has a small hole at the lower end of its side. When the lift is at rest, the water jet coming out of the hole hits the floor of the lift at a distance d of 1.2 m from the person. In the following, state of the lift's motion is given in List I and the distance where the water jet hits the floor of the lift is given in List II. Match the statements from List I with those in List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists.
List I List II
A. Lift is accelerating vertically up. $P.$ $d = 1.2m$
B. Lift is accelerating vertically down with an acceleration less than the gravitational acceleration. $Q.$ $d > 1.2m$
C. Lift is moving vertically up with constant speed. $R.$ $d < 1.2m$
D. Lift is falling freely. $S.$ No water leaks out of the jar
questions.solution:
In P, Q, R no horizontal velocity is imparted to falling water, so d remains same.
In S, since its free fall, ${a}_{eff} = 0$
$∴$ liquid won't fall with respect to lift.

questions.q: In the figure, a ladder of mass m is shown leaning against a wall. It is in static equilibrium making an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal floor. The coefficient of friction between the wall and the ladder is ${\mu}_{1}$ and that between the floor and the ladder is ${\mu}_{2}$ . The normal reaction of the wall on the ladder is ${N}_{1}$ and that of the floor is ${N}_{2}$ If the ladder is about to slip, then
questions.solution:
Condition of translational equilibrium
${N}_{1} = {\mu}_{2}{N}_{2}$
${N}_{2} + {\mu}_{1}{N}_{1} = Mg$
Solving ${N}_{2} = \dfrac{mg}{1 + {\mu}_{1}{\mu}_{2}}$
${N}_{1} = \dfrac{{\mu}_{2}mg}{1 + {\mu}_{1}{\mu}_{2}}$
Applying torque equation about corner (left) point on the floor
$mg\dfrac{l}{2}cos ⁡ \theta = {N}_{1}lsin ⁡ \theta + {\mu}_{1}{N}_{1}lcos ⁡ \theta$
Solving $tan ⁡ \theta = \dfrac{2 - {\mu}_{1}{\mu}_{2}}{2{\mu}_{2}}$

questions.q: A bob of mass $m$, suspended by a string of length ${l}_{1}$, is given a minimum velocity required to complete a full circle in the vertical plane. At the highest point, it collides elastically with another bob of mass $m$, suspended by a string of length ${l}_{2}$, which is initially at rest. Both the strings are mass-less and inextensible. If the second bob, after collision acquires the minimum speed required to complete a full circle in the vertical plane, the ratio $\dfrac{{l}_{1}}{{l}_{2}}$ is
questions.solution:
As shown in the figure shown above, the minimum speed required by the bob of mass $m$ attached to the string of length ${l}_{1}$ in order to complete the full circle is $\sqrt{5g{l}_{1}}$.

When the bob goes to the highest point, its speed becomes $\sqrt{g{l}_{1}}$. Here, it strikes with the identical mass, which is tied to the string of length ${l}_{2}$. The speed delivered to the object is $\sqrt{g{l}_{1}}$. This should be equal to $\sqrt{5g{l}_{2}}$ so that this bob could complete a full circle.   
$\sqrt{g{l}_{1}} = \sqrt{5g{l}_{2}}$
$⇒ g{l}_{1} = 5g{l}_{2}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{l}_{1}}{{l}_{2}} = 5$

questions.q: A hollow, right circular cone of base radius $R$ and height $h$, with its tip at the origin is rotating about the $Z$-axis with an angular velocity $\omega$, as shown in the figure. The cone carries a total charge $Q$ uniformly distributed on its curved surface. The magnitude of magnetic field at a point $(0, 0, z)$, where $z \gg R$ and $z \gg h$, is $\dfrac{n\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{Q R^2 \omega}{z^3}$. The value of $n$ is:
questions.solution:
For a point on the axis at a distance $z \gg R$ and $z \gg h$, the rotating cone can be considered as a magnetic dipole. The magnetic field on the axis of a dipole is given by:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{2M}{z^3}$

where $M$ is the magnetic dipole moment of the cone.

To find $M$, consider an elemental ring on the cone at a vertical distance $y$ from the origin, with vertical thickness $dy$. The radius of this ring is $r = \dfrac{R}{h}y$ and its slant length is $dl = \dfrac{\sqrt{R^2+h^2}}{h}dy$.

The surface charge density of the cone is $\sigma = \dfrac{Q}{\pi R \sqrt{R^2+h^2}}$.

The charge on the elemental ring is:

$dq = \sigma (2\pi r dl) = \dfrac{Q}{\pi R \sqrt{R^2+h^2}} \left(2\pi \dfrac{R}{h}y \dfrac{\sqrt{R^2+h^2}}{h}dy\right) = \dfrac{2Q}{h^2}y dy$

The current due to the rotation of this ring is:

$dI = \dfrac{dq}{T} = \dfrac{dq \omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{Q\omega}{\pi h^2}y dy$

The magnetic moment of this elemental ring is:

$dM = dI (\pi r^2) = \left(\dfrac{Q\omega}{\pi h^2}y dy\right) \pi \left(\dfrac{R}{h}y\right)^2 = \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{h^4}y^3 dy$

Integrating from $y = 0$ to $y = h$, the total magnetic moment is:

$M = \int_{0}^{h} \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{h^4}y^3 dy = \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{h^4} \left[\dfrac{y^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{h} = \dfrac{Q\omega R^2}{4}$

Alternatively, using the gyromagnetic ratio for a uniform charge distribution, $\dfrac{M}{L_{ang}} = \dfrac{Q}{2m}$. The moment of inertia of a hollow cone is $I = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2$, so the angular momentum is $L_{ang} = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega$. Thus, $M = \dfrac{Q}{2m} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\omega\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}QR^2\omega$.

Substituting $M$ into the magnetic field formula:

$B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{2}{z^3} \left(\dfrac{1}{4}QR^2\omega\right) = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{QR^2\omega}{2z^3}$

Comparing this with the given expression $B = \dfrac{n\mu_0}{4\pi} \dfrac{QR^2\omega}{z^3}$, we get:

$n = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$

Answer: $0.5$

questions.q: In a vacuum chamber, a particle of charge $1\ \mu\text{C}$ and mass $1$ mg is projected with a velocity $(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j})$ ms$^{-1}$ from the $XZ$ plane at time $t = 0$ in an electric field of $1\hat{i}$ Vm$^{-1}$. At $t = 0.2$ s, the electric field is switched off and a magnetic field of $6\hat{j}$ T is switched on. The acceleration due to gravity is $-10\hat{j}$ ms$^{-2}$. Correct option(s) is/are:
options: The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.3$ s is $15$ cm.
The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.4$ s is $10$ cm.
The radius of the trajectory of the particle for $t > 0.2$ s is $20$ cm.
The particle will be in the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.35$ s.
questions.solution:
For the time interval $0 \le t \le 0.2$ s, the particle is under the influence of the electric field and gravity.
The charge-to-mass ratio of the particle is $\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{10^{-6}} = 1$ C kg$^{-1}$.

The acceleration of the particle is:
$\vec{a} = \dfrac{q\vec{E}}{m} + \vec{g} = 1(\hat{i}) - 10\hat{j} = \hat{i} - 10\hat{j}$ ms$^{-2}$

Given the initial velocity $\vec{v}_0 = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j}$ ms$^{-1}$ and initial vertical position $y_0 = 0$ (since it is projected from the $XZ$ plane), we can find the velocity and position at $t = 0.2$ s.

Velocity at $t = 0.2$ s:
$\vec{v}(0.2) = \vec{v}_0 + \vec{a}t = (\hat{i} + 2\hat{j}) + (\hat{i} - 10\hat{j})(0.2) = 1.2\hat{i}$ ms$^{-1}$

Vertical position at $t = 0.2$ s:
$y(0.2) = y_0 + v_{0y}t + \dfrac{1}{2}a_y t^2 = 0 + 2(0.2) - \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(0.2)^2 = 0.4 - 0.2 = 0.2$ m $= 20$ cm

For $t > 0.2$ s, the electric field is switched off and the magnetic field $\vec{B} = 6\hat{j}$ T is switched on. The magnetic force $\vec{F}_m = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ acts only in the $XZ$ plane because $\vec{B}$ is along the $y$-axis. The vertical motion is only affected by gravity.

Let $t' = t - 0.2$ be the time elapsed after the fields are switched. The initial vertical velocity for this phase is $v_y(0.2) = 0$.
The vertical position as a function of $t'$ is:
$y(t') = y(0.2) + v_y(0.2)t' - \dfrac{1}{2}gt'^2 = 0.2 - 5t'^2$

Evaluating the options:
At $t = 0.3$ s ($t' = 0.1$ s):
$y(0.1) = 0.2 - 5(0.1)^2 = 0.2 - 0.05 = 0.15$ m $= 15$ cm. (Option A is correct)

At $t = 0.4$ s ($t' = 0.2$ s):
$y(0.2) = 0.2 - 5(0.2)^2 = 0.2 - 0.2 = 0$ m $= 0$ cm. (Option B is incorrect)

At $t = 0.35$ s ($t' = 0.15$ s):
$y(0.15) = 0.2 - 5(0.15)^2 = 0.2 - 0.1125 = 0.0875$ m $\neq 0$. (Option D is incorrect)

For the radius of the trajectory for $t > 0.2$ s, the particle moves in a helical path. The radius of the circular projection in the $XZ$ plane is determined by the velocity perpendicular to the magnetic field, $v_{\perp} = 1.2$ ms$^{-1}$.
$R = \dfrac{mv_{\perp}}{qB} = \dfrac{10^{-6} \times 1.2}{10^{-6} \times 6} = 0.2$ m $= 20$ cm. (Option C is correct)

Answer: The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t = 0.3$ s is $15$ cm.; The radius of the trajectory of the particle for $t > 0.2$ s is $20$ cm.

questions.q: A conducting solid sphere of radius $R$ and mass $M$ carries a charge $Q$. The sphere is rotating about an axis passing through its center with a uniform angular speed $\omega$. The ratio of the magnitudes of the magnetic dipole moment to the angular momentum about the same axis is given as $\alpha \frac{Q}{2 M}$. The value of $\alpha$ is _______ .
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & d M=d I A \\ & A=\pi r^2=\pi(R \sin \theta)^2 \\ & d I=\frac{d a}{T}=\frac{\sigma(2 \pi r)(R d \theta) \omega}{2 \pi} \\ & d I=\frac{\sigma 2 \pi R^2 \omega \sin \theta d \theta}{2 \pi}\end{aligned}$ $\mathrm{dI}=\sigma \mathrm{R}^2 \omega \sin \theta \mathrm{~d} \theta$ Magnetic dipole moment : $M=\int d M=\int_0^\pi \sigma R^2 \omega \pi R^2 \sin ^3 \theta d \theta$ $M=\sigma R^4 \omega \pi \int_0^\pi \sin ^3 \theta d \theta \quad\left(\because \int_0^\pi \sin ^3 \theta d \theta=\frac{4}{3}\right)$ $\mathrm{M}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2}\right) \mathrm{R}^4 \omega \pi\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)$ Magnetic dipole moment $\mathrm{M}=\frac{\mathrm{QR}^2 \omega}{3}$ Angular momentum $\mathrm{L}=\left(\frac{2}{5} \mathrm{MR}^2\right) \omega$ $\frac{\mathrm{M}}{\mathrm{~L}}=\frac{\mathrm{QR}^2 \omega}{3 \times \frac{2}{5} \mathrm{MR}^2 \omega}=\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{2 \mathrm{M}}\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)$ $\alpha=\frac{5}{3}=1.67$

questions.q:
An infinitely long wire, located on the $z$-axis, carries a current $I$ along the $+z$-direction and produces the magnetic field $\vec{B}$. The magnitude of the line integral $\int \vec{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{d l}$ along a straight line from the point $(-\sqrt{3} a, a, 0)$ to $(a, a, 0)$ is given by
[ $\mu_0$ is the magnetic permeability of free space.]
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \ell}|=\mathrm{rd} \theta \\ & \Rightarrow|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}|=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \\ & \Rightarrow \int \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \ell}=\int|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}||\overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \ell}| \cos 0^{\circ} \\ & =\int\left(\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}\right) \times(\operatorname{rd} \theta) \\ & =\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi} \mathrm{d} \theta=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi}\left[\theta_2-\left(-\theta_1\right)\right]\end{aligned}$
[ $\theta_1$ is anticlockwise hence taken negative]

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \tan \theta_1=\frac{\mathrm{a} \sqrt{3}}{\mathrm{a}}=\sqrt{3} \\ & \theta_1=\frac{\pi}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \tan \theta_2=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{a}}=1 \\ & \theta_2=\frac{\pi}{4} \\ & \Rightarrow \int \mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \ell=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi}\left[\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{4}\right] \\ & =\frac{7 \mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{24} \\ & \Rightarrow \text{ Ans. Option (1) }\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Which one of the following options represents the magnetic field $\overset{\to}{B}$ at $O$ due to the current flowing in the given wire segments lying on the $xy$ plane?
questions.solution:
Magnetic field due to a straight wire will be zero if the line of the wire passes through the point of interest. Therefore, In the above figure,

${B}_{BC} + {B}_{DE} + {B}_{FG} = 0$

Therefore,

$\overset{\to}{B}net = \overset{\to}{B}AB + \overset{\to}{B}CD + \overset{\to}{B}EF$

Magnetic field due to a finite wire is given by,

$B = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{4\pid}\left(sin\alpha + sin\beta\right)$

Using above formula,

$\overset{\to}{B}AB = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{4\piL} \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

Magnetic field due to a circular arc is,

$B = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2R} \times \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi}$

Therefore,

$\overset{\to}{B}CD = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{4\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)}\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$ and $\overset{\to}{B}EF = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{8 \times \left(\dfrac{L}{4}\right)}\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

Therefore, net magnetic field

$\overset{\to}{B}net = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{4\pi \times L}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{4\left(\dfrac{L}{2}\right)} + \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{8 \times \left(\dfrac{L}{4}\right)}\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{B}net = \left(\dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2L} + \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2L} + \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{4\sqrt{2}\piL}\right)\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{B}net = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{L}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{2}\pi}\right)\left(- \overset{^}{k}\right)$

questions.q:
A small circular loop of area $A$ and resistance $R$ is fixed on a horizontal $xy$-plane with the center of the loop always on the axis $\overset{^}{n}$ of a long solenoid. The solenoid has $m$ turns per unit length and carries current $I$ counter clockwise as shown in the figure. The magnetic field due to the solenoid is in $\overset{^}{n}$ direction. List-I gives time dependences of $\overset{^}{n}$ in terms of a constant angular frequency $\omega$. List-II gives the torques experienced by the circular loop at time $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6\omega}$, Let $\alpha = \dfrac{{A}^{2}{\mu}_{0}^{2}{m}^{2}{I}^{2}\omega}{2R}$.

List-I List-II
(i) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{j} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)$ (p) $0$
(ii) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{i} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{j}\right)$ (q) $- \dfrac{\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$
(iii) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{i} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)$ (r) $\dfrac{3\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$
(iv) $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(cos\omegat\overset{^}{j} + sin\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)$ (s) $\dfrac{\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{j}$
(t) $- \dfrac{3\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$

Which one of the following options is correct?
options: $i \to q, ii \to p, iii \to s, iv \to t$
$i \to s, ii \to t, iii \to q, iv \to p$
$i \to q, ii \to p, iii \to s, iv \to r$
$i \to t, ii \to q, iii \to p, iv \to r$
questions.solution:
Note: This question was given bonus by JEE council.

The magnetic field in a solenoid is given by, $\overset{\to}{B} = {\mu}_{0}mI\overset{^}{n}$. Therefore, the flux through the loop will be,

$ϕ = \left(A\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left({\mu}_{0}mI\overset{^}{n}\right)$

For case I:

$ϕ = \dfrac{BA}{\sqrt{2}}cos\left(\omegat\right)$

The emf will be,

$ε = \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

Therefore, the current in the loop will be,

$i = \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

The magnetic moment of the loop will be,

$\overset{\to}{m} = iA\overset{^}{k} = \dfrac{B{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{k}$

Therefore, the torque

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{m} \times \overset{\to}{B} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\left(\overset{^}{k} \times \overset{^}{n}\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{τ} = - \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left[\overset{^}{i}\right]\sin^{2}\left(\omegat\right)$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{τ} = - \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left[\sin^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right] = \dfrac{- \alpha}{4}\overset{^}{i}$

Hence, $\left(I\right) \to q$

For case II

$ϕ = 0$

Therefore, we can directly write $τ = 0$

Hence $\left(II\right) \to p$

Following the same process as in case I for case III

$ϕ = \dfrac{BA}{\sqrt{2}}cos\left(\omegat\right)$

$i = \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

$\overset{\to}{m} = \dfrac{B{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{m} \times \overset{\to}{B} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}R}sin\omegat\left(\overset{^}{k} \times \left(sin\omegat\overset{^}{i} + cos\omegat\overset{^}{k}\right)\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omegasin\left(\omegat\right)}{2R}sin\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\sin^{2}\left(\omegat\right)\overset{^}{j}$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \dfrac{\alpha}{4}\overset{^}{j}$

Hence, $III \to s$

Following the same process as in case I for case IV

$ϕ = \dfrac{BA}{\sqrt{2}}sin\left(\omegat\right)$

$i = - \dfrac{BA\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}cos\left(\omegat\right)$

$\overset{\to}{m} = - \dfrac{B{A}^{2}\omega}{\sqrt{2}R}cos\omegat\left(\overset{^}{k}\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = \overset{\to}{m} \times \overset{\to}{B} = - \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left(\overset{^}{k} \times \overset{^}{j}\right)\cos^{2}\left(\omegat\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = + \dfrac{{B}^{2}{A}^{2}\omega}{2R}\left(\overset{^}{i}\right) \cdot \cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$

$\overset{\to}{τ} = + \dfrac{3}{4}\alpha\overset{^}{i}$

Hence, $\left(IV\right) \to r$

Two concentric circular loops, one of radius $R$ and the other of radius $2R$, lie in the $xy$-plane with the origin as their common center, as shown in the figure. The smaller loop carries current ${I}_{1}$ in the anti-clockwise direction and the larger loop carries current ${I}_{2}$ in the clockwise direction, with ${I}_{2} > 2{I}_{1} . \overset{\to}{B}\left(x, y\right) denotes the magnetic field at a point \left(x, y\right) in the $xy$-plane. Which of the following statement(s) is (are) correct?

$
options: $\overset{\to}{B}\left(x, y\right)$ is perpendicular to the $xy$-plane at any point in the plane
$\left|\overset{\to}{B}\left(x, y\right)\right|$ depends on $x$ and $y$ only through the radial distance $r = \sqrt{{x}^{2} + {y}^{2}}$
$\left|\overset{\to}{B}\left(x, y\right)\right|$ is non-zero at all points for $r < R$
$\overset{\to}{B}\left(x, y\right)$ points normally outward from the $xy$-plane for all the points between the two loops
questions.solution: (A) Magnetic field at the plane of the ring is perpendicular to the plane. However, they bend as they move forward. From the graph, it is clear that${B}_{net} = 0$for some value of$r \in \left(0, R\right)$. Sooption (C) is incorrect (D) For the graph, it is clear that$B = - ve ⇒$in$⊗$direction for$r \in \left(Rto2R\right)$, so option D is also incorrect.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Paragraph
A special metal $S$ conducts electricity without any resistance. A closed wire loop, made of $S$, does not allow any change in flux through itself by inducing a suitable current to generate a compensating flux. The induced current in the loop cannot decay due to its zero resistance. This current gives rise to a magnetic moment which in turn repels the source of magnetic field or flux. Consider such a loop, of radius $a$, with its center at the origin. A magnetic dipole of moment $m$ is brought along the axis of this loop from infinity to a point at distance $r(\gg a)$ from the center of the loop with its north pole always facing the loop, as shown in the figure below.

The magnitude of magnetic field of a dipole $m$, at a point on its axis at distance $r$, is $\frac{\mu_{0}}{2 \pi} \frac{m}{r^{3}}$, where $\mu_{0}$ is the permeability of free space. The magnitude of the force between two magnetic dipoles with moments, $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, separated by a distance $r$ on the common axis, with their north poles facing each other, is $\frac{k m_{1} m_{2}}{r^{4}}$, where $k$ is a constant of appropriate dimensions. The direction of this force is along the line joining the two dipoles.

QuestionThe work done in bringing the dipole from infinity to a distance $r$ from the centre of the loop by the given process is proportional to:
questions.solution:
For a super conducting loop, net flux passing through it will remain constant.

${\left({ϕ}_{total}\right)}_{i} = {\left({ϕ}_{total}\right)}_{f}$

As area is same, therefore,

$\dfrac{{\mu}_{0}m}{2{\pi r}^{3}} = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2a}$

$⇒ I = \dfrac{am}{{\pi r}^{3}}$

$⇒ I ∝ \dfrac{m}{{r}^{3}}$

The current carrying superconducting loop will also behave like a magnet, whose magnetic dipole moment is given by,${m}_{1} = NIA = ( 1 ) \left(\dfrac{am}{{\pi r}^{3}}\right) \times \pi{a}^{2} = \dfrac{m{a}^{3}}{{r}^{3}}$

$⇒ {m}_{1} ∝ \dfrac{m}{{r}^{3}}$

The repulsive force felt on the magnet will be

$F = \dfrac{K{m}_{1}{m}_{2}}{{r}^{4}} = \dfrac{\left({K}^{'}\right)\left(\dfrac{m}{{r}^{3}}\right)\left(m\right)}{{r}^{4}} ∝ \dfrac{{m}^{2}}{{r}^{7}}$

${W}_{ext} = - ∫ Fdr = - K ' ∫ \dfrac{{m}^{2}}{{r}^{7}}dr$

Using $∫ {x}^{n}dx = \dfrac{{x}^{n + 1}}{n + 1}$

We get,

${W}_{ext} ∝ \dfrac{{m}^{2}}{{r}^{6}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An $\alpha$-particle (mass $4$ amu) and a singly charged Sulphur ion (mass $32$ amu) are initially at rest. They are accelerated through a potential $V$ and then allowed to pass into a region of uniform magnetic field which is normal to the velocities of the particles. Within this region, the $\alpha$-particle and the sulphur ion move in circular orbits of radii ${R}_{\alpha} and {R}_{S}$, respectively. The ratio $\left(\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}}\right)$ is __________ .
questions.solution:
When a particle moves on a circular path in a magnetic field then,

$∵ R = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mE}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mV}}{\sqrt{q}B}$

According to given data,

$∵ V = \text{constant}\text{\text{ and }}B = \text{constant}$

$∴ R ∝ \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{q}}$

$\dfrac{{R}_{\alpha}}{{R}_{S}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{m}_{\alpha}}{{q}_{\alpha}} \times \dfrac{{q}_{S}}{{m}_{S}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{32}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{R}_{\alpha}}{{R}_{S}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{4}$

Then, $\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}} = 4$

Then, $\dfrac{{R}_{S}}{{R}_{\alpha}} = 4$

questions.q: Two identical moving coil galvanometer have $10Ω$ resistance and full scale deflection at $2\muA$ current. One of them is converted into a voltmeter of $100mV$ full scale reading and the other into an Ammeter of $1mA$ full scale current using appropriate resistors. These are then used to measure the voltage and current in the Ohm's law experiment with $R = 1000Ω$ resistor by using an ideal cell. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
options: The resistance of the Voltmeter will be  $100kΩ .$
The measured value of  $R$  will be  $978Ω < R < 982Ω .$
The resistance of the Ammeter will be  $0.02Ω$  (round off to  ${2}^{nd}$  decimal place)
If the ideal cell is replaced by a cell having internal resistance of  $5Ω$  then the measured value of  $R$  will be more than  $1000Ω .$
questions.solution:
Voltmeter rom galvanometer arrangement.
Given: ${R}_{g} = 10Ω$ and ${I}_{g} = 2\muA$
Required voltage range, $V = 100 \times {10}^{- 3}volts$
$⇒ V = {I}_{g}\left({R}_{g} + {R}_{v}\right) = {10}^{- 1}$
$⇒ \dfrac{{10}^{- 1}}{2 \times {10}^{- 6}} = {R}_{g} + {R}_{v}\left(as, {I}_{g} = 2\muA\right)$
$⇒ 5 \times {10}^{4}Ω \approx {R}_{v} ( {R}_{v} < {10}^{5}Ω ) ⇒$ Option $( A )$ is incorrect.

Galvanometer to Ammeter arrangement
$\Delta{V}_{G} = \Delta{V}_{S}$
${I}_{g} ⋅ {R}_{g} = \left(I - {I}_{g}\right) ⋅ S$
$⇒ S = \dfrac{{I}_{g} ⋅ {R}_{g}}{I - {I}_{g}} = \dfrac{2 \times {10}^{- 6} \times 10}{{10}^{- 3} - 2 \times {10}^{- 6}}$
$⇒ S = 2 \times {10}^{- 5} \times {10}^{3} = 2 \times {10}^{- 2}$
$⇒ S = 20mΩ ⇒ ( C )$ is correct.
Circuit diagram for ohm's law

Resistance ammeter,
${R}_{A} = \dfrac{20 \times {10}^{- 3} \times 10}{10} = 20 \times {10}^{- 3}Ω$
$i = \dfrac{ε}{\left(\dfrac{1000 \times 50 \times {10}^{3}}{51 \times {10}^{3}}\right)} = \dfrac{51ε}{5 \times {10}^{4}}\left(∵ {R}_{A} \to 0\right)$
${i}^{′} = i\left(\dfrac{{R}_{v}}{51 \times {10}^{3}}\right) = \dfrac{ε}{1000}$
Measured resistance $∴ {R}_{m} = \dfrac{{i}^{′} \times 1000}{i} = \dfrac{ε}{51ε} \times 5 \times {10}^{4} = \dfrac{5 \times {10}^{4}}{51} = 980.4Ω$
If the voltmeter shows full scale deflection then
$\dfrac{ε}{980} \times \left(\dfrac{1000}{51 \times {10}^{3}}\right) \times 5 \times {10}^{4} = {10}^{- 1}$
$∴ ε = 999.6mv$
Since ${i}_{A} = 1mA$ so max reading of R can be $\dfrac{999.6mV}{1mA} = 999.6Ω$

The torsional constant of the suspension wire is ${10}^{- 4}Nm{rad}^{- 1}$ . When a current flows through the galvanometer, a full scale deflection occurs if the coil rotates by $0.2rad$ . The resistance of the coil of the galvanometer is $50Ω$ . This galvanometer is to be converted into an ammeter capable of measuring current in the range $0 - 1.0A$ . For this purpose, a shunt resistance is to be added in parallel to the galvanometer. The value of this shunt resistance, in ohms, is __________.
questions.solution:
$\begin{cases}n = 50turns & A = 2 \times {10}^{- 4}{m}^{2}\end{cases}$
$\begin{cases}B = 0.02T & K = {10}^{- 4}\end{cases}$
$\begin{cases}{Q}_{m} = 0.2rad & {R}_{g} = 50Ω\end{cases}$
$\begin{cases}{I}_{A} = 0 - 1.0A & τ = MB = C\theta, M = NIA\end{cases}$
$B {I}_{g} NA = C\theta$
$0.02 \times {I}_{g} \times 50 \times 2 \times {10}^{- 4} = {10}^{- 4} \times 0.2$
${I}_{g} = 0.1A$
For galvanometer, resistance is to be connected to ammeter in shunt.

${I}_{g} \times {R}_{g} = \left(I - {I}_{g}\right)S$
$0.1 \times 50 = \left(1 - 0.1\right)S$
$S = \dfrac{50}{9} = 5.55$

The wire located at $x = + R$ carries a constant current ${I}_{1}$ and the wire located at $x = - R$ carries a constant current ${I}_{2}$. A circular loop of radius R is suspended with its centre at $\left(0, 0\sqrt{3}R\right)$ and in a plane parallel to the xy - plane. This loop carries a constant current $I$ in the clockwise direction as seen from above the loop. The current in the wire is taken to be positive if it is in the $+ \overset{^}{j}$ direction. Which of the following statements regarding the magnetic field $\overset{\to}{B}$ is (are) true?
options: If ${I}_{1} = {I}_{2}, then\overset{\to}{B}$ cannot be equal to zero at the origin $\left(0, 0, 0\right)$
If ${I}_{1} > 0and{I}_{2} < 0, then\overset{\to}{B}$ can be equal to zero at the origin $\left(0, 0, 0\right)$
If  ${I}_{1} < 0and{I}_{2} > 0, then\overset{\to}{B}$  can be equal to zero at the origin $\left(0, 0, 0\right)$

questions.solution: $( A )$ At origin, $\overset{\to}{B} = 0$ due to two wires if ${I}_{1} = {I}_{2}, hence\left({\overset{\to}{B}}_{net}\right)$ at origin is equal to $\overset{\to}{B}$ due to ring, which is non-zero. $( B )$ If ${I}_{1} > 0and{I}_{2} < 0, \overset{\to}{B}$ at origin due to wires will be along $+ \overset{^}{k}$ direction and $\overset{\to}{B}$ due to ring is along $- \overset{^}{k}$ direction and hence $\overset{\to}{B}$ can be zero at origin $( C )$ If ${I}_{1} 0, \overset{\to}{B}$ at origin due to wires is along $- \overset{^}{k}$ and also along $- \overset{^}{k}$ due to ring, hence $\overset{\to}{B}$ cannot be zero $( D )$

questions.q: In the $\text{xy - plane}$, the region $y > 0$ has a uniform magnetic field ${B}_{1}\overset{^}{k}$ and the region $y < 0$ has another uniform magnetic field ${B}_{2}\overset{^}{k}$. A positively charged particle is projected from the origin along the positive $\text{y} - \text{axis}$ with speed ${v}_{0} = \pims^{- 1}$ at $t = 0$, as shown in the figure. Neglect gravity in this problem. Let $t = T$ be the time when the particle crosses the $\text{x} - \text{axis}$ from below for the first time. If ${B}_{2} = 4{B}_{1}$, the average speed of the particle, in $ms^{- 1}$, along the $\text{x} - \text{axis}$ in the time interval $T$ is ________.
questions.solution:
Average speed along the \(\mathrm{x}\)-axis
\(\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{x}}\right)=\frac{\int\left|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{x}}\right| \mathrm{dt}}{\int \mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}_1+\mathrm{d}_2}{\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{t}_2} \rightarrow(1)\)
We also have,
$\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{r}_1=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB}_1}, \mathrm{r}_2=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB} \mathrm{B}_2} \\
&\text{ since } \mathrm{B}_1=\frac{\mathrm{B}_2}{4}
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{r}_1=4 \mathrm{r}_2 \rightarrow(2)\)
Time$ in $\(B_1 \Rightarrow \frac{\pi B}{q B_1}=t_1\)
Time in \(\mathrm{B}_2 \Rightarrow \frac{\pi \mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{qB}_2}=\mathrm{t}_2\)
Total distance along \(\mathrm{x}\)-axis \(\mathrm{d}_1+\mathrm{d}_2=2 \mathrm{r}_1+2 \mathrm{r}_2=2\left(\mathrm{r}_1+\mathrm{r}_2\right)=2\left(5 \mathrm{r}_2\right)\)
Total time \(\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{t}_1+\mathrm{t}_2=5 \mathrm{t}_2\)
\(\therefore \text{ Average speed }=\frac{10 \mathrm{r}_2}{5 \mathrm{t}_2}=2 \frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB}_2} \times \frac{\mathrm{qB}_2}{\pi \mathrm{m}}=2\)$

A particle with charge $+ Q$ and momentum p directed along $x$ -axis enters region 2 from region 1 at point ${P}_{1}\left(y = - R\right) .$ Which of the following option(s) is/are correct?

$∴$    particle will enter region 3 through point  ${P}_{2}$ for $B > \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{p}{QR}$

Column 1 Column 2 Column 3
1. Electron with $\overset{\to}{v} = 2\dfrac{{E}_{0}}{{B}_{0}}\overset{^}{x}$ (i) $\overset{\to}{E} = {E}_{0}\overset{^}{z}$ (P) $\overset{\to}{B} = - {B}_{0}\overset{^}{x}$
2. Electron with $\overset{\to}{v} = \dfrac{{E}_{0}}{{B}_{0}}\overset{^}{y}$ (ii) $\overset{\to}{E} = - {E}_{0}\overset{^}{y}$ (Q) $\overset{\to}{B} = {B}_{0}\overset{^}{x}$
3.Proton with $\overset{\to}{v}$ =0 (iii) $\overset{\to}{E} = {- E}_{0}\overset{^}{x}$ (R) $\overset{\to}{B} = - {B}_{0}\overset{^}{y}$
4. Proton with $\overset{\to}{v} = 2\dfrac{{E}_{0}}{{B}_{0}}\overset{^}{x}$ (iv) $\overset{\to}{E} = {E}_{0}\overset{^}{x}$ (S) $\overset{\to}{B} = - {B}_{0}\overset{^}{z}$
In which case will the particle move in a straight line with a constant velocity?
questions.solution:
Given: A charged particle is introduced at the origin \((x=0, y=0, z=0)\). initial velocity \(=\vec{v}\),
uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\).
uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\).
Also the values are given the table.
we need to find the cases where the particle will move in a straight line with constant velocity.
To move a particle with constant velocity;
Fnet \(=0\),
\(\Rightarrow\) The electric force \(=\) magnetic fore e.
\(\begin{gathered}
q E=q v B . \\
E=v B .
\end{gathered}\)
Now checking the options.
$\begin{aligned}
&\text{ A) (II) (iii) (s). } \\
&\text{ (II) }=\vec{v}=\frac{E_0}{B_0} \hat{y} \text{. } \\
&\text{ (iii) }=\vec{E}=-E_0 \hat{x} \\
&(s)=\vec{B}=B_0 \hat{Z} \text{. } \\
&-E_0 \hat{x}=E_0 \hat{B O} \hat{y}(B O \hat{z}) \\
\end{aligned}\)
\(\therefore\) (II) (iii) (s) is$ the correct option

$F ∝ \left(L + R\right)$

The distance of each wire from the centre of the loop is $d$. The loop and the wires are carrying the same current $I$. The current in the loop is in the counterclockwise direction if seen from above.

Question: When $d \approx a$ but wires are not touching the loop, it is found that the net magnetic field on the axis of the loop is zero at a height $h$ above the loop. In that case
options: current in wire 1 and wire 2 is the direction PQ and RS, respectively and $h \approx a$
current in wire 1 and wire 2 is the direction PQ and SR, respectively and $h \approx a$
current in wire 1 and wire 2 is the direction PQ and SR, respectively and $h \approx 1.2a$
current in wire 1 and wire 2 is the direction PQ and RS, respectively and $h \approx 1.2a$
questions.solution:
The net magnetic field at the given point will be zero if.
$\left|{\overset{\to}{B}}_{wires}\right| = \left|{\overset{\to}{B}}_{loop}\right|$
$⇒ 2\dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2\pi\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {h}^{2}}} \times \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{{a}^{2} + {h}^{2}}} = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I{a}^{2}}{2{\left({a}^{2} + {h}^{2}\right)}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}}$
$⇒ h \approx 1.2a$

A point charge is moving with speed u between the wires in the same plane at a distance ${X}_{1}$ from one of the wires. When the wires carry current of magnitude $I$  in the same direction, the radius of curvature of the path of the point charge is ${R}_{1}$ . In contrast, if the currents $I$ in the two wires have directions opposite to each other, the radius of curvature of the path is ${R}_{2}$ . If $\dfrac{{X}_{0}}{{X}_{1}} = 3$ , value of $\dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{2}}$ is

${B}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{{\mu}_{0}}{2\pi}\right)\left(\dfrac{3I}{{x}_{0}}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{{R}_{1}}{{R}_{2}} = \dfrac{{B}_{2}}{{B}_{1}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{3}}{\dfrac{1}{9}} = 3$

questions.q: A galvanometer gives full scale deflection with $0 \cdot 006A$ current. By connecting it to a $4990Ω$ resistance, it can be converted into a voltmeter of range $0 - 30V$. If connected to a $\dfrac{2n}{249}Ω$ resistance, it becomes an ammeter of range $0 - 1 \cdot 5A$. The value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
Given a galvanometer of resistance (of resistance ${R}_{G}$) get converted into a voltmeter of range $0 - 30V$ , when a resistance of ${R}_{S} = 4990Ω$ is connected in series of it and give full scale of deflection with current ${I}_{G} = 0 \cdot 006A$.


Than from equation ${I}_{G} = \dfrac{V}{{R}_{S} + {R}_{G}}$
$0.006 = \dfrac{30}{4990 + G}$ $⇒ {R}_{G} = 10Ω$

Now this galvanometer is connected with a shunt resistance to convert into ammeter of range $0 - 1 \cdot 5A$

Given ${I}_{G} = 0.006$, so current passing shunt will be 
${I}_{S} = I - {I}_{G} = 1 . 5 - 0 \cdot 006 = 1.494A$
Since ${R}_{G}$ and ${R}_{S}$ are in parallel, ${I}_{G}{R}_{G} = {I}_{s}{R}_{S}$
$0.006R = 1.494\left(\dfrac{2n}{249}\right)$ ;   $∵$given ${R}_{S} = \left(\dfrac{2n}{249}\right)$  
$∴ n = 5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A steady current $I$ flows along an infinitely long hollow cylindrical conductor of radius $R$. This cylinder is placed co-axially inside an infinite solenoid of radius $2R$. The solenoid has $n$ turns per unit length and carries a steady current $I$. Consider a point $P$ at a distance $r$ from the common axis. The correct statement(s) is(are):
options: In the region $0 < r < R$, the magnetic field is non-zero.
In the region $R < r < 2R$, the magnetic field is along the common axis.
In the region $R < r < 2R$, the magnetic field is tangential to the circle of radius $r$, centered on the axis.
In the region $r > 2R,$ the magnetic field is non-zero.
questions.solution:
If we consider a point at a distance $r$ from a common axis such that $0 < r < R$, the magnetic field is non-zero because inside infinite solenoid magnetic field is, $\overset{\to}{B} = {\mu}_{0}ni$ and due to the hollow cylinder it is zero. Hence, net magnetic field is non-zero.

If $2R < r$, then magnetic field due to an infinite solenoid is zero but there will be a non-zero magnetic field because of hollow cylinder. Hence, net magnetic field is non-zero.

If $R < r < 2R$, then the magnetic field due to solenoid is along the axis and magnetic field due to the hollow cylinder is in circular form. Hence, the net magnetic field is neither along axis nor in tangential direction.

questions.q: Consider the motion of a positive point charge in a region where there are simultaneous uniform electric and magnetic fields $\vec{E}=E_{0} \hat{j}$ and $\vec{B}=B_{0} \hat{j}$. At time $t=0$, this charge has velocity $\vec{v}$ in the in the $x$-y plane, making an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis. Which of the following option(s) is (are) correct for time $t>0$ ?
options: If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, the charge moves in a circular path in the $x$ - plane.
If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, the charge undergoes helical motion with constant pitch along the $y$-axis.
If $\theta=10^{\circ}$, the charge undergoes helical motion with its pitch increasing with time, along the $y$-axis.
If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, the charge undergoes linear but accelerated motion along the $y$-axis.
questions.solution: If $\theta=0^{\circ}$, the charged particle is projected along $x$-axis, due to magnetic field, $\vec{B}$ the charged particle will tend to move in a circular path in $y-z$ plane but due to force of electric field $\vec{E}$, the particle will move in a helical path with increasing pitch. Hence options (A) and (B) are wrong. If $\theta=10^{\circ}$, we can resolve velocity into two rectangular components. One along $x$-axis $\left(v \cos 10^{\circ}\right)$ and one along $y$-axis $\left(v \sin 10^{\circ}\right)$. Due to $v \cos 10^{\circ}$, the particle will move in circular path and due to $v \sin 10^{\circ}$ plus the force due to electric field, the particle will undergo helical motion with its pitch increasing. If $\theta=90^{\circ}$, the charge is moving along the magnetic field. Therefore the force due to magnetic field is zero. But the force due to electric field will accelerate the particle along $y$-axis.

$\begin{array}{l}

\frac{\mu_{0} I_{t}}{2 \pi a}-\frac{\mu_{0} I_{c}}{2 \pi\left(\frac{3}{2} a\right)} \\

=\frac{\mu_{0}}{\pi a}\left[\frac{\pi a^{2} J}{2}-\frac{\pi a^{2} J}{12}\right] \\

\text{ or, } \mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{5 \mu_{0} a J}{12}

\end{array}$

Comparing it with $\frac{N}{12} \mu_{0} a J$ We get $N=5$

Take the circular tube as a long solenoid. The wires are closely wound. Magnetic field inside the solenoid is

In the given problem,

Induced emf, $e=-\frac{d \phi}{d t}=-\left(\frac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{L R}\right) \cdot \frac{d I}{d t}$
Induced current,

i=$\frac{e}{R}=-\left(\frac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{L R}\right) \frac{d I}{d t}$Magnetic moment $i A=i \pi r^2$ or $\quad M=-\left(\frac{\mu_0 \pi^2 r^4}{L R}\right) \cdot \frac{d I}{d t}$
Given, $\quad I=I_0 \cos 300 t$
\therefore \quad $\frac{d I}{d t}=-$300 I_0 \sin (300 t)

Substituting$ in Eq. (i), we get\begin{aligned}$M & =$\left(\frac{300 \pi^2 r^4}{L R}\right) \mu_$0 I_0 \sin 300 t \\
\therefore \quad N & =$\frac{300 \pi^2 r^4}{L R}
\end{aligned}$Substituting the values, we get

$\begin{aligned}$N & =$\frac{300(22 / 7)^2(0.1)^4}{(10)(0.005)}$\\
& =5.926
\end{aligned}$ or \quad N \simeq 6$

questions.solution:
Induced emf $e=-\frac{d \phi}{d t}$. For identical rings induced emf will be same. But currents will be different. Given $h_A>h_B$. Hence, $v_A>v_B$ as $\left(h=\frac{v^2}{2 g}\right)$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In an experiment for determination of the focal length of a thin convex lens, the distance of the object from the lens is $10 \pm 0 . 1cm$ and the distance of its real image from the lens is $20 \pm 0 . 2cm$. The error in the determination of focal length of the lens is $n %$. The value of $n$ is _____.
questions.solution:
Given:

Object distance $= 10 \pm 0 . 1cm$

Image distance $= 20 \pm 0 . 2cm$

As per lens formula

$\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} . . . \left(i\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{\left(- 10\right)} = \dfrac{1}{f}$

$⇒ f = \dfrac{20}{3}cm$

Differentiate equation $\left(i\right)$ on both sides, we get

$\left(- \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}\right)dv - \left(\dfrac{- 1}{{u}^{2}}\right)du = \left(\dfrac{- 1}{{f}^{2}}\right)df$

For calculating maximum error, we will add all values

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{{f}^{2}}df = + \dfrac{1}{{v}^{2}}dv + \dfrac{1}{{u}^{2}}du$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{df}{f}\right) \times 100 = \left[\left(\dfrac{0 . 2}{{20}^{2}} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{{10}^{2}}\right)\dfrac{20}{3}\right] \times 100$

$= \left(\dfrac{0 . 2}{4} + \dfrac{0 . 1}{1}\right)\dfrac{20}{3} = 1$

Therefore,

$\dfrac{df}{f} \times 100 = 1 % = n$

The voltage applied across this combination is $V = \left(5 . 00 \pm 0 . 02\right)V$. The percentage error in the calculation of the energy stored in this combination of capacitors is __________.
questions.solution:
For the purpose of calculation of error, fundamental formula is considered

$\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{{C}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{C}_{2}} ⇒ C = 1200pF$

$- dC{C}_{1}^{2} = - d{C}_{1}{C}_{1}^{2} - d{C}_{2}{C}_{2}^{2}$

$dC = 6pF$

Equivalent capacitance $= \left(1200 \pm 6\right)pF$

$E = 1 / 2{CV}^{2}$

$( dE / E = dC / C + 2dV / V ) \times 100$

$= 1 . 3 %$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Paragraph: If the measurement errors in all the independent quantities are known, then it is possible to determine the error in any dependent quantity. This is done by the use of series expansion and truncating the expansion at the first power of the error. For example, consider the relation $z = \dfrac{x}{y}$. If the errors in $x, yandzare ∆ x, ∆ yand ∆ z$ , respectively, then

$z \pm ∆ z = \dfrac{x \pm ∆ x}{y \pm ∆ y} = \dfrac{x}{y}\left(1 \pm \dfrac{∆ x}{x}\right){\left(1 \pm \dfrac{∆ y}{y}\right)}^{- 1}$

The series expansion for ${\left(1 \pm \dfrac{∆ y}{y}\right)}^{- 1}$, to first power in $∆ y / y, is1 ∓ \left(∆ y / y\right)$. The relative errors in independent variables are always added. So the error in $z$ will be

$\text{\Delta}z = z( \dfrac{\text{\Delta}x}{x} + \dfrac{\text{\Delta}y}{y} ) .$
The above derivation makes the assumption that \(\Delta r / x \ll 1, \Delta y / y < 1\). Therefore, the higher powers of these quantities are neglected.
Question : Consider the ratio \(r=\frac{(1-a)}{(1+a)}\) to be determined by measuring a dimensionless quantity a If the error in the measurement of a is \(\Delta a(\frac{\Delta a}{a}<<1)\), then what is the error \(\Delta r\) in determining \(r\) ?
questions.solution:
$r = \left(\dfrac{1 - a}{1 + a}\right)$
$\dfrac{∆ r}{r} = \dfrac{∆ \left(1 - a\right)}{\left(1 - a\right)} + \dfrac{∆ \left(1 + a\right)}{\left(1 + a\right)}$
$= \dfrac{∆ a}{\left(1 - a\right)} + \dfrac{∆ a}{\left(1 + a\right)}$
$= \dfrac{∆ a\left(1 + a + 1 - a\right)}{\left(1 - a\right)\left(1 + a\right)}$
$∴ ∆ r = \dfrac{2 ∆ a}{\left(1 - a\right)\left(1 + a\right)}\dfrac{\left(1 - a\right)}{\left(1 + a\right)} = \dfrac{2 ∆ a}{{\left(1 + a\right)}^{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A person measures the depth of a well by measuring the time interval between dropping a stone and receiving the sound of impact with the bottom of the well. The error in his measurement of time is $\deltaT = 0.01$ seconds and he measures the depth of the well to be L = 20 meters. Take the acceleration due to gravity $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$ and the velocity of sound is $300m{s}^{- 1}$ . Then the fractional error in the measurement, $\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$ , is closest to
questions.solution:
Total time taken,

$T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}} + \dfrac{L}{c}$, $c$ is the sound speed in air.

Now, for an error $\deltaL$ in L,

We have an error $\deltaT$ in T

So, $T + \deltaT = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(L + \deltaL\right)}{g}} + \dfrac{\left(L + \deltaL\right)}{c}$

$= \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}\left(1 + \dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)} + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(1 + \dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

Since, $\dfrac{\deltaT}{T}$ is very small, hence

$\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$ is also small, so taking binomial approximation

$T + \deltaT = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(1 + \dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

$⇒ T + \deltaT = \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\right) + \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) + \left(\dfrac{L}{c}\right) + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

$⇒ \deltaT = \sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{g}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) + \dfrac{L}{c}\left(\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right)$

$⇒ \deltaT = \left[\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{2g}} + \left(\dfrac{L}{c}\right)\right]\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$

$⇒ 0 . 01 = \left[\sqrt{\dfrac{20}{2 \times 10}} + \left(\dfrac{20}{300}\right)\right]\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}$

$⇒ 0 . 01 = \left[1 + \dfrac{1}{15}\right]\dfrac{\deltaL}{L} ⇒ \dfrac{\deltaL}{L} = \dfrac{0 . 15}{16}$

$%error = \left(\dfrac{\deltaL}{L}\right) \times 100%$

$= \dfrac{15}{16}%$

$\approx 1%$

questions.q: In an experiment to determine the acceleration due to gravity g, the formula used for the time period of a periodic motion is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{7\left(R - r\right)}{5g}} .$ The values of R and r are measured to be $\left(60 \pm 1\right)mmand\left(10 \pm 1\right)mm,$ respectively. In five successive measurements, the time period is found to be 0.52s, 0.56s, 0.57s, 0.54s and 0.59s. The least count of the watch used for the measurement of time period is 0.01s. Which of the following statements (s) is (are) true?
options: The error in the measurement of r is 10%.
The error in the measurement of T is 3.57 %.
The error in the measurement of T is 2%.
The error in the determined value of g is 11%.
questions.solution:
T Absolute error
1 0.52 $- 0.04$
2 0.56 00
3 0.57 $+ 0.01$
4 0.54 $- 0.02$
5 0.59 $+ 0.03$
${T}_{avg} = 0.556$ $= 0.56$



Avg. absolute error $\dfrac{0 . 04 + 0 + 0 . 01 + 0 . 02 + 0 . 03}{5} = 0 . 02$
Percentage error in time period$= \dfrac{∆ T}{T} \times 100% = \dfrac{0 . 02}{0 . 56} \times 100% \approx 3.57%$
Percentage error in radius$= \dfrac{∆ r}{r} \times 100% = \dfrac{1}{10} \times 100 = 10%$
Also, $g = \dfrac{28\pi\left(R - r\right)}{5{T}^{2}}$

Percentage error in $g$,=$\dfrac{∆ g}{g} = \dfrac{∆ R + ∆ r}{R - r} + \dfrac{2 ∆ T}{T}$
$\dfrac{∆ g}{g} \times 100% = \dfrac{1 + 1}{50} \times 100% + 2\left(3.57\right)%$$\approx 11%$

questions.q: The energy of a system as a function of time $t$ is given as $E\left(t\right) = {A}^{2}\left(- \alphat\right)$ , where $\alpha = 0.2{s}^{- 1}$ . The measurement of $A$ has an error of 1.25%. If the error in the measurement of time is 1.50%, the percentage error in the value of $E ( t )$ at $t = 5$ s is
questions.solution:
Energy $E = {A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}$
For small % errors, we can, do differentiation
$dE = 2A\left(dA\right){e}^{- \alphat} + {A}^{2}\left(- \alpha{e}^{- \alphat}dt\right)$
Fractional error $= \dfrac{dE}{E} = \dfrac{2A{e}^{- \alphat}\left(dA\right) + \left(- \alpha{A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}\right)dt}{{A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}} = 2\left(\dfrac{dA}{A}\right) + \left(- \alpha\dfrac{dt}{t}\right)t$
% error $= 2\left(1.25%\right) + \left(0.2 \times 1.5%\right) \times 5$
$= 4%$ (errors always add up)
Alternate solution:
$E = {A}^{2}{e}^{- \alphat}$
Taking natural logarithm on both sides,
$ln\left(E\right) = ln\left({A}^{2}\right) + \left(- \alphat\right)$
Differentiating
$\dfrac{dE}{E} = 2\left(\dfrac{dA}{A}\right) + \left(- \alphadt\right)$
For small fractional erros, errors always add up
$\left|\dfrac{dE}{E}\right| = 2\left|\dfrac{dA}{A}\right| + \alpha\left(\dfrac{dt}{t}\right) \times t$
$= 2\left(1.25%\right) + \left(0.2\right)\left(1.5%\right)5$
$= 4%$

For a load $M=2.5 \mathrm{~kg}$, an extension $l=0.25 \mathrm{~mm}$ in the length of the wire is observed. Quantities $d and l$ are measured using a screw gauge and a micrometer, respectively. They have the same pitch of $0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$. The number of divisions on their circular scale is 100 . The contributions to the maximum probable error of the $Y$ measurement
options: due to the errors in the measurements of $d$ and $l$ are the same.
due to the error in the measurement of $d$ is twice that due to the error in the measurement of $l$.
due to the error in the measurement of $l$ is twice that due to the error in the measurement of $d$.
due to the error in the measurement of $d$ is four times that due to the error in the measurement of $l$.
questions.solution:
The maximum possible error in $Y$ due to $l$ and $d \frac{\Delta Y}{Y}=\frac{\Delta l}{l}+\frac{2 \Delta d}{d}$ Least count $=\frac{\text{ Pitch }}{\text{ No. of division on circular scale }} =\frac{0.5}{100} \mathrm{~mm}=0.005 \mathrm{~mm}$

Here, $\Delta d=\Delta l=0.005 \mathrm{~mm}$

Error contribution of $l=\frac{\Delta l}{l}=\frac{0.005 \mathrm{~mm}}{0.25 \mathrm{~mm}}=\frac{1}{50}$

Error contribution of

$d=\frac{2 \Delta d}{d}=\frac{2 \times 0.005 \mathrm{~mm}}{0.5 \mathrm{~mm}}=\frac{1}{50}$

Hence contribution to the maximum possible error in the measurement of $y$ due to $l$ and $d$ is the same.

The reading on the main scale is $2.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ and that on the circular scale is 20 divisions. questions.q: A student uses a simple pendulum of exactly $1 \mathrm{~m}$ length to determine $g$, the acceleration due to gravity. He uses a stop watch with the least count of $1 \mathrm{~s}$ for this and records $40 \mathrm{~s}$ for 20 oscillations. For this observation, which of the following statement(s) is/are true?
options:
Error $\Delta T$ in measuring $T$, the time period, is $0.05 \mathrm{~s}$

Error $\Delta T$ in measuring $T$, the time period, is $1 \mathrm{~s}$

Percentage error in the determination of $g$ is $5 \%$

Percentage error in the determination of $g$ is $2.5 \%$
questions.solution:
$T=\frac{40 \mathrm{~s}}{20}=2 \mathrm{~s}$.
Further, t=n T=20 T or $\Delta t=20 \Delta T\therefore \quad \frac{\Delta t}{t}=\frac{\Delta T}{T}
or \Delta T=\frac{T}{t} \cdot \Delta t=\left(\frac{2}{40}\right)(1)=0.05 \mathrm{~s}$
Further, $T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ or $\quad T \propto g^{-1 / 2}$
\therefore $\frac{\Delta T}{T} \times$100=-$\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{\Delta g}{g} \times$100

or $\%$ error in determination of $g$ is

$\begin{aligned}\frac{\Delta g}{g} \times$100 & =-200 $\times \frac{\Delta T}{T}$\\
& =-$\frac{200 \times 0.05}{2}=-$5 \%
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ correct options are (a) and (c).

questions.q: A student performs an experiment to determine the Young's modulus of a wire, exactly $2 \mathrm{~m}$ long, by Searle's method. In a particular reading, the student measures the extension in the length of the wire to be $0.8 \mathrm{~mm}$ with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.05 \mathrm{~mm}$ at a load of exactly $1.0 \mathrm{~kg}$. The student also measures the diameter of the wire to be $0.4 \mathrm{~mm}$ with an uncertainty of $\pm 0.01 \mathrm{~mm}$. Take $g=9.8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ (exact). The Young's modulus obtained from the reading is
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} Y & =\frac{F L}{A l}=\frac{4 F L}{\pi d^2 l} \\ & =\frac{(4)(1.0 \times 9.8)(2)}{\pi\left(0.4 \times 10^{-3}\right)^2\left(0.8 \times 10^{-3}\right)}=20 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{ N} / \mathrm{m}^2\end{aligned}$
Further $\quad \frac{\Delta Y}{Y}=2  \left(\frac{\Delta d}{d}\right)+\left(\frac{\Delta l}{l}\right)
\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad \Delta Y & = \left\{2\left(\frac{\Delta d}{d}\right)+\left(\frac{\Delta l}{l}\right)\right \}Y= \left\{2 \times \frac{0.01}{0.4}+\frac{0.05}{0.8}\right\} \times2.0 \times10^{11} \\
& =0.2 \times10^{11}  \mathrm{ N}/  \mathrm{m}^2 \text{$ or $}}(Y+\Delta Y)=(2+0.2) \times10^{11}  \mathrm{ N}/  \mathrm{m}^2
\end{aligned}$ The correct option is (b).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Passage: A container of height $2$ m, length $2$ m and breadth $1$ m is made of insulating vertical walls and two large area horizontal metal plates ($M_1$ and $M_2$) which extend far beyond the vertical walls in all directions. The container is partitioned into two equal chambers with a thin insulating vertical wall. The partition wall contains a small hole of cross-sectional area $\sqrt{10}$ cm$^2$ near its bottom edge. Initially the hole is closed and the left chamber of the container is completely filled with a liquid of dielectric constant $\epsilon_r = 15$ and the right chamber is empty ($\epsilon_r = 1$). At time $t = 0$, the hole is opened and the liquid flows from the left chamber to the right chamber. In both the chambers, the space above the liquid has $\epsilon_r = 1$ and is maintained at atmospheric pressure. The schematic of the container at a time $t > 0$ is shown in the figure.
[Given: acceleration due to gravity is $10$ ms$^{-2}$.]


Question: The height (in m) of the liquid in left chamber at $t = 500$ s is:
questions.solution:
Let $A$ be the cross-sectional area of each chamber and $a$ be the cross-sectional area of the hole.
From the given dimensions, the area of each chamber is $A = 1 \text{ m} \times 1 \text{ m} = 1 \text{ m}^2$.
The area of the hole is $a = \sqrt{10} \text{ cm}^2 = \sqrt{10} \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.
Let $h_1$ and $h_2$ be the heights of the liquid in the left and right chambers at time $t$, respectively.
By conservation of volume, $A h_1 + A h_2 = A H$, where $H = 2$ m is the initial height of the liquid in the left chamber.
$\Rightarrow h_1 + h_2 = 2$

The velocity of efflux through the hole is given by Torricelli's law:
$v = \sqrt{2g(h_1 - h_2)}$

The rate of flow of the liquid is:
$-A \dfrac{dh_1}{dt} = a \sqrt{2g(h_1 - h_2)}$

Substitute $h_2 = 2 - h_1$ into the equation:
$-A \dfrac{dh_1}{dt} = a \sqrt{2g(2h_1 - 2)}$

Let $y = 2h_1 - 2$. Then $dy = 2 dh_1$, which gives $dh_1 = \dfrac{dy}{2}$.
The differential equation becomes:
$-\dfrac{A}{2} \dfrac{dy}{dt} = a \sqrt{2gy}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{\sqrt{y}} = -\dfrac{2a\sqrt{2g}}{A} dt$

Integrating both sides from $t = 0$ to $t = 500$ s. At $t = 0$, $h_1 = 2$ m, so $y(0) = 2(2) - 2 = 2$ m.
$\int_{2}^{y} y^{-1/2} dy = -\dfrac{2a\sqrt{2g}}{A} \int_{0}^{500} dt$
$[2\sqrt{y}]_{2}^{y} = -\dfrac{2 \times (\sqrt{10} \times 10^{-4}) \times \sqrt{20}}{1} \times 500$
$2\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{2} = -1000 \times 10^{-4} \times \sqrt{200}$
$2\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{2} = -0.1 \times 10\sqrt{2}$
$2\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{2} = -\sqrt{2}$
$2\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{2}$
$\sqrt{y} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

Squaring both sides, we get:
$y = 0.5$

Since $y = 2h_1 - 2$, we have:
$2h_1 - 2 = 0.5$
$2h_1 = 2.5$
$h_1 = 1.25 \text{ m}$

Answer: $1.25$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A table tennis ball has radius $(3 / 2) \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$ and mass $(22 / 7) \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg}$. It is slowly pushed down into a swimming pool to a depth of $d=0.7 \mathrm{~m}$ below the water surface and then released from rest. It emerges from the water surface at speed $v$, without getting wet, and rises up to a height $H$. Which of the following option(s) is(are) correct?
[Given: $\pi=22 / 7, g=10 \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{~s}^{-2}$, density of water $=1 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$, viscosity of water $=1 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~Pa}$-s.]
options: The work done in pushing the ball to the depth $d$ is $0.077 \mathrm{~J}$.
If we neglect the viscous force in water, then the speed $v=7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.
If we neglect the viscous force in water, then the height $H=1.4 \mathrm{~m}$.
The ratio of the magnitudes of the net force excluding the viscous force to the maximum viscous force in water is $500 / 9$.
questions.solution:
Work done in pushing the ball

W=(v \rho g) d-(v $\sigma$g) d

Where,
$\rho \rightarrow$ Density of water
$\sigma \rightarrow$ Density of ball

$\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow W=$\frac{4}{3} \pi$R^3 $\times$10 $\times$0.7$\left[$1000-$\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{10^{-3}}{R^3}\right]$\\
& W=0.077 $\mathrm{~J}
\end{aligned}

[$1 is correct]
\Rightarrow  When ball is released at bottom same work (i.e. $0.077 \mathrm{~J}$ ) is done on ball.

$\begin{aligned}$& \therefore $\frac{1}{2}$m v²=0.077 \\
& v=$\sqrt{\frac{0.077 \times 2}{\frac{22}{7} \times 10^{-3}}}$\\
& =7 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}

[$2 is correct]
